The complete Master's Manual contains the rules for running your own Imagine Role playing 
games. Within you will find rules that add new dimension to characters, magic, combat and 
much more. This volume has all the Game Master will need to create and run his or her own 
races, classes, skills, spells, invocations, magic items and entire worlds.

===== PAGE 6 =====
ame Mastering is an art form. The Game Master, or GM, creates the setting for adventures. 
The GM creates the whole of the world and paints it with broad and subtle strokes alike, popu-
lating it with aJI manner of beings, creatures and dangers. The game experience is filtered 
through the Game Master. It is a demanding but rewarding challenge. 
So many abilities are needed to assume the role of a successful Game Master. The GM must be able to act out 
the personalities, if not the voices, of the beings the players meet. Artistry and mechanical drawing ability 
help the GM create visually believable worlds. Knowledge of philosophy and history aid the GM in creating 
or running political factions in the new world. Above all, imagination is needed in large doses. If in your 
mind's eye you picture a world and you cannot help but add to it, you have what it takes to become a Game 
Master. 
Imagine, unlike many other role playing games, provides the templates necessary to construct a completely 
different world. Too often sketchy detail and hidden information has kept a capable GM from creating their 
own world. I do not believe settings are cut from the same bolt of cloth. Too often a GM has had to change 
the basic rules of the system just to create his or her world, only to be labelled a variant and lose core players. 
With Imagine, such changes are welcomed, and if made within the ample framework provided can add to, not 
detract from, the core rules. 
Imagine changes the basic rules contract most role playing systems operate under. You do not as a GM simply 
open the Player's Guide and use only what is found there for character development. In most role playing 
systems, a warrior on one GM's world gets the same skills or abilities as a warrior from any other GM's 
world. Imagine provides the flexibility to change what "warrior" means. Maybe the world is set in an Eastern 
culture and every warrior begins with Martial Knowledge. 
They may be called Warriors or they may be called thralls. In Imagine these are choices GMs make and we 
trust them to do so by giving them the keys to take apart the classes, races and even the skills. 
Even if you don't intend to do much more than a few sessions from a town to a nearby dungeon, the extra 
effort spent filling in the details of your world will pay off both in believability and player involvement. You 
will decide upon the deities, races, classes, skills, factions, governments, magic, divine magics, poisons, beasts 
and even the diseases that run rampant in your world. Most of the effort that went into this book was in 
choosing what resources to provide to aid the GM's design process. 
Even should you choose a pregenerated world, details have been provided so that you may further flesh out 
those areas in which you have interest. May you provide enjoyment in all your gaming sessions. 
W. Michael Tenery III

he Player's Guide provides the normal 
range of attributes between 5 and 20. 
Through magical means, or because of 
special race considerations, a being may 
rise above or fall below this 5-20 range. 
The extended range is between 0 and 
30; these tables are presented on pages 11-16. The fol-
lowing section presents infonnation which helps deal with 
the expanded attribute ranges. 
Mob,f}?mt; AttR1butes 
There are many effects in the system that allow for temporary 
attribute increases. A modified attribute will change all skills 
based upon that attribute, and stopping to recalculate the new 
skill chance can slow down game play. There is a simple way 
to deal with this problem, called the attribute increase rule. 
The Attribute Increase Rule 
For skills whose chance is based solely on that attribute: 
Every temporary + 1 to the attribute rating increases the total 
chance by 5%. 
For skills whose chance is based on the average of that attribute 
and another attribute: 
Every odd numbered temporary + 1 to either attribute rating 
increases the total chance by 5%. 
If both attributes increase, of course the bonus should only be 
used once. 
Example: Weapon Parry is based upon Strength and Agility. If 
a character had a temporary Strength increase of+ 1, then the 
chance would go up by 5%. If a character had a temporary 
Strength increase of +2, the total chance would still only 
increase by +5%. However, a temporary Strength increase of 
+3 would raise the total Weapon Parry chance by +10%. 
Though not always precise, this rule is far simpler to use in 
game play than a recalculation of a temporary attribute increase. 
It should not be used for permanent attribute rating increases. 
Maximum Attribute Increases 
No matter what method is used, attributes can only be increased 
to a degree that relates to the power level of the being. These 
limits keep the mortal from having the attributes of a deity, even 
with magical aid.

All temporarily lost attributes return at a rate of l per hour. If

Attribute Saves 
Normally, attribute saves cannot exceed 90%. This means that 
a character who has a Strength save of 90% and somehow gains 
a + 10% to his save still only has a 90%. Bonuses to saves 
merely serve to negate penalties. Thus if a character had -20% 
to a save, the +10% would reduce this to -10%. A character 
with a 60% attribute save who had a + 10% bonus would then 
have a 70% save, but if the same character were given a +50% 
bonus the save could still only be raised to 90%. The only way 
attributes saves can go above 90 is when the attribute itself 
becomes 21 or better. Thus an individual with a 23 Strength 
can have a 93% attribute save, though it will never exceed this 
number even with bonuses, exactly as above. 
Contests of Attributes 
Whenever a character is involved in a contest of attributes, his 
attribute save can never be raised above its natural value. This 
means that a character with a 75% can never make a save by 
more than 74%. 
Example: Two characters are wrestling and are involved in a 
contest of Strength. One is an Ogre with a 20 Strength (90% 
save), the other a Human with an 16 Strength (80% save). Both 
characters use the Force skill (which can be used to add to a 
Strength save) to increase their chance. The Ogre rolls a 70%, 
thus only making his Strength save by 20%, but he makes his 
Force roll by 40%, thus making the Strength save by 60%. In 
addition, he gets a +20% bonus (from his higher rating) and 
thus makes his total save by 80%. The Human rolls makes his 
Strength save by 60%, then makes his Force roll by 30%, and 
thus could make the roll by 90%. However, he cannot make the 
roll by 90%, as his save is only 80%. Thus he makes the roll by 
the best possible value, 79% and loses. 
This is not to say that the Human could not find some way to 
increase his Strength rating, thus increasing his save. He could 
also find a way to gain a bonus to the Strength save and 
increase it to, but not above, 90%. For example, if he were 
fighting an opponent with a 14 Strength and thus gained a 
+ l 0% to his attribute save in a contest, he could in fact raise his 
save to a 90%, thus winning the contest by 89%. It is in such 
cases that a 90% save and a 91 % are worlds apart, for if both 
contestants roll the best possible rolls, the 91 % will always win. 
Attribute Recognition 
Characters may wish to "size up" other characters or opponents. 
If someone is attempting to determine another's attribute, they 
should make an attribute save of the same type as they attribute 
they wish to size up. Success indicates they know the attribute 
within +/-ld4 points. Critical success means knowledge of the 
exact rating.

StRenr;th Extensions 
Attribute Rating: the Beings Strength 
rating after all modifications. 
Attribute Save: the Beings percentage 
chance to have a positive outcome in a sit-
uation resolution. 
Attack Modifier: the modifier applied to 
the Beings chance to hit an opponent when 
using melee weapons. This does not 
include missile weapons. 
Damage Modifier: the modifier that is 
applied to the amount of damage from the 
weapon that strikes an opponent when 
using melee or hurled weapons, but not 
fired missile weapons. The damage modi-
fier is doubled for melee weapons held in 
two hands. 
Load Limit: the multiplier against the 
Beings weight that produces the maximum 
load he or she may carry. Also See 
Encumbrance in the Player's Guide. 
Weapon Speed: a modifier to the attack 
speed for all weapons used by the being. 
This modifier cannot adjust weapon speed 
lower than the minimum weapon speed.

Attribute Rating: the Beings Agility rat-
ing after all modifications. 
Attribute Save: the Beings percentage 
chance to have a positive outcome in a sit-
uation resolution. 
Attack Modifier: the modifier applied to 
the Beings chance to hit an opponent when 
using missile weapons or thrown melee 
weapons, but not melee weapons when 
used in hand to hand combat. 
Defensive Adjustment: a modifier 
applied against an attacker's combat "to 
hit" roll when attacking the being, provid-
ed the being is not restrict.ed from move-
ment and is attempting to avoid the attack. 
Initiative Adjustment: a modifier to a l 0 
sided die used to determine in which sec-
ond a being may begin his actions. 
Modified initiative rolls in excess of -10 
increase the amount of time a being gets to 
act, adding one new second per point 
rolled below -10. The bonus of +10 sec-
onds is the most that can be achieved this 
way. (See combat for dealing with extra 
seconds.) 
Weapon Speed: an adjustment modifier to 
the attack speed for all weapons used by 
the being. This modifier cannot adjust 
weapon speed lower than the minimum 
weapon speed.

Perception 
The elf knelt down low to the floor and examined the lower part 
of the wall. "There," he said, and pointed to a tiny scratch in 
the wall, about an inch above the floor. "How did you ever see 
that!?" asked Brom, for the wall was full of little scrapes and 
scratches, and none seemed any more important than the other. 
Instead of a reply, however, the elf simply shook his head. 
Perception is defined as "a capacity for comprehension." The 
most common misunderstanding of Perception is to think that it 
means only that a person is aware of his environment. This is a 
much too limited view of how the Perception attribute charac-
teristic is used. All creatures are capable of noticing their envi-
ronment through the use of one sense or another. Perception is 
intended to include the comprehension of the information of 
which the individual has become aware. This basically means 
that Perception is not a sense, but represents the understanding 
of the information which has been sensed. When a character 
opens his eyes, the GM does not say, "OK, make a Perception 
test to see if you can see what is in front of you". Vision is 
defined by whatever type of sight the character or being has, 
and the rules for vision apply to where and what the individual 
should see. Once it has been determined that the being can see 
something, next he may use Perception to understand minute 
and subtle details about the information that his vision has 
given him. 
8 
Remember that Perception is the average of all mental attrib-
utes, and this does not necessarily have anything to do with 
vision. To illustrate this point, take the example of an animal. 
Animals all have less than an average of 5 in their mental attrib-
utes, which means that no animal is going to ever have more 
than about a 4% average. In addition, they should have at least 
a -10% penalty, which means that animals all have 0% percep-
tion or worse. This does not mean that an animal cannot see 
someone coming at him, and in fact many animals usually have 
good vision. So why does the animal have no Perception 
chance? Well, say a bear sees a man walking in the woods. He 
is very aware that a creature is there. He has an excellent sense 
of smell, and so probably smelled (and heard) the man long 
before he saw him. But this bear has no real knowledge, no 
intelligence, and is certainly not wise. So his instincts take over 
and he reacts accordingly. He may be driven to attack because 
he thinks only in terms of basic drives; threats, mating and 
hunger. However, the man has a mind. He may have good 
Wisdom, and so he sees this bear and thinks, "it would be haz-
ardous to my health to get near this bear". He may have a high 
Knowledge, and thus think "this is a Grizzly Bear, and it can rip 
me to shreds." He also may have a high Intelligence, and think 
"I need to devise a plan to carefully and quietly escape." This 
all compounds into the fact that when a character sees a form in 
the woods, his Perception tells him that it is a big nasty bear. 
Now of course this is such common knowledge that it really 
requires no actual roll. But often, when the information is 
obscure or very subtle, a test will need to be made. 

===== PAGE 19 =====
Perception Roll Outcomes 
1. A sense must always first be used before a Perception check 
is made. If something is out of the range of a character's 
senses, then he can't make a Perception check; you don't roll a 
Perception check to see if something is out of a character's 
senses. Skill rolls are made for the senses which use skills 
(Listen and Smell). Normal vision, taste and touch do not need 
rolls. 
2. After it has been determined that the character can sense the 
object of a Perception check, the roll is made. If the character 
is passively sensing, then the roll is normal. If the character is 
actively sensing, the roll is doubled. In all cases, however, the 
Game Master is the one who should call for the Perception 
check, and often he may make it without telling the player. 
3. If the roll is successful, the player should get appropriate 
information. If the roll is a critical success (a rare thing with 
Perception) the Game Master may award exceptionally good 
information. If the roll is failed, then the character notices 
nothing unusual at all. 
A successful Perception check should give the character some 
bit of useful knowledge. Perception checks, however, should 
never rule out the need for an informational skill. Character's 
should not generally make Perception checks to get information 
about the weaknesses of a creature (this should be Bestiary 
Lore) or the fact that there are tracks on the ground (this should 
first be Track). Only as a last resort should Perception checks 
be given for such things, and then really just to the character's 
who have those skills anyway. For example, say a Ranger char-
acter is moving through the forest and the player does not think 
about asking to look for tracks, but the GM has a really nasty 
ambush set up and wants to give him a chance to avert disaster. 
In this case, the Ranger might get a Perception check to see if 
his character would have comprehended the fact that he is walk-
ing all over fresh tracks. If he makes the roll, the GM says 
"you notice you're walking all over fresh tracks." He can then 
opt to make a Track roll and gain much more information. 
Examples where Perception checks should be made: 
1. A character closely inspects a wall. A Perception roll is 
made to notice that the wall hides a secret door. 
2. The characters are looking at the stars one night and a shape 
moves across the sky. A Perception check for each one will 
determine if they notice it, and perhaps gain a bit of information 
about what it looks like. 
3. A character is feeling around in an area where he cannot see, 
inside a dark room. The GM has him make a Perception check 
to see if he can feel where the door is.

Affinity 
l'ullarae and I entered the tavern together. Almost within 
moments he was striking up conversations and making friends 
while I struggled to find one person who even noticed me. 
Maybe it was his chann or Elven looks, our perhaps his faith in 
the priesthood, regardless, in a crowded room, he never failed 
to gather a throng of interested people. 
Affinity represents the phenomena known as "the cult of per-
sonality." It creates the condition which we sometimes call 
"starstruck." People can sometimes lose their minds and do stu-
pid things when they make an Affinity roll for a certain person. 
In terms of a relationship, Affinity might be the feeling that 
some people have when they run into a person in their life 
which they feel they have known all their life. They experience 
a connection which is unusually strong. In some cases, it is so 
strong that they may be soul mates. 
Affinity can be passive or active. When used passively, the GM 
can decide to make an Affinity roll when a being walks into a 
room or into a crowd. Immediately this gives a chance for 
many of the people in the room to take notice of the person and 
feel a certain amount of power coming from them. Even if the 
person is an enemy, they ought to have a certain amount of 
respect or fear (depending on the personality of the viewer) of 
the character. When used actively, the character is trying to use 
their ability to influence people directly, and these rolls are at 
times two the normal chance. This may be "turning on the 
charm," or it may be throwing attitude about. Walking up to the 
barkeep and saying, "I am Lord Harkus of Talladia, and you 
will clear these patrons out of this pub immediately," would be 
a good time for an active Affinity roll. If the roll is failed, the 
barkeep will resist and claim that he is being oppressed, or . 
whatever. If successful, the barkeep will decide that it is in his 
best interest to do as he is told by this important person. And 
what's more, he probably will be glad about it, as he is obvious-
ly in the presence of greatness. 
As Game Master, deciding when to use Affinity is crucial. Do 
not let the roll be abused, and remember that it is always up to 
the GM when it can be used. Used too often and the character 
seems to attract a throng of followers wherever she goes. Used 
too little, and she seems like a common person who cannot 
influence people at all. 
It is important not too use Affinity when in fact the more com-
mon Charm roll should be made. Affinity should be saved for 
more special cases. For example, a Charm roll is not made 
when a being has a prejudice toward the character, but an 
Affinity roll can be made. In this case, a guard who is really 
not supposed to let anyone into the storehouse just might do so 
for a person when the GM makes an Affinity roll for that char-
acter. The best use of the Affinity roll for the GM is in helping 
make decisions about how a particular person will behave when 
the GM is not really sure himself. In the example above, the 
GM may really feel like the guard would not Jet the character 

===== PAGE 20 =====
into the storeroom, but the player may have done such a good 
job of roleplaying that the GM is not sure what to do. Making 
the Affinity roll is a great solution. Remember also that if the 
player chooses to remain anonymous, speak little and remain in 
the background, then an Affinity roll does not need to be made. 
Affinity Roll Outcomes 
A successful Affinity roll does not allow the affected being to 
be controlled or manipulated outside of his alignment or sacred 
vows. It is also not a complete trust but an acceptance that trust 
will likely follow if the individual is as special as he seems. 
While there is a sense the person is special, there is plenty of 
room for them to prove they are not. A high Affinity is not a 
replacement for good social interaction, true desirability and 
earned trust. 
Conversely, a failed Affinity roll only produces indifference, 
creating a sense that the individual is just another person in the 
sea of others. It is not loathing, hatred, or even a desired aver-
sion. It does not preclude a later liking for the individual either. 
Sometimes one does not notice the good qualities of another 
and only through time do they come to occupy one's thoughts. 
A low Affinity is not a reflection of the trustworthiness, or 
desirability or ability to interact with others. It is only a meas-
ure of the person's ability to create the first impression. 
Intelligent magical/divine items or artifacts may help a being 
they have an Affinity for, revealing something of themselves or 
activating a power or ability at a crucial time. Some Artifacts 
will not operate at all unless the item has an Affinity with the 
being. 
Modifying Affinity 
Affinity is highly situational. There are several instances when a 
Game Master may want to modify the Affinity roll. lf someone 
is amongst her own race, an obvious bonus should apply. 
Conversely, some groups are very mistrustful by nature and 
unlikely to develop an Affinity for anyone who is not of the 
group. Several sample modifiers are provided. This should not 
be thought of as an exhaustive list but a sample of how to modi-
fy Affinity rolls. The Game Master should feel free to modify 
with these as a guide.

Fortune 
After Yelzik fell into the crevasse, I thought his frail bones had 
scattered to an icy grave-but then I heard his croaking voice, 
groaning for help from just over the edge. Yelzik's hands held 
him to the barest of ledges, but it was enough. I pulled him up 
and he lived, saving us all when we next faced fortunes fury. 
Fortune is a measure of purest luck. It is a chance-however 
slight-to avoid the gravest of dangers and to win when the odds 
are stacked against one. It is only applied during extreme situa-
tions to determine the character's fate, and then only at the 
whim of the Game Master. Fortune is used as a last chance 
when death or gravest danger will be the outcome, and yet 
there is a chance (however small) to avoid the situation. It 
should never be used when a character directly causes the situa-
tion and has "sealed his own fate." If a character falls off a cliff 
he will likely get a Fortune roll to land on a ledge just below. lf 
he jumps without paying attention he should get no such roll. 
Fortune can also be used as a test in a situation where only the 
luckiest will win. Imagine three identical swords, sheathed in 
ice in a frozen waste. When touched, two of them cause all the 
swords to be disintegrated, but the third is an artifact of great 
power that can only be destroyed by Disintegration. lf the char-
acter makes his intention known to 'let fate decide' the GM can 
roll his Fortune to give the character an idea of which one to 
pull. Fortune rolls are also used to determine additional starting 
money. Successful rolls determine a multiplier against the base 
starting money (see Equipment in the Player's Guide). If 
Fortune is rolled successfully, it can also be optionally added to 
the starting Equipment roll for barbaric races. Fortune should 
not be confused with the Endure roll (provided by Will Force). 
While Fortune can represent the last chance to avoid death, 
Endure is used to survive when death is already a result. Both 
of these should be used sparingly or the Game Master runs the 
risk of allowing a character to believe himself invincible, or 
worse destroy the player's suspension of disbelief altogether. 
Fortune Roll Outcomes 
Fortune should not always be a get-out-of-jail-free card. 
Usually, the GM may wish to cause some consequence to occur, 
but perhaps this will not be nearly so bad as the death scenario. 
For example, after the character has fallen off of the cliff and 
made his Fortune roll, the GM may determine that he is holding 
on barely, and will still need to make a climb roll at a strong 
penalty to be completely safe. Another example might be that a 
blow which would have killed a character instead does only 1/2 
damage. All of this is at the GM's discretion. 
Modifying Fortune 
Fortune represents fate, and thus can only be modified by 
songs, poems, ballads, rituals, powers, abilities, spells, invoca-
tions or effects which provide luck points, unluck points or 
influence points. The modifiers for each such effect are sup-
plied with the effect itself.

The ChaRacteR Burlbrnr; S}?stem 
This system is presented as an alternative for the attribute rolling sys-
tem in the Imagine Player's Guide. It is up to each GM which charac-
ter creation system he will allow his players to use. This system 
allows a player to make sure that he will be able to qualify for a certain 
class, but it requires experience in character creation because the player 
needs to know what class and race he wishes to play from the start. 
The system works by giving the player a set number of points to be 
spent on attributes and certain special abilities. The number of points 
allowed corresponds to the attribute rolling methods found in the 
Imagine Player's Guide. This allows the GM to choose the character 
types to fit the power level of his campaign setting, just as with the 
rolling method. 
Spending Points 
Players receive 40 build points to distribute amongst attributes and 
abilities. Each attribute is considered to start at the base rating (based 
on character type) and can be increased or decreased from that value.

Attributes can be decreased to gain build points. However, each attrib-
ute decrease supplies one character build point only. Thus, lowering 
attributes to absurd levels will produce only a minimal number of build 
points. 
Manipulating Social Class: All Social Class increases must be negoti-
ated with the Game Master, and can only be modified at his discretion. 
Racial Modifiers 
All standard racial modifiers apply to the base attribute ratings before 
any points are spent in the system. This means that a player will want 
to examine the attribute modifiers of a given race as he is building the 
character. For Civilized Humans, a standard +3 points is given, so that 
humans spend 43 points instead of 40. 
Racial Maximum Attributes 
The number of individuals which have attributes at their racial maxi-
mums should be fairly rare. Because of this, a player can only buy a 
limited number of attributes up to his character's racial maximum. 
This is based on the character type as well as race, and is listed in the 
"# of RM" column below. Obviously this means that a player must 
decide which race his character will be before spending points. 
Abilities and Disabilities 
No ability on any list can be bought more than once, and no disability 
can be taken more than once. Each ability will have a point cost asso-
ciated with it, and each disability will have a point gain associated 
with. Gained points can be spent on either abilities or attributes. In 
addition, each character type is allowed only a certain number of abili-
ties or disabilities (shown below).

highly specialized character as opposed to a well balanced one. The 
system allows both types of characters.

Abilities and disabilities are options which allow for interesting 
character development. Abilities represent special talents or 
gifts a being may utilize, and disabilities represent deficiencies 
or abnormalities a being must overcome. Many methods can be 
used to select and apply abilities and disabilities. When used 
with the character buying system, a player can spend build 
points to gain abilities and can take disabilities to gain build 
points. When used with the standard attribute rolling method, 
the GM can decide from several options: 
1) The Game Master can have the player roll on the table 
below, in which case he must roll for both an ability and dis-
ability. Under this method, a character may get an ability with 
no disability, but also risks getting a disability with no ability. 
2) The GM can allow the player to roll for an ability, but in 
return they must also roll a disability.

Emotion Effects 
Emotional effects are penalties that occur when a character is under the 
effects of a certain emotion. The emotion can be chosen or rolled ran-
domly, and in all cases the GM is the final arbiter of when the emotion 
"activates" the effect. 
Random Generation Method: roll d4. 
Attribute Buying Method Cost: gain 1 point. 
1) Combat: -10% to combat skills. 
2) Magic: -10% to magical skills. 
3) Divine Magic: -10% to divine magical skills. 
4) Stealth/Tntrusive: -10% to stealth/intrusive skills.

This section of abilities and disabilities allows the Grune Master to 
secretly roll or choose a latent ability and /or disability for the charac-
ters in his group. The player should not be informed of this latent abil-
ity, and the GM can introduce it at any time he wishes. For exainple, if 
the character had +20% to Weapon Parry and failed a roll by 10%, the 
GM would inform him that his character somehow managed to pull off 
the parry (hmmm ... ).

===== PAGE 31 =====
II 
he new races provided in this section are to be 
used at the option of the Game Master. They 
are listed here as opposed to the Imagine 
Player's Guide either because they can be 
unbalancing, or because they require an indepth 
understanding of certain rules that are also 
found in this book. The Civilized Giant and Fairy for example, 
require special rules for combat and weapons, not to mention 
the fact that they can be overpowering. Feel free to use some, 
all, or none of the new races at your discretion. Provided also 
in this section are rules involving special characteristics, abili-
ties and disabilities that can be used to expand the races. 
Breaking racial restrictions for class 
Many racial restrictions to class are based on special talents. 
Dwarves cannot be Mages generally due to their lack of ability 
to manipulate Aura to produce spell effects. Dwarves have 
other advantages based on being technophiles and so a balance 
is established. If you decide to break racial class restrictions, 
do so because it makes sense for the situation and make sure 
there is a good reason recorded so that whenever another player 
asks to do the same thing you are able to explain why the 
exception was allowed. Create a heretical or outlandish teacher 
that refused to follow convention and took on an apprentice 
who had no talent but had great desire, or you can allow the 
learning to occur by magical means. You can also make it a 
product of the character's background as opposed to rolling on 
the Special Background Table. 
Attribute Qualification for Class by Race 
Some races are unable to qualify for a class under normal cir-
cumstances because their Racial Attribute Maximums are below 
the required levels. In this case the requirements can be waived 
for anyone who possesses the racial maximums for each attrib-
ute required, allowing the diminutive Fairy to be a Knight. 
Racial Mixing 
Racial mixtures in general can be dangerous. A player could 
abuse the system by using the flexibility of being able to mix 
races to take the best of both races without suffering the worst 
of either. You as a Game Master are all that stands between the 
realistic mixed-race character and the spray-on cheese variety 
that results in a power gamer looking for every edge. Try not to 
let players make characters in a vacuum. Most abuse comes 
when a player makes twenty characters without guidance and 
brings back the ultra-hero that is the best of the lot. He then 
begs that you let him play ultra-hero. Don't. The best charac-
ters are made interactively between the player and the Game 
Master. The Game Master should help the player to find the 
character's background and distinctive personality. Create a sit-
uation wherein the player will decide what he wants to be. You 
are the balancing force. Elves have advantages in Magic and 
Agility but lack Strength and ability to resist poisons. Dwarves 
have a strong resistance to poisons and have great strength but 
are slower and sink in water. You may find yourself being more 
21 
flexible when there are fewer members in a party of adventurers 
or the characters are in a heroic style of play. As with every-
thing else herein, ultimately the choice is yours. 
Bizarre Racial Mixing 
Some individuals will want to use unusual racial mixing combi-
nations to try and produce the best possible results and not for 
any role playing reason. For instance while there is no rule pre-
venting someone mixing Barbaric and Civilized Human it is 
nonsensical in most situations. Sure the half-aboriginal guide 
who was weaned by his wild mother and later was returned civ-
ilization and raised by his more civilized father is possible, but 
how likely is it? It worked for Edgar Rice Burrough's Tarzan. 
If this sort of building of a character by putting together the best 
part becomes prevalent, we suggest you give disabilities as a 
matter of course and/or begin giving hereditary diseases. 
Alternately, you as GM can just veto the character for use in 
your game. 
If the player insists on making every character a part Ogre-
Forest Avian-Gray Elf, then start using disabilities (see 
Abilities/Disabilities) to balance the character. Allow the natu-
ral racial tensions in your world to make that character style 
non-viable or just force the player to take some of the disadvan-
tages with the advantages of the racial mixes. It should be 
noted the races are very balanced as a whole. 
Trace Race: You may choose to tell the character he has the 
trace of another race, or make it subtle enough to be a secret 
that is later discovered. Choose two of the areas below and 
modify the character accordingly. 
1) Endurance: If the trace race has an Endurance bonus, add + I to 
starting Endurance. If the trace race has an Endurance penalty, subtract 
- I from the starting bonus. 
2) Attributes: Choose I attribute modifier for the trace race and add 
or subtract it as the modifier indicates. If the character already has a 
racial modifier for that attribute then average it instead. Attribute max-
imum for that attribute is the higher of the two races. 
3) Racial Skills: The character can learn 1-3 racial skills from the 
trace race either being taught them or because they represent inborn 
abilities. 
4) Resistance Modifiers: A single resistance modifier is added or sub-
tracted as the modifier indicates. If the character already has a racial 
modifier, then average it instead. 
5) Abilities/Powers(Special Modifiers): One special power or ability 
is given from the trace race. 
6) Starting Age: This is normal for the parent race but the life span is 
averaged. 
7) Characteristics: One or two characteristics from the trace race are 
manifest in a subtle fashion. Perhaps not pointed Elven ears, but a 
sharpness to the ear that may suggest Elven heritage. 
8) Class Options: One additional class type possibility is added from 
the trace race.

ChetahL 
Chetahl are a nocturnal race of cat-like humanoids. With superior agility 
to other races, these creatures have incredible balance and leaping skills and 
are often found in high, hard to reach places. Their fur can be many colors 
and patterns, giving them the ability to blend in their natural surroundings. 
Like their cousins of the feline kingdom this race has the ability to see in 
nighttime conditions. Unlike their cousins they walk on two legs, not four. 
The Chetahl basic society is tribal and hierarchical. Their natural habitat 
can be anywhere, but the colder the climate the thicker their fur. Females 
hold all the positions of power and even though males tend to be stronger, 
females are afforded more respect. This is partly due to the birth rate of 
males, which is outnumbered by females 10 to I. In their culture, males have 
no say as to who their mates are, often being shared by many different 
females. As a race Chetahl are considered one of the cleanest and hold 
grooming to high standards, even making a symbolic ritual of the act. 
Considered fussy by some races, it is not unusual to see a Chetahl adorned in 
extravagance, especially with their love for jewelry and things that sparkle. 
This does not diminish their warrior skills however, as they are one of the 
fiercest races in combat. Chetahl moods are like quicksilver, content one 
moment and angry the next. Because of this they can be of any alignment.

DaRk Av,an 
Dark Avians can best be described as a race of bird-like 
humanoids. Dark Avian facial structure resembles that of an 
owl and their feathers are similar as well, making silent flight 
possible. While very agile, this race tends more toward the 
magical arts and because of this it is not unusual to find mages 
and priests among them. They are nocturnal by nature and are 
considered one of the best at hunting after dusk. Hand signs are 
a large part of their natural language like many of the other 
races that hunt at night. 
The society of Dark Avians is tribal and clan-like. Being 
patriarchal, young avians are inducted into the tribe with dark 
rites and a ritual that involves a hunt. Many do not survive the 
induction, insuring those that do are competent enough to take 
their place in the tribe hierarchy. Clan leadership is decided not 
II \ll':'I Y.,WI ~ I~ 
only by contests of strength and physical prowess, but also by 
'-
battles of wits. Needless to say, the losers of such challenges will find themselves scorned, driven from the tribe and maybe even 
killed. Usually found in deep forests, this race tends toward arrogance with outsiders and mostly trade with Dark Elves and 
Mountain Avians, considering all other races as inferior. Forest Avians are treated with a tribal-like hatred and often attacked on 
sight. Other races are barely tolerated and usually only when something is to be gained. Dark Avians are aggressive by nature and 
usually neutral to evil in alignment.

FaJR)? 
Fairies are the most magical of all beings. They live in cloud cities or in very 
enchanted woods, and their homes are usually unseen and very protected. There is 
a Fairy Queen or King who rules over all Fairies and lives hidden within the Fairy 
realm. 
Fairies are mischievous beings and will often play tricks on their larger neigh-
bors. Usually these tricks are not life threatening but those who capture, kill or 
generally abuse Fairydom can expect retaliation, and this is usually something that 
suits the crime and makes a fool out of the criminal. They are great magical 
craftsman and most Fairies possess magic items of one type or another (Game 
Master discretion for type and numbers). A Fairy birth is a rare and mystical event. 
Fairies can produce offspring no more than once a century. 
Fairies are ancient cousins of the Elves but they consider most Elves boorish. 
Other races they look upon with disdain and little tolerance. They rarely take sides in a 
conflict between races. Their society is an ordered chaos, with an "anything goes" atti-
tude, except in the actual permanent harming of another Fairy or Elf. Still there are 
nobles and commoners and a very long lasting order to the levels of their society. A Fairy 
can be of any alignment.

C1v1lJzeb Giant 
Of all the player races, the Civilized Giants are the largesL They are a peace-loving, intellectual race that live in large communities in hidden 
valleys and away from the bustle of most other races. Their society is organized in much the same way advanced human kingdoms are. Unlike 
humans however, they are master crafts-people and only the Dwarves match them in respect to their scholarly pursuits. To this end they are very 
friendly with the Dwarves and conduct a lucrative trade with them. Civilized Giants, like the Dwarves, are masters of machinery and innovation. 
ln spite of the many fields in which Civilized Giants are without equal, they do have limits. Unlike many of the other races their magical knowl-
edge is at limited at best. Because of their great size their magic is inherent in their nesh and bones and any magic they would try to cast or use 
would be bent by their magical nature; hence, they cannot use any magic with respect to Aura. This also means that they cannot activate magical 
items that require the wielder's Aura. Although they themselves cannot cast spells, they are affected by them. Though it is belied by their great 
size, most Civilized Giants seek intellectual pursuits in their lives. Civilized Giants abhor violence unless it is deemed absolutely necessary. To this 
end they feel that physical violence is not only barbaric but will go so far as to ostracize Civilized Giants from their society who choose a violent 
path in their Jives. Because of this aversion to violence, in Civilized Giant communities, Warriors are extremely rare as are weapon-smiths and 
armorers. This causes Civilized Giant weapons and armor to cost many times the normal amount (because of both size and availability). Most 
weapons and armor acquired by Civilized Giants are made by their good friends the Dwarves. ln addition, most standard equipment costs twice as 
much because of its size. Civilized Giants look like large humans with the exception that the only hair they have is eyebrows and some on top of 
their heads (they cannot grow facial hair). They are between eleven and sixteen feet tall and are usually very heavy framed. As a race they tend 
toward good alignments.

Gnome 
Gnomes are a smaJI, fairy-sized race that can be found anywhere in the wilderness. They have a 
natural affinity with all animals and consider themselves the protectors of nature. Other wilderness 
dwelling races revere the advice of Gnomes, and it is not unusual to see many Gnomes walk the 
druidic path. They make their homes in hollowed out trees and small caves where they live in 
large communal villages. Each village serves a purpose, and many times one village will help 
another in need. Often young Gnomes will leave their village to learn what their role will be 
in the world. Gnomes tend to deal with Fairies more than any other race and have adopted 
the Fairy gem currency. 
Gnomes are not as flighty as Fairies but not as dour as Dwarves. One of the longest 
lived races, they have achieved a good balance between work and festivity. Seasonal 
changes are always celebrated, and the Gnome way of life revolves around the patterns 
of nature. The solstices in particular are sacred holidays and no work is allowed on 
those days. Gnomes are slow to trust yet even slower to anger, but once this anger 
has been thoroughly aroused, they are capable of great vengeance and terrible fury. 
With their innate magical skills and superior nightvision, they can be either ferocious 
enemies or dependable friends. Gnomes tend towards neutral alignments.

===== PAGE 37 =====
FoRest GobLm 
Forest Goblins are a small race of bestial-looking creatures. Their appearance is brutish like other 
Goblin races but they are much smaller in physical stature. Their skin color is a light green that nat-
urally blends in well with surrounding foliage. This, combined with their natural sense of smell and 
exceptional eyesight, makes them quite adept at hunting and ambushing. They are also very good at 
moving silently and erasing any trace of their presence. All this, coupled with their knowledge of 
the plants and animals of their environment makes them formidable indeed. 
Forest Goblins arc very tribal and considered by many races as socially inferior. The clan leader 
without exception is the strongest and the most cunning. The average reign of a tribal chief is 
about three years. It customarily takes that long for the tribe to get tired and dispose of him. After 
that a great feast takes place, usually with the former chief being relished in his new place in life 
as dinner. Afterwards the Shaman (who is always revered and feared) declares who are the 
worthy successors and sits back to watch which one will survive the bloodlet-
ting about to take place. The act of succession is the most sacred Forest 
Goblin rite. 
Wood Elves and Forest Avians are the Forest Goblins' mortal ene-
mies. Both races have joined forces numerous times in what can best be 
described as a purge of the Goblins from the forests. No matter how 
many they manage to kill and drive away, the race always comes back 
_ _ 
and replenishes quickly. Due to this, the Goblins will not have any deal-
-,. 
ings with either race. They will also not deal with Forest Midfolk, but ~ 
do not fear them like the other two races. The Forest Goblins tend to 
only barter with other Goblins. They are neutral to evil in alignment.

===== PAGE 38 =====
Mounram Goblm 
If Forest Goblins are considered the smallest of the Goblin races, their opposites 
are Mountain Goblins, who are the largest. As their name denotes, these Goblins live 
in often harsh mountain settings, where only the strong can survive. They are found in 
caves and primitive stone structures, which are much like rocks piled together with a 
space hollowed out to provide shelter. Their skin color is a dark greenish gray and 
their appearance bestial and brutish, more so than other Goblin races. Only Ogres, 
who the Mountain Goblins greatly respect, are bigger and fiercer, but not by much. 
Mountain Goblins have a social structure more primitive than that of their goblin 
cousins. The concept of unique ownership is all but non-existent. If a Mountain 
Goblin sees something he wants, he takes it. If the victim resists, then the Goblin 
introduces him to the concept of "the strongest wins". This simple system seems to 
work. Mountain Goblins are patriarchal but that is about the extent of the organiza-
tional level they possess. 
As a whole, Mountain Goblins do not deal well with other races except Ogres. 
Dwarves and Mountain Avians are considered mortal enemies and frequently attacked 
on sight. Even other races of Goblins have fallen victim to their savage cousins. The 
Mountain Goblins do mine ores and produce inferior metal goods that they have been 
known to trade, but not often. Because they only respect strength, taking is much easi-
er than trading most of the time. As a race, Mountain Goblins are almost always neu-
tral to evil alignments.

===== PAGE 39 =====
GRahL 
Grahl are a race of humanoid, dog-like creatures that are found in almost any climate. 
They are on average tall and large framed with many of the characteristics possessed by 
their smaller kin in the canine world. These characteristics depend on which of the sub-
species of canines they emulate. Most Grahl have paws for feet and hands with claws. 
They are excellent night hunters due to their infravision but are equally as adept in the 
daylight hours thanks to their superior sense of smell. Often their fur grows to match 
the surrounding color of their natural environment, giving them a clear advantage 
in this terrain. 
The Grahl society is based around the clan, which can normally have 100 to 
200 members. Within this clan are packs, consisting of between 6 to 25 mem-
bers. The leader of the clan must be a pack leader, so he first learns how to 
lead. A pack leader is decided by whom is strongest, while a clan leader is 
decided by a test of whom is smartest amongst the pack leaders. The society 
is usually patriarchal, but females have been known to lead at times. 
Advantages of belonging to a pack include safety in numbers and communi-
cating over long distances with a series of howls. As a whole, Grahl do not 
have racial enmity towards other races. There is a slight tension between 
them and the Chetah1 at times, but that is normally the extent of it. Grahl 
freely trade with all races and are also prized as excellent scouts. Grahl 
tends towards neutral alignments.

TRoLL 
The Troll is a horribly ugly and wiry green skinned humanoid which stands gen-
erally just under seven feet tall. It has an amazing regenerative ability that is reflect-
ed in its reproductive ability; it is sexless and breeds by budding once per decade. 
The Troll has no affinity for other Trolls, nor does it have much concern at all for a 
social structure, as a good Troll is almost unheard of. Trolls will take a slight inter-
est in their budded offspring until they eventually tire of it, then will attack the 
young Troll and drive it off. If the infant is lucky enough to survive, it will crawl off 
and regenerate its wounds where it can grow up to become another cruel Troll adult. 
Trolls like to hunt alone, but they are smart enough to band with others when neces-
sary. They can be very cunning hunters and love the taste of humanoid meat, but 
they see all creatures as food or sport and enjoy torturing them when possible. They 
are often referred to as Bridge Trolls because of their habit of hiding under bridges. 
This is as much for the cool and often damp environment as well as for pouncing 
upon hapless victims. Trolls blend well in swamps and dead vegetation and can 
move quickly and quietly when necessary. The Troll respects other evil individuals 
that can best it in combat or who have superior magical ability.

Rock TRoLL 
The Rock TrolJ gets its name both from its extremely tough 
skin and from its prodigious regeneration ability. Its immense 
bulk and pale gray skin have caused some to confuse it with the 
Ogre. While not the brightest of creatures, the Rock Troll's 
amazing size and strength more than make up for its mental 
deficiencies. The Rock Troll prefers to hunt alone or in small 
bands with others of its own kind. These hunting parties are 
enormously feared for their voracious appetites and willingness 
to eat almost any animal or humanoid they happen across. 
They are especially fond of Elven flesh, and will go out of their 
way to hunt the race. Rock Trolls dislike the taste of Mountain 
Goblins, but they do find them to be good allies, and sometimes 
will make deals with them to fight in exchange for food. Rock 
Trolls live in dark caves, where they breed (thankfully very 
slowly) and raise their young. They will only come out at 
night, as even the the slightest shaft of sunlight will tum their 
entire body to stone. Most Rock Trolls are neutral or evil in 
alignment.

HanbLm~ ALK;nments 
Dealing with alignment can be both tricky and perplexing. The 
idea of a alignment is itself very subjective. Your job as GM is 
to help the player stay in character. Alignments are used for 
this purpose. In a perfect gaming world, alignment would be 
unnecessary because such a strong concept of character is creat-
ed that his world view and norms of social interaction would 
replace alignment. But the gaming group and situation can vary 
wildly, creating a need for consistent play from each individual. 
This helps make the setting and situation believable and main-
ta1nable. Also, players will want to expect things of each other. 
Alignment becomes a code for what players will expect from 
each other, as well as what the GM will expect from players. 
The current trend in gaming seems to be for players to play pre-
dominately neutral alignments, as these can represent freedom 
to do whatever they want. Although the fantasy role playing 
game allows for freedoms that society would not normally tol-
erate, it is important to remember that actions do determine 
character. 
This is true both in the game and in real life. A character may 
be a neutral rogue, but only the act of stealing makes that rogue 
a thief. He may play an evil Knight, but only the act of killing 
makes the knight a murderer. As GM, make sure that the 
actions of the character match the supposed alignment that the 
character has chosen. Your strictness will vary, but here are 
some good guidelines to follow: 
1) Fanatical 
a) Killing can be done against anyone but those of the same 
alignment (fanatics are a little nuts, and even good fanatics will 
kill good people if they feel justified). 
b) If non-fanaticals flee, the individual might switch to other 
opponents etc., but they should not run away, and should not 
break off combat once begun .. 
2) Et11L 
a) intrusion (break in) against anyone. 
b) Steal from anyone. 
c) Cheat anyone. 
d) Murder any non-evil (any evil, but must justify). 
e) Trade with or help any non-good. 
f) Defend against any personal attack; aid others only to protect their 
own interests. 
g) May heal or aid non-good only (unless ulterior motive). 
h) Lie or attempt to deceive anyone. 
3) Neumal 
a) Intrusion (break in) against anyone. 
b) Steal from anyone. 
c) Cheat anyone. 
d) Trade with anyone. 
e) Defend against any personal attack; will aid others if they see 
self benefit. 
f) Murder (any fanatical). 
g) Aid (any non-fanatical). 
h) Lie or attempt to deceive anyone. 
34 
4)Goob 
a) intrusion (break in) against evil owned items and places. 
b) Steal from anyone evil, with the intent of keeping something 
powerful out of the evil person's hands, or to return a stolen item. 
c) Trade with any non-evil. 
d) Murder of any evil or any criminal committing or known to 
commit crimes. 
e) Defend against any personal attack: will attempt to aid friends 
when attacked. 
f) May heal or aid any. 
g) Lie or deceive evil, only to protect a greater good. 
5) Active: May initiate attacks directly against anyone to start combat. 
6) Passive: Should initiate dialogue before any direct attack unless 
combat has begun. 
7) Immoral: If a character wants to steal, break and enter, or cheat on 
a regular basis, she should be immoral. 
8) Moral: If a character expects to heal or aid others often, she should 
moral. 
9) Order: Only gets two alignment checks (see below) before loss of 
alignment. 
10) Chaos: These characters are allowed one free action per game day 
that is considered out of alignment. 
Alignment Checks 
This is when an action is taken which is out of alignment for the 
character. Three strikes, and alignment moves one up or down the 
scale if the character is good or evil (fanatical is just the extreme 
end of good or evil). Loss of current experience towards the next 
goal occurs. Loss of commune chance occurs, as well as loss of 
divine skills and possible usage of divine items. GMCs should 
alter the way that they treat a character when the alignment of that 
character alters radically. If divine ability is part of the character's 
make up, she earns the dubious title of "Fallen." For switches 
between active and passive alignments, loss of current experience 
toward the next goal must occur, but no loss of commune or divine 
ability occurs. Tendencies can be switched or changed at a whim 
with no penalty. (Use the three strikes system to determine if the 
tendency changed, and have the player record the change). 
Dealing with Priests 
The GM should always be stricter on alignment with Priests and 
Priest subclasses. By deciding to be Priests, they have made them-
selves both role models and conduits to the deities of the world (its 
hard to follow a role model that changes her opinion constantly). 
Deities do not accept easily their servants changing away from the 
deities' alignment. 
Insanity 
Certain types of situations will temporarily or permanently 
render the character insane. lnsane characters are unaffected by 
alignment. Optionally their experience is frozen while insane, but 
they can do anything they want (only certain types of insanities 
apply). Characters who literally want to do anything and not suffer 
any internal conflict should be considered insane (borderline per-
sonality).

===== PAGE 47 =====
he decision to allow characters to go above 10th 
Title is completely within the GM's prerogative. 
Such characters will require great challenges and 
if let loose, may run unchecked over the other 
inhabitants of the game world. One of the best 
suggestions for the GM is to lead the characters toward retire-
ment by giving them more and more responsibility until they 
cannot adventure anymore. Even retired characters can be 
brought out to play in the occasional high Title, save the world 
epic adventure. However, if the GM and players wish to 
advance the characters and feel they are ready for this level of 
power struggle in the setting, then the information is provided 
in the following section. 
Requirements for Advancement to Higher Titles 
Each class has different attribute requirements to advance beyond 
10th Title. Certain symbols are used to distinguish these: RM 
means the individual must have the racial maximum attribute for 
their race; a "-I" means that the character must have one below the 
racial maximum for the race, "-2" means he must have a rating that 
is within 2 of his race's maximum for that attribute, etc. In addi-
tion, core class skills have minimum requirements. If these condi-
tions are met, then the advancement proceeds based on class exten-
sion tables. 
Goal Advancement 
At each new Goal a character may choose to raise one attribute, at 
a 20% chance, two attributes with a I 0% chance each, four with a 
5% chance each, or any combination of 5% increments be wishes 
within 20%. All racial attribute maximums can be ignored above 
10th Title.

Beyond I 0th Title, Endurance earned is at the maximum possible

value is doubled, then tripled at 14th, quadrupled at 15th, and all 
races have a fixed sum added to them at the higher Titles, shown

As a character becomes immortal and heads down the path toward 
godhood, weapons begin to affect him less and less. At each new 
37 
Title up through 16th, weapons will now affect the character in a 
new manner, described below: 
11th: Normal weapons do 1/2; blessed,+! or better weapons do full. 
12th: Normal weapons do 1/2; blessed,+! or better weapons do full. 
13th Normal weapons do 1/4; blessed do 1/2, +I do full. 
14th Normal weapons do l/4; blessed do 1/2, +l do full. 
15th Normal weapons do none, blessed do 1/4, +l,+2 does 1/2, +3 or 
greater does full. 
16th and up: Normal weapons do none; blessed,+ 1,+2 do 1/4; +3,+4 
does 1/2; +5 or greater do full (as the spell Invulnerability). 
Beings that advance to 11th Title are considered arch mortals and 
as such should have at least one magical or divine magical power. 
A power can be acquired with the skills Empower, Metal Lore, 
Stone Lore or Wood Lore. The spells Permanency and Wish-as 
well as their di vine magic counterparts Permanency and 
Miracle-can also be utilized to give a being a permanent power. 
Sometimes a sponsor will intervene and help a prospective charac-
ter get that extra edge to advance beyond 10th. After making 11th 
Title, racial attribute maximums are ignored altogether and the 
character ceases aging. 
A player's character should not advance to 16th Title. 
Advancement beyond 15th is reserved for the path to divine ascen-
sion, and is shown here for clarification purposes and to allow the 
Game Master to advance a GMC (see glossary) into godhood. 
Arch mortals must possess at least 3 powers in order to become a 
semi-deity. They must also possess the ability to plane shift and 
have at least one supernatural servant. Ascension to 16th Title is 
only granted to those who depose another semi-deity or are spon-
sored by a deity. 
Advancement to 21st Title is for the ascension to godhood. To 
achieve the exalted rank of deity, a being must have at least 5 inter-
nal powers be can call upon. He must have a loyal following of at 
least 1000 who worship him. The being must also have a mini-
mum of three supernatural servants, one of which must be an arch 
supernatural being. He must then choose spheres of influence or 
be granted them (see the Divine Magic section). The being may no 
longer reside on the earthly plane and must have a home on an 
alternate plane. The being must either have sponsorship of a higher 
deity or must depose an existing one. 
Advancement to 26th Title is for arch deities. The requirements for 
advancement to arch deity are 10,000 or more worshippers and 
nine supernatural servants. At least one of these must be an arch 
supernatural being and two must be major supernatural beings. 
The being must have his own plane to rule, and must have a high 
Priest of at least 7th Title as a spiritual leader of his worshippers. 
An arch deity must be deposed for the being to advance to 26th 
Title. 
Advancement to 30th Title represents the supreme end of advance-
ment. This step requires 100,000 or more worshippers and a spiri-
tual leader of 9th Title or higher. 
Non-Acquired Skills at Higher Titles 
No character is allowed to use any of the skills at 11th Title or 
above as non-acquired skills, even if he has already advanced 
beyond 10th Title.

Expanbeb Rules FOR Classes 
0 Title Characters, Personalities and GMCs 
Anyone who has not yet had all of the required training to become a 
class is considered O Title or non-Titled. A GM may wish to start an 
adventurer off as O Title before his training is complete to add flavor or 
create a richer history. When the character has met the required train-
ing, he becomes I st Title and can begin applying experience normally. 
AO Title character can earn up to 499 experience before he makes 1st 
Title. When 1st Title is acquired this experience is applied immediate-
ly. Characters starting off at O Title do not roll their Endurance bonus 
when they get to I st Title. 
Obtaining a Class 
AO Title character must learn his l st Title skills with the learning 
method, described on page 164 of the Player's Guide and expanded on 
pages 85-86 of the Master's Manual. In addition to completing the 
learning time required to gain the necessary skills, he must also be 
exposed to and learn about the higher Title non-acquired skills of his 
class. This time is equal to the total number of non-acquired skiJJs in 
his class (between 2nd and I 0th Title) x8 hours. There is no roll 
required at the end of this time. The following determines the standing 
of the 0-TitJe character:

A character can end a class career at anytime; he simply stops adding 
experience to that class and advancement stops. Sometimes a charac-
ter's career ends when all class skill Knowledge slots have been used 
up. Another reason would be because all divine skills were denied per-
manently to the being for loss of alignment, or for angering a deity. 
If a core skill is not taken, then career advancement stops immediately. 
A career can only be restarted if the conditions stopping the advance-
ment are removed- higher Knowledge, atonement, etc. A final reason 
for ending a career is to start a new one. 
Beginning a New Career or Switching Classes 
1) The player must first declare an end to her current character's career. 
Dual class characters cannot switch careers. 
2) She must learn all the new 1st Title starting skills and complete the 
required class training time as explained under O Title characters. 
3) Current experience is recorded and saved for reference, but is no 
longer used. 
4) She applies all experience gained towards advancement in her new 
profession only. 
S) The new character now begins as a 1st Title character in her new 
profession and is considered I st Class Title for all effects and or abili-
ties based on Class Title. 
6) The skills from the previous class are still available as normal, and 
non-acquired skills of that class can still be attempted. 
7) Special class modifiers are lost for both the original class and the 
new class. 
8) (GM optional) When current experience equals or surpasses the pre-
vious careers experience she can then begin advancing in the previous 
class again just as if she was a dual class character. However, if this 
option is taken, all special modifiers by class are unavailable to the 
new dual class character.

ARcheR (W aRRJoR subclass) 
The Archer represents the skilled marksman. He hones those skills which improve or enhance the ability to fire a mis-
sile weapon (or weapons) at opponents. Historically archers, whether they were crossbowmen of repute or Welsh 
hunters, were known for their ability to take an opponent down at a great distance with one carefully placed shot. Some 
were used as scouts and others were lone hunters who practiced their trade for survival's sake. William Tell was an 
example of a renowned marksman. 
Attribute Requirements: Agility 13, Intelligence 13, Strength 13. 
Special Modifiers: +30% to all core skills, + 10% to combat skills, +5% to stealth/intrusive skills. 
Alignment: Any 
Social Skills: Up to two from the following: Cooking, Firemaking, Fletching/Bowmaking, Foraging/Forestry, Hunting/frapping, 
Riding, Running, Signaling, Skinning/fanning, Survival. 
Core Skills: Brace, Missile Lore, Perfect Shot, Projectile Knowledge, Quick Load. 
Armor Usable: Any chain, any leather, any scale, any shield, composite or half helm, breast plate, arm bracers, leg bracers. 
Weapons Usable: Any missile; any one-handed weapon. 
Goal Advancement: 19 skill points per goal achieved. +l Agility 5%, +I Intelligence 5%. 
Title Advancement: None. 
Racial Restrictions: Any race except Ogre, Troll and Rock Troll.

CavaL,eR (W aRRJoR subclass) 
Cavaliers are liegemen trained in both arms and the fine use of horsemanship. They travel far and wide, meting out jus-
tice and running errands for their lord or lady. Sometimes they alone serve as prosecutor and magistrate. They are men 
and women inducted ceremoniously into high military rank usually after completing service as a page and squire. They 
are often captains in war, and lions in peace. Cavaliers are all considered knights of the realm for purposes of Social 
Class (not to be confused with the worshipful Knight class). 
Attribute Requirements: Agility 13, Strength 13, Wisdom 13, Social Class 15. 
Special Modifiers: +30% to core skills, +10% to combat skills, +5% to disciplined skills.

Courtesan, Cryer, Dancing, Diplomacy, Drilling, Instruction, Falconry, Page, Squire, Soldiering, Story Teller. 
Core Skills: Armor Knowledge, Horsemanship, Law, Shield Parry, Weapon Knowledge. 
Armor Usable: Any. 
Weapons Usable: Any non-missile. 
Goal Advancement: 15 skill points per goal. +l Strength 5%, +l Agility 5%. 
Title Advancement: None. 
Racial Restrictions: Special. Any race, as long as that race has an appropriate mount 
that it can ride. In this case, the skill Horsemanship applies to that mount type (see 
Mounted Combat).

HealeR (PRiest subclass) 
Healers are individuals with a special gift for curing. Their purpose in life is to bring good health to the sick and injured, and they 
often do this without hope of monetary compensation. Healers are generally pacifists, using their weapons primarily for self 
defense. Unlike Priests, healers feel that their purpose of helping the wounded supersedes alignment, and thus they will often heal 
both good and evil individuals alike. This is not to say that they will sanction or aid evil acts, but simply that they find it hard to 
tum away the injured. Only if the Healer has been personally attacked or threatened do they tend to refuse help to someone. 
Attribute Requirements: Piety 15, Will Force 14, Wisdom 13. 
Special Modifiers: +30% to core skills, + 10% to divine magical skills, +5% to magical skills. 
Alignment: Any non-evil. 
Socia) Skills: Required: Chirugeon. Up to 2 from the following: Animal Husbandry, Animal Training, Baking/Cooking, Leeching, 
Midwife, Philosophy, Sing Songs, Recite Poetry, Theology. 
Core Skills: Cure Disease, Cure Insanity, Cure Poison, Divine Knowledge, Healing. 
Armor Usable: Any leather or hide, any half-helm or composite helm. 
Weapons Usable: Dagger, club, rod, knife, sling, quarterstaff. 
GoaJ Advancement: 17 skill points. + 1 Piety 5%, + I Will Force 5%. 
Title Advancement: At 1st Title and beyond, Piety Control increases by 2. 
Racial Restrictions: Any except Troll and Rock Troll.

W,lbeR (Mae subclass) 
Beings of this class have been born with a special talent: the gift of wild magic. This class is an exception in that the practitioner 
need not train to learn his spellcasting skills. Generally, a teacher guides the individual's talents for a time and in such cases the 
nor­mal apprentice training time is halved. The Wilder does not cast spells in the typical fashion, but simply concentrates and 
make s spell-like effects with the skill Wild Magic. Though not as powerful as the true Mage, the Wilder makes up for this with 
versatility. Wilders also have a minor gift with animals that is divine though they often do not recognize it as such. An early sign 
that a being might be a Wilder is that animals show a natural affinity to him. 
Attribute Requirements: Will Force 15, Aura 14, Intelligence 14. 
Special Modifiers: 18 skill points. +I Will Force 5%, +I Aura 5%. All Aura Control modifiers are halved (round down); apply to 
dual class Wilders as well. +30% to Core Skills, +10% to Magic Skills, Wilders have a +5% Affinity with animals. 
Alignment: Any. 
Social Skills: Up to 3 from the following: Chirugeon, Collecting, Drawing, Drudgery, Fire/Making, Painting, Pyrotechnics, Story 
Telling, Ventriloquism, and Writing. 
Core Skills: Absorb Aura, Detect Magic, Speak to Animal, Tame Animal, Wild Magic. 
Armor Usable: Any leather or hide, any half-helm or composite.

Weapons Usable: Club, dagger, knife, rod, spear, staff, sling.

Title Advancement: + I Aura Control per Title. 
Racial Restrictions: No Giants, Dwarves, Troll, Rock Troll, or Goblins.

===== PAGE 58 =====
Jack oF aLL TRabes 
(The Classless Character; GM Optional) 
The Jack of aJI Trades represents the character who has the uncanny knack of absorbing the abilities of those who he 
travels with or has as long term companions. This character has no apprenticeship or career training period and 
advances as shown below. It is unlikely he will ever be recognized as a professional of any class. He is usually merely 
referred to as simply "adventurer." Rogues often pretend to be a Jack of all Trades until their skill usage gives them 
away. The Jack of all Trades may never dual class, end his career, or switch careers. 
Attribute Requirements: Agility 15, Intelligence 15, Knowledge 15. 
Special Modifiers: Primary skill path: + 10% to any one chosen skiJl category. 
Alignment: Any. 
Social Skills: Any, up to maximum allowed by Knowledge. 
Core Skills: None. 
Armor: Any (spellcasters must use Mage restrictions when casting). 
Weapons: Any. 
Goal Advancement: 18 skill points per Goal. 5% chance of increasing any one attribute. 
Title Advancement: Standard ruJes based on the skills chosen.

Learning New Skills 
The character is not planned out ahead of time like other class-
es. Instead, at each Title the character may choose new skills to 
learn based on the format of the table above. So at 1st Title, A 
Jack of all Trades could learn any four common skills and one 
restricted skill, and at 10th Title he could learn any five restrict-
ed skills. At any time, the character may choose to learn a com-
mon skill in place of a restricted skill. 
In order to acquire a new skill, the Jack of all Trades must have 
observed the skill being used by a practitioner of the skill a 
minimum of three times. He must concentrate solely on under-
standing how the skill works. This means the Jack of all 
Trades' obvious concentration will be seen by those around him, 
and it may become known that he is attempting to take the skill 
without the required training. This is almost universally 
frowned upon by the various people in a game setting and may 
be as well by other players. 
48 
The following limitations are also applied to learning skills: 
1. The character may not learn any skill before its minimum 
Title requirement, and must meet all prerequisites for the skill. 
These are found starting on page 238. 
2. The character can only learn one spell casting or invoking 
skiJI (Scroll Knowledge, Divine Knowledge, Hermetic Lore, 
Wild Magic). 
3. No divine skill can be acquired without permission of the 
deity who is responsible for the skill's power. 
4. The GM can set certain skills as off limits, or decide that 
they have additional requirements above the normal. 
5. No restricted skill can go above 90% with skill points except 
for restricted skills which are in the primary skill path. 
Jack of All Trades Extension 
The Jack of all Trades should not advance beyond 10th. If the 
GM decides that he will allow the character to advance beyond 
10th, then the character must qualify for advancement for one 
of the existing classes and advance as that class from 11th on.

Class VaR1ants 
Customizing Classes 
Sometimes a player will want to play a certain class, but would 
prefer that the skill set was slightly more suited to his idea of 
what that class should be. Also, the player may wish to use 
skills presented in the Master's Manual for classes in the 
Player's Guide. In such cases, the player may substitute up to 
three skills from the class/racial skills lists, as long as the these 
rules are followed for each skill: 
1) A skill can only be substituted for another skill of the same 
type (combat for combat, magical for magical, etc.). 
2) Core skills cannot be substituted. 
3) The skill may not already be in the class. 
4) The skill being inserted into the class must meet all of the 
skill requirements listed on pages 238-242. Each skill lists a 
minimum Title requirement, and some have other skills as pre-
requisites, which must be in the class at the same or previous 
Titles. 
5) If the skill which is being removed is a prerequisite for 
another skill in the class, the skill can not be taken out of the 
class (found on pages 238-242). 
6) No more than three skills can be substituted in this way. 
Example: A player wishes to play a Dark Knight, but would 
like to play a variant and use some of the new skills. He wishes 
to substitute in Shield Knowledge and Fearless. The following 
substitutions are chosen: 
Shield Knowledge (combat): Title 4, prerequisite skills are 
Shield Parry and 4 additional combat skills. The player chooses 
Stun at 4th Title, and the skill requirements are easily met. 
Fearless (Disciplined): Title 3. The player could choose to 
remove Horsemanship, but as he wishes to play a mounted 
Knight, he instead chooses Meditate at 6th Title.

as non-acquired.
