===== PAGE 67 =====
he first part of this section covers the effects of 
critical failures and successes, and repeat usages 
and repeat failures for the skills in the Player's 
Guide. The GM can use these effects to balance 
certain skills, and astute players will find that the 
critical successes may greatly increase the application and abili-
ties of their characters. The following terms apply: 
Simple Success: The skill is made, but not by more than 20%. 
Simple Failure: The skill is failed, but not by more than 20%. 
Critical Success: A success of more than 20%. 
Critical Failure: A roll failed by more than 20%. 
Repeat Usage: Notes on any effects when the skill is used mul-
tiple times. 
Repeat Failure: Applied when the character just keeps on try-
ing to make that roll and continues to fail in succession. Three 
repeat failures becomes an automatic critical failure. 
Effects 
Divine Denial: The skill is denied to the practitioner for a peri-
od of 24 hours. 
Fall: Practitioner falls to the ground. 
Fumble: The character must use the fumble rules found in the 
Combat section. If the being is fumbling and a second fumble 
is called for, treat as a fall. 
Me11tal Fatigue: All skills are rolled at a -5% chance. 
Headache symptoms develop, requiring an Intelligence save to 
concentrate. Mental penalties are reduced one per hour of non-
mental activity. One hour following the removal of the last 
penalty the headache is removed. Mental fatigue effects are 
cumulative, adding -5% per level of mental fatigue. 
Off-Balance: Loss of defensive adjustment after maneuver 
( 1 d4+ 1 seconds unless otherwise noted). If already off balance 
when a second off-balance is called for, treat as fumble. 
Extra-Recovery: Additional time is required before other 
actions may be taken. 
Strain: -I STR/ AGL. Each hour of rest or sleep allows an 
attribute save to recover the lost point(s); -5% to the attribute 
save per point lost. 
Skill Restrictions for Non-Standard Sized Races 
The GM may rule that certain skills are simply not able to be 
used by a certain race due to size or shape restrictions. The fol-
lowing are some common examples: 
The Centaur: Breakfall, Slow Fall, Climb, Balance, Acrobatics, 
Disguise (may appear as a large animal only), Martial 
Knowledge (upper body only). 
Martial Knowledge, Martial Lore, Acrobatics, Slow Fall and 
Break Fall: These skill ought never be used by any race that 
cannot jump at least 1/4 of its height. 
57 
ABSORB AURA 
Critical Failure: No further attempts for 1 minute. No further 
attempts at same target for one day, regardless of willingness. There is 
a 1 % chance for each point below 20% by which the skill roll was 
failed of reversing the Aura flow if giving or taking Aura. 
Critical Success: Channelling and absorption can be re-established 
within sight for the remainder of the day with a successful skill roll. 
Repeat Usage: More than double the practitioner's Aura drained in a 
single combat round is added towards Aura cast when computing Aura 
Fatigue. 
ACROBATICS 
Critical Failure: Agility save or off balance. 
Critical Success: Treat as simple success. 
ANIMAL LORE 
Critical Failure: No further information is known at all about the ani-
mal in question until the skrn chance is increased. 
Critical Success: More information may be supplied in addition to the 
information being sought. 
Repeat Failures: No repeat rolls for the same information are allowed 
unless the available resource changes (study material) or the skill 
chance increases. 
ANIMAL PROJECTION 
Critical Failure: No further contact to that animal type can be 
attempted this day, and no further contact with that particular animal 
can be made at all unless the skill chance improves. 
Critical Success: Animal has affinity and will stay in general vicinity 
of practitioner even after the Animal Projection ends. The animal will 
not leave its home terrain under these conditions. Tame Animal is 
allowed at +20%. A critical success can also be used to project 
through a non-sapient magical animal. 
Repeat Usage: Each successful projection on the same animal is 1 % 
easier until it reaches a maximum of 99%. 
Repeat Failures: Each failure lowers the skill chance with that animal 
by 1%. 
ANIMAL SHAPE 
Critical Failure: Results in divine denial for the remainder of the day. 
Critical Success: Practitioner has changed so well into the animal that 
he cannot be distinguished by mannerism or form from the true animal. 
All others may have either a distinguishing mark or mannerism that 
would allow another with Animal Lore or similar knowledge to spy out 
the animal shaped being. 
Repeat Usage: Loss of intellect (See Player's Guide: Animal Shape). 
Repeat Failure: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
AREA SENSE 
Critical Failure: No further attempts can be made in the area until 
one day has passed or the skill chance is increased. 
Critical Success: Questions up to one additional day per point over 
20% success can be asked. 
Repeat Usage: Each success increases the Area Sense chance in that 
area by 1 % for one hour. 
Repeat Failures: Each failure decreases the Area Sense chance in that 
area by 1 % for one hour. 

===== PAGE 68 =====
ARMOR KNOWLEDGE 
Critical Failure: No further attempts can be made with the same con-
figuration of armor until this skill chance is improved. 
Critical Success: Minor adjustments can be made, such as adding or 
subtracting 1-3 pieces of armor to the existing suit, or changing the 
material but not the rigidity level (rigid, semi flexible, flexible), at a 
+20% bonus. This +20% does not apply to the actual level of penalty 
reduction, merely to the chance of success for Armor Knowledge. 
ARMOR LORE 
Critical Failure: No further attempts can be made with the same con-
figuration of armor until this skill chance is improved. 
Critical Success: Minor adjustments can be made, such as adding or 
subtracting 1-3 pieces of armor to the existing suit, or changing the 
material but not the rigidity level (rigid, semi flexible, flexible), at a 
+20% bonus. This +20% does not apply to the actual level of penalty 
reduction, merely to the chance of success for Armor Lore. 
ARTIFACT LORE 
Critical Failure: No information is known about the artifact being 
studied until the skill chance is increased. 
Critical Success: Additional or more pertinent information may be 
supplied in addition to the information being sought. 
Repeat Failures: No further rolls for the same information are 
allowed unless the study material grows or the skill chance increases. 
ASSASSINATE 
Critical Failure: The Assassin is seen by a witness, possibly the 
intended target. Evidence exists that could point to the Assassin. 
Critical Success: The Assassin is unseen and no one can tell from 
where the blow was struck. 
Repeat Usage: Assassinating individuals in the same organization or 
domicile as another who has successfully been assassinated is at + I 0%. 
Repeat Failures: Evidence against the Assassin piles up (drawings or 
description, etc.) increasing the chance of being caught. 
AURA OF PROTECTION 
Critical Failure: Treat as simple failure. 
Critical Success: Treat as simple success. 
AW AKEN PLANT 
Critical Failure: The plant dies in ld4 hours. No Will Force is lost. 
Critical Success: The plant is friendly with the practitioner regardless 
of the plant's alignment. 
Repeat Usage: Each successive usage in a single day's time adds one 
level of fatigue as well as the usual Will Force loss. 
Repeat Failures: Each failure lowers the practitioner one level of 
fatigue. No Will Force is lost when failing this skill. 
AWE 
Critical Failure: The being is not affected by Awe and notices this 
skill is being used by the practitioner. 
Critical Success: Further control spells, skills, invocations or other 
magics are resisted at -20% for the being the practitioner has affected 
as long as he remains within sight. Thereafter, Awe must be rerolled. 
58 
BALANCE 
Critical Failure: If the Balance roll is being made in place of an 
Agility save, then the save is at -20%. 
Critical Success: Allows Brace to be used to maintain position of 
balance, so that no new roll is needed. 
Repeat Usage: Fatigue applies per 10 minutes of usage. 
BALLAD LORE 
Critical Failure: All listeners are allowed+ 10% to saves and resist-
ances from further ballad effects for the duration of that ballad. Vocal 
chords are strained; all Sing, Sing Songs, Recite, and Recite Poetry 
skills are at 1/2 their skill chance for the rest of the day. 
Critical Success: All listeners are required to make a -10% save or 
resistance to further ballad effects for the duration of that ballad. 
Repeat Usage: Three failures becomes a critical failure. 
GM Notes: See the Magic section for new ballads. 
BANISH 
Critical Failure: No further attempts can be made to Banish this tar-
get until the Banish skill chance is increased. 
Critical Success: A specific target area can be named on the home 
plane if said target area is known by the practitioner; + I 0% to the next 
Banish attempt against that target. 
Repeat Usage: Each usage may create a one-use gateway to the other 
plane if another being is waiting at the location and attempts to use the 
gateway to get to the practitioner location. The chance should equal 
the Commune chance of the banished being. 
Repeat Failures: Each failure may notify other beings from the target 
being's home plane of the practitioner and his attempts to Banish 
beings there. The chance equals the Commune chance of the being tar-
geted for Banish. 
BERSERI<ING 
Critical Failure: Must wait 5 seconds to try again in addition to the 
normal time. 
Critical Success: The time is reduced by one second. 
Repeat Usage: Fatigue after the berserk state (See Player's Guide: 
Berserking). 
Repeat Failures: Cumulative -5% chance of fatigue per failed attempt 
in a days time. 
BESTIARY LORE 
Critical Failure: No other information is known about the creature 
studied until the skill chance is increased. 
Critical Success: Additional or more pertinent information may be 
supplied in addition to the information being sought. 
Repeat Failures: No further rolls for the same information are 
allowed unless the study material grows or the skill chance is 
increased. 
BLASPHEMY 
Critical Failure: No further attempts can be made that day to 
Blasphemy in the same fashion, i.e. make unholy water, blaspheme 
opponents or curse weapons. 
Critical Success: Duration is doubled for all effects and special 
usages. 
Repeat Failures: Three failures of the same type of Blasphemy (make 
unholy water, blaspheme opponents or curse weapons) are treated as a 
critical failure. 

===== PAGE 69 =====
BLEND 
Critical Failure: The practitioner does not know that he has failed but 
it is obvious to anyone else. 
Critical Success: The practitioner knows he has successfully hidden 
himself in the foliage. 
BLESS 
Critical Failure: No further attempts can be made in the same day to 
Bless in the same fashion, i.e. make holy water, bless companions or 
bless weapons. 
Critical Success: Duration is doubled for all effects and special 
usages. 
Repeat Failures: Three failures of the same type of Bless (make holy 
water, bless companions or weapons) are treated as a critical failure. 
I / / 
BODY CONTROL 
Critical Failure: The practitioner is considered to be in a non-medita-
tive state and cannot try again until either a successful Meditate skill 
roll is made or at least 10 calm minutes have passed. 
Critical Success: Also counts as a successful Meditate skill roll. 
Repeat Usage: Requires Will Force save for repeat usage within an 
hours time. 
BODY PARRY 
Critical Failure: No defensive adjustment can be applied against 
blows in the same second as the failed Body Parry. 
Critical Success: Area takes - I point of physical damage per attack. 
This 1s subtracted before damage is doubled or tripled for other effects. 
BRACE 
Critical Failure: No defensive adjustment can be applied against 
attacks during or 2 seconds following the failure to brace. 
Critical Success: The braced being can reposition herself once within 
3 feet without a second Brace roll. 
BREAK FALL 
Critical Failure: No Agility save is allowed to further reduce the 
effects of falling (see falling damage). 
Critical Success: The practitioner can return to a standing position in 
1-3 seconds instead of the usual time. 
CALLUNDEAD 
Critical Failure: No further use may be made of the materials for the 
Call Undead formula. 
59 
Critical Success: Undead material (bones, corpse, area, etc.) can be 
reused even after the destruction of the undead being. 
Repeat Usage: Will Force save is required to avoid mental fatigue on 
subsequent usages in any daily period. 
Repeat Failures: Nearby intelligent undead (within I mile per Will 
Force point of the undead) are alerted to the practitioner. 
CANDLE LORI 
Critical Failure: No further Candle Lore usage that day. 
Critical Success: The practitioner feels the success even if the effect 
is over a long distance. 
Repeat Usage: Will Force rolls are required to avoid mental fatigue. 
GM Notes: See the Magic section for new rituals. 
CARTOGRAPHY 
Simple Failure: The cartographer records one dimension inaccurately. 
Critical Failure: All dimensions are inaccurate. 
Critical Success: Indoors, secret doors or hidden areas become obvi-
ous. Outdoors, one geographic fact becomes obvious, i.e. a mountain 
runoff produces the river being mapped. 
CAUSE DISEASE 
Critical Failure: Divine denial lasting only an hour. 
Critical Success: The practitioner knows his hands are charged with a 
disease, and the target being is -20% to Disease Resistance. 
GM Notes: See diseases in the Combat section. 
CHARMING 
Critical Failure: Witnesses make a Wisdom save to notice the skill 
usage. 
Critical Success: None are aware of the skill's usage unless she 
knows the practitioner's ability to use Charming and makes a Wisdom 
save. 
Repeat Failures: Each failure reduces the next skill usage chance 
against that target by -5%. 
CHEAT 
Critical Failure: An Intelligence save by any witness will uncover the 
failed Cheat skill usage. Practitioners of Cheat have +20% to their 
Intelligence save to uncover the cheating and +20% to their Cheat roll 
if they are also trying to cheat. 
Critical Success: Practitioners of Cheat have -20% Cheat roll if they 
also try to cheat after the practitioner. 
Repeat Failures: Increases witnesses Intelligence saves by +5%; 
cumulative for this match or game. 
CLIMB 
Critical Failure: Skill user slips and requires an Agility save to avoid 
falling. 
Critical Success: Next climb roll at this location is +20%. 
Repeat Usage: Fatigue as jogging. 
CONTROL GROWTH 
Critical Failure: No further attempts may be made against this target 
until the skill chance increases. 
Critical Success: Plants will follow simple commands like entwine, 
kill, strangle, etc. and will not need direct control. 
Repeat Usage: Will Force save required to avoid mental fatigue on 

===== PAGE 70 =====
subsequent uses in a 24 hour period. 
Repeat Failures: Three failures against the same target are treated as 
critical failure. 
CONTROL UNDEAD 
Critical Failure: Undead become agitated and will in a combat situa-
tion usually choose the practitioner as the most favorable target unless 
otherwise engaged. No further attempts can be made against the target 
until the skill chance has been increased. 
Critical Success: Other Control Undead skill users are at -20% to 
their attempts to control this undead. 
Repeat Failure: Treat three repeat failures as a critical failure. 
Repeat Usage: If the undead has been controlled by the practitioner 
before, then there is a +10% chance added to the skill roll. 
CONVERT 
Critical Failure: No further attempts may be made against this target 
ever. 
Critical Success: No question of the conversion is made unless a 
good reason presents itself. Knights can be converted to Dark Knights 
and Dark Knights to Knights. The character will retain his Title, but 
must spend the new learn time for all skills not in his previous class. 
Repeat Usage: Each usage of Convert affords a cumulative, favorable 
+ I 0% Control Resistance for the target against further uses of Convert 
by the practitioner. 
Repeat Failures: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
CONVINCE 
Critical Failure: No further attempts may be made against this target 
ever. 
Critical Success: No question of the convincing is made unless a 
good reason presents itself. 
Repeat Usage: Each usage of Convince gives a cumulative, positive 
+10% Control Resistance for the target against further uses of 
Convince by the practitioner. 
Repeat Failures: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
COVER TRACKS 
Critical Failure: Obvious marks increase the likelihood (+20%) that a 
tracker will see that the tracks were covered up. 
Critical Success: The skill user knows she was successful. 
CRITICAL 
Critical Failure: Off balance. 
Critical Success: Weapon is +I to damage before doubling or tripling. 
CRYOKINESIS 
Critical Failure: Skill user is unable to use Cryokinesis for one 
minute and must make a Will Force save or suffer mental fatigue. 
Critical Success: 1/2 Aura requirements. 
Repeat Usage: Further usage in a period of one minute requires a 
Will Force save to avoid mental fatigue. 
Repeat Failures: Treat three failures in a minute's time as a critical 
failure. 
CURE DISEASE 
Critical Failure: No further attempt may be made to remove this dis-
ease from the target until the skill is improved. 
60 
Critical Success: The next attempt to remove the general type of dis-
ease (Bone, Blood, etc.) is at +20%. 
Repeat Usage: Treat three failures for the same target being and dis-
ease as a critical failure. 
GM Notes: See diseases in the Combat section. 
CURE INSANITY 
Critical Failure: Skill user can make no further attempts to remove 
this insanity on the target being until the skill chance is increased. 
Critical Success: Next attempt to cure the type of insanity is at +20%. 
Repeat Usage: Treat three failures for the same being and insanity 
type as a critical failure. 
GM Notes: See the effects of insanity in the Combat section. 
CURE POISON 
Critical Failure: No subsequent attempts are allowed to remove this 
poison from the same target. 
Critical Success: Next attempt to cure this type of poison is at +20%. 
Repeat Usage: Treat three failures for the same target being and poi-
son as a critical failure. 
GM Notes: See effects of poison in the Combat section. 
CURSE 
Critical Failure: No further attempts may be made to curse the target 
being, object or place until the skill is improved. 
Critical Success: The skill user knows he or she was successful. 
Repeat Usage: No repeat usage is allowed against the already cursed 
person, place or thing until the curse is removed or runs its course. 
Repeat Failures: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
GM Notes: The Control Resistance to avoid the curse is made at the 
same modifier used by the practitioner to call the curse; i.e a dangerous 
curse (-10%) lasting days (- 10%) would require a Control Resistance at 
-20% if the practitioner's Curse roll is successful. The GM may fur-
ther modify the Control Resistance roll if she feels it is unbalanced. 
No curse should be used to produce an overall positive effect (GM's 
judgement). 
DANGER KNOWLEDGE 
Critical Failure: No further rolls for one minute allowed. If this 
chance was rolled at the request of the player, have the character make 
a Will Force save to avoid mental fatigue. 
Critical Success: May have a possible hint to the nature of the danger, 
i.e. ambush, trap, etc. 
Repeat Usage: Each additional roll during a one minute period 
requires a Will Force roll to avoid mental fatigue. 
Repeat Failures: Treat three failures in a minute's time as a critical 
failure. 
GM Notes: Works even against hostile beings who have non-detec-
tion, etc. Each practitioner will have a unique sensation that causes 
him to feel danger. Some examples are: an itching, a feeling of being 
watched, a feeling of dread, goose bumps, hairs on the neck or arms 
stand up, a chill, etc. If more than ten Danger knowledge skill rolls are 
rolled in a day at the request of the player, he must make a Will Force 
save to avoid insanity.

GM Notes: See potions in the Magic section. 
PREDICT 
Critical Failure: The skill cannot be used for the rest of the day. 
Critical Success: Additional information may be supplied. 
GM Notes: As with Omen, do not allow Predict to be used if some 
form of other divine magic test, Divination, Omen, etc. was used first 
to try and find information and failed. If a deity or minions thereof 
decide not to reward the first test, then it is unlikely they will honor 
further requests. 
PROTECTION FROM EVIL 
Critical Failure: Make Piety save to avoid divine denial. 
Critical Success: -10% to Control Resistances to avoid the effects of 
the skill. 
Repeat Failure: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
PROTECTION FROM GOOD 
Critical Failure: Make Piety save or suffer divine denial. 
Critical Success: -10% to Control Resistances to avoid the effects of 
the skill. 
Repeat Failure: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
PYROKINESIS 
Critical Failure: Skill user is unable to use Pyrokinesis for one 
minute and must make a Will Force save or suffer mental fatigue. 
Critical Success: 1/2 Aura requirements. 
67 
Repeat Usage: Further usage in a period of one minute requires a 
Will Force save to avoid mental fatigue. 
Repeat Failures: Treat three failures in a minutes time as a critical 
failure. 
QUEST 
Critical Failure: No additional attempts may be made to quest these 
individuals for the particular task until the skill chance is increased. 
Critical Success: The practitioner is able to feel if the Quest has been 
successful or has reached a point at which it cannot succeed (or has 
failed outright). 
Repeat Usage: Only one quest may be in effect per Class Title. 
Repeat Failure: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
READPAST 
Critical Failure: No additional attempts may be made that day to 
learn the past of the being in question. 
Critical Success: More than just a feeling is imparted. A mental 
image of the previous week is replayed. 
Repeat Usage: Each additional success allows a further week of his-
tory. Replaying a previously read week is a + 10% to the skill roll. 
Repeat Failure: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
RECITE 
Critical Failure: Will Force save is required to avoid mental fatigue. 
Critical Success: -10% to victim's saves and resistances. 
GM Notes: See starting lores in the beginning of this section. 
RECOVER 
Critical Failure: Mental Fatigue. 
Critical Success: The being gains the benefit of the Bless skill for an 
hour. 
REGENERATION 
Critical Failure: No extra tries may be made to regenerate the lost 
limb or remove the scarring unless the skill increases. 
Critical Success: No save is required to avoid loss of Will Force. 
Repeat Failure: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
REINCARNATION 
Critical Failure: No further attempts may be made to reincarnate the 
dead being in any form. Make Piety save or suffer divine denial. 
Critical Success: The specific vessel's identity is felt by the practi-
tioner when the ritual is complete. 
Repeat Failure: Three failures are treated as a critical failure. 
REMOVE CURSE 
Critical Failure: No additional attempts may be made to remove the 
existing curse unless the skill is improved. 
Critical Success: The curse is removed and a general impression of 
the creator of the curse is known to the skill user. 
Repeat Failure: Three failures are treated as a critical failure.

Critical Failure: No additional attempts may be made against that

or storm.

ization rules in the Magic section.

reality the trap is not functional. 1n the case of pit traps the pit's walls

type of terrain or on a similar surface (door, floor, etc.)+ 10%.

SHIELD PARRY 
Critical Failure: Make Agility save or suffer off balance. 
Critical Success: - I damage before doubling or tripling modifiers. 
Repeat Usage: Consecutive parries versus the same opponent aiming 
for the same body region have a +10% skill chance modifier applied. 
Blows all striking the same contiguous body areas as the number of 
areas the shield covers in the same second can be parried with one roll. 
For example, a medium shield parries a blow to the head, neck and 
shoulder all in one roll because three arrows would have hit those loca-
tions in the same second and they are contiguous body areas (non 
buckler only).

should be contacted first when speak to dead is begun. This generally 
allows the skill user to then contact further dead. The ghost guides 
will often act like small children and need to have their egos indulged

New SkrlLs 
This part of this section contains the skills which are used by the new classes and those which are used at Titles 11 through 15. The

critical failures or success information listed-this is because these are skills which cannot be learned before 11th Title. Because 
skills above 10th Title are not able to be used as non-acquired, critical failures and successes for these skills are all considered sim-
ple failures and simple successes.

ALTER DESTINY 
Arm,bures: Knowledge, Will Force 
StaRt Bonus: ld6% 
Type: Magical 
LeaRn Tnne: NIA 
Ranm;: 20 
Tnne: I Hour 
Resmrcreb: Yes 
Description: Allows the practitioner to use a wish-like power to 
change the fate or destiny of one individual. 
General Usage: As the spell Wish with the following exceptions: 
1) The future is altered, not the present. The alteration must take place 
at least 24 hours in the future. 
2) Only a single individual is affected. 
3) This has no effect at all on beings over 16th Title. 
4) 1110 a Will Force point is lost when the destiny plays out. If the 
destiny was positive, then the individual pays the WiJI Force cost. If 
the destiny was negative, then the practitioner pays the Will Force cost. 
AURA BLAST 
AttRrbures: Aura, Will Force 
StaRt Bonus: ld6% 
Type: Magical 
LeaRn Tnne: NIA 
Rannt;: 20 
T nne: I Second 
Resmrcreb: Yes 
Description: Allows the practitioner to create a channel of pure 
destructive Aura Fire. 
General Usage: The energy is flung outward and travels in a straight 
line until it either encounters something that it cannot destroy, or it 
reaches its distance limit; it is l ' wide and one mile long per Class 
Title. The blast does its damage by the practitioner dropping his actual 
Aura rating. The blast does 20 points of damage per L Aura rating 
point which is dropped, and the practitioner must make an Aura save 
based on the new rating. If the roll is failed, then he must roll on the 
magical mishap table. After the blast, the practitioner's Aura pool is 
drained to zero, and will return at the normal regeneration rate. The 
practitioner's Aura rating returns at a rate of one per hour. 
The Aura blast destroys soil, trees and plants instantly. The path of 
destruction cut becomes an anti-magic zone and no plant or animal life 
will grow there. On most worlds, the Aura Blast will eventually exit 
the atmosphere because of the curve of the world (Earth's curve is 12 
miles). The only thing that will stop it is a structure which has more 
structural strength than the damage done (IO points of damage = I 
point of structural damage). No save of any kind is allowed against the 
Aura blast.

BATTLE CRY 
AttR1bures: Vitality, Will Force

LeaRn Tnne: NIA 
Rarrnt;: 15 
T nne: 2-7 Seconds 
RestRrcteb: Yes 
Description: Allows the practitioner to give a war whoop, cry or 
scream that unnerves opponents in combat. 
General Usage: When this skill is used the practitioner screams, 
whoops, cries out or emits some other loud noise in addition to her 
other actions. After 2-7 seconds, all non-player opponents under 15

+10%.

BLOOD LUST 
AttRrbures: Vitality, Will Force 
StaRt Bonus: ldl0% 
Type: Combat 
LeaRn Tnne: NIA 
Rarrnt;: 18 
T nne: 2-7 Seconds 
Resmrcreb: Yes 
Description: Allows the user to go into a frenzied state well beyond 
the state of the skill Berserking. 
General Usage: The practitioner gets angry or works himself up into 
the frenzied state and then rolls to go berserk with the skill Berserking. 
If that is successful, a Blood Lust roll is made to see if he has entered 
the state of bloodlust. The following information gives the benefits for 
the Blood Lust skill in place of Berserking and its benefits and effects: 
1) Endurance is doubled, but only for the duration of the Blood Lust. 
2) Strength, Agility, Vitality and Will Force are raised by 4 points dur-
ing this state. 
3) All mental attributes are at -4. 
4) The affected being remains in this state until all enemies on the bat-
tlefield are dead or are reduced to an obvious non-living state. 
5) After Blood Lust ends, Strength, Agility and Vitality are -3, return-
ing at a rate of one point per hour. 
6) When the Blood Lust state ends, the practitioner is considered 
fatigued at one full minute per 30 seconds that he was in the bloodlust 
state. 
7) During Blood Lust, the being does not go into shock and cannot be 
killed by blood loss or asphyxiation. Blood loss and asphyxiation 
deaths are postponed until the end of the Blood Lust state. 
8) Cannot be held, stunned, paralyzed, slept, or knocked unconscious. 
9) While blood lusted the effects of poison, disease and all control are 
temporarily ignored. They will take effect after the Blood Lust. 
10) All possible non-player opponents with a Will Force below 15 will 
require a morale check to engage the blood lusted individual. 
11) The being automatically passes all Control Resistance rolls, and 

===== PAGE 85 =====
ignores any effects which would normally cause a being not to attack. 
Notes: During the transformation into a bloodlusted state, it will be 
obvious that the practitioner has become unhinged. He will have 
symptoms like a bulging neck, bulbous eyes, a particularly viscous 
look, constantly scream, have uncontrollable drooling, etc. 
Special Notes: Damage is re-assessed after the state of Blood Lust. 
Any damage that would have killed or incapacitated the blood lusted 
being now takes effect, as do poison, disease and control effects. 
Critical Failure: Fatigue as described above in 6. 
Critical Success: Takes one less second. 
Repeat Usage: Cumulative -5% to fatigue. 
BONE LORE 
Arm,bures: Aura, Will Force 
StaRt Bonus: Id IO% 
Type: Magical 
leaRn Tnne: NIA 
Rarmc;: 18 
T rrne: 10 Minutes 
Resm1ereb: Yes 
Description: The ability to take or give magic powers between magi-
cal non-living bone objects, and to magically shape non-living bone. 
General Usage: The practitioner chooses a focus and a target. The 
focus may be a bone item or an undead being, as may be the target. 
Ten minutes of concentration is used to draw a single magical power or 
ability out of the focus and apply it to the target. The target may 
instead be the practitioner. The new power is at the Aura level of the 
target item, or twice the Class Title of the target being. 
Special Usage: The practitioner may shape one cubic foot of bone 
material per Class Title per hour. Shaping allows the user to alter both 
shape and change density. Density can be reduced to half normal or 
increased to twice normal. A Bone Lore roll is required before each 
hour of shaping. Bone Lore shaping can be used to separate a piece 
into two parts or to make an edge. Bone Lore can also be used to 
attach new limbs to undead beings; limits are 6 functional arms and no 
more than one brain case. In the cases where a magical bone item is 
separated into two parts, a Magic Resistance must be made by the 
magic item or it is ruined. If the resistance is successful, then all magi-
cal powers and abilities will stay with the largest piece. 
Notes: No normal being may possess more than I power per 2 Titles 
rounded up, by this or any other method. A magic item cannot gain 
more than five powers by transferring them with this or any similar 
skill. If an item is non-magical or a being is O Title, then powers given 
by the Bone Lore function will be at O Aura (no effect). Some care 
concerning transferred powers should be taken in applying new pow-
ers. Where no duration is given, assume I hour per Title of the being 
who receives the new power. 
The new power is usable depending on the Class Title of the being 
using Bone Lore:

Special Notes: Powers that transform other powers, or have the poten-
tial to do so, are not transferable by this skill (Wish, Unlimited Wish, 
Set, Delay, Extend, Intensify, Permanency, Enchantment, Creation, 
75 
etc.). lf Dispel Magic is cast on the power, instead of destroying the 
power it is merely returned to its origin. If Dispel Magic is cast on the 
individual or item that is missing the power, then the power returns as 
well. The only method for permanently keeping a power by this 
method is to have the spell Permanency cast on the power or to destroy 
the original item or being. Any bone-type undead being given a power 
or altered by this method will also radiate magic and be detectable by 
Detect Magic. Dispel Magic can be cast to remove the effects of bone 
shaping on an undead being. The bone shaping is considered to be at 
an Aura Level equal to twice the Class Title of the individual doing the 
bone shaping.

Armrbutes: Wisdom, Piety 
StaRt Bonus: 2d6% 
T £pe: Divine Magical 
LeaRn Tnne: NIA 
RatmI;: 14

Resmrcreb: Yes 
Description: Creates the illusion of death around oneself or others. 
General Usage: The skill user concentrates and forms the mental vis-

ful, a simple passing of the hands over the body and the individual has 
the illusions of death. The individual or practitioner now smells, looks, 
feels, sounds and even tastes like the dead. The individual is allowed a 
Control Resistance if he is unwilling or unknowing. The effect lasts 
one half an hour per Practitioner Title. One individual per Practitioner 
Title can be under the effects of Death Visage (this includes the practi-
tioner). 
Special Uses: This skill can be used to make one type of undead look 
like another type, or make an undead being look like a normal corpse. 
It can also be used to make the undead appear as a living being, though 
mindless undead will still not behave like the living. The skill can also 
allow the practitioner or other affected normal being to hide amidst 
bodies or the walking dead themselves. Since the illusion extends into 
the feeling of a negative energy or supernatural force, even other 
76 
undead will see the affected being as one of them. 
Special Notes: A normal Illusion resistance will allow an individual to 
see through the effects of this skill; however, there should be an 
extremely good reason for the being to feel that the death visage is an 
illusion. Illusion altering effects like Dispel Illusion work as if the illu-
sion was created at an Aura level equal to twice the skill user's Title. 
Critical Failure: No effect happens and no further attempts can be 
made on this individual for one hour. 
Critical Success: The effect is so good that the affected being will 
seem to be undead even to detection abilities, etc. Detect Illusion still 
sees through the death visage. 
Repeat Failure: Treat three failures as a critical failure. 
Repeat Usage: Renewing a death visage on a being is done at -20%.

Common Powers: 
• The item can be sensed anywhere, and the practitioner knows the dis-
tance and direction of the item. The practitioner can tell if the item is 
intact, and this ability works even if the item is on another plane of 
existence. 
• The practitioner may concentrate and project one sense through the 
item (as Sense Projection), wherever it may be. 
• The item can be returned instantly to the practitioner's person for the 
cost of II I 0th of a Will Force point, regardless of its current location. 
Examples of Unique Powers: 
Armour Enchantment (Rating 18/+5%): Inscribed on a piece of armor, 
the object becomes magical and gives a defensive adjustment of 
+ I per 5 Class Titles. In addition, it grants one point of Force 
Armor (as the spell) per Class Title. 
Weapon Enchantment (Rating 18/+5%): Inscribed on a weapon, the 
object becomes magical and gains +2 to hit and +2 to damage per 
5 Class Titles. 
Notes: Only one glyph may be in existence per Practitioner Title.

Knowledge are recorded as scrolls and memorized, spells for Hermetic

When the practitioner wants to cast a spell, he mixes the components 
together and makes a skill roll. Success indicates that the spell was

Special Usage: If the character does not have a recipe, the skill can be 
used to try and create a spell from scratch. In this case, the spell cre-
ation system is used (see the Design section). 
Notes: See the Magic section for a full explanation of how spellcast-
ing with Hermetic Lore works. The GM must determine the specific 
hermetic material(s) that are used for Hermetic Lore and the various 
strengths of the materials. The Magic section also contains a listing of 
hermetics and their relative strengths. 
Special Notes: Just like scrolls with Scroll Knowledge, Hermetic Lore 
recipes for particular spells must be found and learned. The practition-
er can attempt to learn a new spell by making a normal Hermetic Lore 
skill roll if a recipe is found. Unlike spell casting, any spell below 21st 
Aura level may be cast by guessing the formula and making a 
Hermetic Lore roll at half normal chance (see spell creation). 
Critical Failure: Roll an Intelligence save, failure indicates incorrect 
mixing and a possible magical mishap (see the Magic section). 
Critical Success: Duration is increased by 50%. 
Repeat Failure: Treat three failures in one day as a critical failure.

SHIELD KNOWLEDGE 
Armrbures: Strength, Agility 
StaRt Bonus: 2d6% 
Type: Combat 
LeaRn Trme: NIA 
Rarmr;: 14 
Trme: Varies 
RestRrcteb: Yes 
Description: Allows the skill user to overcome penalties with shields 
and to use them to much greater effect. 
General Usage: The skill user practices with a particular type of 

===== PAGE 93 =====
shield and then makes a skilJ roll to become a master with that type of 
shield. Only one shield type may be mastered per Practitioner Title. 
Mastery of a shield type gives the following benefits: 
1) Some of the penalties are removed with that shield type. For every 
25% of the skill, -10% of any penalties which would be applied to the 
Shield Parry roll for that shield type are removed. Bonuses are never 
given, just penalties removed. 
2) For every 25% of the skill, one additional second is given for the 
off-hand time to parry. This can never allow more than IO seconds in 
the off-hand, and thus has no affect on ambidextrious characters. 
3) Whenever the character makes a successful Shield Parry, he can also 
make a Shield Knowledge roll. Success indicates that the shield acts 
like hide instead of armor, thus reducing the amount of damage on a 
one to one basis. 
Example: If a smashing blow hits a plate shield for 40 points of dam-
age, normally half the value of the plate would be subtracted ( 10 
points). In this case, the shield would act like hide and subtract 20 
points from the attack. Damage done to the shield itself is treated as 
normal, and soft parries still apply. 
4) The practitioner can parry multiple adjacent areas with the same 
shield in the same second. The number of adjacent areas is based on 
the shield size: 
Buckler 1, Small Shield 2, Medium Shield 3, Large Shield 4, 
Body Shield 5. 
Thus if one blow came to the head and one came to the neck in the 
same second, the practitioner would need only make one Shield Parry 
roll to block both attacks with a buckler. A Body shield could block a 
blow to the head, neck, upper torso, right shoulder and right arm all in 
the same second. This is of course in addition to the normal areas 
blocked by that shield type (p. 193 of the Player's Guide). 
Critical Success: Damage done to the area(s) is -1 per die rolled. 
Critical Failure: No Shield Parry can be attempted for 2 seconds as 
the shield is loose or in the wrong location for such an attempt.

regrow and reform from the starting material. The recovered being 
will be the same age he was when he died. The person being restored 
must spend one Will Force, and the practitioner must spend one Will 
Force per 10 years that the being has been dead. 
Notes: For beings that have been dead for many centuries, the practi-
tioner can use the Will Force of volunteers (in one Will Force incre-
ments), but he cannot draw more Will Force from them than he will-
ingly gives himself.

Arrmbures: Aura, Will Force

Description: The ability to create spells on the fly without memoriza-
tion or study of scrolls. 
General Usage: The user concentrates and attempts to cast a magical 
effect. The player describes the magical effect including, duration, 
range, area of effect, targets, damage, game mechanics, etc. The GM 
then uses the Spell Creation Guide in the Design section to determine 
if the spell is viable and what Aura Level it is. If the spell is too high 
an Aura Level, then an Intelligence save is allowed to cancel the effect 
and avoid a magical mishap. Otherwise a magical mishap will result if 
the failure chance is rolled (this is rolled before the Wild Magic skill 
chance). If the effect is within the caster's Aura Control, then he can 
place a desired amount of Aura into the effect and attempt to produce a 
result. He must then roll a Wild Magic skill roll. Success indicates 
the spell works. Alternately, the Wild Magic practitioner can simply 
use the effect of an existing spell. The practitioner must know of the 
spell by having used it before, having seen it or having heard of it ( I /2 
Knowledge roll), otherwise he will have to experiment and deal with 
the results. Wild Magic is thus dangerous and can often backfire on 
the practitioner until he has practiced and learned some desirable 
effects. It is recommended that the practitioner (with the help of the 
GM) record successful effects as spells to cast in the future.

Armibures: Aura, Will Force 
SraRr Bonus: I d6%

Aura and draw up to IO points per 5 seconds from the wind. For each 
such draining, the random spell effect is skipped. 
7) The winds last 5 seconds per Class Title.

LeaRnmr; anb TRammr; Expanbeb 
Pages 164-165 of the Player's Guide outline the rules for 
Learning and Training. The following is an expanded explana-
tion for how the Game Master should deal with a character who 
learns new skills outside his class. 
Class/Racial skill slots 
The first requirement of learning a new racial or class skill is 
that a character must have an open race or class skill slot. As 
long as the total number of racial and class slots allowed are not 
yet full, a character can learn a skill outside his class and place 
it into one of these slots. A new list should be created, called 
"trained skills", for the skills which take up a race or class slot 
and are outside the class. When a racial or open class skill slot 
is filled, the player should make a note (next to the skill) of the 
Title that the character is when learning the skill. This is 
because Practitioner Title is based on the Title when the skill 
was learned (exactly like class skills). 
Skill Prerequisites 
On page 236 of the Design section of this book is presented a 
list of the class and racial skills, along with minimum Title 
requirements and skill pre-requisites for each skill. When a 
character wants to learn a skill outside his class, he must meet 
both of these requirements, as well as have an open skill slot. 
These prerequisites will allow a character to learn skills outside 
his class but not be out of balance with other classes who have 
the skill in their class structure. 
Example: A I st Title Warrior wants to learn some stealth/intru-
sive skills. This character has a 14 Knowledge, pretty good for 
a Warrior. This gives him 40 Class skills. The Warrior class 
has 3 I skills, leaving 9 slots open. This Warrior thinks that 
Move Unheard or Move Unseen would be good skills to learn, 
but alas, they have a requirement of 2nd Title. The Warrior 
decides instead to learn Climb. When he reaches 2nd Title, he 
is able to learn both Move Unheard and Move Unseen, filling 
up two other available slots. At 3rd Title, the Warrior decides to 
go ahead and learn Detect Trap (3rd Title requirement). He fills 
up another slot with Lie. At 4th Title he learns Listen, and 
because he now has so many stealth/intrusive skills, he can even 
meet the Escape requirements (Title 4 and any combination of 5 
stealth/intrusive or disciplined skills). The Warrior could learn 
3 more skills at any Title that he chose before his Knowledge 
maximum was met. (All of this assumes that the Warrior is able 
to find teachers for these skills.) 
It is very important to remember that although these skills are 
taking up class slots, they are not class skills. Thus the Warrior 
cannot put his class skill points into them, but must continue to 
train as described on p. 164 of the Player's Guide. This adven-
turer has been clever in learning useful skills, but these skills 
are not his forte and thus he must work at them continuously. 
If the player wishes to have such a character, he should create it 
with the Class Design system in the Design section of this book. 
85 
Learning Restricted Skills 
Leaming and Training are normally reserved for non-restricted 
skills. Yet there are always new members of different classes 
being trained with restricted skills. How do they all learn these 
restricted skiUs? The following rules are presented (at the 
Game Master's option) for allowing characters to learn restrict-
ed skills which are not in their class (such as a Warrior learning 
Scroll Knowledge, for example). The trick is that any expert 
(6 I%+) can teach a skill to a student who would have even a 
I% if it was a common skill (no starting bonus). Any master 
(81 %+) can teach anyone her skill. However, the practice of 
choosing apprentices and students is a time honored one and 
few are likely to break it. Restricted skills are restricted for a 
reason. Unrestricted access to whatever restricted skills a play-
er wants could easily break the balance established in this sys-
tem. 
Example: Say the Warrior in the example above wanted to 
learn Scroll Knowledge instead of stealth/intrusive skills. The 
skill Scroll Knowledge has the following requirements: 
a) minimum Title requirement of 3rd Title 
b) the character must also have acquired either Detect Magic or 
Detect Aura, and have acquired an additional four magical skills 
as well. 
The Warrior needs to learn a few things before he can start 
spellcasting. First the Warrior has to learn Detect Magic or 
Detect Aura. Since both are magical skills with the only 
requirement being 1st Title, the Warrior decides to learn these 
two skills. The Warrior learns Detect Magic, and then goes off 
to do some adventuring. He waits until 2nd Title when he 
returns to learn Detect Aura. Next he learns Identify, which has 
a minimum requirement of: 
a) 2nd Title 
b) Detect Magic or Detect Aura. 
This fills up another slot, for a total of 3 slots. At 3rd Title he 
learns the magical skills Play, Sing and Recite, filling up 3 more 
slots. Finally, at 4th Title, he is able to meet the requirements 
for Scroll Knowledge. All of this assumes that he was able to 
find teachers for all of these skills. The character now has the 
following list of trained skills: 
Detect Magic (Class Title I) 
Detect Aura (Class Title 2) 
Identify (Class Title 2) 
Play (Class Title 3) 
Recite (Class Title 3) 
Sing (Class Title 3) 
Scroll Knowledge (Class Title 4)

Sk,LL LoRes 
Providing Starting Lores to Characters 
There are several skills that require additional information or 
special discoveries to use, called lores. Lores are products of 
skills such as rituals for Ritual Lore and runes for Rune Lore. 
If a character begins the game with one of these skills acquired, 
he should receive at least one of the rituals, lores or spells, etc. 
A good rule of thumb is that for every full 10% chance the 
character has the skill he should be given one lore for that skill. 
For example, if a character started the game with Herb Lore at 
72%, he should be given seven herbs at the start of the game. 
If a character has any of these skills as non-acquired skills 
(meaning he will acquire them later during his advancement up 
to 10th Title) and he currently has a positive base chance in the 
skill, he should know at least one lore for the skill at the begin-
ning of game play. Some skills are used in conjunction with 
other skills such as Sing and Song Lore, and Recite and Poem 
Lore. The Bard class starts with Sing but doesn't acquire Song 
Lore until 3rd Title. Thus he would be given one song for Sing 
one Song for the Song Lore skill (assuming a positive base 
chance). 
Where does this automatic learning come from? It represents a 
teacher or teachers the character had in her prehistory that 
taught her the required lore. Based on the GM's discretionary 
learning rule, a practitioner with 61 %+ skill chance (an expert) 
can teach that skill to anyone who would have a base of at least 
I% despite the possibility of the skill being restricted. A practi-
tioner with an 81 %+ skill chance (a master) can teach the skill 
to anyone. However, in this case she is not teaching the skill so 
much as teaching one Song, Ritual, etc. This means that while 
many Wood Elves have Sing it is the Wood Elven Bards and 
lore masters who have Song Lore who teach the one magical 
song to their young students. 
Classes which will acquire Scroll Knowledge, but do not begin 
with it and also have at least a 1 Aura Control (either from the 
use of the social skill Metaphysics or through an Intelligence 
bonus) may begin the game with a spell already known. One 
additional spell is given at the start if he will acquire Spell Lore 
during normal advancement and has a positive chance and Aura 
Control.

Providing New Lores to Characters 
In an adventuring setting a character may want to acquire a new 
song and yet not have Song Lore (the skill needed to learn the 
songs). How do they do it? Like the learning rules, the singer 
must meet someone who has at least a 61 % chance in the skill 
Song Lore (if the singer has at least a I% chance in the skill 
Sing) or an 81 % (if the singer would have no chance at Song 
Lore). The Song Lorist spends several days, if not over a week, 
attempting to teach the song. The formula for basic learn time 
is 4 hours per rating point of the song in question. If a particu-
lar song is rating 16 then it would take 48 hours of training. 
Remember, no more than 8 hours of training is allowed in a 
day. At the end of that time, the singer makes a Song Lore roll 
with all the bonuses used in Learning (+20% with Teacher, 
etc.). If the roll is successful, the song is learned. If it is failed, 
the student may keep trying until they succeed with a +10% 
each time. 
Rules Summary: 
1) Learning a lore, spell, etc. can be done on one's own if one 
has a 1 %+ base chance and has or will acquire the skill during 
normal class advancement (10th or below). 
2) Alternately, a lorist can teach the lore but must have either a 
61 % skill chance or an 81 % skill chance depending on whether 
the student has a theoretical I% base or no chance. 
3) The number of starting lores is equal to the number of skills 
the player will acquire during his normal advancement to 10th 
Title. Having Sing would give one starting song, having Sing 
and being able to acquire Song Lore through advancement 
would allow two starting spells.

Whenever you are making a piece of armor out of, add the mag-

a 
ou as the Game Master have the difficult task of 
being the focus of all combat activities. You 
must run each and every being from the simplest 
extra to the most complex character, as well as 
keeping up with all of the players. You must 
weigh the needs of realism versus the need to get on with the 
role playing. Your players may be into ultra realism, counting 
on every second to survive opponents as bloodthirsty as they 
are-or perhaps they want you to focus on story telling, with 
combat only a means to an end to achieve storylines. Whatever 
the preference, the following section provides information that 
should allow the Game Master to better run combats in the 
Imagine system. 
Running your first few combats can be confusing because of all 
the many variables you have to deal with. You will most likely 
forget several things the first few times through, but don't 
won-y; it gets much easier with practice. As a result, you may 
wish to omit certain groups of rules until your group gets the 
hang of things. Several items commonly found in your local 
game store can be useful, such as large grid boards, small metal 
miniatures, and erasable markers (for use with the hex boards). 
In addition, we have provided several tools for you in order to 
make things run more smoothly. Below is an outline of the 
steps involved in combat to use as a Game Mastering aid. 
The Steps Of Combat 
I. Sighting 
Sighting does not have to be just visual, but can be any sort of 
detection ability available to a being. Once a being has sensed 
another, combat time and the combat round begins. 
II. Surprise 
Any combatants who have sighted another combatant and have 
not yet been detected get a surprise roll. (Note that initiative 
has not yet been rolled only because at least one being is 
unaware of his attackers. If all opponents are aware of each 
other, then no one has surprise and thus this step is skipped.) 
The attacker(s) now gains ld4+ I seconds of unanswered action 
against his victims. When multiple opponents are involved, the 
simplest way to handle surprise is to make one roll using the 
average Agility of the surprising group and the average Agility 
of the victims. 
Advanced GM note: A surprise roll can be made for each vic-
tim an attacker is trying to Surprise as opposed to a "group sur-
prise" roll. In this case, the surpriser gets I d4+ l seconds against 
only the people for whom the surprise roll was successful. 
m. Initiative 
Characters not involved in surprise should now roll Initiative. 
Initiative is really just about determining if anyone loses sec-
onds in the beginning of the round. Characters do not always 
93 
lose time, but it does happen. Anyone who gained surprise, and 
anyone who was surprised, waits until after the the 1 d4+ 1 sec-
onds has been used up before rolling initiative. Thus, if any of 
these beings rolls poorly for initiative, they will not lose those 
seconds until after the initial surprise time has been used. 
Advanced GM note: The only time this gets tricky is where 
individual surprise is being used, and multiple people are trying 
to surprise one or more individuals, such as in an ambush. In 
such cases, a character may be surprised by one ambusher but 
not another. This is acceptable and in fact makes the game 
much more interesting-it simply means that you need to keep 
track of who gains unanswered seconds against who. In this 
case the surprised people can only act against those combatants 
which they are aware of; the still wait to roll initiative until the 
surprise time has ended. 
IV. The Combat Round 
Though the combat round is considered to have begun, no actu-
al time has passed; until now, the GM has been setting things up 
by determining who gets to act on what second. At this point, 
players begin declaring actions in the order of there initiative 
roll. Now the action starts and second one begins. Players can 
either: 
a) begin using an effect: a spell, skill, power or the like. 
b) hold action and/or size up opponents. 
c) move. 
d) fire missile weapons. 
e) engage and attack in melee combat. 
A. Using Effects 
This is fairly straight forward, as the player simply states what 
skill he wants to begin, what spell he wants to cast, what power 
he wishes to activate, etc. Unless that action gets broken off 
before it is complete, that player has been addressed for the 
length of time that the spell or effect will take. Such effects are 
considered to go off at the end of the time period. For example, 
if a spell takes five seconds and was begun on second one of 
the round, it will take its effect at the end of second five. 
Anything that requires concentration limits the character to 
walking movement, or for flying characters basic flight only. 
B. Sizing Up 
Any character can sit back and watch the action and wait to see 
what happens. While doing this, he can gain information by 
sizing up opponents. A player gets one question for every sec-
ond that his character is not in action time (for general informa-
tion), and about one detailed question for every 2 seconds that 
his character is not in action time. Questions should always be 
answered with only single bits of information, whether detailed 
or general. For example, a player asks if the opponent is wear-
ing a helmet. This takes only one second, and its ok to tell the 
player that it is a metal helm with an open face. But another 
player then wants to know if he is wearing a helm and if the 
symbol of a certain evil god is upon the helm. This would be a 

===== PAGE 104 =====
detailed question and would take 2 seconds. Questions such as 
"Which regions of his body are armored?" are far too broad and 
should be responded with a broad answer such as "Most of his 
body is armored." A good general rule is that questions are 
only answered which give information about one or two body 
regions, with a greater level of detail for two second questions. 
While the player is asking these questions, he can only be mov-
ing, and cannot do any activities which require action time, 
such as swinging a weapon. If an opponent comes within 10 
feet of the character, then that character is forced to choose an 
engagement form, and he likely will not have the time to do any 
lengthy actions. Any further questions he wishes to ask can 
only be done under the restrictions of the type of engagement 
he has chosen and furthermore, cannot ask questions during 
action times. The idea is simply that he cannot really gain gen-
eral infonnation while he is heavily involved in an action. 
C. Movement 
When using miniatures, it is best to have a player move his own 
miniature and you simply make sure the movement is legal. A 
good scale to use is one inch equals five feet. If a character 
wants to run, he must begin his movement by walking in the 
first second, jogging in the second, and running in the third. 
Remember that characters cant just stop on a dime, and must 
slow down in an appropriate manner. 
D. Fire Missile Weapons 
The following steps apply to firing missile weapons: 
1) Detennine Range 
2) Have the player inform you where he is aiming. When firing 
at beings, always remember to ask which body region. Decide 
if it should be a called shot. 
3) Have the player roll to hit, and apply all modifiers to the roll. 
The tables on pages 96-97 will aid you. Modifiers include such 
things as: 
Coverage: ls anything or anyone blocking the shot? If so is it 
full or partial coverage? If full coverage, inform the player they 
have no shot. 
Aiming: Each second of aiming gives+ I modifier to hit, maxi-
mum of +4. 
Weapon: Does the weapon have a modifier when used as mis-
sile weapon? Do the projectiles being used affect the roll? Is 
the way the character is using the weapon affect the roU (two 
projectiles, firing two weapons at once, etc.). 
Skills: Do any skills affect the roll (Missile Lore, Brace, etc.)? 
Relative size modifiers: How big is the target in relationship to 
the being? 
Body Area Size: If you wish, you may modify the roll based on 
the size of the body areas. 
Defenders Penalties: Modify using the defensive adjustment of 
the character, as well as bonuses for magic armor, skills etc. 
4) Based on the target bullseye, determine where the shot hit. If 
the shot missed, you can use the accidental fire zones to see if 
94 
someone else was hit. If a natural "1" was rolled, roll a d6; if a 
6 is rolled some damage may have been done to the missile 
weapon. If the weapon has a wire or string, there is a 75% 
chance the wire has broken. Otherwise the attacker is allotted 
an Agility save. Failure indicates the weapon was thrown or 
slipped from the hand and is thrown 2dl2 feet in a random 
direction. Roll a dl2 to determine basic random direction. 
Treat just as you would the hour marks on a clock (12 equals 
directly in front, 6 equals directly behind.) 
5) If the shot hit, roll damage adding all damage bonuses. 
6) Compare the type of damage to the armor value, and subtract 
off the appropriate damage. 
7) Subtract damage from the Endurance area struck. Assess the 
effects of this damage during Resolution, unless the damage is 
below negative Vitality. 
E. Engagement and Melee Combat 
When a character wants to attack an opponent, he must declare 
which form of engagement he will use. If he declares none then 
simply assume standard engagement, unless the character is at 
charging speed (if the character is at charging speed, you must 
make him decide if he will do a move into or a move by). For 
characters which begin attacking immediately without first siz-
ing up, it is important not to give out too much information. 
The type of engagement will determine how much information 
the player gets. For example, player A is about to engage an 
opponent, and he wants to know what kind of armor the oppo-
nent is wearing. The GM is careful and will not tell player A 
until player A has announced his form of engagement. Player A 
then informs the GM that he wishes to furiously attack. He is 
then allowed no new information other than the simple basics, 
such as the basic race of the opponent (assuming he is familiar 
with that race), what category of weapon he is wielding (such 
as, "it's a big axe") and other such non-specific information 
(never detailed information on armor). Player A then sends his 
character into battle swinging for the intended victim's neck. 
The GM informs player A that his opponent's most heavily 
armored region is his neck, totalling some 40 points. Player A 
grunts when he later finds out that his comrade, player B, chose 
the form standard engagement, and was able to gain the basic 
information that his opponent had no armor upon his lower 
torso. Of course, Player A is now committed to this form of 
engagement until his opponent is incapacitated or until resolu-
tion at the end of the round. After a form of engagement has 
been chosen, the moment of engagement must then be 
addressed. This is where the actual attack takes place. 
Advanced GM Notes: The Moment of Engagement 
Remember that if two opponents have not yet engaged, then 
they are more than 10 feet apart. This generally gives the play-
er ample time to strike his opponent in coordination with his 
weapon speed. When a player chooses his fonn of engagement 
it is assumed that the character is timing the blow to correspond 

===== PAGE 105 =====
-
•l1Il•I•-
with his arrival at an opponent. This may not necessarily work 
out, however, so it is important for you as the GM to be aware 
of the timing to make sure that the player can actually strike his 
opponent at the point of engagement. For example, Brom the 
Warrior sees a Knight standing 30 feet away and decides to 
attack him. Brom advances upon his opponent (choosing the 
standard engagement form) and plans on striking him with his 
long sword. The combat round begins normally, and as Brom 
wields a 5 second long sword, we know that his weapon will 
make contact at the end of second 3 (action time) and that he 
will recover in the next 2 seconds (recovery time). His oppo-
nent, the Knight, is fighting with a short sword, and thus can 
strike at the end of second 2 and recover in the 2 seconds after 
that. If the two opponents were already engaged then the 
Knight would strike Brom first. However, as they are more 
than IO feet away, it so happens that Brom can time his attack 
to correspond with the weapon speed of his long sword. He 
thus plans on talcing 3 seconds to get to the Knight. Then, 
because his reach is longer, he will be allowed to strike first. 
Let us say, however, that the Knight sees Brom coming and 
decides to counter advance. The GM determines by the speed 
of the two individuals that the Knight can actually make it to 
Brom in 2 seconds. Therefore the Knight may actually strike 
first, and is able to get the advantage of his faster weapon. 
However, he must deal with Brom's blade, which will strike on 
second 3. 
Melee Attacks 
The following steps apply to melee weapon attacks: 
1) Determine who has the longest reach when the opponents 
first engage. That person strikes first. 
2) The player should state any skills he is using with his 
weapon. This may modify his weapon speed and roll to hit. 
3) Have the player inform you what body area he is trying to 
hit. Decide if it should be a called shot. 
4) Have the player roll to hit, and apply all modifiers to the roll. 
The tables on page 96 will aid you. Modifiers include such 
things as: 
Weapon: Does the weapon have a modifier when used for a 
certain kind of damage type? Does the weapon have a magical 
bonus? 
Skills/Effects: Do any skills or similar effects modify the roll? 
Relative Size Modifiers: How big is the target in relationship to 
the being? 
Body Area Size: If you wish, you may modify the roll based on 
the size of the body areas. 
Defenders Penalties: Modify using the defensive adjustment of 
the character, as well as bonuses for magic armor, skills etc. 
5) Based on the target bullseye, determine where the strike hit. 
If the attack missed and the player rolled a "1 ", have the attack-
er make an Agility save. If the save is made no fumble occurs 
but there is a loss of ld4+1 seconds spent recovering (use the 
95 
fumble charts). Loss of a weapon involves throwing the 
weapon away or loss of grip. The weapon is thrown 2d 12 feet 
in a random direction. Roll a dl2 to determine basic random 
direction; treat just as you would the hour marks on a clock 
(with 12 directly in front and 6 directly behind). Retrieval of the 
weapon takes ld6+1 seconds. 
6) If the blow hit, roll damage adding all damage bonuses. 
7) Compare the type of damage to the armor value, and subtract 
off the appropriate damage. 
8) Subtract damage from the Endurance area struck. Assess the 
effects of this damage during Resolution, unless the damage is 
below negative Vitality. 
V. Resolution 
This is the phase when ending effects for the round are handled. 
Resolution can be used for any effect which requires a roll 
every IO seconds, such as storm spells (or the GM can keep up 
with the times of these effects). All special injury effects and 
Vitality saves are made at this point. 
Overall Endurance 
Certain special effects apply to a being's overall Endurance. 
Overall Endurance simply refers to the attribute characteristic 
Endurance, as opposed to the Endurance for any one specific 
body area. This number can be adjusted from things such as 
poison and blood loss. Adjustments to overall Endurance do 
not require that the rest of the body areas be recalculated, even 
though they are all based on Endurance. If basic Endurance 
goes below zero, however, the being must make a Vitality save 
every round (in combat) or every minute out of combat to stay 
conscious. This roll is made at -5% per every point under 0. 
Overall Endurance returns at twice the normal healing rate. 
Healing can be applied to a character's overall Endurance, just 
as if it were its own body area. 
Death 
Death occurs when any vital area is reduced below negative 
Vitality, or overall Endurance is reduced below negative 
Vitality. Characters can be magically healed within IO seconds 
of vital death wounds and 10 minutes for death from loss of 
overall Endurance or any other method. After death, the spirit 
will stay near the body or place of death for one day per Will 
Force point. The spirit is considered an invisibly-phased ghost 
which has no ghostly powers except movement (fly), life sense 
and magical sight. Anyone who can Speak with Dead or Spirit 
Dance will get +20% to contact the being while he is in this 
near permanent death state (mostly dead).

Special Note: Ducking, falling to the ground or jumping out of the way of indirect fire is possible. A wary secondary opponent (other than the target opponent) may 
declare her intention to get out of the way (before to hit is rolled). lf he does so, he gives up his current action and ducks, rolls, dives or jumps either towards cover

the field of fire altogether. Direct targets may not attempt this, and must use the Dodge skill.

Usm~ Expanbeb Combat" Rules 
MR. lrnnanoe 
The timing in combat can be greatly clarified to both the play-
ers and the Game Master by a fellow who is a friend to us all, 
"Mr. Initiative." Mr. Initiative is basically a visual system that 
the GM can use to keep up with the timing relationships of all 
combatants in the 10 second combat round. Feel free to photo-
copy Mr. Initiative. As a GM, you may wish to use this so all 
players can see, or keep it hidden behind your GM screen. 
Some GMs even like to give a copy to each player so that they 
can keep up with their own timing. Use whichever method you 
prefer. This system also works well as a teaching tool to help a 
get the hang of combat, eventually needed only for the most 
complex combats. 
Using Mr. Initiative 
Surprise seconds: This part of the chart is for those seconds 
that a character gains when he surprises an opponent, but initia-
tive has not yet been rolled and the actual combat round has not 
been entered. Use this area as a "mini round" to show how 
many seconds have been gained by the surpriser. Once the sec-
onds have been used, roll initiative and enter using the other 
sections. 
Split Second: Have each player roll initiative. Roll initiative 
for any opponents that you are controlling. Ask everyone what 
their modified initiative number is. Once you know this num-
ber you can then place that player's marker on the correct sec-
ond of the Mr. Initiative chart. When a player has generated a 
negative number then you place her marker onto the Split 
Second section. Note that the split second section does not 
allow extra seconds to be gained in the actual combat round, 
and is considered part of the first second. 
Combat Round: This darker area is used to keep up with the 
actual combat round itself. All players should have some sort 
of a marker, whether this be a token, or preferably a second 
miniature. If the player's modified initiative roll was positive, 
then place their marker on the specific second on the combat 
round section. Once the players in the split second section 
begin taking action, they will be placed here as well (on the 1st 
second). As players begin fighting, their marker will be moved 
along the seconds in correlation with their actions. It is a good 
idea to try and not let any one player get too far advanced into 
the combat round (in relationship to the other players). Thus 
you may move one player's marker ahead, then move another 
player's marker ahead of that, going back and forth until the 
end of the round. 
Extra event time: When a player's modified initiative roll is 
- l l or Jess, that player gains extra event time. Specifically, he 
gains I second worth of event time for each value below -JO, so 
that a player who has a -15 actually gets 5 extra 'seconds' of 
combat time in the actual combat round. Note that certain 
spells and effects can also speed a character up and provide him 
with extra time as well. This section actually breaks each sec-
ond up into two parts. Add the extra event time gained in the 
second half of each second, represented with a "b." When all of 
the extra time has been used up, move the player's marker onto 
the actual combat round. For example, the above character who 
gained 15 seconds would have his marker moved from la to lb 
to 2a to 2b and so on until he reached 5b, at which point his 
marker would advance to second 6 of the actual combat round 
section. 
Off hand seconds: This section is not meant to parallel the 
combat round like extra seconds. It will require an extra marker 
or token, but this should not be a miniature as it is not repre-
senting the character. It is merely used to represent the amount 
of time that the character has used in her extra hand. When all 
5 seconds have been used (for non-ambidextrous characters) the 
marker simply remains until the next round and the character 
can take no further action with that hand. The IO seconds are 
provided for ambidextrous characters only. When the player's 
primary hand marker reaches 6 seconds, start moving the off-
hand marker along with it. 
Current combat round: You can use a die or simply mark a 
number in the box provided. This will let you know how many 
rounds of combat have passed as well as what number the actu-
al combat round is. 
Carry over seconds: When a character takes an action that 
will carry over into another round, you simply place his charac-
ter marker in the appropriate box. Each time you increase the 
current combat round by one, move all the carry over markers 
one space vertically upwards (10 spaces down). When a marker 
is on the lowest level (1-10) then you move that marker onto 
the actual combat round when the current combat round number 
advances. Effectively this number tells you how long it will be 
until the character is able to perform the intended action.

Expanded Rules 
Martial Knowledge Throws 
Throws can unbalance the game and are difficult at best. They are an 
optional portion of Martial Knowledge and so are included here. All 
successful throws require ld6+ I seconds for the victim to recover 
unless the opponent has the ability to jump to his feet, in which case it 
requires 1-3 seconds. Damage for each throw is based on striking 
packed earth, or wood. Hitting water removes damage, stone adds + I 
per die, metal +2 per die. One additional die is rolled for damage per 
50 pounds of opponent over 200 and + I is added to rating per 50 
pounds over 200 (maximum of 6 dice +6). ld4 random areas are dam-
aged by this method if the throw is successful. 
Arm Throw (Rating 16/+{)%): The martial artist grabs the arm of the 
opponent (d20, IQ or better) and the martial artist must then win a con-
test of his Strength versus the opponents Agility to throw the opponent 
to the ground. If the Martial Artist makes a second Agility save, he has 
an Arm Hold as well. Takes 3 seconds and does d6 damage. 
Leg Throw (Rating 17/-5%): The martial artist uses her leg to capture 
the leg of the opponent (d20, 10 or better) and then the martial artist 
must win a contest of her Strength (at -20% to the martial artist) versus 
the opponents Agility to throw the opponent to the ground. A martial 
artist who makes a second Agility has an Leg Hold as well. Takes 4 
seconds and does d4 damage. 
Shoulder Throw (Rating 18/-10%): The martial artist grabs the arm of 
the opponent (d20, IO or better) turns, and rolls the opponent over the 
shoulder onto the ground. The martial artist must win a contest of her 
Strength (at +20% to the martial artist) versus the opponents Agility to 
throw the opponent to the ground. If the martial artist makes a second 
Agility save, she has an Half Neck hold as well. Takes 3 seconds and 
does d8 damage. 
Body Throw (Rating 19/-15%): The martial artist grabs the arm of the 
opponent (d20, IO or better) turns, bends, and flips him onto the 
ground. The martial artist must win a contest of his Strength (at +30% 
to the martial artist) versus the opponents Agility to throw the oppo-
nent to the ground. If the martial artist makes a second Agility save, 
he has an Arm Hold as well. Takes 5 seconds and does d8 damage. 
Spin Throw (Rating 18/-10%): The martial artist attempts one of the 
other throws above but adds momentum by spinning. The opponent is 
-20% more to Agility save in the contest to avoid the throw. The oppo-
nent is released at the end of the throw so no hold is possible. Adds I 
second and adds +2 damage per die rolled. 
Martial Lore Throws 
Punch Throw (Rating 19/-5%): Any Upper Body Punch is used in 
combination with a Leg Throw. Both are simultaneous but the punch 
must be successful in order for the throw to have a chance of working. 
Kick Throw (Rating 20/-10%): Any Lower Body kick is combined 
with an Arm, shoulder or Body Throw. Both are simultaneous but the 
kick must be successful in order for the throw to have any chance of 
succeeding. 
101 
Slam (Rating 21/-15%): A Strength save is added to any throw except 
leg to add force to the throw and slam the opponent against a hard 
object. Damage is ld6 per 5 full points of martial artist's strength 
+ I d6 for every 50 pounds over 200 of the victim (maximum of +6d6). 
Damage is I additional die per full 5 points of the martial artist's 
Strength, and adds +2 seconds to the other Throw .. 
Martial Disarm (Rating 20/-10%): The ability to disarm an oppo-
nent's melee weapon with bare or gloved hands. To determine success, 
a contest of skill (at rating 20) vs. the opponent's Agility is rolled. If 
the practitioner wins, the weapon is disarmed. If the Skill roll itself 
fails and the melee weapon has a cutting attack, then one half of the 
weapon's damage is applied randomly to one of four body areas, either 
hands or forearms, left or right. If the skill roll is made by one quarter 
or less and the practitioner wins the contest of skill vs. Agility then the 
weapon can actually be taken from the opponent and transferred to the 
practitioner. 
Break Fall 
A Break Fall practitioner may negate damage from a grappling or mar-
tial throw with a successful skill roll.

Expanded Rules for Penalties to Skills 
The Players Guide gives modifiers for individual pieces of 
armor that can be applied to combat skills; these penalties can 
be removed by the skills Armor Knowledge and Armor Lore. 
In addition to those penalties, the GM can apply the penalties 
listed below for a character wearing either a suit or simply sev-
eral pieces of an armor type. These penalties should be applied 
not combat skills. but instead to certain disciplined and stealth/ 
intrusive skills where common sense dictates. These penalties 
should be added to those listed in the players guide, but are not 
themselves cumulative. For example. a character in a full suit 
of plate gets -20% to relevant skills, not -20% for each piece. 
Examples of a few skills where these penalties should apply: 
Move Unheard, Climb, Martial Knowledge and Martial Lore.
