Survival Rule of Thumb 
As a fundamental survival rule of thumb, human-like beings can 
not go longer than three minutes without air, three days without 
water and three weeks without food. While it's possible to 
reach these limits, and even surpass them without perishing, it's 
not a recommended course of action. 
Asphyxiation and Drowning 
A character can survive without oxygen for ten seconds for each 
point of Vitality they have. Once that time limit has been 
reached, the effects of asphyxiation begin. Every ten seconds, 
ld6 are subtracted from the character's Basic Endurance (ld6+l 
if drowning). At the onset of asphyxiation, a Will Force save 
must be made to remain calm or damage is doubled. When 
Endurance has been reduced to zero, the being will appear very 
pale and must begin making Vitality saves to remain conscious 
(-5% to the save for each point below zero). Once Endurance 
reaches the negative Vitality rating of the being, the lungs have 
collapsed and the heart stops beating. One minute later, if 
Endurance is not raised above the negative Vitality rating of the 
being, then it will die. A Churigeon roll will resuscitate the 
being and raise Basic Endurance to one above negative Vitality. 
Should a being survive the ordeal, restoration of Basic 
Endurance is based on the healing rate of the character (defined 
by Vitality). However, Basic Endurance is restored at a rate of 
minutes instead of days, and a period of ten minute intervals 
instead of weeks. 
Dehydration 
For each full day without water, all physical and mental attrib-
utes of a character are reduced by four. Additionally, three lev-
els of fatigue are assessed, eventually requiring Vitality saves to 
avoid passing out. Once adequate water has been ingested, 
attribute points are restored at the rate of eight per day. 
Starvation 
All physical and mental attributes of a character are reduced by 
one for each full day they go without food. Also, the character 
suffers from a level of fatigue each day, which eventually 
require him to make Vitality saves to remain conscious. 
Attribute points are restored at the rate of two per day once ade-
quate food has been consumed. 
Falling Damage 
Falling damage is based on distance and the surface struck. An 
Agility save reduces damage taken by one dice, and the number 
of damaged areas by one. If a character is wearing metal armor, 
add 1 die per 30' of falling, and treat falling damage as crushing 
damage.

Vitality point. The nausea effect returns in one week per Vitality point if no 
longer imbibed regularly. 
2 Once the being is unconscious he must make a new Vitality save every hour or 
move further down the table. Remember to subtract 5% of negative cumulative 
modifier to Vitality save per 50 pounds of body weight per hour. 
3 Death will be as a result of heart stoppage within Id IO minutes of reaching 
this level of alcohol/drug poisoning. 
Notes: Combat Modifiers are suffered when drinking. Berserking is only 
rolled if the GM feels the being has been provoked. When aJJ cumulative modi-
fiers to Vitality saves are removed, the affected being will move up one level of 
intoxication (No# of failed saves) per 50 pounds of body weight per hour. 
Example: A Ranger with a 15 Vitality and a weight of 187 pounds meets a 
young lass and thinks he can impress her by chugging three beers in succession. 
He has them quickly enough that we combine them into one Vitality save. His 
Vitality gives him a 75% Vitality save -15% (-5% per beer x3). He rolls a 47%; 
he is not intoxicated. She thinks him foolish and so offers him a whisky. He is 
now at 75% -25% (+10% more for the whisky plus the previous beers). He 
rolls a 58%, 8% over the 50 he needed. He is now at the first level of intoxica-
tion and were he to get into battle he would suffer the penalties listed above. 
He decides wisely to stop drinking because its a rough looking bar and recovers 
15% of his accumulated penalty that hour ( 187 pound weight/ 50 = 3 x 5% = 
15%). If he continues down the road to being sober the next hour, he will recov-
er the remaining I 0% penalty and the level of intoxication.

death to their victims. Poisons can be stopped by magic or herbs.

Tolerance: A being can build a tolerance to any particular poison that has a 
"None" listed in the "Resist Effect" column. She takes small doses once per 
week. Each dose requires a Poison Resistance. Failure indicates that the being 
has the effect of a poison of V levels lower, for 1/2 of the typical duration. 
Success indicates an improvement of 5% Poison Resistance against that particu-
lar type and source of poison. Thus, it is possible to make oneself nearly 
immune to that poison. Some poisons either do not allow for immunity because 
of the source or because of their magical nature. GM discretion should be used 
when allowing players to build up immunities. 
GM Advice on Poisons: Most medieval systems thrived on intrigue, and the 
nobles and their ilk had and used poison. However, the average person had lit-
tle access to it. If your average character can easily acquire poison, it can be 
overbalancing as most creatures or beings will succumb to it eventually. It 
doesn't challenge the Warrior to poison his every armored spike and blade and 
then roll all over his opponents until they die of poison, or you of boredom. 
Keep poison rare. Also in most societies the use of poison is considered 
immoral and is often illegal.

Insanity is usually caused by a the Insanity skill or a traumatic 
event in the character's life. The Insanity rules should be used 
with extreme care. Insanity should not become so rampant that 
all the characters need to be restrained for the good of society. 
The tables below provide some of these as sample stresses. A 
character stressed as described below gets a Will Force save to 
avoid becoming insane. If the character makes the roll, there is 
no effect. If the roll is failed, the next tables determine category 
and then specific type of insanity. Healing can occur over time 
or through one of several skills, magic or divine abilities such 
as Cure Insanity.

Depressive Disorders 
Depression: Inability to act or to feel necessary. The being has feel-
ings that everything is pointless. Characters who experience this will 
want to sleep a lot as well. Depression can be alleviated by the charac-
ter experiencing events that are comforting or soothing to him. If this 
happens, the GM may waive the time rolled on the duration table. 
Depressed characters are -2 to all physical and mental attributes. 
Fugue State: A state in which the character is withdrawn, befuddled, 
and generally unreachable. The character may wander around aimless-
ly and/or mumble to himself. The character has no actions and is unus-
able but will act to save his own life. If the character is truly threat-
ened with such a situation, then a new save is allowed to break out of 
the fugue state. 
Manic Depressive (bipolar disorder): A state in which the character 
is alternately extremely depressed and maniacally uplifted and exuber-
ant. Characters in the maniac phase are in a constant berserker state 
(see the Berserking skill.) Characters in the depressive phase are 
depressed as described in depression above. The character is most 
always in one of these two states. 
Neurotic Disorders 
Amnesia: A rare disability that causes a character to forget a specific 
event or a segment of the past. Sometimes even only a certain knowl-
edge the character possesses is lost. Roll or choose below for effect.

Hypochondria: Characters with hypochondria have internalized their 
fears. They seek attention by complaint about their ailments. 
Insomnia: The inability to fall asleep due to anxiety. The character 
afflicted by this ailment may not be able to get a full night's sleep. 
Have the character roll a Will Force save each time he desires to sleep. 
If the roll fails, it takes the character several hours( ld6) to fall asleep 
and she is fatigued I level per hour of sleep missed the next morning. 
Phobia: A phobia is an extreme fear or loathing of something such as 
a fear of heights. A character with a phobia will avoid the feared thing 
at all costs, even to his own detriment. A character attacked by an 
intelligent tree might have a phobia of trees and will not enter forests 
for any reason. The GM should pick an appropriate phobia for the sit-
uation or make one up as necessary. The following are a few exam-
ples:

Sleepwalking: The character who sleep walks is so troubled by his 
fears that he walks about in sleep. Waking this person up is difficult 
unless you can get him to lie down first. Have the character roll a Will 
Force save every night to see if he sleepwalks. 
Tic: A jerky muscular contraction of one specific area that either 
occurs continually or during times of stress. Some common nervous 
tics are jerky hands or a twitching eye. 
Stammering: Characters who stammer cannot speak without difficul-
ty. This is especially damaging to characters who use magic spells. 
Each time the character truly concentrates on saying words (casting a 
spell) they must make a Will Force save or the words come out garbled 
and the spell fails. 
Psychotic Breaks 
Schizophrenia 
A) Simple (01-65%): Inability to separate reality from fantasy. 
Characters with this will experience illusions of sound, sometimes 
sight and very rarely touch. Sometimes these individuals, over time 
,can believe they are famous figures of importance or notoriety. 
B) Paranoid (66-90%): Paranoid schizophrenics are experiencing a 
specific delusion that they are being watched and even hunted. This 
type of schizophrenic can often appear very normal but will act very 
defensively about their particular paranoia. 
C) Catatonic (91-00%): These schizophrenics have withdrawn com-
pletely into themselves to the point where they will rarely move or 
respond to anything. A random lucid moment may occur from time to 
time but the character is no longer able to function or feed themselves. 
Depressive Personality: This is similar to chronic depression except 
it is constant and seems unending. The character may even kill them-
selves if faced with another stress (roll Will Force save). This type of 
character is very non-functional and may not be able to act in many 
situations. 
Antisocial Personality: When the being becomes antisocial they lose 
whatever alignment they had and become True Neutral. He may seem 
quite charming but will be unable to form lasting friendships or rela-
tionships. Beings like this may break off from any groups they are in 
or sell their supposed friends out for gain. 
105 
•I•-
Borderline Personality: Being loses alignment and may appear to be 
several alignments depending on his whim of the moment. These 
beings are very dangerous, unpredictable and will do almost anything 
on a dare. An extreme borderline personality might cut off his own 
head on a dare. 
Conversion Reaction: This is similar to hypochondria save that the 
victim actually gets a debilitating disease or impairment continually 
due to the stress experienced. For instance, a character who sees her 
friend die tragically may become blind so she will not have to see such 
an event again. The illness is incurable save by the methods listed 
under Insanity rules. 
Multiple Personalities: Beings with multiple personalities exhibit 
extremely different personae. The being switches back and forth 
between personalities at random or if keyed by specific events. 
Usually one of the personalities is strongest and will be displayed more 
frequently. This may be the original core personality. The number of 
different personae differs, but most often is two (perhaps one good and 
one evil). Each may become different classes have different align-
ments and attitudes and will have different experiences. Sometimes 
the personalities know about each other, but this is not always the case. 
Rarely three or more personae will display themselves. Choose or roll 
below for number.

Divine Magical Diseases 
Divine Magical diseases are created through divine and super-
natural forces. They can be transferred through means other 
than earthly (bacteria, viruses, etc.). Some of the ways to create 
a magical disease are through the skill Curse, a 1/2 skill roll of 
the Cause Disease skill and the skill Plague. 
Cause Disease 
Cause Disease can be used to create a magical disease in a vic-
tim at a half skill chance. The effect depends on the disease 
being created and is limited to the individual who is infected 
with the disease (the exception is Lycanthropy, which can be 
passed on). 
Cursed Diseases 
The skill Curse can cause a magical disease of a set type, with a 
set duration and seriousness at a 1/2 skill chance. A mortal may 
only curse a single individual at a time with a disease however. 
Lycanthropy 
Divine Plagues 
These plagues can be created by an immortal with the skill 
Curse or Plague, or with a divine or supernatural source. A 
divine plague is a type of divine magical disease whose dura-
tion and effect is completely controlled by the supernatural 
influence who created it. The variables of the disease are set at 
the time of creation. For example, every individual struck with 
it could have a terminal case that lasts three days while the dis-
ease itself lasts three years. The divine plague can also target a 
single entity type or community, such as all Elves or everyone 
living in and around a particular city. An immortal or divine or 
supernatural source can also cause Lycanthropy as a disease for 
multiple victims with a half skill chance of Plague or Curse. 
The number of victims cannot exceed the same number of wor-
shippers and followers of divine or supernatural being. 
The Plague Invocation 
This invocation creates a divine disease that effects a set num-
ber of people and then does not pass on to any additional vic-
tims. This invocation cannot be used to cause Lycanthropy. 
The curse of the beast-the disease of the change. They walk amongst us, unseen and unknown, turning in dark of night by moons 
light. Some wizened beasts even change by the whim of their deranged minds. Fear them then, for they have forgotten what it 
means to be man, elf or dwarf. Magic or silver will harm them but only silver will Leave them scarred. Sadly, when the night's dark 
Labor is done and a beast Lies dead, it loses its animal shape, making many would be heroes appear as simple murderers to those 
that do not see the change. Ware' the claw or the bite or you will be the next. 
There can be as many types of lycanthropy as there are animal types. The victims are referred to as were-animal, i.e. werewolf, 
werebear, etc. This disease is said to be an infection of the spirit that ties the animal nature to the being, making him not entirely 
either man or beast. It is ftrst created by a Curse or divine disease but then propagates, passing to victims who are wounded-but not 
killed-by the lycanthrope in its animal or half-animal form. At first the change brings madness and loss of memory for the victim. 
Later the victim may master the beastly impulses, retaining mental control while changed and finally controlling the change itself. 
Few lycanthropes live this long, for they are always hunted. Their divine magical nature can be seen by the wise, with the skills 
Detect Supernatural, Sense Supernatural, and the invocation Discern Divinity. When any one of those skills is combined with a suc-
cessful Bestiary Lore or Animal Lore skill roll, the type of Lycanthropy is identified as well. Many of the effects of lycanthropy are 
determined by the skills Evoke and Animal Shape as noted below. While in most settings, lycanthropes change with the full moon; 
however, other mechanisms can be chosen to set a cycle as well.

Duration of disease: The length of time the victim has been infected. 
Will Force (WF) saves are non-optional. The being must make this save to determine the outcome whenever the condition is met. 
Moon Change: The Will Force save (with modifier) to avoid changing during a full moon. 
Stress Change: When the victim of this disease is severely stressed, such is in a combat situation, this is the save required to avoid changing form. 
Using the skill Berserking requires this chance to be checked once per IO seconds.

Retain Control: This is the chance the victim is able to retain mental control while in half-animal or animal form. 
Change by Choice: This is the chance the victims can bring on the change themselves.

The Change 
If the victim does not retain mental control halve all mental 
attributes (do not halve them again if the changed Lycanthrope 
goes berserk). Beings not in control are in a fugue state, 
remembering little, save a flash here and there after they return 
to their true form. If the change was based on the moon cycle, 
then it lasts until just before dawn, when the sky begins to 
change, whether the victim sees the change or not. Moon 
changes will occur even if the moon is obscured or the victim is 
deep underground. After a full night of the change the victim 
wakes up exhausted (-5 levels of fatigue). Changes because of 
stress last until ld6+ l minutes after the stressful situation or 
individual is gone. If the victim changes by choice she can 
change back with a normal Will Force save. After a stressful or 
self-determined change the victim is fatigued one level. For 
either change, add any additional penalties if the victim went 
berserk during the change. Anytime a victim reverts back after 
an uncontrolled change, a Will Force save is required to avoid 
Insanity. Once the victim is stricken insane, no further rolls are 
required regardless of the number of changes, until that insanity 
is cured or leaves the victim. It should be noted that most 
lycanthropes go insane long before they learn to control the 
change. Victims that are killed while changed revert to 
humanoid form I d6+ 1 minutes after death. 
lmmullities (ill humalloid fonll): 
Normal weapons do no damage, blessed and +l/+2 magical 
weapons half, +3 and higher as well as silver weapons do full. 
Special Abilities (ill humanoid form): 
Berserking at +20% 
Detect Supernatural at +30% 
Slow Regeneration: ld4 points are healed per 10 minutes. 
When limbs are fully healed, they are fully-grown back. Vital 
areas still cause death. 
Special Note: damage done with silver weapons heals at the 
normal healing rate of the being and is the only form of damage 
that can leave scarring. 
Immullities (while changed): 
Normal weapons do no damage, blessed and + 1/+2 magical 
weapons half, +3 and higher as well as silver weapons do full. 
Immune to fear, hold, paralysis, and control. 
Immune to disease 
Special Abilities (while changed): 
Berserking at +50% 
Detect Supernatural at +50% 
Greater Regeneration: ld4 points are healed to all wounded 
areas per 10 seconds. When limbs are fully healed, they are 
fully-grown back. Loss of vitals still causes death. 
Special Note: damage done with silver weapons heals at the 
normal healing rate of the being and is the only form of damage 
that can leave scarring. 
Half-Animal Form 
The Lycanthropy type will be of an animal. For the powers and 
abilities in this state, treat the being as if he were fully evoked 
(per the skill Evoke). Determine the evoke powers for that type 
of animal and apply all of them to this being while in half-ani-
mal form. Use the level or Class Title of the being for power of 
the abilities. This creature will appear as halfway between the 
being's humanoid form and the animal's. Personal attributes are 
halved while in half-animal form even if control is maintained. 
Animal Form 
The being will appear to be the largest possible form of the cur-
rent animal. Treat as if the being has used the skill the skill 
Animal Shape with +50% to the Endurance of the animal. Has 
the physical, personal and mystical attributes of the animal. 
Curing/Suppressing Lycanthropy 
When the victim damages another being with natural weapons 
(claws, beak, bite, etc.) for more than 10 points of flesh dam-
age, and that wound is not healed completely by the next night-
fall, a Disease Resistance is required to avoid lycanthropy of the 
same type as the victim. It takes exactly one month for the 
lycanthropy to be considered active in the victim. During this 
month the disease can be cured with holy water, see curing 
lycanthropy. 
Cure Disease: The victim can be cured by the skill Cure 
Disease at half chance but only for the first few days. The 
number of days the being is eligible to be cured in this manner 
is one day per Vitality point of the victim. 
Holy Water: The victim can cured by holy water by taking one 
dose per day for a month. At the end of the month the chance 
of curing the Lycanthropy is 100% -5% per daily dose missed. 
If a daily dose is taken then the diseases is completely sup-
pressed that day. However on days of a full moon a Will Force 
save is required for the victim to force himself to take the dose. 
Holy Ground: The victim will never make the change while on 
the holy ground of a deity they recognize or worship. Holy 
ground is defined as a place of worship sanctified (blessed) or 
where Blessed Ground has been invoked. Sacred Groves also 
count as holy ground. Conversely, unholy grounds are consid-
ered very stressful and require one check per hour for change, 
including the moment of first arrival. 
Prison of Silver: If the victim is trapped within some sort of 
confinement made or plated with silver, then the change will be 
suppressed. Even a collar of silver will suppress the change. 
Walls/Spheres of Protection: If the being passes through the 
invocation form of Wall or Sphere of Protection then the being 
will revert to true form. If the being is completely surrounded 
by Walls or Spheres of Protection then the disease will be sup-
pressed, whether the victim has passed through them or not.

Lifespan: A character can expect to live 1120th of her potential lifes-

growth.

Enum.onmental Conb,nons 
Depending on the campaign style and flavor, players may ven-
ture into unfamiliar environmental conditions. The rules and 
guidelines herein attempt to cover the gambit of the more fre-
quent environments players may adventure through. As a base-
line, Earth-like variables are referenced when presenting infor-
mation. 
These environmental conditions are not frequently visited due 
to the harsh nature they inflict on inhabitants. For extended 
durations within these conditions, it is advisable that mechanical 
devices or magical effects are utilized to offset or negate the 
effects of pressure (an environmental suit or the spell 
Invulnerability) and provide a breathable environment (an iron 
lung or the spell Breathless). 
Water Environment 
Pressure 
As depth increases in water, so does pressure. Using the gas 
mixture pressure conditions found on Earth as the baseline 
(roughly 80% nitrogen, 20% oxygen), the pressure on the body 
is increased by one atmosphere every 33 feet in salt water. So, 
at 0 ft. sea level, one atmosphere of pressure is applied to the 
body. At 33 ft. below sea level, two atmospheres worth of pres-
sure is applied to the body. For the astute, the pressure differ-
ence between salt water and fresh water is negligible at low 
depths, so differentiation is not made here. 
So, how does this translate into game mechanics for Swimming 
and Diving? The Diving social skill is a condensed representa-
tion of bow long a swimmer can hold his breath underwater at 
varying depths before asphyxiation occurs. For every increas-
ing atmosphere change, a diver needs to make a roll versus his 
Diving skill at cumulative -5%. (Conversely, when ascending 
through atmospheric changes the cumulative Diving penalties 
reduced by 5%.) A normal failure indicates the diver was not 
able to accommodate the pressure changes and will begin to 
asphyxiate 30 seconds sooner than normal. When ascending to 
the surface, note must be taken of any critically failed Diving 
rolls. If any occur, the diver has lost consciousness for Id4 
minutes due to oxygen starvation and sudden pressure changes. 
Vision 
When in contact with water, a human-like eye fails to transmit 
close to 90% of the details to the brain. This blurriness occurs 
due to the loss of focus of refracted lightwaves on the retina 
(the part that transmits the lightwaves as images to the brain). 
Needless to say, it's difficult to see underwater.

Luminance is also another factor to consider in an underwater 
environment. Assuming some mechanism allows for the opera-
tion underwater, mundane light sources are roughly 20% as 
effective as normal. The effects of magical luminance unde,wa-
ter remain the same. Infravision remains as effective underwa-
ter as it is above water. Night Vision and U1travision is useful 
to a depth of 200 feet during daylight hours - any depth or time 
after that requires a supplemental light source. 
With a diving mask, poor underwater vision can be corrected to 
a degree, but other factors come into focus. The field of view 
through a flat viewport is reduced from 180 to roughly 90 
degrees. Unless expertly accounted for in the manufacture, 
objects viewed through masks or viewports seem closer (25%) 
and bigger (33%) than they actually are due to refraction. 
Assuming enough light exists to see, the vision ranges are dou-
bled when using a mechanical device or magical effect to cor-
rect underwater vision. 
In circumstances where vision is not corrected, a penalty of -
50% is applied to the Lip Reading skill when used underwater. 
Hearing 
Sound travels roughly five times faster in water than in the air. 
However, when sound travels from one medium (water) to air 
(the ear), some amount of the soundwave reflects off the air sur-
face. Therefore a -25% to the Listen skill is applied while 
underwater. (However, for each atmosphere, add +5% to the 
Listen skill due to the compression of the sound wave.) 
Additionally, a being must make a Knowledge save to correctly 
interpret what was said. The more the save was failed by, the 
more garbled the message translated by the being. For the same 
reason, but at a greater degree of separation, conversations 
above water cannot be understood below water (and vice versa). 
For each syllable spoken aloud underwater, the being will 
reduce their time to asphyxiation by 15 seconds. 
Movement and Fatigue 
Each 10 minutes of swimming activity requires a -5% cumula-
tive Swimming skill roll. For each Swimming skill roll failed, 
one level of fatigue is assessed to the swimmer.

===== PAGE 121 =====
Combat 
For beings not adapted to an underwater environment, the 
defensive adjustment is negated and the following modifiers are 
applied: -4 to hit, +4 initiative and -20% to combat skills. 
Unless a combatant has corrected underwater vision, an addi-
tional -2 to hit is applied. Thrusting, piercing, crushing and 
constricting are the only effective attack types (cutting or 
smashing with a melee weapon is not possible). Ranges of mis-
sile weapons are reduced by 75%. Every time a being is hit 
with a weapon while holding his breath underwater, a success-
ful Diving skill roll must be made. If the skill roll fails, then 
the being is 30 seconds closer to asphyxiating. 
High Altitude Environment 
Pressure 
As altitude increases, atmospheric pressure decreases. Not tak-
ing into account that the atmosphere is thicker at the equator 
than at the poles, the atmospheric pressure of the Earth is 
halved around 18,000 ft. In terms of game mechanics, the neg-
ative effects of high altitudes (lower pressure) on a being are 
best represented through fatigue (often referred to as altitude 
sickness). 
Vision 
No modifiers. 
Hearing 
Listen skill rolls are -5% per 5,000 ft. above sea level, due to 
the declining atmospheric pressure. 
Movement and Fatigue 
Take the altitude (in ft.), divide by 1,000 ft. and then subtract 
the being's Vitality rating from that number. A negative or zero 
number indicates the altitude does not have an effect on the 
being. A positive number indicates the constant fatigue level 
the being will be at when fully rested. For example, a moun-
taineer with a 14 Vitality is climbing a mountain and her current 
altitude is 16,000 ft. (16,000 ft./ 1,000 ft.) - 14 = 2. Even with 
complete rest, she would always be fatigued two levels. 
An iron lung (a device containing a limited supply of com-
pressed but breathable air) or the spell Breathless will negate 
the effects of high-altitude induced fatigue for the duration they 
are in use. 
Combat 
No modifiers. 
High Temperature Environment 
Pressure 
No modifiers. 
Vision 
Barren outdoor environments exposed to the sun can have air 
temperatures regularly exceed JOO degrees Fahrenheit, while 
ground temperatures can be upwards of 200 degrees Fahrenheit. 
Under these conditions, the ground releases stored heat into the 
atmosphere, since the air is cooler than the ground. When this 
occurs, distortion of images close the horizon occurs. This 
shimmering effect can make mountains look only a few hun-
dred yards away when they are in fact IO miles away. Coupled 
with the long-term exposure to the heat and sun without ade-
quate water, this environmental effect is often the explanation 
given for delusional mirage sightings. 
In terms of game mechanics, when the ambient temperature of 
an area is more than 100 degree Fahrenheit, apply the follow-
ing: 
Far Sight: Negated; treated as Normal Sight 
Exceptional Sight: Negated; treated as Normal Sight 
Infravision: Negated. 
Night Vision: No changes. 
Ultravision: No changes. 
Hearing 
No modifiers. 
Movement and Fatigue 
Stored heat within the ground is released into the atmosphere, 
creating lifting thermals. Avians or animals that fly over areas 
with thermals can travel twice as long before requiring rest. 
Unless adapted to the environment, each being has one constant 
fatigue level when fully rested for every 5 degrees over IOOF. 
Combat 
See Movement and Fatigue. 
Vacuum (Void) Environment 
Pressure 
By definition a vacuum (such as outer space) is devoid of any 
atmosphere. A mechanical device or magical effect is required 
to survive for more than 30 seconds at a time. 
(Hyperventilating before entering a vacuum will provide 
enough oxygen for survival during this brief time period.) 
Vision 
No modifiers. 
Hearing 
Sound is a pressure wave and does not travel in a vacuum. 
Therefore, it is not possible to talk or attempt a Listen roll in a 
vacuum as there is no method for the sound to travel. 
Movement and Fatigue 
Requires assisted movement (gravity, magnetism, tow-line or 
propulsion) to travel in a given direction. 
Combat 
No modifiers.

Mounteb Combat 
A mounted combatant is a dangerous foe, moving effortlessly 
through lines of opponents and unleashing devastating attacks 
to those on the ground below. Presented here are a number of 
modifiers and rules to handle common situations involving 
mounted combat. 
Type of Mount 
The most common type of mount in a medieval setting is the 
horse. In a fantasy setting, though, many type of magical crea-
tures can be ridden into battle. The skill Horsemanship can 
apply as a general skill to any animal which the GM allows the 
character to ride. The rule for Horsemanship is that the charac-
ter must spend one week and make a successful Horsemanship 
roll to be able to use his skill on a particular mount. Failure 
means another week must be spent and another roll made. 
Some mounts will have a bonus and some may have a penalty 
to the roll. Flying mounts decrease the chance by 20%; aerial 
combat is dealt with on the next page. 
Attacking and Defending 
While on a steed, an attacker is considered to be attacking from 
above, allowing +2 to hit and +2 to damage. Those that attack 
a mounted opponent are considered attacking from below and 
are -2 to hit and -2 to damage. 
Missile Fire 
For each full 10 feet per second the steed is travelling, a -2 
penalty to hit is applied. Each 25% chance in Horsemanship 
reduces this penalty by 1. In addition, people firing at mounted 
opponents are -2 to hit for each full 10 feet per second the steed 
is travelling, unless the opponent is riding directly at or away 
from the attacker. 
Move Through 
Mounted opponents moving 10 feet per second or more must 
choose either the move by or the move into maneuver. The 
character gets all charging bonuses. Weight damage is not 
added for the move by. In the move into, the rider can attack 
followed by the steed striking the opponent and doing ldlO 
damage per 50 lb. of difference in weight. A contest of the 
steed's Strength vs. opponent's Agility determines if the oppo-
nent is struck (-5% to the lighter opponent per 50 pounds of dif-
ference). If the mount loses the contest, the rider can make a 
Horsemanship roll to avoid the mount making the standard 
Agility save to keep balance. The body area that is struck is 
often the upper torso but it can be any random area that aligns 
with the forequarters of the steed. If the move into is success-
ful, the damage may exceed 50 points and thus the knock down 
rules apply; the opponent must make an Agility save at -1 % per 
point of damage over 50 or fall down. If this happens, the steed 
may be allowed to Trample. 
Trampling: Hoofed animals are squeamish about stepping on 
soft, squishy beings and will attempt to avoid doing so if they 
can. Thus normally a steed will make an Agility save to avoid 
trampling anything. The save is at -20% for each individual 
moved over in succession. However, if the steed is a trained 
mount (trained with the Animal Training skill) such as a 
warhorse, or a Horsemanship roll is made, the steed will tram-
ple instead. The attack is successful if the steed rolls a IO or 
better (modified) on a d20. The appropriate trample damage for 
the steed is then applied. Weight and Strength damage modi-
fiers are applied to the attack as welJ. The damage already 
takes into account a prone opponent, so it is not doubled. 
Thrusting Charge 
A thrusting charge is one where the rider takes any weapon with 
a thrusting attack and sets it in one second. Polearms and 
lances almost all have penalties to hit when thrusting, but when 
used in a thrusting charge these penalties can be removed with a 
successful Horsemanship roll (no bonuses, just penalties 
removed). A thrusting charge attack is very difficult to stop; 
instead of making a Weapon Parry roll to stop the attack, the 
defender must win a contest of his Weapon Parry vs. the attack-
er's Weapon Knowledge. Shield Parry is treated as normal. 
Bracing in the Saddle 
The weight damage of a mount is not normally added into the 
attack of the rider. However, lf a rider is braced in a saddle, 
then the the weight damage of the steed is added to the attack. 
This takes 2 seconds and is done by making both a successful 
Brace skill roll and a Horsemanship roll (bonuses for Brace are 
also allowed). In a move into, however, there is then a required 
Strength save to retain the weapon if it strikes the opponent. 
Failure indicates loss of the weapon and only 1/2 damage is 
done. 
Fixed Point Saddle 
A fixed-point saddle allows polearms and lances to be snapped 
in to the saddle. This gives them -2 to hit, and the character 
also cannot remove the thrusting penalty for the weapon, but all 
thrusting charges count as being braced in the saddle with no 
rolls required. This is generally only used by characters who 
are not adept at Horsemanship. 
Steed Attacks 
If a steed is trained (or inclined to do so) it may attack oppo-
nents. This should not be allowed if the rider's steed is moving 
faster than 1 O feet per second, except for trampling and move 
into damage. A Horsemanship skill roll is usually required for 
the steed to attack. 
Unseating the Rider 
Knock down damage (50 points or more in one blow) can 
unseat the rider. An Agility save at -1 % per point done over 50 
is required to avoid being unhorsed. A Horsemanship roll with 
the same penalty can be rolled instead. Buckled saddles add 
+20% to the save and harness saddles add +40%. 
Falling from a Steed 
When a rider falls from a steed he must make an Agility save to 
land safely. Failure indicates ld6 damage done +ldlO damage 
per 50 lb. over 200 (6dl0 max) to ld4 random areas. Apply 
double damage if the steed was charging when the rider was 
thrown.

===== PAGE 123 =====
FL y,nr; Combat 
Flying combat is a dangerous ballet of death, with opponents 
circling and diving towards one another. Strikes often result in 
immediate death, sometimes for both the attacker and the oppo-
nent. Even strikes that do not kill often cause a combatant to 
fall to his death. 
Flying Mounted Combat 
All the rules for mounted combat apply to those who are riding 
flying mounts. 
Attacking and Defending 
When flying, anyone attacking from above gets +2 to hit and +2 
to damage, and those that are attacking from below and are -2 
to hit and -2 to damage. 
Missile Fire 
For each full 10 feet per second a flyer is travelling, a -2 penal-
ty to hit is applied when firing a missile weapon. In addition, 
people firing at flyers are -2 to hit for each full 10 feet per sec-
ond the steed is travelling, unless the opponent is riding directly 
at or away from the attacker. 
Flying Move Through 
Flyers moving 30 feet per second or more must choose either 
the flying move by or the flying move into maneuver. The flyer 
gets all diving bonuses: +3 to hit, x3 damage and +3 to be hit. 
All normal move through rules apply. In addition, if the flyer is 
diving on an opponent who is on the ground or other fixed sur-
face, the diver must make an Agility save at -30% to avoid 
crashing and receiving the falling damage from 60 feet. When 
moving less than 30 feet per second, this damage is normal, but 
is doubled when moving at diving speed. 
A Flying move into is a very dangerous type of engagement that 
has the flyer moving into opponent. In this maneuver the flier 
strikes the opponent and does ldl0 per 50 lb. difference in 
weight. A contest of flier's Strength vs. opponent's Agility 
determines if the opponent is struck. The body area that is 
struck is often the upper torso but it can be any random area 
that aligns with the strike point of the flyer. If he hits, the flyer 
automatically takes falling damage as above. Against most 
opponents the surface is treated as soft earth. If the flyer misses 
he still must make an Agility save at -30% to avoid crashing (if 
the being is on a solid surface) and taking falling damage as 
above. 
Thmsting Dive 
If a rider is mounted on a flying steed and is braced in the sad-
dle (see Mounted Combat) with a thrusting weapon then the 
weight damage of the steed is added to the attack. However, 
there is then a required Strength save at -30% to retain the 
weapon if it strikes the opponent. Failure indicates loss of 
weapon and only l/2 damage done. The usual +3 to hit, x3 
damage and +3 to be hit applies. A fixed-point saddle allows 
polearms and lances to be snapped in to the saddle (see mount-
ed combat). 
Inte"upting Flight 
Knock down damage (50 points of damage in one attack) can 
interrupt a flight. An Agility save at -1 per damage point over 
50 is required to avoid loss of flight. With a flying steed, a 
Horsemanship roll with the same penalty can be made instead. 
If the roll is failed the flyer will be out of control for I d4+ I sec-
onds, and can then make an Agility save as above to regain 
flight. If failed the flyer must wait another ld4+ l seconds. 
See stalls and falls for falling speeds, and see falling damage for 
damage. 
Maneuvering 
It is recommended that a hex map be used to show the move-
ment of fliers, and that a 20-sided dice (next to the flier) be 
used to show relative altitudes. Each hex equalling 5' is a good 
standard. 
Level Flight: This is the set speed of the flier and is used for 
most all other calculations. Level flight is x4 walking speed or 
whatever is specified by the spell or effect. 
Shallow Dive: The flier loses I foot of altitude for every 5 trav-
elled and is 50% faster. 
Dive: The flier loses l foot of altitude for every foot travelled. 
Speed is I 00%. An Agility save and 5 seconds is required to 
tum a dive into a shallow dive. Failure indicates the dive has 
become a steep dive. 
Steep Dive: The flier loses 5 feet for every l travelled. Speed 
is 200%. An Agility save at -20% and 10 seconds is required to 
tum a steep dive into a dive. Failure indicates the steep dive 
has become a fall. 
Slow Climb: The flier gains l foot of altitude for every 10 
moved forward. Speed slows to 75%. 
Climb: The flier gains I of foot altitude for every 5 moved for-
ward. Speed slows to 50%. This is considered strenuous and 
requires a Strength save every minute or a stall results. 
Steep Climb: The flier gains I of foot altitude for every 2 
moved forward. Speed slows to 25%. Considered very strenu-
ous and requires a Strength save every 30 seconds or a stall 
results. 
Stalls and Falls: When the air moving below the wing of the 
flier is slow enough to produce less lift than required to hold the 
flier's weight then a stall occurs. This results in loss of flight, 
or falling. An Agility save can tum the fall into a steep dive 
(I 0-30 seconds) and the successive saves can transform it into 
level flight (see steep dive and dive). Stall conditions vary; still 
air, tail winds and speed all are factors. A good rule is anytime 
the flier is travelling less than half the speed of normal level 
flight a stall is a likely result. During the stall (and the recov-
ery) the flier is considered to be falling and will fall at a rate of 
32 feet per second, increasing by 32 feet every second until 
reaching terminal velocity (see below). 
Terminal Velocity: Maximum falling speed. This varies by the 
113 

===== PAGE 124 =====
shape (wind resistance) of the object/being, but a good average 
is 225 miles per hour or 330 feet per second. Needless to say 
death is the very likely result of striking anything at that speed. 
Turning in the Air 
Turning is based on the size of the flyer. 
Small Fliers: Less than IO' long or under 20' in wingspan. 
Slow Turn: This is a turn of 30 degrees for every 30 feet trav-
elled, or 1 foot per degree. It results in no loss of altitude but 
slows movement by 15%. This turn would be shown by a six 
hex movement with a one hex facing turn when going between 
the 3rd and 4th hexes. 
Banking Tum: This is a turn of 30 degrees for 15 feet travelled 
or 2 feet per degree. It results in a loss of altitude of 5 feet per 
5 feet travelled. Movement is slowed by 25%. Requires an 
Agility save to avoid stall. It is accomplished by moving three 
hexes with a one hex turn between hexes 2 and 3. 
Sliding Turn: This is a tum of 30 degrees in 5 feet. Requires a 
Strength save and Agility save -20% to avoid stalling. 
Movement is slowed by 50%. IO feet is lost for every 5 feet of 
turn. It allows a single hex face turn within one hex. 
Medium Fliers. (between than 11' and 20' long or between 21 
to 36' in wingspan) 
Medium Fliers: Between 11 ' and 20' long or between 21' and 
36' in wingspan. 
Slow Tum: This is a turn of 30 degrees for every 60 feet trav-
elled. It results in no loss of altitude but slows movement by 
15%. This turn would be shown by a twelve hex movement 
with a one hex facing turn when going between the 6th and 7th 
hexes. 
Banking Turn: This is a turn of 30 degrees for 30 feet travelled. 
It results in a loss of altitude of 5 feet per 5 feet travelled. 
Move-ment is slowed by 25%. Requires an Agility save to 
avoid stall. It is accomplished by moving six hexes with a one 
hex face turn between hexes 3 and 4. 
Sliding Turn: This is a turn of 30 degrees in 15 feet. Requires 
a Strength save and Agility save -20% to avoid stalling. 
Movement is slowed by 50%. IO feet is lost for every 5 feet of 
turn. It is accomplished by moving three hexes with a one hex 
face turn between hexes 2 and 3. 
lArge Fliers: Longer than 20 feet or greater than 36' in 
wingspan. 
Slow Turn: This is a turn of 30 degrees for every 120 feet trav-
elled. It results in no loss of altitude but slows movement by 
I 0%. This turn would be shown by a twenty-four hex move-
ment with a one hex facing turn when going between the 12th 
and 13th hexes. 
Banking Turn: This is a tum of 30 degrees for 60 feet travelled. 
It results in a loss of altitude of 5 feet per 5 feet travelled. 
Movement is slowed by 25%. Requires an Agility save to avoid 
stall. It is accomplished by moving twelve hexes with a one 
hex face turn between hexes 6 and 7. 
Sliding Tum: This is a turn of 30 degrees in 30 feet. Requires 
a Strength save and Agility save at -20% to avoid stalling. 
Movement is slowed by 50%, and l 0 feet is lost for every 5 feet 
of turn. It is accomplished by moving three hexes with a one 
hex face turn between hexes 3 and 4. 
Air Current Phenomena 
The GM can choose to introduce these phenomena into aerial 
combat as he sees fit. 
Ridge lift: When wind blows against hills or mountains it cre-
ates an updraft along the face of the hill or mountain. This cre-
ates lift equal to and average of 1/4 of the strength of the wind 
as upward lift. A 40 mile an hour wind hitting a hill face pro-
duces a IO-mile an hour updraft. 
Thermal Updrafts: In the hottest parts of the day, updrafts can 
occur providing lift of anywhere from ld6 feet per second to l 0 
to 60 feet per second depending on the strength of the thermal. 
Downdrafts: Pockets of cold air can result in sudden down 
drafts. They vary in strength but can cause loss of ld4 feet in 
per seconds to as much as l 0 to 40 feet per second. 
Wind Sheers(Turbulence): The most deadly anomaly for the 
flier. This is the edge of an updraft and a downdraft and causes 
unstable air. Agility saves are required for the flier when 
encountering this phenomenon. The penalty to the save should 
equal the strength of the turbulence or from 0% to -50% save. 
Failure of an Agility save results in immediate fall. 
Ground Effect: Near the ground (l-12 feet) air resistance 
changes and flight has more lift. This tends to increase the 
speed of the flier by 25%. It is why Agility saves are required 
to land. 
Flare: A flier can attempt to purposefully stall on landing and 
alight in an exact spot. It requires an Agility and a Strength 
save and requires the flier to be moving at 1/2 level flight 
speed.

The Duel 
These expanded rules are designed to extend the two-person 
combat into a full duel. They are most useful when applied in 
one on one combat situations, but feel free to integrate them 
into normal combat as well. 
Keeping at Bay 
When using any thrusting weapon, it is possible to menace an 
opponent so effectively as to keep that opponent at bay. This 
forces a situation that requires the opponent to deal with the 
weapon before counter-attacking. An opponent's failure to deal 
with the weapon offers a free opportunity to attack at the 
moment the opponent attacks or attempts to close. The 
mechanics of this maneuver are listed below. Henceforth the 
combatant keeping an opponent at bay is referred to as the men-
acer. 
Me11acing weapon 
The menacing weapon is required to be at least 18" long and 
must be a thrusting or piercing weapon. 
Reach Advantage 
Differences in reach ( I/3rd being's height+ weapon length) 
larger than a foot are obvious to both opponents while either is 
attempting to keep the other at bay. This means that a combat-
ant cannot keep an opponent at bay if that opponent has more 
than one foot of reach advantage. It also means that if a com-
batant has over one foot of reach advantage, he cannot be kept 
at bay by his opponent. 
Me11acing 
When one opponent engages another who is wielding a legal 
menacing weapon, the menacer can declare that he is attempting 
to keep the opponent at bay. First, the menacer must have "set" 
the weapon before engagement. Then the menacer declares a 
target (body region) on the opponent at whom he is pointing the 
weapon and must make a successful Weapon Knowledge roll. 
The opponent is now considered to be menaced. Common 
sense should be used; menacing someone's foot might be possi-
ble in some bizarre postures but ordinarily should not be 
allowed. No other actions (other than those listed below) may 
be taken with the weapon being used to menace. 
Keeping the menaced opponent at bay 
Each time the opponent makes an attack, the menacer is 
allowed to make a Weapon Knowledge roll. If the menacer is 
successful, he immediately rolls to hit against the area of the 
opponent's body being menaced. No penalties for body size or 
defensive adjustment are applied, as the menacer already has 
the weapon trained on the body area. Note that the menacer 
does not use the attack speed of the weapon to determine how 
long it takes to perform the attack (all menacing attacks take 
one second). If the menacer hits, the opponent's attack auto-
matically misses. The menacer can then make another Weapon 
Knowledge roll and the opponent is considered kept at bay, and 
if he tries to attack again, then the same steps are repeated. If 
the menacer misses, the opponent can then roll to hit as normal. 
In addition to this, he is considered to have closed with the 
menacer and is no longer being kept at bay. 
Pressing 
Once an opponent has closed he can declare that he is pressing 
his opponent. This means that the opponent is attempting to 
keep from being menaced again by staying close to the oppo-
nent. If the menacer desires to separate from a presser for pur-
poses of gaining distance to menace again, a contest of Agility 
occurs between the two opponents. If the presser wins, there is 
no separation. If the menacer wins, he manages to back up 
quickly enough to once again menace his opponent by making a 
successful Weapon Knowledge roll. In order to do so, the men-
acer must have room to back up. If the opponent does not press 
the attack, the menacer can make a new Weapon Knowledge 
roll to once again menace his opponent. An attacker cannot 
press an opponent if he is slower than half the opponent's 
speed. This means that if the menacer is twice as fast as the 
attacker, he can move faster backwards than the presser can 
forward. 
If two menacers are keeping each other at bay and either closes, 
then both get the menacing attack. The attacks are considered 
simultaneous regardless of slight differences in reach (a foot or 
less). 
Removing the menacing weapon 
A menacing weapon can be remove so that the opponent is no 
longer considered kept at bay and may close with the menacer. 
The menacing weapon can be removed in the following ways: 
1) Beat the Weapon: The opponent can beat the menacing 
weapon aside if he wins a contest of his Weapon Parry skill ver-
sus the menacer's Weapon Knowledge skill. [f the attacker 
wins, the opponent is no longer considered menaced and may 
close on his opponent. If the menacer wins, he keeps the oppo-
nent at bay. 
2) Lunge: If an opponent is being kept at bay by a menacer 
who does not have more than one foot of reach advantage, he 
can attempt a Junge. Lunging is used often used when two peo-
ple are menacing each other. In a lunge, the opponent is not 
trying to close on the menacer, but simply get in a free attack. 
When the opponent lunges, the menacer must make a successful 
win a successful contest of his Weapon Knowledge versus his 
opponents Weapon Knowledge to keep the menacing weapon 
trained on the lunging opponent. lf the menacer wins, the 
attack misses automatically. If the attacker wins, he gets a free 
I second quick attack (a lunge can only be performed by a 
weapon which can make a I second quick). As the attacker is 
not trying to close, the lunge attack negates the menacing attack 
which would normally be allowed. However, the menacer auto-
115 

===== PAGE 126 =====
matically continues keeping the opponent at bay after the lunge 
attack is complete, regardless of the result. Whenever an oppo-
nent lunges, the menacer can choose to counter attack. If he 
does so, he cannot return to keeping his opponent at bay after 
the lunge is complete, and the attacker is now allowed to press 
the attack. Whenever an attacker is lunging, all of his Agility 
saves are halved and he is allowed no defensive adjustment. 
Me11acing opponents with shields 
Keeping an opponent at bay who has a shield is very difficult. 
An attacker cannot be menaced if he has a shield larger than a 
buckler, and the standard combat rules apply. 
Menacing charging opponents 
Charging opponents are moving too fast to stop, and thus can-
not technically be kept at bay. In this case, there are but a few 
options: 
1) The attacker can abort his attack and attempt a Feint if he has 
enough time. In this case he of course gets no attack but will 
not be hit if the Feint roll is successful. 
2) He can attempt to beat the menacing weapon as described 
above. If he loses the contest, the menacer gets the free attack 
without penalties from body size or defensive adjustment. He 
also gets the +2 to hit allowed against charging opponents, and 
if the opponent is has used Brace, he has another +2 to hit and 
+2 damage, and the total damage is doubled. 
Cloak and Net Fighting 
"Never have I seen two more matched swordsman, in height, 
grace or speed. We watched them duel until both were lathered 
in a sheen of sweet and their shirts pinked with their own blood. 
In the end it was the sweep of a cloak that hid the winners fatal 
blow." 
One well-practiced style of fighting uses a cloak to obscure 
attacks and turn aside an opponent's blows, or even trip up the 
opponent. The word cloak is used, but a cape, jacket, blanket or 
the like are equally effective. In some cases a net may be used. 
The word "cloak" in parenthesis denotes those moves which 
may only be attempted with a cloak, while (cloak or net) indi-
cates that either may be utilized. A cloak is generally used in 
one hand while a weapon is carried in the second, hence the 
term "cloak and dagger·•. 
Cloak as a weapo11 
The cloak fighter must take cloak (or net) as one of his weapon 
proficiency slots or else he will suffer the non-proficiency 
penalty for the either of those. Using moves with both requires 
that both proficiencies be taken. All standard rules for Weapon 
Knowledge apply (see the skill Weapon Knowledge). 
Cloak parry (cloak or net) 
The cloak is used to parry with by turning a thrusting/piercing 
weapon aside, while sweeping the cloak away from the body. 
This requires a successful Weapon Parry roll; it is completely 
ineffective against any other form of attack besides 
thrusting/piercing. The cloak will take little damage from such 
attacks and at most the weapon will leave a hole or smaJI tear. 
This maneuver takes I second. 
Trap weapon (cloak or net) 
Trap Weapon may be used with a cloak or net at +30% to the 
Trap Weapon Skill roll. This takes 3 seconds. 
Obscure attack (cloak 011ly) 
The cloak can be used to hide a thrusting/piercing attack. The 
attacker must win a contest of Weapon Knowledge verus his 
opponents Agility. If he wins the contest, the opponent cannot 
Weapon Parry the attack, and the opponent's normal defensive 
adjustment is removed. The opponent may still Shield Parry or 
Body Parry the attack. This takes as long as the attack speed of 
the attacking weapon and one additional second for recovery. 
Obscure form (cloak only) 
The cloak can be used to hide the true location of a body region 
(head and neck may not be obscured). If a successful Weapon 
Knowledge is rolled then the area is obscured. Obscured 
regions are -4 to be hit. This maneuver takes 2 seconds. 
Cloak entangle (cloak or 11et) 
The cloak can be used to trip an opponent (per the Trip skilJ) at 
+ I 0%. This usage requires a releasing of the cloak so that no 
further actions may be taken with the weapon until it is recov-
ered. This takes 3 seconds. 
Other Dueling Moves 
Riposte: By using a Quick Parry followed by a Quick Attack a 
weapon may be knocked aside during an opponent's attack, fol-
lowed by a quick attack at 1/2 damage. The total time for this 
move cannot exceed 2 seconds, and only weapons with a modi-
fied speed of 3 seconds can perform this move. A contest of the 
attacker's Weapon Knowledge vs. the opponent's Weapon Parry 
determines if the riposte is successful (still need s roll to hit). 
Quick Draw Attack: Used in some Asian duels, this move can 
be can be performed with a successful Weapon Knowledge roll. 
The quick draw attack allows a weapon to be drawn from its 
scabbard and attacked with all in the normal weapon speed, but 
does only 1/2 damage.

All Thrnr;s B~ an b Small 
Expanded rules for non-standard sized beings 
Imagine combat rules were designed primarily with humanoids 
between three and nine feet tall in mind. Standard equipment 
fits best with the model of the moderately sized humanoid. 
These are the rules are for handling beings and creatures small-
er or larger than this ideal. 
Size Classification 
Tiny: Any being or creature under I foot in height or average 
width. 
•Weight and Strength damage penalties are not a factor 
when using weapons specially designed for tiny-sized 
beings. These penalties are only applied if a normal 
sized weapon or larger is somehow used. 
•No sub body areas are used for calculating (finger, toe, 
brain, etc.) because they represent too smaJJ a target 
and cannot be struck except by destroying the body 
area containing them. 
Small: Any being or creature over a 1 foot but Less than 3 feet 
in height or average width. 
•Weight and Strength damage penalties are not a factor 
when using weapons specially designed for small-sized 
beings. These penalties are only applied if a normal 
sized weapon or larger is somehow used. 
•No sub body areas are used for calculating (finger, toe, 
brain, etc.) because they represent too small a target 
and cannot be struck except by destroying the body 
area containing them. 
Medium: Any being or creature between 3 feet and 9 feet. 
•Use standard rules, except that weight and Strength 
damage bonuses do not apply to giant sized weapons, 
and penalties do not apply to undersized weapons. 
Huge: Anything over 9 feet but Less than 12 feet in height or 
average width. 
•The being has a Bear Hug grappling move, which works 
like the Martial Knowledge move Torso Hold (p. 96 of 
the Player's Guide) but does 3d6 (+Strength and 
weight) constriction damage per 5 seconds. 
Gia11t: Anything over 12 feet but less than 18 feet in height or 
average width. 
•Gains Bear Hug (as above) and Smash grappling moves. 
Smash is as Punch but does 3d6 smashing damage. 
Mammoth: Anything over 18 feet but Less than 25 feet in height 
or average width. 
•Gains Bear Hug, as above, except that damage is 6d6. 
Gains Smash, as above, except that damage is 6d6. 
Gains the Squish grappling move: Squish is as Kick 
but does 7d6 crushing damage. 
Titanic: Anything over 25 feet in height or average width. 
•Gains Bear Hug, as above, except that damage is 8d6. 
Gains Smash, as above, except that damage is 8d6. 
Gains the Squish grappling move: Squish is as Kick 
but does 9d6 crushing damage. 
Modifying the use of the Attack Bullseye 
The target bullseye functions normally when creatures of the 
same size are attacking one another. When creatures with great 
discrepancies in size fight, the use of the bullseye needs to be 
modified a bit for realism. 
When a creature is attacking another being who is two size cat-
egories or more below him (medium attacking tiny, etc.), use the 
bullseye in this manner: 
•For purposes of targeting only a center hit on the attack 
chart strikes the creature. 
•The hit location is determined randomly after a hit is suc-
cessful as described above. All attacks which are not 
thrusts or piercing attacks will strike not one but I d4 
body areas; these areas must be adjacent to the ran-
domly hit area. 
•If a specific body area is desired to be struck a called shot 
is needed. 
When a creature is attacking another being who is one size cate-
gory below him (medium attacking small, etc.), use the bullseye 
in this manner: 
•Any hit area listed on the attack chart strikes the creature. 
•Hit location is determined randomly after a hit is success-
ful as described above. 
•If a specific body area is desired to be struck a called shot 
is needed. 
When a creature is attacking another being who is one size cate-
gory above him (medium attacking huge, etc.), use the bullseye 
in this manner: 
•Torsos (or trunks) are oversized areas (all hit and gray 
areas on the attack chart strike this body region). 
When a creature is attacking another being who is two size cat-
egories or more above him (medium attacking giant, etc.), use 
the bullseye in this manner: 
•All body areas but hands, feet and neck are oversized 
areas (all hit areas on the attack chart strike this body 
region). 
When a creature is attacking another being who is three size 
categories or more above him (medium attacking mammoth, 
etc.), use the bullseye in this manner: 
•All body areas are oversized areas (all hit areas on the 
attack chart strike this body region). 
•If a missile weapon fired at a body region misses (white 
area) then the rules for accidental fire zones can be 
applied to determine if another body region was hit. 
Note on Weight Damage 
Several effects cause beings to take extra damage based on its 
own weight over 200 lb. This weight damage maximizes at an 
extra 6 dice of damage. Examples are found in the grappling 
Martial Throw, and Falling Damage.

Exotic Weapon Descriptions 
Crossbows: All exotic crossbows jam if a fumble is rolled. These are dangerous weapons that take a sophisticated craftsman to produce. 
Over-under Crossbows: A variant on the crossbow that has a special grip and a second crossbow under the hand as well as over. A pinkie trigger 
sets off the under crossbow. The heavy version is too long to be worn by anyone under 7' tall. 
Double Crossbow: A second quarrel slot and crossbow bar is mounted above the 1st and there is a two-stage trigger allowing both to be fired in the 
same second or fired individually. 
Repeating Crossbow: A crossbow with a cocking mechanism that drops additional bolts into the firing slot as well as resetting the tension on the 
string. Early versions fired 3 bolts before requiring a full reload (3x normal reload for weapon); later versions held 5 and required 5x normal 
reloading time. 
Hom Bow: A special bow made out of horn and extremely flexible; it has the damage of a composite bow but the pull and range of a long bow. 
Welsh Bow: A very thick bow that handles as a strong great bow, requiring a little extra strength but doing slightly better damage.

Damar;mr; Ob,ects anb StRuctuRes 
All items are subject to the object strength and object threshold 
rules. Damage done above the object threshold of an item is 
applied to the object strength of an item, and if the remaining 
damage exceeds the object strength of the item then the item 
breaks. Otherwise it has its object strength lowered by I point. 
The following are object thresholds for materials for average 
sized objects (roughly weapon sized). These numbers can be 
used for most objects which are not part of a large structure.

Very large objects follow basically the same object threshold 
and object strength rules with much higher numbers. Because 
of its mass, it takes much more damage to affect a large object. 
To simulate this, the above object threshold numbers are gener-
ally doubled for large objects of roughly I 0'x IO' in surface 
area and anywhere from I to 5 feet thick. Also, if a single blow 
of a small object such as a weapon exceeds the combined object 
strength and thresholds of a large object such as a door or wall, 
it can be assumed that only a hole was made in the object as 
opposed to the whole thing breaking, as would happen with a 
weapon. In this case, every IO points of damage reduces the 
object strength of the object by I point. When a large object is 
reduced to 1/2 of its object strength, it can be considered to col-
lapse and be in ruin. This often applies in siege warfare when 
assaulting castles.

The following rules can be applied when characters are attempt-
ing to lift heavy objects: 
1) A character can pick up an object that is less than 1/2 his 
load limit without penalty. 
2) A character can pick up an object between 1/2 and full load 
limit, regardless of what he are currently carrying (as long as he 
does not try to move as well) but is considered to be under 
fatigue rules from the moment the object is lifted. Each level of 
fatigue requires a successful Strength save or strain is the result. 
3) A character can pick up an object that is over his load limit 
by attempting a Strength save at -40%, with an additional penal-
ty of -10% per 10 pounds over his load limit. The skill Force 
can be substituted here, without the -40% penalty, but including 
the -10% penalty per 10 pounds over load limit. A failed roll 
requires a normal Strength save to avoid strain. Holding such 
an object causes fatigue at twice the normal rate. Each level of 
fatigue requires a successful Strength save or strain is a result. 
4) A character can lift over his head an object that is less than 
1/4 his load limit without penalty. 
5) A character can lift over his head an object between 1/4 and 
full load limit, regardless of what he is currently carrying (as 
long as he does not try to move as well) but is considered to be 
under fatigue rules from the moment he lifts the object. Each 
level of fatigue requires a successful Strength save or strain is 
the result. Characters can lift over their head an object that is 
over their load limit by attempting a Strength save at -60%, 
with an additional penalty of -10% over the load limit. The 
skill Force can be substituted here with a -20% chance, also 
including the -10% penalty per 10 pounds over load limit. A 
failed roll requires a successful Strength save to avoid strain. 
Holding such an object causes fatigue at twice the normal rate. 
Each level of fatigue requires a successful Strength save or 
strain is a result. 
The following rules are applied to drag or push a heavy object: 
1) A being can drag 2x his load limit and move at 1/2 speed. 
2) A being can drag 4x his load limit and move at 1/4 speed. 
3) A being can push 2x his load limit and move at 1/4 speed. 
4) A being can push 4x his load limit and move at 1/10 speed. 
Strain 
Strain can occur in any circumstance the GM sees fit, such as 
when a Force roll is critically failed. A character that has 
become strained has Strength and Agility temporarily reduced 
by one per incident of straining. Each night while the character 
sleeps, a Strength and Agility save is rolled for temporary attrib-
ute rating loss due to the strain. Only one save is allowed for 
Strength and one for Agility. If the save is made, then one point 
is restored to the attribute for which the save was made. The 
save is -5% per strained point. 
Mental Combat 
Expanded 
Mental combat represents the powerful ability to dominate, 
influence or mentally attack others. Because it can be extreme-
ly dangerous, several checks have been placed on it through 
skills and spells; the spells Mind Set and Mind Change, as well 
as the invocation Fortitude are defenses against any form of 
mental attack or intrusion. In addition, the following rules 
affect the way mental combat plays out. 
Increases and Decreases in Will Force 
Various effects can raise or lower a being's Will Force rating. 
When the Will Force rating is increased or decreased, the new 
rating is used for purposes of mental combat and for determin-
ing any effect based on the Will Force rating (Control 
Resistance, etc.). Since battling in mental combat almost 
always results in the temporary loss of Will Force by those 
involved, even the winner of a mental combat can find himself 
in a very vulnerable position. Lost Will Force returns at a rate 
of one per hour until it returns to the natural rating, and gained 
Will Force is lost at a rate of one per hour until the natural rat-
ing is reached. Mortals can never exceed a 25 Will Force rating 
under any circumstances. Raising the Will Force rating should 
not be confused with increases to the Will Reservoir which 
immortal creatures possess. Any creature who gains Will Force 
to its reservoir does not get to use it for mental combat, as it is 
not an actual rating increase. 
Note on Will Drain: When a mentalist successfully Will Drains 
an opponent, he does not get the Will Force of the being; the 
being's rating simply decreases. 
Optional Mental Combat Rules 
Some Game Masters feel that mental combat is unbalancing, 
while others enjoy making it an integral part of their games. 
Any of the following optional rules can be employed to either 
increase or decrease the role of mental combat in a game world: 
1. A being who has an active method of engaging in mental 
combat (Thought Projection, active Improved Telepathy, etc.) 
can make a Will Force save to break free of mental combat. 
This works even if the being is not the one who initiated the 
combat. A Thought Projection roll can be made instead. 
2. Whenever a being with an active method of engaging in 
mental combat is being mentally "spied" upon (such as Mind 
Dance, etc.) the being can make an Intelligence save to notice 
that another mind is present. 
3. For every full 50% a practitioner has in the skill Thought 
Projection, he gains + l to all mental combat rolls. 
4. Although a being assumes a trance like state when in mental 
combat, he can still walk; however he should make an 
Intelligence save to avoid walking into objects or something 
similar.

M0Rale 
Morale simulates the mood of non-players (GM Characters, personalities and extras) and how they react in combat. Players are 
never required to make these rolls. When the situation turns grim, morale determines whether the loyal fo11owers stay loyal or turn 
tail and run for their lives. Base Morale is set by racial type and is modified by Title or creature level. A leader can add to the 
morale of his followers by having high Appearance, Charm, and Social Class. 
The recognized leader in a group is the only one who may apply modifiers to the group's Morale. There can be only one leader per 
group. Morale checks can be made as for an entire group or rolled individually as the GM sees. This is usually based on the impor-
tance and power level of the combatants who are checking morale, as well as whether or not the group is acting as a group or more 
like individuals. A leader can attempt to rally fleeing followers by showing a banner, symbol of heraldry (flag, shield, etc.), or with 
a loud musical device (horn, drum, trumpet, etc.). Each attempt to rally can only be made once per combat round. If morale is 
rolled for a group it is averaged amongst the members of the group to determine the morale percentage. Creatures and beings with-
out minds are exempt from morale checks. A failed morale check usually requires the GMC, GMP or GME to flee as far from the 
situation as would seem prudent or make him feel safe. Other results depend on the type of morale check.

ConstRucnon Costs 
As a general rule, it will take I month to build a structure per 20,000 
gold spent in its construction. These required laborers are needed: 
I Architect 
I Miner per 500 Gp spent in excavation 
I Stone worker per 5000 spent in construction 
1 Wood worker per 5000 spent in construction 
1 Engineer for structures over I 00,000 gp in construction costs 
1 General laborer for every 2000 spent in construction costs. 
Using half of the required laborers will cause the job to take twice as 
long; using double the required laborers and it will take half as long, 
etc. A builder must have an architect and an engineer, if required or 
the structure will be unsound and may collapse. A builder wilJ not 
benefit from having more than triple the required laborers.

Magical Weapons and Armor 
Blessed weapons 
A non-magical weapon can be made nearly the equivalent of a +I 
weapon with the skill Bless. Some undead and special creatures take 
less damage from blessed weapons than true magical weapons, but oth-
erwise a + 1 magical weapon and a + 1 blessed weapon are identical. 
Silver Weapons 
Silver weapons count as +l for purposes of determining if they can 
affect a creature, unless the creature says that it is not affected by silver 
weapons. They do not get an actual + 1 bonus, however. 
Materials from Produce spells 
The produce spells (wood, metal, clothing, stone) will produce magical 
materials of + I per 5 Aura with a maximum of +6. This equates to a 
30 Aura Produce Metal spell being able to produce a +6 magical 
sword, albeit temporarily. A permanency or Enchantment is required 
to make the material permanent. 
Weapon Enhancing Spell Effects 
The spells (or effects), Sharpness, Disruption, Piercing, Accuracy and 
Seeking also will allow a weapon +l to hit magically, per 5 Aura with 
a cap at +6 or 30 Aura. 
Armor Enhancing Spell/Invocation Effects 
The spell or invocation Protection can add additional magical bonuses 
to armor. 
Combining the above 
All such combined effects are subject to the cumulative effects rule in 
the Player's Guide. 
Quality magical weapons and armor 
It should be noted that quality weapon rules are superseded if the 
weapon is magical. 
Armor and Weapons from magical metals 
Magical materials can be used to create weapons of between + I and +6 
depending on the type of magical material and quality of that type. For 
instance, low grade Mithreel is considered +I while high grade is +2. 
To determine the armor value for armor made from magical metal, first 
add the magical bonus to it from the metal. Then, because magical 
metals have their armor value doubled, the new value is doubled. This 
bonus is only doubled when the value is inherent to the metal, so that 
+2 magical steel still only doubles to 40. 
Example: Chain mail has an armor rating of 15. When made from +2 
Mithreel, this becomes 17, then doubled (for magic) it becomes 34. 
Thus plate mail made from the same material would be (20+2) x 2 = 
44. Armor damage is listed in the form of a ratio. 
Damaging magical weapons or armor 
When magical weapons and armor take damage, there is a chance that 
they can lose their powers. For each point of damage over the object 
threshold (for weapons) and armor value (for armor) that an item takes, 
there is a 1 % chance of the item losing its enchantment, thus all pow-
ers, abilities, etc. Charged items will explode (per the spell Explosion) 
at I Aura point per of charge remaining in the item.

Changing Objects with Wood Lore, Metal Lore, Stone Lore and Bone Lore 
With these skills a player can change the shape and density of a normal object. This changes the properties of the object in question, 
specifically the density and damage threshold (tensile strength). Some objects (especially blades) become stronger but less flexible 
when their density is increased. A blade is meant to be flexible and thus skills are harder with the weapon even though it is stronger. 
Armor is also meant to be flexible and can impair movement if it is made denser by the magical shaping of these skills. Thus both 
armor and weapons are afforded skill modifiers if the density changes. Use the table below when objects are changed as noted.

Examples 
The Axe of the Loresmiths (a Dwarven Axe) 
Dwarven Smiths are not content to merely forging and then 
tempering weapons and wish to create an axe that will that will 
take the punishment of the king's champion. A tempered battle-
axe is 3 and 1/2 feet long, has strength of 60, a damage thresh-
old of 40 and is -10% to use for combat skills. The Dwarven 
loremasters take the battle-axe and use Metal Lore to increase 
the density to the maximum, adding 100%. The axe now has 
the following properties; 
Length: 2.8 feet (3.5 feet x .80%) 
Strength: 120 (60 + 100% or x2) 
Damage Threshold: 60 (40 + 50% xl.S) 
Skills (Combat): -30% (-10% as weapon, -20% for increasing density) 
Heavy Chain Long Shirt of the Loresmiths (Dwarven) 
The Dwarven smiths are equally adept at creating the finest 
armored links. A heavy chain long shirt has the following prop-
erties; 16 armor value and damage thresholds of 1/15, 1/15, 
1/ 15, and 1/20 for cuts, thrusts, smashes and constricting 
respectively and -5% to skills. To achieve even greater results 
the lore masters increased the density of the links two fold 
(x I 00% ). The chain now has the following properties: 
Width and Length: See note 
Amzor Value: 21 (16 + S, chain is semi-flexible) 
Damage Threshold: 1/23, 1/23, 1/23, 1/30 (I/IS, 1/15, 1/15, 1/20 
+SO% or xl.S) 
Skills (Combat+Stea/th Intrusive): -25% (-5% as armor, -20% for 
increasing density) 
Note: The Dwarven smiths needed to make the chain mail 
twice as wide and 120% as long as the dwarf who was to wear 
it because the chainmail was shrunk by increasing its density. 
This means that the chain mail now weighs 160% (xl.6) of the 
normal weight (200% width and 120% length averaged). The 
size is adjusted for the being for whom it is made (dwarven 
sized) before multiplying any additional weight modifier. 
Using armor designed for another being 
1. Height requirements: The armor must have been designed to 
fit a being within +/-6" of the height of the character trying to 
wear it (for flexible and semi-flexible pieces; within +/-3" of 
height for rigid pieces). 
2. Weight requirements: The armor must have been designed to 
fit a being within +/-20% of the weight of the character trying 
to wear it (for flexible and semi-flexible pieces; within +/-10% 
of weight for rigid pieces). 
129 
If the armor has been made to fit a shorter being (within the 
above requirements), then it can only be worn if it was made to 
fit the same frame size or one frame size larger than the charac-
ter trying to wear it. 
If the armor has been made to fit a taller being (within the 
above requirements), then it can only be worn if it was made to 
fit the same frame size or one frame size smaller than the char-
acter trying to wear it.

Aura Rating and the Aura Pool 
Aura has, in addition to its normal rating, an external pool, which-for 
mortals-cannot exceed twice the attribute rating. However, any 
amount which exceeds the rating through skills Like Absorb Aura is 
considered to be in the pool, but does not apply to the attribute rating 
for purposes of determining anything derived from that attribute. Thus 
a Mage with a 20 Aura rating might absorb 40 points of Aura into his 
pool, but the rating itself would not increase. If a being's Aura pool 
ever exceeds twice his Aura rating, then he will burst into flames. 
Aura Control and Aura Pool Maximums 
There are many modifiers in the system that can increase Aura Control. 
The cumulative magical effects rule should apply, but even beyond that 
there are Limits set on Aura Control by Class Title. In addition, the 
number of Aura in some beings Aura Pools is allowed to exceed dou-
ble their Aura rating number. Beings are simply incapable of drawing 
or having more Aura than these limits. (Burning Aura is not Limited by 
these numbers; see Burning Aura in the Player's Guide).
