IntRobucnon to Game MasteRrn~ 
Being a Good Game master is part art and part science. 
The science is in the details, and knowing how to use the 
game mechanics in a hurry and under pressure to resolve 
conflicts. It means having at least a loose understanding 
of subjects like politics, geography, sociology, psycholo-
gy, etc. The art is in weaving the world, the story and the 
player choices into a coherent whole-in making it all 
seamless and as real as possible an experience for the 
players. Suspension of disbelief is a requirement for con-
tinued play. The players have to see in their mind's eye 
what is happening and not be distracted by situations that 
do not make sense or do not seem coherent to the setting. 
Success as a GM is measured by players who come back 
for more. Continued failure at these basics will bring an 
end to the game. The following section is designed to give 
an overview of Game Mastering in the Imagine Role 
Playing System™. 
GM Discretion 
Several times throughout the system the term game 
Master Discretion is mentioned. By this is meant that, in 
the end, a Game Master is in charge of the Game and 
must use his best judgement on how things ought to work 
in his game world. This should not be misinterpreted to 
mean that the Game Master can go making up whatever 
rules he feels like; in fact, doing so will cause the players 
to lose faith in the GM and they will not wish to play in 
his game any longer. You should always remember as the 
GM that your purpose is entertain. The Imagine system is 
not perfect, but it is very well thought and and attempts to 
cover a myriad of situations and allow for vast possibili-
ties. Changing these rules without a solid understanding 
of the game's fundamental mechanics will no doubt cause 
an eventual unbalance somewhere. When rules arguments 
or conflicts arise in a game (and they will) the best solu-
tion is for the GM to use his best discretion and make a 
quick ruling. Later the players can discuss the situation 
and try and come up with a fair solution. One option is to 
access the Imagine web site and ask the designers a ques-
tion, and this more often than not can solve the problem. 
In any case, the show must go on. No one can have fun if 
the game is always stopped by rules arguments. 
161 
Stfles Of Game MasteRrn~ 
Many times rules are not the problem, but simply the Game 
Master's style of running things needs improvement. The styles 
presented below are intended to help the growing Game Master 
understand both where he currently is and where he wants to 
go. These are stereotypes; an individual GM rarely fits com-
pletely one of these stereotypes, but instead is generally a com-
bination of different styles. Use these to understand the 
strengths and weaknesses of GMjng styles. All GMs at some 
point fall into one or more of these styles. In some cases, it 
may even be appropriate to alter one's style based on the 
behavoir of players. 
Monty Haul 
"I knew he was a Monty Haul when I felt guilty about every-
thing I had and knew that no other GM would Let me play that 
character." 
Play Style: Typical sessions involve where to find the best and 
most powerful items. The GM drops loot hints and the players 
come a runrun'. Magic shops can be common. Cottage GMC 
industries grow around helping the characters spend their loot. 
Eventual breakdown is likely, and players may move on to more 
challenging GMs. The world seems more comical than cohe-
sive. 
Strengths: Characters will have a plethora of nifty toys to play 
with. 
Weaknesses: Boredom will result from either from inability of 
foes to match the overstuffed characters, or a rise of powers 
between friends and foes will occur that resembles nuclear esca-
lation. Worlds suffer; beljevabi]jty is sacrificed wholesale on 
the alter of power. 
Conflict Points: Boredom, fights over loot, disrespect of the 
GM. 
The Hack and Slasher 
"He has a book of creatures and he's not afraid to use it. Plot? 
What plot? In the end, isn't it about who lives and who dies?" 
Play Style: The world is divided into those who fight and those 
who are killed by those who fight. SWS (Super Weenie 
Syndrome) becomes an oft used tactic, where the GM takes a 
normally weak critter and amplifies its power to surprise and 
distress those foolish players. Boss Syndrome appears even 
more commonly-this syndrome arises when monsters are found 
in stronger and stronger varieties and power until the greatest is 
finally dispatched. 
Strengths: Players will face a wide assortment of ready to 
fight critters. 
Weaknesses: Purpose beyond survival is trivialized. 
Conflict Points: Believability, been there done that, division of 
combat experience, djsrespect of the GM. 

===== PAGE 172 =====
The Miser 
"Treasure? Whats that? We fought off a goblin hoard with 
sharpened sticks and a makeshift avalanche and all we found 
were a handful of coppers, some rusty armor pieces and few 
tarnished weapons. " 
Play Style: The characters pool their resources to solve most 
any situation, or they simply lose. Frustration and desperation 
are constant companions. The GM agonizes over every thing 
the characters come across. The players who are unable to 
overcome challenges will drift away from play. Everything 
costs more than the characters have and everything seems to 
sell to GMCs for less than its worth. Those players that thrive 
are masters of the impossible, winning conflicts with wit, wis-
dom or the serviceable end of an oblong smashing device-a 
club. 
Strengths: The players earn every penny. Master players can 
enjoy the challenge of a miserly GM. 
Weaknesses: The players feel gypped. Less masterful players 
become frustrated. 
Conflict Points: Treasure, character ability to overcome obsta-
cles, armor and weapons for warrior types, spells for mage 
types, invocation usage for priestly folk. 
The Contestant 
"Every play session was a contest. It was us against the GM, 
sometimes losing and sometimes beating his challenges. " 
Play Style: Anything is possible. This GM pulls from a bag of 
tricks creating situations to challenge the ability of the charac-
ters-and when meta-gaming-the ability of players. The players 
can lose believability in the setting and the game itself as any-
thing more than a contest against the GM. 
Strengths: There is a sense of a game to be won or lost. 
Competative players may enjoy the game. 
Weaknesses: The player can become weary of the contest and 
lose character motivations and purposes. 
Conflict Points: Anything is potential for a contest between 
the GM and the play group. 
The Best Friend 
"He could never quite bring himself to kill us. Garyeth got 
swallowed whole by a dragon and the GM Let him cut his way 
out from the inside. " 
Play Style: Play style is normal, except when death rears its 
ugly head. Then the GM wades in; throwing fake rolls behind 
the screen, or helping the players overcome the impossible. The 
players gain a sense of invulnerability and may begin doing 
things that would ordinarily get them killed because they rely 
on the friendly GM not to kill them. 
Strengths: The GM is often well liked. The players feel safe. 
Weaknesses: The players may not feel challenged. 
Conflict Points: Death, Boredom, favorite players of the GM, 
disrespect of the GM. 
The Bully 
"He just never Liked Jerry. Jerrys characters had a habit of 
dying under questionable circumstances. " 
Play Style: Play tends to be cliquish; there are many inside 
jokes and information that's not readily available to new players 
and less Liked players. The GM has preference for some players 
over others. Friends may talk to the GM outside the play ses-
sions and get info that aids them in play. The GM supports 
those players who defend him to others. The GM doesn't 
respond well to criticism, and often engages in sneaky and sus-
picious methods that end up in the harm or death of characters 
belonging to players he doesn't like. 
Strengths: If the GM Likes you life is good. 
Weaknesses: If the GM doesn't like you life is harsh and short. 
Conflict Points: New players, disrespect of the GM. 
The Tyrant 
"I wanted to search the canyon for bandits but the GM made us 
head into the cave. The Leader GMC Looked into our hearts; he 
was godlike and directed us like toy soldiers in a child's sand-
box." 
Play Style: The GM controls the direction of play. The indi-
vidual who has different ideas finds herself out on a limb. 
When total control is necessary, the GM's super character 
arrives to lead the party into the promised land. The players 
always have a sense of being led. Players who do not resist the 
GM's control may find accomplishment in meeting the set chal-
lenges placed by the GM. 
Strengths: Abundant structure allowing new characters to get 
used to play. 
Weaknesses: Player freedom is often ignored. 
Conflict Points: Player choices, directions travelled, powerful 
GMCs. 
The Braggart 
"In his own mind he was the best GM ever. It was daunting to 
try and play his games because all you heard about was the 
great adventures he had run before." 
Play Style: This GM makes epic scale adventurers where the 
characters must live up to their roles as famous heroes or infa-
mous villains. There isn't a lot of room for someone to pursue 
minor goals or be recognized for lesser achievements. Master 
players have the opportunity to receive notoriety for their play 
but the best of them won't need it. 
Strengths: If the party achieves a fantastic result this GM will 
start a legend about them. 
Weaknesses: Too much greatness overshadows smaller accom-
plishments. 
Conflict Points: Character Histories, Character achievements. 
162 

===== PAGE 173 =====
The Actor 
"His world is the stage and he is all the actors. The party spent 
an hour role playing with the bartender to get the name of the 
local baron. " 
Play Style: The story unfolds at the players. They are thrust 
into the drama and expected to act the parts. The GM acts out 
encounters with every GMC. The bartender always has an out-
rageous accent or speaks with a drawl. Foreshadowing is com-
mon. The master player has to keep up with the GM, staying in 
character and uncovering the plot unfolding around them. 
Strengths: Entertaining, flamboyant, plays with a style that 
captivates players. 
Weaknesses: May overshadow his gaming group, stealing the 
limelight from their play. Sometimes play is held up too long. 
Conflict Points: Roleplaying standards, character motivation 
and disagreements with GMCs results in lost leads. 
The Philosopher 
"There is always a moral to his adventures. The party agonized 
over whether to kill the innocent boy who was possessed by an 
evil god or believe the promise of the god and watch him 
destroy the village in the hopes he would free the boy after." 
Play Style: Games are long and involved. Often their meaning 
is only revealed after endless wrangling over the ethical choices 
presented. The GM stands a good chance of loosing players 
having an opposing point of view. Games with these GM's 
often have a meta-game that is played in and around the actual 
game as the GM watches the players reactions to situations and 
gauges their choices. 
Strengths: This GM makes you think. He challenges both the 
character and its player's point of view. 
Weaknesses: Sometimes players just want to play and not be 
lectured to, even subtly. 
Conflict Points: Morals, character motivation, belief struc-
tures. 
The Deceiver 
"We ended up in the wrong city at the wrong time fighting the 
wrong foes; somehow this amused the GM to no end. " 
Play Style: Something mysterious happens (again). The play-
ers start shaking down everything that doesn't run away for 
clues. Things that run away, they hunt down and beat up for 
clues. When they think they have enough clues they set off to 
solve the mystery. The Master player ferrets out the true clues 
from the false ones and solves the mystery, sometimes to the 
annoyance of the GM. Failure means the GM has successfully 
deceived the players. 
Strengths: The characters (and their players) will have a true 
mystery to solve. 
Weaknesses: Continuous mysteries don't always make for 
great foundation upon which to role play and can be tedious. 
Conflict Points: Who, what, where, why, when and how. 
The Intriguer 
"This GM's game has political undertones. He seems fair even 
when he kills someone, but I couldn't always tell if it was sup-
posed to happen like that. " 
Play Style: Game play is slow and cautious-a dance between 
characters and the GMCs. Although the game resembles a mys-
tery, motivations are the key to unlocking the puzzle of intrigue. 
True dangers can be avoided by knowing what each faction 
wants and what they fear. The master player walks through the 
Intriguer's world, turning opposing factions against each other 
and making friends of foes. 
Strengths: The game has games within games where charac-
ters are thrust into factional conflicts, party conflicts, personal 
conflicts and the GM's hand is rarely shown. 
Weaknesses: Cynicism grows, players mistrust each other and 
most anyone they meet. 
Conflict Points: Relationships, hidden motives, potential 
threats. 
The Strategist 
"The enemy warriors held their ground, while their priests 
healed the wounded and their mages picked us off one by one. 
Just when we thought we were about to tum things around the 
rogue skirmishers attacked from the rear." 
Play Style: This GM's game is a combination of hack and 
slash and a contest with real reasoning behind how the GMCs 
fight and operate. Play is spent finding getting intelligence on 
the opponents before engaging them to increase the chances of 
victory. Rarely are opponents taken head on. The master play-
er breaks the opponent's organization and then defeats only the 
opponents necessary to achieve the group's goals. 
Strengths: His GMCs fight with coordination and strategy that 
rivals the play group's tactics. 
Weaknesses: Believability suffers, because unless foes are 
mind-linked, they realistically would usually fight as individu-
als unless trained soldiers. The GM's hand can be seen in these 
tactics. Every fight becomes a struggle to out think the GM. 
Conflict Points: Combat, character/player strategy/tactics. 
The World Builder 
"Everything was detailed. She had maps of maps. Histories, 
creatures, gods, religions, nations, factions, heroes, villains-
heck even weather patterns. When you played in her world you 
felt you had gone someplace. " 
Play Style: Play style involves exploration of a rich world. 
Characters should be able to see the inherent conflicts in the 
details they uncover and become part of the world's structure. 
Destruction of places in the world may be resisted or downright 
thwarted by the over protective GM. The master player thrives 
in a detailed world that presents endless opportunities to role 
play. This type of player learns how to weave their own story 
into the fabric of the world. 
163 

===== PAGE 174 =====
Strengths: Believability is often very high. There is a strong 
context for role playing. 
Weaknesses: Sometimes the world gets too much attention and 
the player's entertainment too little. The story itself may suffer. 
Conflict Points: Too much to do and explore. Player freedom 
to create and destroy may be curtailed. 
The Storyteller 
"The GMC's always seemed to have a story to tell and we 
seemed to be living one. Sometimes you can take a step back 
and see the story unfold around you. " 
Play Style: Characters begin play often with a lead in and 
GMC's may have scripts that are read from to enhance the 
story. The coherence of the story is maintained and loose ele-
ments weaved back together again by the artful GM. Danger 
comes when the players wish to do boring and inherently mun-
dane tasks. The skillful storyteller fast forwards through this 
material as much as possible. The GM resists the paths that 
might harm the story and this can create frustration. 
Strengths: Who doesn't want to be a character in a rich story? 
Weaknesses: Sometimes the story overwhelms the character's 
choices, and they feel pushed. Rules often suffer and the play-
er's can lose the sense that they are in control of their actions. 
Conflict Points: Less interesting choices are resisted. Player 
freedom may suffer. 
The Master 
"She is a chameleon. Just when I think I have this GM figured 
out she surprises me. I can never tell if she is rooting for us or 
trying to kill us. She is descriptive when the players seek infor-
mation and deceptive when they aren't paying attention. There 
are always people lined up to play her games." 
Play Style: Perhaps an unattainable absolute, the Master com-
bines all styles and uses the right one at the right time. Play 
matches the players. It can entertain, enlighten, educate, 
engage, and influence both the characters and their players at a 
pace and temperament that suits them. Meta gaming is kept to 
a minimum. This GM will desire feedback from the players to 
make corrections in style and substance of further play. The 
games are usually memorable and if the characters lose or die 
the players rarely blame the GM. The master player is at home, 
role playing, seeking storyline and plot, uncovering the myster-
ies of the world and overcoming conflicts. This is the game 
every good GM wants to run and everyone wants to play in. 
Strengths: Uses the best style to fit the situation at hand. 
Weaknesses: Minimizes the downside of any style used. 
Conflict Points: Only ones the players make for themselves. 
PoweR Le"eL OF the Game 
In addition to the styles of Game Mastering, a GM should con-
sider at what power level he wishes his game to be run. The 
first tool for this is the different character types (nonnal, adven-
turer, heroic and legendary). The closer a GM wants his game 
to be run at the mundane level (low magic, less of the fantastic 
and more of a medieval setting) then the closer the characters 
should be to nonnal. Having characters with low attributes 
means that they will often fail attribute saves and skill rolls, and 
will have little access to their non-acquired skills. For this rea-
son it can be good to begin Grune Mastering with character's at 
nonnal or adventurer level. 
Heroic and legendary characters generally always have access 
to all of their non-acquired skills. While this is very exciting 
for experienced players, it can be very frustrating to the new 
GM. Not only does it mean that you will have to know how all 
of the skills work, it also leaves you open to "scenario busters". 
Scenario busters are those skills and abilities that will end a sce-
nario very quickly if the GM is not aware of them and has not 
thought to prepare for them. There is no substitute for knowing 
the system, but it can help greatly to watch out for these sce-
nario busters: 
1) locating abilities. Anything ability which can detect where 
something is at a distance can really wreck an adventure that 
involves finding a hidden treasure. Some examples are Path 
Find and Scrying. One solution offered to the GM which 
should not be overused is the spell Non-Detection, which pre-
vents the effects of these abilities. 
2) "Peeking" skills. Similar to locating abilities, these are abil-
ities that give away the true nature of the major opponents or 
items in an intrigue adventure. For example, lets say that the 
GM designed an adventure where an evil villain had infiltrated 
the ranks of a good guy organization. If the party uses Detect 
Evil on the villain, the scenario pretty much ends. Now of 
course the villain would be prepared for this and would use an 
ability like "Mind Change" or Non-Detection. 
3) Specialized effects. These are effects which directly target 
and destroy a certain type of scenario. If you are writing an 
undead adventure and fail to take into account the skills of the 
two Priests and two Knights in the group, then you may be in 
for a short adventure. 
4) Rapid travel. Sometimes it can ruin an adventure if the GM 
has not considered all of the mobility options in Imagine. 
Characters can fly, levitate, and at higher Titles, teleport. Make 
sure that you have considered the implications of these abilities. 
5) Mental Combat. If you are not setup to deal with it, mental 
combat characters can walk all over their opponents. Read the 
mental combat rules and decide if you wish to include it in your 
game. This book also provides several checks on mental com-
bat which can be employed to balance it. 
164 

===== PAGE 175 =====
6) Martial combat. If someone in your group wants to play a 
character with Martial Knowledge (there's always one) then 
make sure you have at least a fair understanding of these rules. 
Otherwise this character will more than likely be attempting 
things reserved for anime. The most important thing about mar-
tial combat is mal<ing sure that the character is not trying to 
combine too many actions into one, in too short a time period. 
1n all cases, the best thing to do is look over the characters in 
your adventuring group and make sure you are aware of all of 
their abilities. If someone can use a skill that you are not famil-
iar with, look it up and read it. This will both allow you to 
write an adventure that is appropriate to the character's abilities 
as well as prevent the adventure to not be a challenge. 
Title Breakdown 
Another element which determines the flavor of your game 
world is the Title at which the character's are playing. The 
game gets very different at high Titles, and a GM ought to be 
aware of how the game is played within certain Title ranges. 
1st through 3rd Title: In this Title range, characters are on a 
search for the most basic of possessions. It has been said that 
the difference in a I st and 2nd Title character is equipment. 
Getting that suit of armor is so important for combat, and often 
new characters die simply from a lack of good equipment (this 
is one of the reasons that Social Class is so important). At this 
range, characters do not have access to overly powerful skills or 
abilities. The spells and invocations have been set up with this 
in mind. With a few exceptions, a character cannot go above 
Piety or Aura Control 9 until 4th Title. Most of the scenario 
buster invocations and spells do not start until Piety level and 
Aura Level I 0. In addition, most of the classes are set up so 
they "come into their own" around 3rd Title. 
4th through 6th Title: Characters begin to gain abilities and 
skills of some power at this point. All final core skills fall with-
in this range, for no class has a core skill beyond 6th. Some 
players feel that these are the most exciting Titles to play a 
character, for most of the basic skills have been mastered and 
the skills in these ranges are a lot of fun without being too over-
balancing to a game. Still, the GM needs to watch out for sce-
nario busters here to a much larger degree. At this point spell 
using characters are capable generating higher Aura Controls 
than might be expected. Warriors have skills that can crush 
many opponents in a short time, such as Critical and Sweep. 
7th through 10th Title: At this point things begin to get very 
powerful. At 7th Title, a character earns his class name as a 
Title and begins moving into a new power range. Spells and 
invocations used here are exceptionally powerful and the GM 
has to be prepared to meet his characters with equally powerful 
opponents and creatures or else the characters will annihilate his 
encounters. The GM must be prepared to do a lot of work to 
make his adventures interesting and challenging at this point. 
The experience curve here begins to sharpen, and it can take 
much longer to advance in Title. For this reason, as well as the 
fact that the game begins to enter a fantastic power level, many 
players like to retire their character's at 7th Title. 
11th Title and above: The game becomes supernatural at this 
point. Characters are almost not even playing the same game 
anymore. Their motivations are about building armies and find-
ing worshippers. The characters have entered the politics of the 
deities and are leaving the concerns of the earthly world behind. 
Travel to other planes is not uncommon. The Game Master is 
required to do an enormous level of preparation. This level of 
game is not for everyone. 
ThReabs: An Open Enbeb GM Stfle 
The Master's Manual provides a healthy dose of information for 
GMs to create and develop their own campaign setting. 
However, making all of that information available to players 
can be an overwhelming task for the GM. How is it there are 
people who are ready to GM at anytime with nothing more than 
a notebook and dice? How do they take so little information 
and weave it into an adventure time after time? 
No matter how prepared you are for your players, they will 
inevitably stumble into an underdeveloped area of any cam-
paign world. When this happens, you have three choices: tell 
the players you need more time to develop the area and stop the 
game, tell the players they cannot go there, or use improvisation 
and general background. As amazing as it sounds, you can 
almost always do the latter without the players realizing they 
have done something unexpected. 
Threads - The Tools 
1. A notebook with ample paper. 
2. Graph paper to record the new areas you make up as you go. 
3. A list of factions in your setting and their basic purpose. 
Exhaustive detail isn't necessary, but you should know their 
motivations and conflicts. 
4. A list of influential and powerful people in your setting, 
along with their purposes, aims and the factions to which they 
belong. You don't have to make a character out of each one but 
their class and any special abilities should be noted. 
5. Several general maps of generic areas. They don't have to be 
filled in nor set into specific places. Keep around a few layouts 
to inns, a dungeon level, a town, etc. so you have them for ref-
erence and can create almost anything by borrowing elements 
from them. 
6. A list of creatures and extras that can be developed as more 
focus is placed upon them. 
7. Imagination - keep your notebook with you and write down 
odd ideas you get at weird times. 
165 

===== PAGE 176 =====
Weaving - Using the Tools 
So how do you start when you don't have an adventure pre-
pared, but they want to play now? 
1. Dedicate at least a page within your notebook to each one of 
the characters. Write their name, race, origin, background and 
anything else you can think of that would be interesting to have 
them involved in the future. 
2. Use the situations information on p.176. Pick a suitable situ-
ation and place some or all of the characters within it. Draw the 
starting area as any inn or another gathering locale. Create a 
very brief background including name and something notewor-
thy about the area. As the situation resolves, write down how 
certain characters reacted or interesting things that might have 
come from the resolution of the situation. Let the players digest 
the situation and as they talk amongst themselves. Then, take 
this information and setup one or two more situations based on 
the first. 
3. As the situations begin to become a scenario, start thinking 
about a place you want the characters to end up to tie off sever-
al of the situations that you have created. Start creating situa-
tions that lead the characters towards this objective. 
4. Map any new areas your players explore. 
5. Use your faction list to create situations where there is oppo-
sition to the party or individuals. If the opposition becomes too 
great, or you deem appropriate, use supporting factions as well. 
6. Use leaders or important figures to underscore big moments 
in the adventure or get the characters crucial help or informa-
tion. They can also be used as direct opposition to the players. 
7. Everything interesting that happens that could create future 
situations should be written down on a character's page or the 
general threads page. 
In essence, you are weaving the adventure together. You are 
using the creative process to pull at certain threads, start new 
ones, tie off others and create a complex and appealing whole. 
If the GM weaves the entire adventure together ahead of time 
and then refuses to allow the characters to deviate, it can fall as 
flat as the GM who badly improvises unknown areas. The note-
book you populate with your writing will become your world 
bible. 
Your notebook will grow and your world will be fleshed out as 
you go. The greatest danger from this process is that you will 
forget what has happened or not remember important details 
accurately. Thus anything that might be important must be 
written down. Also you will need more concrete encounters. It 
is one thing to throw Saurians at your party in several situations 
or even a Saurian guard who bas a few skills. It is quite another 
to throw in a Saurian war leader who has bis own history, skills 
and abilities. 
You will find that you must flesh out some personalities into 
full blown GMCs. There will be no helping this and if you 
resist too long you will end up in situations where the charac-
ters are face to face with an encounter that will fall flat because 
you don't have enough information to run it correctly. In 
essence you are doing everything the "prepare ahead" GM is 
doing. You are just doing it as you go, or just before you need 
it. Beware of taking too large a bite with "save the world" cam-
paigns in the early stages of your setting development. 
If you keep good notes and maps, when you are done you will 
have a well-defined campaign setting and can expand upon it 
infinitely. The collective memory of the players is nearly 
always greater that the GM's on any given day. A combination 
of preparation and inspiration is going to make the best playing 
experience long term but don't let lack of preparation mean that 
you can't start. With the Player's Guide, Master's Manual, a 
notebook and some dice you can start a new adventure anytime. 
CoheRent CReatuRe EncounteRs 
Most of us have been there as players. You open one door and 
a fire breathing Hydra pops out and a glorious battle ensues, but 
then you open the next door and a Werewolf attacks. The sense 
of unreality creeps in and its all over. Though you may rise to 
the challenge of the fight, something important is irretrievably 
lost: suspension of disbelief. 
As a GM, this is one of the most important details. Players will 
be drawn into coherent believable worlds and will become 
bored with worlds that make no inherent sense. J .R.R. Tolkien, 
in a famous lecture on writing fantasy, talked mostly about 
world building and history. These are important tools that will 
aid immensely in suspension of disbelief. However, there is 
one very easy way to gain suspension of disbelief without those 
tools. Make coherent creature encounters. 
So how do you do it? Does it mean putting only one kind of 
creature for the party to encounter? Does it mean that you have 
to bore the party with lack of variety simply to create realism? 
No, neither of these things are required. In fact, the example 
given above of the Hydra and the Werewolf might actually be 
explainable if the right details are added. But let's start simple. 
There is usually a controlling group to a game world area. Few 
areas are filled with equal numbers of creatures unless they are 
all mindless or do not compete in any way. So start with a con-
trolling group. If it is a race of some type of intelligent crea-
tures, create a hierarchy from the lowest farmer to the highest 
king. Place these in locations that make sense in your planned 
area. 
Also, avoid the "big boss" syndrome. Inexperienced GMs grav-
itate toward making a single very powerful creature who is 
always the most dominate creature in the area. Sometimes this 
can be fun but should be avoided in becoming the standard. It 
166 

===== PAGE 177 =====
makes the goal or target far too easily understood and that much 
easier to achieve. Oftentimes, it is not the ruler who is the 
strongest or most powerful creature. Rather, it is a lieutenant or 
associate that has more ability. So if you make a Goblin chief, 
make him a powerful Warrior but make the Goblin Shaman the 
greater of the two in ability. This will add an element of com-
plexity to the plot line. 
Now supplement the leaders with domesticated or controlled 
creatures used and owned by the controlling group. If the situa-
tion dictates, you can place other creatures that exist either as 
parasites to the controlling group, or in opposition to it. Even 
open conflict between groups is possible but then you may need 
to change your encounters to show scenes of open hostility 
between the two groups. For instance, deep underground Dark 
Dwarves and Dark Elves could be vying for control of a large 
cavern and network of tunnels. Draw battle lines and have sev-
eral skirmishes set up between the two races. 
All creatures need to eat. Assuming they are carnivores, there 
needs to be a supply of some sort of hunting game or domesti-
cated animals as a food source. These animals can be creatures 
in their own right and dangerous to the party. 
Finally, there are ways to add even more exotic creatures to cre-
ate believability and amazing encounters. Suppose the first 
example of the Werewolf and the Hydra was desired by the 
GM. How could that situation be made believable? Create a 
third character, a Dark Priest. This character has a rod that will 
control the Hydra, which is used to keep out intruders. Make 
the Werewolf a cursed family member of the Dark Priest and 
suddenly the encounter can make a lot more sense. But without 
these details, the players will not understand and scoff at the 
encounters presented to them. Make sure you have supporting 
details to make the supporting cast believable. 
You do not need to have or use all types of encounters 
described, just draw on them as you design your encounter area. 
With these rules as your guide to developing coherent creature 
encounters you will create situations and scenarios that will 
embroil the party in excitement and adventure. In a role play-
ing game, that is the overriding goal for the GM. 
Example 
1) Controlling Group: Goblins who have a hill cave system 
and raid travelers passing on a local road. Nine Goblin women, 
four Goblin hunters, and a Goblin cook, two human slaves, 
fourteen Goblin Warriors, three Goblin guards, a Goblin 
Shaman and a Goblin chief. 
2) Domesticates: Five Dire Wolves and a Wyvern are con-
trolled and used by the Shaman. One trapped Electric Jelly 
used for waste disposal. 
3) Parasites: A great spider is surviving by killing weaker 
Goblins and those few travelers who escape the Goblin attacks. 
Drained bodies of Goblins and travelers are piled on one side of 
the spider's clearing. 
4) Opposition: Two Ogres are plotting to kill the chief and the 
Shaman and are killing the occasional lone Goblin. The Ogres 
hope to take over and enslave the Goblins to get a ready supply 
of free food and because they enjoy the fear they can create in 
the Goblins. They have holed up in a secondary and smaller 
cave system nearby. 
5) Food Sources: The woods have mule deer, rabbits, wild 
boars, black bears, mountain lions, and birds of various kinds. 
All are used as a food source by the Goblins. 
6) Exotics: The Shaman can summon a totem wolf. 
T1me anb Deta1L 
The pace of a game can often determine whether or not the 
players have a good time, or whether the game becomes a 
drudgery of mundane events. Different situations call for dif-
ferent ways of dealing with time. For example, there is no 
point in making your players explain each and every action they 
are going through as they get dressed in the morning. However, 
combat requires a slowed down second-by-second approach to 
time. It may be helpful to think of time in three different fash-
ions, and you may even wish to let your players know in which 
time frame you are running your game at any given point. The 
three types of time the GM must juggle are real time, game time 
and combat time. Real time is the time that is transpiring in the 
real world; this is dealing with time as it actually passes. When 
a player spends four hours with the GM and his friends, then 
four hours within the time-space he perceives has transpired. 
Game time is the time that is transpiring within the GM's cam-
paign setting. Game is time is almost always elapsed, meaning 
the GM "speeds up" game play by fast forwarding through 
insignificant events. For example, take the character that 
spends an hour walking along a road. Instead of the player 
spending an hour of real time role-playing the task of walking 
for an hour in game time, the GM elapses the one hour into just 
a couple of seconds of real time. To the character an hour has 
passed, while to the player only a few seconds have passed. 
Real Time and Game Time can be thought of as two infinitely 
linear lines. The players exist within Real time, while the char-
acters exist within Game time. Game time can run in 
sycronization with real time, it can be elapsed, or it can be in 
combat time. Finally, combat time is the time slowed down 
version of events that occur during fighting. 
Real Time 
Using real time can be extremely frustrating for many players. 
You may excite or upset your players when you get out the stop 
watch and say, "You have ten minutes to solve this puzzle." If 
you do it every game session, it's likely you will upset them, or 
at the very least they will secretly enroll you in Sadists 
Anonymous. Real time does not have to be obvious to players. 
167 

===== PAGE 178 =====
As GM, you can be carrying on a conversation with a player, 
having a GMC stall for time-perhaps to see how long you can 
keep them in one place before the characters are surprised by an 
ambush. Very few players want to deal with their characters in 
real time on a constant basis, as this becomes an exercise in 
triviality. Players convene to have fun with a game, not to 
wade through hours of detail to get to do one thing they enjoy. 
Real Time should be used vary sparingly. Become the master 
of the moment and save such uses for the thrilling climax to a 
campaign of many months. 
Game Time 
In addition to serving as the chronological measurement within 
a game setting, game time is used to represent the time it takes 
to resolve the mechanics of game play. The Imagine Role 
Playing SystemTM simulates real time conflict resolution. 
Skills, spells and effects have stated times they require to elapse 
within game time before the desired result can occur. 
Elapsed Game Time: When players are becoming bored or the 
GM wants to fast forward to the next important situation or 
event, then elapsed time is the answer. A GM should allow 
time to pass quickly between uneventful situations, then drop 
into real time for encounters. For example, you as GM may say 
something like, "You walk for three hours through the dark-
ened, tangled growth without event. Then, you notice a strange 
flower growing near the base of a tree." Let the party deal with 
the discovery and then elapse more time. "You continue for 
another two hours and then you notice the forest has gotten 
rather still. There are no longer the sounds of soft scurrying 
from creatures running away from you, or the cries of birds 
accompanying your movements. It is then you notice the red-
skinned creatures approaching you." In this example, several 
hours of game time elapsed. Yet, in real time no more than a 
few minutes were spent dealing with the herb and listening to 
the GM describe the surroundings. 
A GM must be mindful about being predictable in his use of 
elapsed game time. During play, you might occasionally stop 
elapsed time on a whim to describe some unusual or unrelated 
feature of the terrain or setting just to keep the players on their 
toes. Otherwise the moment you stop elapsed time, everyone 
will draw their swords and expect to be jumped. Also respond 
to your players; if you're in elapsed time and your players say 
they want to search for herbs or take more time to study their 
surroundings, drop back into real time, describing what they see 
or find. Elapsed time is your tool to keep the game flowing and 
interesting, providing the detail needed for each situation. If 
you listen to your players and see how they react to your use of 
elapsed time, you will soon strike a happy balance that will 
keep the game smooth playing. 
Combat Time 
This is time as it is described in the Combat section of the 
Player's Guide. It is much slower than real time, moving along 
the second-by-second timing system that allows the GM to 
determine exactly how things are happening in relationship to 
each other. Combat time is based on seconds in order to simu-
late a balanced combat, but in truth most actions do not take as 
long in real time as their listed seconds. It is done this way 
because l second is the slowest unit of time with which most 
people are familiar and thus is a simple way to handle combat. 
PRops 
What makes a great game stand out in the player's imagination? 
Is it the challenges faced, breathtaking descriptions of the world 
or something else? Certainly, challenges and descriptions are 
important and begin the process of bringing the player into the 
world you have weaved together. An often overlooked finishing 
stroke to the completion of the suspension of disbelief are 
props. Most Game Masters use one form of prop or another to 
represent characters and opponents during combat situations. 
This can be as simple as crude drawings on a piece of paper or 
painted miniatures in elaborate hand crafted terrain. Spend 
some time adding to the experience your players will feel by 
making a small part of your world tangible. Having props in 
your game will keep your players coming back for more. 
You can play by just describing the action, but the more intense 
and complex, the more likely you are to lose crucial detail or 
even comprehension. Sure you can have a Goblin leap over the 
table, land behind the party, and attack with his scimitars. 
However, unless you use some sort of prop it is likely you will 
forget exactly where you put that Goblin when six more attack 
from all sides. 
The first time you whip out the ye ole' inn diorama that you 
spent three days making you will probably get lots of attention. 
However unless you have time to make more versions of inns, 
the believability you initially gained will be lost when ye ole' 
inn becomes ye every inn. If you're so inclined, most model 
and train stores can get you started. Game stores that sell 
miniature battle games often sell pre-made terrain as well. Save 
handcrafted terrain for epic battles, special beginnings or 
moments you really have time to punch up. An erasable mat is 
an excellent way of drawing temporary terrain. 
There are other kinds of props that can really bring your players 
into the experience and are easier to make than dioramas. Maps 
allow the player to directly see your world. They need to be 
interesting and yet not give away every detail. Parchment 
works great for creating a rustic feel. Even if you created your 
map on a computer you can usually use a print feeder to put in 
parchment paper. You can crinkle it, rip pieces off, scrape off 
some of the ink with a knife, burn the edges, write notes on the 
168 

===== PAGE 179 =====
map from previous owners, etc. All of these techniques give 
the map an authentic heir. Given the choice, most players 
would much rather be handed a parchment map that looks 
rather worn, than a crisply printed digital map. 
Use a similar technique when making scrolls and messages the 
players may find. Think Like the person who made the scroll or 
message. What was its intent? Should it be obvious or vague, 
in some sort of code or not? Longer works like histories, spell 
books and diaries can be created with relative ease. 
Puzzles that involve connecting pieces together can be done by 
distributing cut outs and allowing the players to physically 
assemble them. A talisman, sword or other item prop can be 
constructed out of construction paper or a manila folder and 
then split up into puzzle pieces. Try to do your best to disguise 
the way the pieces fit together unless you want the puzzle to be 
fairly easy. One good way to do this is to make an unusual pat-
tern on the pieces that could fit together in multiple ways. 
Magic items are usually hard fought for and much cherished. 
You can make the experience a memorable one for the character 
by making a magic item card. Use what talents you have to 
draw a reasonable facsimile of the item on the non-lined side of 
an index card. If artistry is not your forte, recruit a friend who 
can draw. Also the Internet is a great source of clip art. When 
the player gets the magic item, they will feel like they actually 
acquired something and have something to show for it. You 
will be surprised by how much difference a card can make. 
If you tend to vacation in places where you happen upon junk 
jewelry and other cheap odds and ends, grab them. A real atten-
tion getter is showing the players something physical that repre-
sents what the characters find. If something they acquired can 
be held, felt, prodded and wondered about, then you have their 
full attention. Old or foreign coins can make great game coins. 
Dice pouches can become belt pouches to be pilfered or looted. 
Runnmr; Factions 
Conflict is at the heart of every story. Without it characters are 
going through the motions: living without a common purpose; 
or worse, arriving at their goal with little challenge. The party 
itself is the simplest faction in any game-a band of noble or 
ignoble few who stand as one against capricious fate. 
Humanoids are social animals, and even extremely shy beings 
will band together to protect themselves in times of turmoil. So 
it is that factions are of paramount importance to any setting. 
Fledgling Game Masters often ask what is it that makes a set-
ting interesting, but believable. While piles of statistics (the 
facts and figures) can be useful, they are shadows when com-
pared against the factions in your setting. It is factions that cre-
ate conflicts, story line and even history. 
Consequently factions are the first element to create in the set-
ting and the one to update most often. This element is a rich 
material to weave stories from. With well-described factions 
and even the crudest area maps, play can begin in minutes. So, 
how does one create factions and what specifically can be done 
with them? 
Choose the largest area of influence. Is the setting made up of 
kingdoms? Is there a central form of government or a dispersed 
one? No matter, pick the most powerful and create the faction 
that makes up this element. Choose the type of faction, create 
the leader and the other factional elements (See Factions in the 
Setting section). Decide what the goals of the faction are, how 
they hold power, what they stand for and against and finally 
who are its principal enemies? Are these enemies factions in 
themselves? Who is the strongest of these enemy factions? 
Now create that faction. With just these two factions conflict is 
created. Perhaps they are in a struggle for supremacy or one 
has fallen and the other usurped its rightful place. The charac-
ters can be embroiled between these two sides, caught up in 
machinations far beyond their ability to control. Create as 
many sides as you deem fit. Perhaps a setting is extremely fac-
tionalized, with rival houses forever jockeying for position in a 
grand game of influence and intrigue. 
Don't end there, create factions that are neutral to the greater 
conflicts or non-aligned. Remember the type of culture the fac-
tions are created in. If the people are generally like-thinking 
then numbers of different factions will be fewer while individu-
alistic cultures may have multitudes of distinct factions. Fill in 
the setting with factions that grow up around the places of 
wealth and power, for this is where factions form. Even a 
group of beggars, lead by a semi-retired brigand, represent 
power of a kind. When each current faction is complete, devel-
op a back-history. Who founded it? How has the faction drift-
ed since? What were its greatest moments? What deeds is it 
known for? How is the faction viewed by the setting's citizens? 
What were the past conflicts and how did they resolve? 
Characters can then uncover these tidbits as they become 
important or are chanced upon. Believability soars and a long 
term sense of the setting grows. 
Now the factions are ready for use. As the character's (or 
group's) deeds and misdeeds become known to a faction, record 
the character's factional standing with that group. Open fac-
tions may attempt to help, hinder, recruit or harm the character 
right away. Secretive factions will tend to take a wait and see 
approach until more is known. As the factions begin to involve 
the character, some will test loyalty or attempt to uncover the 
character's true motives. Generally, factions take an interest in 
a character that shows promise and is aligned with the faction, 
or seems dangerous and is at odds with them. Factions often 
ignore the neutral parties, sometimes until it is too late. 
169 

===== PAGE 180 =====
A character does not have to be handed a mission by a faction 
to feel its influence. It can exact a toll on the character's finan-
cial activities, curtail freedoms in response to a character's 
actions, or oppose the character with threats or direct response 
or it may simply use the character for whatever purpose seen fit. 
Each case will depend on how the faction views the character 
and how the character is seen to respond. As a character rises 
in power, factions wilJ become more interested in the character's 
doings. The military factions of an empire rarely waste their 
time with what a working farmer thinks but may become inter-
ested if that over-taxed farmer stirs his peers to riot or rebel. 
Likewise a street thief is unlikely to care about a hardworking 
seamstress, but one who now makes dresses for the royal court 
may come in handy as a source of infonnation. 
The GM represents the faction and its interests. Remember to 
involve the factional elements in the enfolding story. When fac-
tions are forgotten, the story will suffer and the motivations of 
the GMCs the characters meet, will seem hollow or entirely 
selfish. It is never too late to factionalize a setting and add true 
depth to the game. Creating specific factions is handled in the 
Setting section. 
ALK;nmentless Imru;rne 
Their is a sentiment among some that the best role players don't 
need the artifice of alignment to create and play their characters. 
For the in-depth role players who feel this way, alignments 
actually get in the way because they can place artificial restric-
tions on the player who is following the life script of the char-
acter envisioned. 
So why do we use alignments? What pitfalls are there to run-
ning without strong alignment boundaries? How and when can 
we move beyond them and still create a believable and playable 
experience? How can the good GM avoid these and create an 
even richer experience for the mature role player? What about 
skills like Detect Good and Detect Evil and the overall conflicts 
between Light and darkness? 
In the most simple terms, alignments create expectations and 
the beginnings of a role to fill. When you sit down to play you 
want to know what to expect from your fellow players and how 
the world will react generally to the role you have picked to 
play. If every time you played, your fellow party members 
behaved in a different way, and the game master characters 
acted completely differently, you would most likely become 
frustrated-or at the very least the world would loose some of 
it's believability. When you meet an active good character and 
you are an active good character there is some expectation that 
you can generally agree on a variety of issues without serious 
conflict. When that same active good character discovers an 
active evil one you expect friction and rightly so. When the 
Game Master observes an active good character kill a simple 
shopkeeper it is apparent that the character is not behaving as 
the alignment chosen and acts accordingly with the penalties 
and modifiers proscribed. 
Why do we care as players and Game Masters whether people 
follow these alignments? Because alignment represents one of 
the roles the character is suppose to play-class, race and reli-
gion being others. The heavy in a movie would seem nonsensi-
cal if he was nice one minute, awful the next and there was nei-
ther rhyme nor reason for it. As players, you generally don't 
want to have your character suddenly at odds with the people 
you have played with every week just because suddenly every-
one has gotten bored with the role they picked and decides the 
opposite would be fun. Not every gamer is at the same level of 
maturity or understands the reasoning behind staying in-charac-
ter. Alignments impose at least a limit on behavior that allows 
you to know when someone has stepped out of the bounds of 
the agreed upon play. The play group may all want to play an 
evil group out to do mayhem to the world, but at least they will 
know that they are an evil group and that they can't get away 
with the same things good groups can. Alignments thus help 
bring motivation to the character, while still allowing a range of 
play. If one removes alignments for everyone the play that 
results can degenerate in mixed audiences. There will be peo-
ple that play very motivated characters with an understanding 
for their role and worldview. There will also be people that 
show up and kill whatever they see or even each other for loot 
and yet later feign piousness when praying to the gods because 
it suits them. The god of law and morality would brook no trai-
torous killers for her divine gifts and as well the god of murder 
would accept no law-abiding, peaceful disciples to his ranks. 
With these problems how can you move beyond alignments? 
The first test is the maturity level of the group. Do they bicker 
at every turn regardless of alignment? Do they fall in and out 
of character at a whim? Have they been warned for having 
conflicts cross the boundary between in and out of game? If 
they do not do these things and the Game Master is ready for 
more upkeep, then he may be able to let alignments fall away. 
Alignmentless Mechanics/Rules 
1) Remove all alignments but the most general concept of Good 
and Evil and do not force the players automatically to assume 
these concepts in play unless it is befitting. 
2) In order to explain and understand the character's personali-
ty without an alignment the player must choose as many of the 
descriptive words as possible from Roles in the Setting Section. 
These will give a launching place to begin taking on the char-
acter's role. While these should shift over time they should 
rarely have dramatic changes without dramatic causes. 
Adherence to the roles chosen is a good way to determine if 
someone is playing their character well. 
3) Factions should become a primary motivating factor for 
how character's behave. The GM needs to have a list of all 
known factions in his world. A record must be kept for each 
player; by the GM, showing the status that player has with those 
factions. This is how these factions will react to that player. 
170 

===== PAGE 181 =====
This is referred to as factional standing ( see Factions in the 
Setting Section). 
4) Assume everyone is alignmentless unless they serve a super-
natural power or deity that is considered Good or Evil. These 
powers will have factions that follow them which are considered 
good and evil in the loosest terms. 
5) Reduce the effectiveness of the spells Read and Reveal Aura. 
They can either a) show gray (for alignmentless) black for those 
that serve darkforces and white for those that serve the forces 
of light, or b) continue to reveal color, but these colors do not 
represent specific alignments but moods and emotions. 
6) Detect Alignment only reveals whether someone serves a 
dark or light power and takes twice as long to work. 
5) Detect Good and Detect Evil only detect beings who serve 
the appropriate force. 
7) The only penalty for changing one's stance on the conflict 
between light and dark is the loss of divine magic. 
8) There are some acts that are so strong that they can lead a 
character to be considered Good or Evil without serving a 
divine being. 
a) If a player murders with no justification beyond the gratifica-
tion of some need or want that player can be considered Evil. 
The Game Master may allow the character to lose the stigma of 
Evil only after a period of remorse is shown in play that befits 
the heinousness of the murderous act(s). Performing such acts 
may attract the attention of evil factions. 
b) A player that helps others with no gain can be considered 
good. This person must do so in an obvious and constant fash-
ion to be considered good. Good status can be easily lost if the 
player becomes selfish and lapses into selfish acts. Performing 
171 
such acts may attract the attention of good factions. 
JO) Invocations must be granted based on a list from each deity 
which the GM must create. 
Removing Alignments does not mean that you have to lose the 
conflict between forces who follow good and those who follow 
evil. It just means that the character's places in such conflicts 
may be less clear or more transitory. This is all to the better in 
a rich game where players my find themselves squeezed into 
these conflicts. Some of the best characters in fiction are reluc-
tant heroes or accidental villains. Let the play decide where the 
characters fall in this spectrum. 
As you make the transition to alignmentless play watch careful-
ly how the characters are played. Do they have wild swings in 
factional standing? Are they following the roles they choose for 
their character in the Setting section? Are they in conflict with 
their fellow players? Are you finding it difficult to interact with 
them? If these are happening your group may not be ready for 
this advance type of play. Honestly many groups enjoy the 
expectations and roles created by alignments and wiJI always 
play with them. This is why we present this concept as the base 
level of play in Imagine. 
If you have made the transition and it is going well, remember, 
you have more to do now as Game Master. As they interact 
with factions you need to note the rise and fall with those fac-
tions. You need to remind the players to update their role 
choices as they grow or change over time. Expect good play 
from the alignmentless character. Ask them about why they did 
something and how they feel about their interactions. You as 
GM must now participate in the player's characterizations to 
understand where they are coming from and whether it is fit-
ting, desirably with the expectations of play.

Using the Imagine Game Mechanics 
Applying Attribute Saves 
Attribute saves are one method of situation resolution; that is, a 
mechanic used to determine the success or failure of a character 
achieving a desired end. Skills are generally used to determine 
if a complex or trained action is successful, whereas attribute 
saves often are used to negate an undesirable outcome, such as 
not dropping a rope, not falling off a cliff, not going insane, etc. 
Some saves are used as part of a contest either against oppo-
nent's save or against opponent's skill (see Player's Guide; con-
tests of attributes). Saves in general are very high before they 
are modified. Even an average person has a 13 rating in an 
attribute, producing a 65% save. Therefore, if there is any diffi-
culty at all, it is common to apply modifiers. Also remember 
that saves are not allowed to go above their natural chance (see 
attributes for a full explanation). The following suggests how 
to modify an attribute save based on the difficulty level of the 
situation: 
Difficulty level 
Easy 
Normal 
Difficult 
Challenging

Modifier 
+10% 
+0% 
-10% 
-20% 
-30% 
Attribute Save Examples 
The following discusses the many uses of attribute saves. This 
is not meant to be an exhaustive list; you as Game Master must 
use your discretion in applying both the save and applicable 
modifiers. Where the save suggested is so variable as to be 
unpredictable, no modifier is suggested- let the situation deter-
mine the modifier (see using modifiers). 
Strength 
Strength saves are used most often when a character is trying to 
hold onto something. Some examples, with suggested modi-
fiers, are: 
• The character has stabbed an opponent, and is trying to 
remove the blade that is stuck within him. 
• A character is trying to lift himself up onto a ledge or some 
similar higher ground, or is trying to hang onto something in 
rushing water. 
A~ty 
. 
The Agility save is probably the most commonly made save m 
Imagine. It is used for any general circumstance that requires a 
nimble touch or light foot. Some examples: 
• The character wishes to step over a trip wire, or walk across a 
thin ledge to the other side of a pit. 
• Someone throws an object across the room and the player 
wishes to catch it. 
Vitality 
Vitality saves are most often made when a wounded character 
wishes to remain conscious. They can also be made: 
• To avoid vomiting when the character eats something which 
does not agree with them, but is not poisonous or diseased. 
• The character is very ill but wants to stand up. 
• The character is not exposed to an actual disease, but is 
exposed to conditions which may cause a disease, such as being 
freezing cold and wet (save to avoid catching cold). 
Sometimes it may seem that a Will Force save is appropriate as 
well, so the main distinction of the Vitality save is that involves 
the functions of the body, not the spirit (the spirit may be will-
ing but the body may not cooperate). 
Intelligence 
The Intelligence save is another very common save, and some-
times it can be overused when in fact another mental attribute 
save would be more appropriate. The best use for an 
Intelligence save is when problem solving is involved: 
• The Game Master has not worked out an actual game or puz-
zle, but simply wants to see which characters can pass a certain 
point in an adventure. 
• The GM has devised a clever puzzle, but he thinks perhaps it 
has been made too difficult. If the character makes an 
Intelligence save he may get a hint. 
• As a last chance when a character just is not getting something 
which ought to be obvious. For this reason, it is sometimes 
called the "duh" save. 
• Sometimes if a player comes up with a brilliant idea, but is 
playing an exceptionally stupid character, the GM may require 
that he make an Intelligence save for his character to be able to 
think of the idea. 
Wisdom 
The Wisdom save is sometimes referred to as the common 
sense save. Whereas the Intelligence save is good for getting 
someone out of a mess, the Wisdom save allows for a brilliant 
insight of wisdom before the mess has been gotten into: 
• Anytime the character is about to do something incredibly 
stupid. The character is about to go into the room where five 
other people walked into, screamed horribly, and never came 
out. {Make a Wisdom save} 'That might not be such a good 
idea ... " 
• The character is trying to gain some insight into a situation 
involving human interaction, where no real clues are offered for 
problem solving. {Make a Wisdom save} "You get the feeling 
that the innkeeper really does not like his wife ... " 
Knowledge 
Anytime a player may know general trivia in a gameworld is a 
prime time for a Knowledge save. Usually this is when the bit 
of knowledge is outside of the realm of a skill or the specific 
172 

===== PAGE 183 =====
background. 
• This is a good way to handle the old "My character grew up 
in this world, he ought to know blah blah ... " 
Player: "Would I know where this wine came from?" 
Game Master: "Make a Knowledge roll..." 
• This is also a good save when player's want to remember 
something from a previous game session that they failed to 
record. 
Player: "What was that guys name again-Lord whatchajigger?" 
Game Master: "Make a Knowledge roll..." 
Appearance 
This save can be used when trying to determine if someone 
considers the character good looking. Everyone has different 
tastes, and even with a good Appearance save, sometimes the 
roll will be failed. So if a young woman has a 90% Appearance 
save, then there are about 90% of the people who meet her 
think "wow, what a looker" but the other 10% think "well she is 
attractive, but I really don't see what all the fuss is about". 
When a character makes an Appearance save, things should 
generally go better for that character when dealing with the 
individual. Note that this is not the same as the affinity roll 
which is much more powerful. 
• Appearance saves are general made to attract attention, espe-
cially from those of the opposite sex. 
• Beauty can command a certain amount of authority in at least 
making someone listen, for a time. If the fair knight was about 
to be ripped apart by the crowd he might make an Appearance 
save to see if his fair presence alone will give him enough 
respite to attempt to sway the crowd. Then of course Charm or 
an appropriate skill would need to take over or the knight would 
still be doomed. 
Charm 
Charm is the spark of friendship or indifference that begins 
within minutes of meeting. There are many factors that modify 
the Charm save such as race, class or profession. Where there 
is prejudice or hatred a Charm save cannot be used. There are 
multiple situations that require determination of whether there is 
a general liking or indifference to the being. The success of this 
save determines whether someone is general liked or disliked. 
It does not cause the affected being to act out of the ordinary, 
just have a good feeling about the character. This save should 
not be used in place of Affinity, which is much more powerful. 
• When a person is introduced to a group, such as a debutante 
ball or a meeting with a guild. 
• When the character is attempting to make conversation or be 
seen, such as a party or in an open tavern. Roll a Charm save 
for those who the character actually meets or is introduced to. 
Social Class 
Social Class saves are rarely used but can be powerful when 
made. This save is applied when the character is attempting to 
convince others that he is in fact of a certain status. For exam-
ple, if a person of high Social Class was caught in another land 
and brought before a king,, a social class save might allow the 
king to realize that he was talking to an individual with good 
breeding and who was obviously someone of importance. 
In general, Social Class saves primarily to seek audience with 
other nobles and to be seen in courts and places of station as 
being worthy. Social Class can also be used to as an implied 
threat. 
• To bully a local innkeeper into a free meal because of the 
character's nobility or station. 
• In seeking audience with the king. 
• Getting a guard to step aside in the 'name of the king' 
Aura 
Generally when an Aura save is required, the appropriate skill, 
adventure or rules explanation will call for it. Aura saves are 
used when a character is desperately trying to activate a magic 
item that has not been identified. The success of the save indi-
cates that one power may have been activated. Aura saves are 
sometimes made when Aura has been overused and Aura 
fatigue sets in. 
• To activate one power of an unidentified magic item for the 
fust time. 
• Aura fatigue. 
• Optionally, when the Aura pool reaches zero, an Aura save can 
avoid a physical shock from temporarily having no magic. That 
physical shock results in the body going into shock for the peri-
od of time it takes to regenerate at least one Aura point. 
Piety 
Piety saves should be used when some sort of divine test is 
required. The GM may opt to make a Piety save required when 
a character wants to activate a divine item for the first time. 
Another good time to use the Piety save is when the characters 
have violated a sacred place to see if they arouse the anger of 
spirits. Supernatural beings will almost always attack those 
who fail their Piety saves first. 
• This save is most often used when a Priest attempts to paint 
someone as a heretic or non-believer. If the save is made then it 
obvious to all that the character is a pious person and above 
suspicion. 
• To prove to a minion or Priest that one has divine favor. 
• To avoid arousing the anger of supernatural beings in a sacred 
or unholy place. 
Will Force 
Will Force saves are used when a test of willpower is called for. 
Such cases might be: 
• To keep from crying out in pain when having a bone set or 
being tortured, etc. 
• To keep from vomiting at something repulsive. 
• Used to maintain concentration when invoking. 
• Overcome a phobia or avoid being driven insane. 
• To force oneself to continue to physically act despite near fail-
ure of the body.

Tasks 
Attribute saving throws provide good, fast resolution to 
unplanned situations that arise during play and require a test of 
ability against difficulty. Skills provide a measure against prac-
ticed ability and natural talent (attributes) versus difficulty. 
Between the two are tasks. Tasks are created to deal with situa-
tions where the Game Master desires a more repeatable test 
than an attribute saving throw, with on-the-fly situational modi-
fiers, and yet falls short of a trainable skill. Tasks allow the 
Game Master to create tests the player's must overcome that are 
more like skills but do not require advanced training. Also it is 
an opportunity to record a set of modifiers so that tasks are fair-
ly applied to each person who attempts them. Tasks should be 
prepared ahead of time and are generally written into an adven-
ture. Using them on the fly is generally too cumbersome and 
can slow game play, however they may be used if the GM feels 
they are appropriate. Tasks are created in this manner: 
Step 1: Describe the task. 
Indicate how the task is performed or overcome. Describe any 
circumstances surrounding the task and visual cues or descrip-
tions that may be part of the task. 
Step 2: Choose the attributes that apply. 
Pick one (or two) attributes that will be tested during the task. 
If more than two attributes will be tested, break the task up into 
more than one task leading to an overall goal. 
Step 3: Assign a difficulty rating. 
Remember that an attribute save against an average adventuring 
character produces between a 65% and 75% success rate on 
average. If you rate your task between 5 and 7, you produce 
the same average result, so modify up or down based on the dif-
ficulty compared to a simple attribute save. Consider how 
involved and how taxing the task will be. Is the task relatively 
easy, or a true test of ability that only a few will pass? 
Rating 
Task Difficulty 
4 or less 
Trivial 
5-7 
Easy (equivalent to most attribute saves) 
8-10 
Difficult 
11-13 
Hard 
14-16 
Harsh 
17-19 
Unforgiving 
20 or more 
Hopeless 
Step 4: Determine any modifiers 
Skills or conditions that might affect the outcome of the task 
should be recorded ahead of time, along with their modifiers to 
the task. This allows the task to be repeatable without the risk 
of making up different modifiers (as can happen with on the fly 
attribute saves). If it is determined that having (or successfully 
rolling) a skill provides a bonus of 10% to the task, it should 
always provide that 10% bonus. By recording it at this time it 
is guaranteed that the modifiers will always be + 10%. 
174 

===== PAGE 185 =====
Step 5: Set the Results (failure and success) 
Failure results in some undesirable outcome, or at the very least 
a failure of the task. Success produces positive results and a 
completion of the task. Optionally, critical success and failure 
conditions may be applied. 
Examples 
The Rope Swing 
Description: The Game Master is developing a scenario and 
places a deep spiked pit with a rope overhanging, allowing 
someone to swing from one end to the pit to the other if they 
have the knack. Although we could use Climbing to determine 
if they could climb the rope, that won't get them across the pit. 
We could have the individual make a Strength save to hold on, 
and an Agility save to swing across but then the difficulty could 
only be changed by adding in modifiers to two saves. A task 
better serves the overall goal of creating a repeatable test. 
Attributes: Strength is required to hold oneself aloft, Agility to 
swing across. This is a task testing Strength and Agility. 
Difficulty: The rope is thick and coarse allowing for an easy 
grip but the swing is far and footing on either side unsure. 
Therefore we will set the difficulty rating at 6. 
Modifiers: The successful usage of the skills Balance and 
Climb each provide a +20% to the chance. 
Results: Failure indicates that the tested has not made the other 
side. Critical failure means that tested has fallen into the pit. 
Success indicates the tested has safely made the other side. 
There is no critical success for this task. 
Darlok the Rogue attempts to make the other side. He grabs 
hold of the rope and swings. He has a 15 Strength and a 17 
Agility (on average of 17) against the rating of 6 this gives him 
a 55% ((17-6=ll)x5%). He also has the skills Climb and 
Balance. He makes the Climb skill roll but fails the Balance, 
increasing his chance from 55% to 75% (55% + 20% for suc-
cessful Climb). He rolls a 67% and makes the other side. 
Later Darlok's Friend, Yitza the Midfolk, brags that he can do it 
better and faster (now making Darlok's single feat a contest). 
Yitza has a 14 Strength and an 18 Agility (16 average) but is 
better at Balance and Climb and is confident he can beat 
Darlok's 67% roll. He bets his friend a few coins and takes his 
swing; 16 against 6 task rating produces a 50% chance (( 16-
6= I 0)x5% ). He makes both his Balance and Climb rolls, 
adding an additional +40% (+20% for each successful skill). 
With a 90% chance he rolls, getting a 70%, rolling 3% higher 
than Darlok. Darlok rolled a 67% against a 75% skill chance, 
so Darlok made his attempt by only 7% (75-67)%. Yitza rolled 
a 70% but had a 90% chance making it by 20% (almost a criti-
cal success), easily beating Darlok's showing. Darlok grumbles 
and pays Yitza his winnings. 
The Beauty Contest 
Description: Every year the city of rnidvale holds a beauty 
contest to determine the most beautiful, graceful and talented 
woman in city. Many compete for the prize but only one is 
crowned the Queen of rnidvale. 
Attributes: Although beauty is relative, Appearance measures 
the basic desirability and is an obvious attribute for this test. 
Because the contest involves talent Charm is also factor. 
Difficulty: This is a hard test, only a few women can compete 
for this honor. Therefore the difficulty rating will be set at 10. 
Modifiers: There are 5 judges each year; successful bribery of 
a judge increases odds by +20% per judge bribed. Only one 
individual can successfully bribe a judge-this will be whoever 
pays the most. Courtesan Social Skill provides a modest boost 
to performance in the contest of + 10% 
Results: Critical Failure means the contestant washes out in 
the early rounds. The winner and runner up are determined by 
the highest relative rolls in the contest. If all contestants fail 
then the lowest failure wins but the beauty contest itself is con-
sidered to be bad that year and not as good as in previous years. 
Nine women compete in the contest. One of the more average 
women (Anita) has bribed two of the judges, giving her a +40% 
edge, more than making up for her lack of high Charm. Only 
one other woman (Rhea) is a serious threat, a natural beauty 
from the outer farming districts of rnidvale, who is also quite 
charming. The other seven women fail their skill rolls, five crit-
ically fail and washout early. Anita has a 13 Charm and a 15 
Appearance (14 average) giving her only a 20% chance ((14-
10=2)x5% ), but the fix is in and her bribery has upped her odds 
to 60% (+40% for the 2 bribed judges). Rhea has an 18 
Appearance and a 17 Charm ( 18 average). This gives her a 
modest 40% chance ((18-10=8)x5%). Rhea rolls a 38 and is 
judged worthy but Anita rolls a 53. Anita is the winner (at least 
among the judges) because she has made her roll by 7% where 
Rhea made it by only 2%. The judges proclaim Anita the win-
ner but the common folk are suspicious.

CReatrn~ the Game 
No matter what anyone tells you, the true fun of the game is not 
the mechanics, but in the playing of the game itself-the adven-
tures that the players will experience. The game is what you, 
the Game Master, produce for your players. All of Imagine's 
rules and information is just a framework so the true game can 
be played. The style of the Game Master will influence the way 
that he runs his adventures. There are those that will glance 
through this book, look over a few things and then will start a 
loose, "fly by the seat of your pants" game. These Game 
Masters shrug off the need to prepare for a game or to plan out 
a session. If you are one of these, then the following sections 
may seem next to useless, as they describe how to organize and 
plan the game. However, players appreciate a well planned 
game and when Game Mastering Imagine, one will find that the 
game runs much smoother with some time spent on preparation. 
The other advantage of a prepared adventure is that provides a 
repeatable event that can conceivably be played over again with 
different groups. 
Running a game can be divided into five types: situations, sce-
narios, adventures and campaigns. They are defined as follows: 
Situation: These are single scenes where a single conflict arises 
and must be dealt with, ignored, pursued, erased, built-up, 
extended, met, etc. Situations can also be events that are mere-
ly for informational purposes or lead to other situations, scenar-
ios, etc. These situations are further divided into likely tasks 
and events. 
Scenario: A short story which is made up of a series of events 
that lead to some sort of a conclusion. Scenarios generally can 
be completed in a single game session, which may then have 
many possible situations and outcomes. 
An Adventure: A series of scenarios. 
A Campaign : A series of adventures. 
Situations 
If you want to role play for only a few hours, all you need to do 
is create a single or a few situations that will quickly develop 
and resolve. Sample situations are provided here for ideas:
