Running a Situation 
1) Pick a situation. Write down the specifics of who are the 
principle participants in the situation. Rarely will it be required 
to develop a full GMC for one situation. Use personalties or 
extras. Determine who are playing what roles in this situation. 
Create or write down words they might say, or general replies to 
questions that might be asked. 
2) Set possible resolutions if it is a conflict or overcoming type 
situation. 
3) Create tie-ins to other situations that might arise because of 
this situation. 
4) Set experience value of completing the situation if it is a task 
or overcoming type situation.

of the more important Situations is a good place to start. It is 
important to have a minimal setting to house the Scenario. A 
cast of extras, personalities and one or two GMCs needs to be

Scenario Building Guide 
1) Create or choose the starting setting. Draw or prepare maps 
of your setting areas. 
2) Create an event-task list out of possible situations. 
a) Create the initial event (situation) that begins the scenario. 
b) Create the task (situation) that lies at the heart of the 
scenario and create resolutions, some of which can lead to 
other situations or scenarios. Make failure consequences as 
well as possible extra rewards for excellent play. 
c) Create events that will happen based on time passing. 
d) Create tasks required to support the main task. Make 
consequences for more important tasks that are failed or not 
tried at all. 
e) Create tasks and events as subplots or sideplots to the main 
plot. 
3) Create the GMCs who are central to the plot and where they 
live, sleep, hangout, their goals and activities. 
4) Create the personalties and extras that will flush out your 
scenario. 
5) Write up any location-based encounters or encounter keys. 
Make reference to existing tasks/events that may transpire in 
the area. 
6) Check reward balances for situations and events within the 
whole scenario. Adjust accordingly and serve at room 
temperature. 
Adventures 
Adventures are more complex in that they usually involve a 
beginning, a middle and an end. Adventures consist of several 
scenarios strung together around a common theme or situation. 
Follow these: 
1) Create a starting scenario as outlined above that starts the 
adventure, handles background info, early research, equipment 
purchases and availability of resources needed to complete or 
plan the adventure as a whole. The starting scenario in an 
adventure usually ends when the players begin to journey to the 
real goal. This part of the adventure is called "finding out", and 
uses lots of informational skills. 
2) Create 1-3 scenarios that represent the middle piece. The 
middle piece can represent false leads, wrong paths, devise situ-
ations, and lead up to what will be in the final scenario. These 
situations are created as much to get the players to their final 
destination or situation as to prepare them to face it. When the 
players enter into solving the main situation directly the middle 
piece is done. The middle pieces are collectively called "get-
ting there." 
3) Create 1-2 final scenarios that represent the solving of the 
adventure. Many possible outcomes should be created, 
whether this is the overthrowing of the warlord, the unmasking 
of the master assassin, or returning the lost artifact. Have con-
tingencies for as many possible situations as you can in this 
piece. Have tie-ins to previous plot points that were developed 
in the earlier stages of the adventure. The final piece is called 
aptly, "finishing it." 
177 

===== PAGE 188 =====
Notes: Sometimes the adventure is held in a small setting, or 
the central situation defining the adventure does not call for 
three or more scenarios. Under these circumstances remove the 
"getting there" middJe piece. Whatever middle situations would 
normaJiy be used to connect the beginning and the end are 
saved and split between "finding out" and "finishing it." These 
can be treated as elapsed time. 
Campaigns 
A campaign has a grand theme, usually a large area event, a 
great reward, or a dangerous outcome if failed. There wilJ be 
many sub-plots and several key GMCs that will play a part 
directly and/or indirectly in the long term campaign. The cam-
paign should require more of the player, more time, more com-
mitment; a campaign can take months of real time to complete. 
Your major theme should have far reaching consequences, and 
after its completion the world itself will be changed. 
Sample Campaigns 
Save a race: A race is dying out or in grave danger. 
Create World Peace: Some how the party can stop wars, stop 
conflicts and keep the world at peace. 
Great War: Fight a great war, of races, or good against evil. 
Found a Nation: Start a new culture. 
Save a Nation: A culture is in trouble. 
Destroy an Artifact: Remove a dangerous power from existence. 
Find or create Artifact: Make, build, uncover, find an artifact. 
End Magic: Remove magic from the world. 
Lost Race: Uncover the secrets of a lost race. 
God War: The gods themselves are at war. 
Armageddon: The end of the world is nigh. 
Save the World: Keep the world from being destroyed. 
Travel of the Planes: Seek adventure in alternate planes/dimen-
sions. 
Conquer the world: Become the ultimate leader(s). 
Godhood: Become deities. 
Bring down a God: Fight a deity. 
Apocalypse: Cataclysmic event. 
Planar War: War between the planes. 
Dimensional Invasion: From afar a foe comes. 
End Injustice: Stop an injustice like slavery, etc. 
Rebellion: Fight to change a culture for good or ill. 
1) Create 1-2 adventures as lead-ins. Decide which GMCs will 
be paramount during the campaign as villains, patrons or allies. 
Present them in these early situations even if it is through infor-
mation rather than a direct meeting. Often the first adventure 
masks the importance of the campaign by disguising it as a sim-
ple mission. The resolution of the first adventure often brings 
realization of the campaign. 
2) Create as many adventures as you need to handle sub-plots, 
resolve early conflicts, isolate the final solution. Create GMCs 
and GMPs that will come and go and will have periodic con-
tact with the players to create a consistency. 
3) Create 1-3 adventures that determine resolution of the central 
theme. One entire adventure here might be thrown away if the 
completion of the theme happens early. Preparation here is 
most important because the conflict has been building for many 
game sessions. Make sure to use as many tie-ins to earlier 
events as possible and to adjust the strengths and powers of any 
beings, or items in the final conflicts. 
RewaRbs 
Part of the excitement of adventuring is the rewarding experi-
ence it can bring your players in terms of advancement, gain of 
power, magic, knowledge and control of their environment. 
Rewards are divided into these types as noted below and themes 
for their use and management are suggested. 
Experience 
Imagine is a system that generalizes the idea of adventure relat-
ed learning into experience. Experience is checked against the 
single Universal experience chart for advancement. Goal 
advancement represents incremental improvement and Title 
advancement represents evolutionary improvement. But when 
too much experience is given too quickly, its perceived value is 
lost and the life span of a character is shortened by arriving too 
early at its end. When too little is given, the character's growth 
can stagnate. How then does one keep experience balanced? 
Because of the two Title cap, no character can advance more 
than two Titles at a time. Still this is an outside edge. If this is 
the sole block to advancement then in five sessions a character 
could rise from 1st to 10th Title. In most cases a two goal limit 
is more desirable. How then do you limit experience? A good 
first step is to remove experience for magical treasure. This is 
an option that is not always necessary, especially when the 
treasure itself usually leads to more direct power and is there-
fore its own reward. Next, limit combat experience. If the 
creature has been fought by the group before, reduce experience 
by 5% or 10% each time until by the 10th or 20th time the party 
has fought skeletons (and are no longer learning anything new), 
they gain no experience. Do not reward combat experience for 
random killing that does not relate to the objectives at hand for 
the scenario, adventure or campaign. The main thing is to avoid 
the encounters sought by players for experience sake. It is often 
said that whatever you reward you get more of. Therefore 
reward successful, directed combat more than casual, looking 
for experience, killing. The experience shown for encounter 
combat in the Experience section is the maximum potential that 
should ever be rewarded. Reward the highest amount for 
encountered leaders, obstacles to scenario goals, etc. Reward 
less for tangents of the storylines and even less, if any at all, for 
outright departures from it. Intelligence Experience, as offered 
in Imagine, rewards players for intelligent choices and risks. 
Avoid rewarding dice rolls. Convincing the local Priest that 
their dead friend should be resurrected is worth experience, hav-
ing every Priest in your party randomly rolling a skill and then 
rewarding the "lucky roll" is not.

Magic 
ls your world magic light, or magic heavy? Will the players be 
required to have magic items to survive or merely gain addi-
tional power with them? How easy is it to produce magic items 
in your world? Since the Imagine spell and invocation systems 
provide clear methods for producing items, higher level charac-
ters will want to do this unless you have placed artificial barri-
ers within the world. You may say that every item requires a 
loss of a life as well as Will Force, or that only at certain rare 
moments (or places) can items be enchanted or imbued. Or you 
may want to allow many items. Whatever you decide, make 
certain that your GMCs, GMPs and GMEs have a proportional 
share of magic and that the party does not seem to have a dis-
proportional one.

dard which the GM can use to gauge the amount of magic items 
characters might have at various Titles. The table assumes a 
game world with an amount of magic which would be expected 
in a typical high fantasy setting. Of course these are guidelines, 
and a character need not have these exact ratios.

Of course these are guidelines and should help you decide how 
often to give out items, but remember that some characters may 
wind up with more and may suddenly defeat an opponent or 
character who has several herself. Remember this when giving 
items to the character's adversaries. 
Knowledge 
Information within a game world is it's own sort of power. 
There are secrets, lost lores, hidden factions, shadow govern-
ments, lost civilizations and the like. Imagine has a rich list of 
infonnational skills and social skills. These should be fed regu-
larly by the Game Master. Background in the setting must be 
complete enough to provide, history, secret lores, lost arts, leg-
ends, etc. When creating scenarios, make certain to include the 
use of as many informational skills as possible. Information is 
always the back story behind any gaming experience. The more 
the players learn, the more it will be etched on their memories 
and the more believable it will be for them. You as a GM can 
never have too much infonnation. About a quarter of a GMs 
game development time should be spent creating background 
information for the setting and the scenario. The reward of 
being prepared is the ability to reward the exceptional players 
for their interest in your game setting. 
Power 
Characters gain power by becoming influential in factions, con-
trolling expanding regions and resources, or by gaining direct 
control of populations. This should ever be a balancing act. 
The more the player character controls, the less time he should 
have for actual adventuring and the less likely he can do so 
without direct intervention by rival factions. If the king of the 
west decides he wants to personally clear out the Goblin hordes 
from the swamps he may get away with it the first time but 
opponents will seize future opportunities to kill the king, or take 
over his holdings in his absence. Under ideal conditions, power 
becomes consuming and a character gracefully retires from 
adventuring life to pursue other interests. Many a well played 
character survived to higher Title only to retire into a public life 
of leadership. Some players find much satisfaction in achieving 
this goal and often consider themselves to have "won" at that 
point. 
Summary 
Control experience rewards through; 
a. Experience Cap (2 Titles, or 2 goals). 
b. Reduce by 5% to 10% each encounter of a previously 
overcome creature. 
c. Combat experience is rewarded fully for direct scenario 
objectives only, not killing sprees. 
d. Reduce or remove experience for treasure. 
e. Do not reward lucky rolls with Intelligence Experience. 
Base magic as reward through; 
a. How magical the setting is. 
b. Requirements for survival (at higher Titles). 
c. The amount of magic carried by GMCs in the setting. 
d. How restrictive producing the item is within the setting. 
e. How much control over the setting magic provides. 
Base knowledge as reward through; 
a. Develop settings to answer informational skill rolls. 
b. Develop scenarios with informational skills in mind. 
c. Make and protect secrets, lost lores, dead cultures, etc. 
d. Knowledge adds structure and believability. 
e. The GM can never have too much information. 
Base power as a reward through; 
a. Remember to give responsibility with power. 
b. The more power one has the more powerful one's 
enemies. 
c. An adventuring career may be curtailed or ultimately 
abandoned. 
d. Can be the final goal of an experienced character. 
The greatest reward is a good play experience. You as a Grune 
Master determine just how rich that environment can be. 
Players will sense when you are unable to handle their interests 
and unable to create a rewarding playing experience. The play-
ers may never realize the full potential of what you offer them, 
but a good time can still be had by all.

AwaRbmr; ExpeR1ence 
Experience is a crucial aspect of any Imagine game. Too much 
and the characters run over the world, imposing their wills upon 
it. Too little and they become bored, unable to advance, and 
unable to tackle progressively more challenging situations. 
When designing adventures pay particular care to the amount of 
experience that is available. If the character or party would 
advance too quickly, then perhaps the adventure is not suitable. 
Again, too little available, probably means that there is no chal-
lenge involved. 
Experience is acquired at different times and in different ways. 
Chiefly these are combat, intelligent moves (intelligence experi-
ence), good roleplaying (role-playing experience) spell acquisi-
tion (spell experience), healing (healer's experience), and treas-
ure (magic items, potions, and herbs experience). 
Combat Experience 
When to Award Experience 
Two methods can be used to distribute experience. The second 
is more realistic but not always practical for gamers who cannot 
play often or for long sessions. They are: 
1) Experience is awarded at the end of the gaming session. 
2) Only experience gained through treasure is given immedi-
ately; all others are given to a character as he awakens the next 
morning (or the next time he sleeps). If a character does not 
sleep or rest for at least a four hour period he cannot immedi-
ately absorb the events of the previous day. In such cases, save 
the experience and apply it the foUowing day. If the character 
does not adequately sleep for more than three days then he loses 
one day of stored experience for each day over three he is 
unable to sleep. The character will likely be extremely fatigued 
at this point and is unlikely to earn much experience anyway. 
As a rule of thumb no character can store more than three day's 
worth of experience. Treasure experience which is given imme-
diately is only given once. 
Combat experience is detennined by the value of the creature(s) which have been fought. Creatures which have already been creat-
ed have an experience value attached. When creating opponents or creatures of your own, the following table is used to detennine 
experience value. This value will be modified by several factors, explained below.

Modifiers to Combat Experience 
The amount of experience received for each combat can be 
modified by several factors. The first is a set of modifiers that 
have to do with certain conditions of the combatants at or dur-
ing combat:

The total experience of a creature or opponent can be very high, 
and this number is intended to be awarded only in the most 
extreme cases where the party has truly earned the experience. 
In most cases, only a percentage of the experience should be 
given. The percentage of experience is based upon two addi-
tional factors to those listed above. These are called "risk to 
self' and "means of kill" modifiers. 
Modifers by Risk to Self 
At combats end, the GM should set a value called "risk to self'. 
The number is an assigned percentage, in 10% increments, 
which basically which reflects the risk of death or serious injury 
that a character or group faced while in the combat The total 
experience of a creature is then multiplied by this number, and 
that is the actual amount of experience that the character(s) 
should receive. 
Example I: A Ranger waits in ambush with a loaded arrow and 
while hidden with the skill Blend. When an unsuspecting 
Goblin walks past, the Ranger rolls for surprise and is success-
ful. He then aims for 3 seconds and fires into the unarmored 
neck of the Goblin, who never even knew what hit him. 
Goblin total experience: 200 
Risk to Self: 10%. 
Modified experience: 200 x 10% = 20 
Example 2: A Warrior madly wades into five heavily armored 
Goblins of 2 levels higher than his Title and somehow kills 
them all without dying. 
Goblin total experience: 200 each 
Risk to Self: 100%. 
Modified experience: 200 x 5 = 1000 x 100% = 1000 
Modifiers by Means of Kill 
A second important modifier is caUed "means of kill". The 
number is an assigned percentage, in 10% increments, which 
reflects the failure chance of the tools and methods being used 
to win the combat relative to the opponent(s) being fought. The 
lower the percentage, the more likely that the means of kill 
would be successful, and the higher the number, the greater the 
chance that the means of kill would be unsuccessful. The total 
experience of a creature is then multiplied by this number, and 
that is the actual amount of experience that the character(s) 
receive.

===== PAGE 193 =====

using +6 arrows of Piercing with the Seeking ability. 
Goblin total experience: 200

10%.

Example 2: Assume the Warrior in the example above went into 
the fight bare handed or with a simple club. 
Goblin total experience: 200 each 
Risk to Self: 
100%. 
Means of kill: 100% 
Modified experience: 200 x 5 = 1000 x 100% x 100% = 1000 
Dividing Combat Experience 
There are many ways to divide combat experience amongst a 
party, but in general the character(s) who had the most involve-
ment in the combat, or removed the most opponents from the 
contlict, should receive the lion's share of experience. A good 
recommendation is to gauge proportionally how much each 
character was responsible for the outcome of the conflict and 
divide the experience accordingly. If the Priest gives his all to 
destroy the undead leader and yet is rendered unconscious at the 
very last moment of the battle, but his Midfolk sidekick finishes 
the badly wounded undead leader off with a lucky sling shot 
(blessed by the Priest), the Priest should still receive most of the 
experience with the Midfolk getting the remainder. Were it not 
for the Priest they would never have stood a chance against. 
This method will tend to reward the Warriors over other classes, 
which is as it should be. Other classes have their own methods 
of receiving experience. Players and GMs are free to agree on 
any other alternate method of experience distribution. 
Treasure Experience 
The character who correctly identifies a magic item, potion, 
herb, or anything else of value is given 10% of its experience 
value and 90% is given to the finder of the treasure. Parties can 
agree to split experience equally for treasure if they wish. 
Rogue and rogue subclasses, however, are the only classes that 
get experience for money earned. They earn one experience 
point per 5 gold pieces in value appropriated (stolen, swindled 
or found). Other classes do not earn experience from gold, 
gems and similar valuables which are purely monetarily based. 
However, they can be a factor in improving Social Class and 
thus may provide intelligence experience if used wisely. Note 
that treasure experience is optional and some Game Masters 
may choose not to apply it.

Experience Value for Other Lores (poems, songs, formulae, 
found rituals, etc.): Base experience equals 50x the rating of 
the skill. It is further modified by the rating of the lore. If the 
lore found has a lower rating than the skill rating, use the fol-
lowing method: for every one point that the rating of the ritual 
is below the rating of the skill, subtract 25 experience. 
This translates into the following formula: 
(S0x skill rating) - (skill rating - lore rating) x 25 
If the lore found has a higher rating than the skill rating, use the 
following method: for every one point that the rating of the rit-
ual is above the rating of the skill, add I 00 experience. 
This translates into the following formula: 
(S0x skill rating) + (lore rating - skill rating) x 100 
Lores researched are worth half of the normal experience value. 
Lores traded for or purchased are worth 1/4 value.

Adventure Bonuses: Characters that do extremely well during 
an adventure may be awarded a bonus at the end. Bonuses are 
a based on the total experience received during the course of the 
adventure. Bonuses range from 1-10% of the experience gained 
on an adventure. Perhaps Namba the Warrior has lead her party 
through danger and peril and has done extremely well, both in 
the goals of the adventure and in how well she played. The GM 
elects to give her a 5% experience bonus. She earned 12,500 
experience on the adventure. Her bonus would be 5% of 
12,500 or 625 experience received the next game day. 
Experience for Other Actions 
The GM should realize that players will continue to do those 
actions which get rewarded with experience, and that experi-
ence can provide a means for directing the players. For exam-
ple, some GMs give a small experience bonus to those players 
who show up on time. Still others will give experience to a 
player who can give a brief summary of what happened at the 
last gaming session (an excellent technique for getting everyone 
in the mood and remembering their character's current situation 
after a long time between game sessions).

erhaps the true key to successful

Master who has a well devel-

Most garners who have partici-

the difference between a game where the world was 
an endless scenario of random monster encounters, 
and one where there was tangled web of politics, col-

factions. The first is certainly worthwhile for an 
evening's entertainment and often gets people 
involved in role playing, but the latter keeps them 
corning back. It is this difference that keeps your 
players scheduling games and making time for your 
game over others. I have often heard formulas for 
success, such as spending four hours preparing for 
every hour of game time or use as many props (lost 
maps, fantasy coins, etc.) as possible. Still others 
urge stage voices or sound effects. Use these effects 
as you wish, but focus on your setting. Create a 
believable setting and you will overcome more obsta-
cles before you even begin to play. Create the planes 
of your universe, the forces that drive it, the gods 
that rule it. Set the races that populate it and fill it 
with magic, monsters and mayhem. Some settings 
will have few if any strange creatures. Some fantas-
tic worlds will approach a "Disneyesque" quality as 
they possess legions of fantasy beings and creatures. 
As with everything else in this book, it's yours to 
decide. This section will round out the volume and 
bring together the other sections to allow you to pro-
duce your own Imagine game setting. 
Terms Used for Settings 
Module: A section of a world, including its cultures, his-
tory, leaders, magic, classes, etc. 
World: A collection of modules which make up a planet. 
Plane: A collection of worlds and general laws which 
make a universe. 
Multiverse: A sum of planes. 
Setting: The sum total of all of these parts and player 
experiences.

The Planes 
The planes are an area that can be overlooked in a setting. 
It is easy to wave your hands as a GM and make the planes 
unreachable and not a factor of the setting. Fantastic planes 
with strange energies, effects and connections to other planes 
will instead allow your players to enter a realm rich with possi-
bility. Perhaps they will find a gateway to another dimension, 
or an item that draws on the power of fire from the plane of 
fire. When you have decided which planes you want, it may 
help to draw a structure to these planes or make a chart showing 
their linkages. The following are examples of planes that you 
may wish to include in your multi-verse. 
T fpes OF Planes 
Earthly or Prime Plane 
This is where the characters live and die. Unless you are ready 
to have characters be created or born on other planes and have 
them live their lives there this will be your setting for most 
adventures. 
The Phase plane 
"He stood before us as a pale ghost, breathless and unable to 
move except to raise an arm or turn his head. Our hands 
passed through him and no sound issued from his lips even 
when it was obvious he was trying to speak to us. If it weren't 
for the lip reading ability of our Rogue Jess , we would never 
have known he was phased. " 
The phase plane can be reached by spells, invocation or skills 
like Phase, Planewalk, and the like. This place needs to be 
accessible in all settings, otherwise spells, skills, invocations, 
abilities and effects that access the phase plane will not func-
tion. This plane is not technically a plane of it's own; instead it 
is forever connected to the prime plane. It is sometimes 
referred to as the plane of shadows or the betwixt. Beings, 
creatures and objects on the phase plane can be seen on the 
prime plane but appear grayed, faded out, and semi-translucent. 
While on the phase plane people and objects on the prime plane 
appear to be phased out, and phased beings and objects appear 
more distinct and clear. 
The appearance of the phase plane itself is a misty fog with no 
direct source of light. Because it exists parallel to the prime 
plane, light from the prime plane will provided a dim and dif-
fuse light of half the luminosity and strength on the phase plane. 
The sun itself does not provide a visible ball on the phase plane, 
but rather a diffuse light that will make it appear to be twilight 
with no obvious source. In all cases visibility is never more 
than a few hundred feet even with a phased light source. There 
is no obvious ground or sky. The phase plane has no up or 
down except in relation to the prime plane and is infinite. 
There is no gravity. Objects and beings placed on the phase 
plane remain motionless unless propelled by magic or pushed 
against by a force of more mass. If a person pushes off a large 
phased boulder he will go away from the boulder at a rate equal 
to the strength of his push minus the difference in mass. So if 
he is out-massed by the boulder by 2 to I, he will move at 1/2 
the strength of his push and the boulder will move away at 1/4 
the strength ( 1/4 of the force being lost in the push itself). The 
medium of the phase plane is such that motion is reduced by 
I/10th of it's force per minute, coming slowly to a rest in 10 
minutes. Only something that applies constant force can main-
tain constant speed. 
There is no air on the phase plane. Beings transported to this 
plane are in a kind of breathless limbo, neither breathing nor 
requiring breath. Because of this, phased beings fatigue at 
twice the normal rate and are considered to be exerting them-
selves even standing still. There is no need to eat or drink 
while phased, but a toll is still enacted against the body, aging 
phased beings at twice the normal rate. Beings or animals that 
die on the phase plane do not pass on to the higher planes 
unless directly summoned by divine will (or minions thereof), 
instead becoming ghosts, (or sometimes worse), haunting this 
plane for all time. Sound does not carry well on the phase 
plane, losing strength four times as quickly as on the prime 
plane. Smell and taste are non-existent, but touch is unaffected. 
Beings on the phase plane cannot communicate or take any 
actions against those on the prime and vice versa. This includes 
mental attack or magical force. Some effects (Phase Weapon) 
create objects that are distinct in both planes and overcome this 
problem, and are the only exception. These objects can be 
moved on one plane and will move effortlessly through the 
other plane, unless the object strikes something on either plane. 
There are a couple of known ways to communicate between 
phase and prime plane, these include the spell (or effect) 
Interdimensional Message, hand gestures or somatic languages, 
and lip reading. 
Planes of the Elements 
Air (cold), Fire (heat), Water (acid), Earth (electricity), Magic 
(Aura). These 5 planes can be used to represent the basic forces 
from which magical energy is drawn. Air provides air elemen-
tals of both divine and magical types, and through the chill of 
its winds, frost and cold based magics. Fire represents the fun-
damental magical energy of fire and the elementals of fiery 
countenance and temperament. The plane of water in concen-
trated form allows the drawing of magical acids and the hard 
pounding froth of the elementals of wave and surf. The earthly 
plane houses iron and magnetism, and beneath its surface elec-
tricity is stored in magical rock. The unyielding earth and 
rocky elementals come from this plane. The plane of magic is 
the chaos of pure unused energy that is neither light nor dark, 
that is prismatic and blinding. Without this plane or some other 
form of magic source, magic use is impossible (see magic 
sources in the Magic section). 
Planes of Light and Darkness 
The planes of light (luminous, life) and darkness (void, death) 
188 

===== PAGE 199 =====
are planes usually used as the source of Life magic and death 
magic. They are made up of energies that sustain and promote 
life and those that degrade and diminish life, or replace life 
itself with a living death (undead). Without these planes it 
becomes difficult to explain positive and negative magics or the 
existence of undead beings. 
Ether or Astral 
This plane can Lay between worlds or it can be a connecting 
point between all other planes. It is often the location used by 
the spell Cache. This plane should be considered very sparse 
but may have it's own beings and places of unusual note. 
Plane of Dreams (The Veil of Illusion) 
This plane is often considered to be illusionary and the source 
of illusions and glamours. Some abilities allow for the extension 
into this plane without actually leaving the earthly plane. The 
skill Mind Dance or Thought Projection allows the practitioner 
to join others' dreams and alternately enter this dream plane. In 
the dream plane anything that can be willed can be made (Will 
Force save). Often horrors appear because the weak willed 
allow their fears to run rampant. This can be a great plane to 
add depth and dimension to your world, allowing contact to 
dreamers and might even prompt an additional class of dream 
weaver or dream walker. 
Upper Plane(s) 
This can be the home of good gods. They can share one plane 
or each have their own as you see fit. These planes are paradise-
like and are often gardens or grand cities of perfections where 
souls gather to pay homage to their deities or serve them in 
strange ill understood fashions. The Upper planes often cause 
pain, damage or ailment to beings of evil. 
Middle Plane(s) 
This can be your home for the neutral gods. These planes are 
also closest to the earthly or prime plane. These planes are not 
as idyllic as the Upper planes, but are often linked in greater 
fashion to the daily workings of the prime plane. These minions 
are more likely to be meddling in the affairs of mortals than 
either gods of the upper or lower planes. 
Lower Plane(s) 
This can be the home of the evil gods. These halls of Hades 
and perdition exist to torment dead mortals and provide pleas-
ure to their evil masters. The evil beings that run in the 
extremes of the Lower planes are twisted, malice filled beasts 
whose very existence is often at the pleasure of whatever master 
they serve. Good beings can suffer pain, damage or ailment 
from visits to these places of ice and fire, terror and torment. 
Racial home planes 
Other races may not be naturally occurring on the prime plane 
and may be linked to other planes. Fairies and Elves are oft 
times connected to a plane of Fey (Faerie). Dwarves may come 
from a rockhome where there is no sky at all just great furnaces 
of warmth and tunnels. 
Order and Chaos 
Two great planes when used together. Order seeks to bind 
things together, to create a logical consistent whole. Chaos 
seeks to tear things apart and allow individual freedom. 
Parallel worlds 
Places very similar to the current prime plane but with strange 
differences, like a world having an alternate plane of earth. 
Strange planes 
Some example concepts for such planes are: forms (Plato), 
patchwork, time, garbage, lost items, machines, nexus, insanity. 
PRopeRtJeS OF Planes 
Effects of Magic and Divine Magic 
Different planes affect magic in diverse ways. Some ideas: 
•Magic/divine magic operates as normal. 
•Magic and/or divine magic doesn't operate at all. 
•Magic and/or divine magic power is increased. (higher 
Aura/Aura Control and/or higher divine invoker Title/Piety 
Control). 
•Magic and/or divine magic power is decreased. (lower 
Aura/Aura Control and/or lower divine invoker Title/Piety 
Control). 
•Energy effects are changed: (increase, decrease, fizzle or com-
pletely altered). 
•Some type of effect is altered (life, death, illusions, etc). 
•Source of magic or divine magic is altered. 
•New spells or effects may be possible. Special spells, invoca-
tion or skills that only work on this plane. 
Planar Boundaries 
Define the boundaries of the plane and how they connect or do 
not connect to other planes. 
Closed: No direct open connection to other planes, and travel 
there by magic is usually blocked. 
Open: No direct connections to other planes but travel there by 
magic is permitted. 
Direct: 1 or more planar boundries are connected to other 
planes. 
Veiled: One or more openings (veils) appear randomly or by 
some pattern connecting this plane to one or more other planes. 
Gated: Fixed or permanent gates or gateways exist between 
this and other planes. 
Merged: This plane and one or more other planes are merged 
or just offset from each other (Prime and Phase). 
Altered: Any of the above, but crossing the planar boundary 
causes some alteration to the being who crosses it which may or 
may not be undone by recrossing the boundary. 
Life 
Life is considered a force as represented by Will Force. It can 
be disrupted or affected by different planes. The following are 
189 

===== PAGE 200 =====
suggested ways that life force is affected on various planes: 
Ideal: Paradise for the soul. Lost Will Force (non-permanent 
losses) returns at twice the normal rate (2 per hour usually). 
Aging is slowed to half the normal rate here. 
Normal: No effects. 
Requires Aid: Less air in the plane; may require magic to sus-
tain beings who breathe it. 
Fixed: Aging is stopped. 
Ages: Aging is accelerated. 
Detrimental: Has a negative effect on life energy. Fatigue or 
mental fatigue may be result. Damage, physical or otherwise, 
may be taken. 
Toxic: Poisons beings in any of a variety of ways, air, foods or 
something similar. 
Hellish: Has a strong negative impact on life energy. Will 
Force lost does not return when lost on this plane. Aging is 
twice normal. Kills instantly or requires periodic saves or 
resistances to avoid death. 
Planar Special Effects 
Adding these spices in the right quantity can make your planes 
very unique and make them even more unlike the earthly plane. 
No Wishes/Miracles: This plane is too touched by order to be 
warped by wishes or miracles. 
Spontaneous Wishes/Miracles: Chaos touches directly upon 
this plane and as such wishes and miracles can be a daily event, 
though often unexpectedly occurring at odd rhythms or through 
some power. 
Wild Magic: This plane is plagued by regions where magic 
runs wild. In these places spells and effects are likely to warp 
and become other spells or effects. Magic effects just go off in 
these regions, perhaps with no rhyme or reason. 
Rifts: This plane has areas that are voids. These rifts must be 
crossed with magic and may isolate portions of the plane. 
Parallel Universe Contact: This plane occasionally connects 
with parallels of itself. Sometimes creating very bizarre results 
such as when good and evil individuals switch places, or when 
a ruler in one dimension becomes a pauper in the next. 
Crossover can occur at random or through some sort of rhythm. 
Spheres of Life: In this plane the life energy creates for itself a 
sphere of life allowing for survival in an otherwise unsurvivable 
environment. The sphere is governed by the Will Force of the 
being and grows or shrinks with gains or losses in Will Force 
such that complete loss of Will Force, even temporarily, will 
cause the sphere to completely dissipate possibly killing the 
individual or exposing them to the harmful effects of the plane. 
Everpresent Luck: Random amount of luck are added to every 
action. 
Everpresent Unluck: Random amounts of unluck are added to 
every action. 
Wild Fate: Random amounts of luck or unluck are added to 
every action. This could be determined 50%/50%, be set by the 
day or by some bizarre rhythm or pattern. 
Fate: Each being has a fate. Their fate allows influence points 
that can be applied within some length of time. The number of 
influence points and the length of time are set by the GM. 
Perhaps everyone is born with a random amount of fate (say 
5d4) that they can use up in their lifetime or each person gets 
ld4 influence points to use per day. Influence points differ from 
luck or unlucky points in that they can be used after the die is 
cast to influence it in their favor. 
Time is threaded: Time is a river with many crossed streams 
and channels. There are many paths and time travel or future 
sight only sees one of these paths. When you travel towards the 
future, you travel to one of many possible or simultaneously 
existing futures. 
Predestination: The future is set. In this plane if someone 
looks into the future they see exactly what is going to happen. 
The future is firmly set by a present that is known. All is fixed. 
Free will is illusionary. 
Astrology: The movement of stars, celestial bodies or other 
phenomenon really does affect living beings. This means that 
same beings may be lucky one day, unlucky the next. They 
may have a greater or lesser power on a certain day, etc. 
Immortals among us: Occasionally, immortals are born into the 
mortal society. This may be by a set plan or may be random. 
These immortals may have special powers or they may just 
have the gift of immortality. One suggestion is that they become 
the only beings allowed to advance beyond 10th Title in these 
planes. 
Undeath follows death: Plane of the living dead. Anytime 
something dies it is reborn as some form of undead. The form 
of undead can be set, determined by Will Force or a variety of 
factors involved. 
Reverse Aging: Beings spontaneously appear in advanced age 
and then age backwards until they disappear at normal birth. 
The cause and effect law must be suspended in this plane. 
Life is Wheel: Life is truly cyclic all beings store Karma points 
based upon their actions. If they store enough Karma, then they 
advance at death to the next stage of life. Perhaps by being 
born as a criminal and then saving a child from a life on the 
streets, they can earn enough points to become a craftsman in 
the next life. The soul is literally recycled and goes from host 
to host. The soul does not travel on to a higher plane, or if it 
does, it does so only for a period of respite between lives. The 
soul can inhabit any creature, though the creature may not sense 
the soul and the soul may not manifest itself in obvious ways. 
Worlds are created by sleeping beings: This plane is all in the 
mind of one or more beings. Should those beings awaken all 
will end (at least until that being dreams again). Some manifes-
tation of that being should exist on that plane. 
Forces in conflict 
An interesting thing to do is to create forces that are in conflict 
on your plane. These conflicts allow for high adventure when 
one is threatening to over-balance the other or merely to serve 
one or the other force. Below are some sample conflicting 
190 

===== PAGE 201 =====
forces for your multiverse are provided. You can use these to 
produce themes or grand scale backgrounds within your setting: 
Good vs. Evil: Good or evil wiU prevail; which is stronger? 
Growth vs. Decay: Life expands; death conquers. 
Expansion vs. Compression: Everything becomes contiuously 
more sparse; everything narrows. 
Complexity vs. Simplicity: Complexity produces greater results; 
simplicity is easier. 
Spiritualism vs. Hedonism: Spirituality produces lasting happi-
ness; hedonism produces instant happiness. 
Natural vs. Supernatural: Natural life will overcome; supernat-
ural life is eternal. 
Magic vs. Divinity: Magic is controllable; divinity controls. 
Mundane vs. Magical: Mundane is the right way to be; magic 
gives power. 
Wisdom vs. Bliss: Wisdom comes from seeking; bliss comes 
from acceptance. 
Knowledge vs. Ignorance: Knowledge allows better choices; 
ignorance is freedom to choose blindly. 
Form and Substance of Planes 
Each plane has a form, even if that form is a nothingness. 
Many forms are listed below as ideas; some of these can be 
combined. 
Void: Empty of all things except for possible native beings. 
Gulfs of Void: Mostly empty with some pockets of life or exis-
tence. 
Ether: An ether permeates everything and extends forever in 
all directions. This ether suspends living things in it that are not 
propelled by magic. 
Energy: The plane consists of energy flowing in many shapes 
and directions. The energy depends on the plane as does the 
shape and form of the energy seen. 
Flat: The plane is literally a geometrical plane. A one or two 
sided single sheet of land that may be boundless or have a set 
dimension. 
Pocket: This plane is a pocket, with some sort of defined or 
established boundary around it. 
Crystal Spheres: This plane is made up of spheres of worlds 
that are surrounded by crystals. These crystals give off light but 
do so in patterns of day and night that cycles as they give off 
light and then recharge. (The light moves around the crystal 
creating a full day and night.) Each crystal has a set lifespan. 
When the crystal fails so does light, then life. 
Great Ocean: The plane is made up of a vast sea of liquid on a 
flat surface. It may be bottomless and endless or it may have 
set boundaries. There can be islands or continents or it could be 
all ocean in all directions forever. There may be breathable air 
in a sheet above the ocean or there may be nothing but the 
ocean itself. 
Great creature: The world is on the back of a great creature 
that is supported by the cosmos. It may be a great turtle, for 
instance. There may be many such creatures or only one. 
Normal Universe: This plane has normal stars and star forma-
tions, planets and moons, etc. There are vast distances between 
these objects that are not easily travelled. Beings can only live 
on those that provide an abundance of materials needed for life.

Magic is the element of fantasy which makes it truly unique, 
and you as a Game Master must decide how great a role it will 
play in your world. If magic is scarce it will be hoarded, fought 
over and desired. If it is common, it will become a necessary 
building block to surviving as a character. In some settings, 
Mages, Witches and other spellcasters are feared and hunted 
like animals. They hold strange power and talent that the "nor-
mal" folk are trying to eradicate from the world. In other 
worlds, magic is as common and mundane as baking. Use the 
information and tables that follow to enhance the magical expe-
rience and help you decide how magic will color your game 
world.

Everyone commands Aura at different levels and Aura regener-

many who pursue mage-craft. It is common enough to generate 
abilities referred to as magical skilJs.

Material 
A particular substance such as crysteel or chromantium is 
deemed to be magical in nature and the source of magic for this 
world. The area of normal magic is determined by the size of 
the piece. Each cubic inch of material should be deemed to add 
magic to one mile diameter circle and each doubling adds an 
additional mile. Alternately, a small portion could be made into 
objects of power that radiate magic. Those within range of the 
objects or material can feel it if they have Detect Magic and can 
draw upon it as a source of magic. If you choose to deal with 
magic in this way, you will need to make decisions on how it 
will affect certain skills (such as Hermetic Lore.)

Magic involves great secrets, and these secrets are locked into 
specific locations called taps. Unbelievable energies must be 
tapped into to achieve magic. These secrets are priceless and 
wars are fought over the secrets of tapping magic. They are 
tapped into by word, deed, magical keys or ingredients. 
Possibly even some undiscovered mechanisms awaits to unlock 
the keys to magic. Sources are divided into types and their 
effects are based on type. 
Using Magic: Most magical skill usage requires a certain 
amount of Aura to be available but not consumed. Necessary 
available Aura is equal to 2 times the Practitioner's Title. Use 
of the powers in a magic item require taps themselves. The 
greatest of items are infused permanently with links into the 
taps. Direct magical links to taps exist in limited numbers, tap-
ping directly into these unlimited sources of magical power. 
There may be only one tap in a world or there may be dozens. 
Great battles are fought over such places of power. 
Personal Aura Level: Beings do not have Aura available for 
anything but defensive needs unless they have a permanent 
magical tap. Each "point" of permanent magical tap allows the 
available Aura for immediate use to rise by the number of 
points in the permanent tap. It can never rise above the actual 
Aura rating of any being. 
Access to Taps: The standard mage should start the game with 
up to three lesser permanent taps. In this type of world every 
spellcaster needs Absorb Aura to survive so a +20% modifier is 
given to the skill for everyone whether they possess the skill or 
will later obtain it in the future through advancement. Each tap 
is accessed by a successful Absorb Aura skill roll. (However, 
no Aura containers may be created with the skill Absorb Aura). 
In this setting taps can be connected to magic items as part of 
the enchantment process. Taps can be active or non-active. 
The magic user can be tapped into one source per Title and is 
allowed one additional active tap per Title.

Combinations 
You can make strange combinations of the above types like Iey 
lines and focal points, or material and tapped. Think up your 
own using the preceding information as guidelines to help you 
develop your own unusual sources of magic. 
Metaph}?sical Laws 
Magic needs laws and principles just as the physical world 
does. This allows the Game Master to add believability to the 
force of magic which is the hardest thing to do in any fantasy 
setting. If players want to make new spells or effects make sure 
none of the metaphysical laws are broken. These laws are 
meant to be representative of a fantasy magic system and in no 
way are meant to be seen as real laws of any form of real magic 
or belief. You may have different laws for each plane in your 
multiverse or the entire multiverse may obey the same laws. 
The following are some suggested laws. 
Magic Equilibrium: In magical worlds you will need a law that 
allows magic to exist without destroying your entire multiverse. 
This law states for every magical effect there is an equal and 
balancing effect even if that effect is spread out over a large 
area or on another plane. This means that when you draw Aura, 
you are drawing from one place to another place. Aura just 
doesn't appear inexplicably, though your players need not know 
this unless they have Metaphysics. It also means that when you 
destroy a world another world may be created or alternately, 
many worlds saved. This effect can be dispersed in the same 
world or it can affect other planes. 
Sympathy: Like things hold power over each other. A hermetic 
spell can only be cast affecting the victim if something that is a 
part of or resembles the victim is involved. 
Empathy: All things affect other things in subtle ways. Beings 
are connected based on life energy and thus can employ this 
"connectedness" for a positive benefit. 
Power equals effect: The more magical or divine power called 
upon, the greater the effect. You cannot have a greater effect by 
applying less power, nor can you decrease the effect by apply-
ing more power. 
Duration Requires Power: Duration requires power. The 
longer the duration the greater the power required. Permanent 
duration can only be achieved through methods shown below. 
Range Requires Power: The greater the area affected or the 
longer the range the more power is required to be wielded. 
Longer is Greater: The longer something takes, the greater the 
effect or chance of an effect. 
Residue: Magic breaks planar boundaries and as such it creates 
a residue that can be sensed by those attuned to it. This magic 
residue may or may not have properties of its own. 
Order vs. Chaos: The more magical energy used to force magic 
into an ordered form the more likely the remaining residue will 
be chaotic or wild in nature. Magic seeks to escape the prison 
of order as it is wild and chaotic and does not like to be bound. 
True Name: You cannot know a being and sense that being 
without knowing her true name. That being cannot be sum-
moned unless the true name is known. 
Control: It is harder to control something the more it is at risk 
and the farther from its nature you try to change it. 
Alteration: All altered beings/objects know their true nature 
and this true nature can always be restored by some mechanism. 
Illusion: The illusion fools the mind not the senses. Those 
with no mind cannot be fooled. You cannot make a plant feel 
water in its roots. 
Life vs. Death: Life strives to survive; death strives to undue 
life and its works. A living being cannot use magics of death 
for long without it affecting their lifeforce and undead beings 
cannot promote life without it affecting their negative life force. 
Supernatural: All that is not native to a plane is supernatural. 
Soul, Spirit and Body: The soul is the true individual and can 
only be destroyed by a form higher than itself. The spirit is the 
life's force while alive and is represented by Will Force. The 
body is the vessel which contains the spirit and thus the Soul. 
Undeath is Equal to the Form: If the body or physical remains 
are reanimated, only a lesser undead is created. If the spirit is 
utilized along with or instead of the body major, undead can be 
created. If the soul is utilized, then and only then are greater 
undead created. 
The Mind: The mind is the location of the spirit within the 
body (but not the soul). If the mind is damaged the spirit suf-
fers but not the soul. The mind and spirit can be recreated from 
the soul though only if the soul desires it. 
Life Binds: The soul binds the life energy (spirit, composed of 
Will Force) to the body. The soul can, through magic, voluntar-
ily give up some of its life energy to bind permanence to magic 
effects. This same energy is required to restore life from death. 
Divine Magic is Indirect: The application of divine magic is 
through indirection. Though the Priest calls the divine magic, it 
is the divine agent that uses that magic not the priest. 
Lesser Permanence: Lesser direct, non-divine magical effects 
194 

===== PAGE 205 =====
(4 Aura or less) will become permanent when a great amount of 
energy (20 Aura or more) is applied to them because their effect 
creates a magic shadow that remains. 
Spirit Accepts What the Mind Rejects: The spirit accepts magic 
and the mind rejects it. Thus, the mind must grow to accept the 
spirit in order to accept greater levels of control over magic. 
The mind rejects magic within itself; thereby, the mind must 
release its hold to allow the being to have magic effects on him-
self (which explains experienced-based control of magic.) 
Mind Wills the Spirit: Magics of an external sort (those cast on 
others) are supported by the spirit through control of the mind 
(which explains the limit

Artifacts 
Artifacts are created as other magic items, but they must have 
the unique properties of 14 and 20 listed in the unique proper-
ties table (near indestructibility and cannot be identified). They 
can be created by deities, semi-deities, arch mortals (planes-
walkers) and mortals who voluntarily give up their life perma-
nently in the creation process. In addition, they must have a 
destruction process that may or may not be known and are often 
wrapped in history, legend and prophecy. Artifacts also have 
one special power that once used causes the item to be lost to 
the user.

Repairing Magic Items 
A magic item that has been destroyed by being broken or dam-
aged can be repaired in the following ways: 
1) Cast Mend on the object. After this, the item has lost its 
magic and Enchantment must be recast with Aura points equal 
to or greater the original Aura of the item. 
2) Use Wood Lore, Stone Lore, Metal Lore or Empower to 
attempt to repair the item. If any of the item is missing, Repair 
must be cast in conjunction with the lore skill. If all the pieces 
of the item are present, then the chance of repairing is the 
chance of the lore. 
3) The GM can define if the Will Force used during 
Enchantment is returned to the caster when the item is 
destroyed or is the target of Disenchant. If this is the case, then 
new Will Force must be spent to fix the item. 
Aura Containers 
Aura containers count as miscellaneous magic items, worth 20 
experience per point of storage capacity. Cast spells cannot be 
absorbed. Aura moved through use of the skill counts towards 
Aura Fatigue. Critical failure while trying to produce an Aura 
storage item can result in an magical explosion (per the spell 
Explosion) equal to 1 Aura per Aura point of the container. The 
chance of explosion equals 2% per percentage point over 20 by 
which the skill was failed.

Phrs,caL laws 
These are things often taken for granted or ignored all together 
such as gravity, entropy, etc. Some or all of these laws may be 
in place, absent or altered as you see fit. You may ask why you 
should bother with the natural laws and principles; after all, 
isn't this fantasy? Having at least a general idea of these laws 
and principals will allow you to break them. You can then pro-
duce fantastic effects and create truly bizarre but consistent 
planes that excite the players without fostering their disbelief. 
Planar romps can too often degenerate into cartoon-like 
episodes unless some care is expended understanding the places 
they will visit. This list below is not meant to be an exhaustive 
list, but describes most of the major laws and principles that 
define us. Some of the more mathematically or complex laws 
and principles are not included, so as not to have too little or 
too complex a bearing on the setting. The laws of thennody-
namics are very important but cannot be easily modified or 
explained simply enough to apply in game mechanics. Many of 
the mathematical laws and principles won't help to define a 
more interesting plane, though mathematicians and theologians 
might disagree. You also don't have to be a nuclear physicist to 
have a basic understanding of how the world works and thus 
how to break it's laws. The following are basic laws and princi-
ples: 
Entropy 
Entropy causes the breakdown of organization and is responsi-
ble for death and the deterioration of items and places after their 
construction. Entropy can be classified as fast or slow. Fast 
entropy would accelerate this process, causing things to rapidly 
fall apart Slow entropy decelerates this process, resulting in 
longer a longer lifespan of matter. The reverse of entropy is 
that things get better with time, creating a "practice effect.". 
You can start with something that is like an envisioned ideal 
and practice it till it meets that ideal. David Brin describes this 
in his book The Practice Effect. 
Life Resists Entropy 
Though not a principle it ought to be. Life is the only force in 
the universe that can resist entropy. Even though individual 
members of a species are destroyed the species seems to 
improve over time and even if that species fails other species 
are improved to take its place. Jf life didn't resist entropy, 
beings would be devolving, becoming lesser with each genera-
tion until they were literally a spec of goo, though some argue 
that life merely keeps pace with entropy If life overcomes 
entropy easily, beings evolve quickly and each generation will 
bring a new change. 
Conservation of Matter 
Matter is never destroyed, it merely changes fonn. Without this 
law things may disappear and the universe shrinks or gets used 
up. Alternately it could reverse allowing for the spontaneous 
creation of matter in strange or unusual places. 
Conservation of Energy 
Energy is stored and does not disappear until used. This is why 
the arrow speeds up as it leaves the bow. Energy is conserved 
as momentum in the arrow as it leaves the bow building up 
speed until air resistance and gravity removes this energy. If 
there is no conservation of energy, it may be much harder to 
move or much easier. It may allow for the sudden and random 
movement of objects or energy just is randomly applied to 
objects. This can cause some dangerous and deadly effects like 
a being getting electrocuted for no apparent reason than the air 
decided to give off electricity. 
Uncertainty 
Hesinberg proved that you can only know for certain two things 
about any object, and that you cannot know its weight, speed 
and direction all with certainty. If you could know everything 
about every object then you have no uncertainty as to what 
would happen. The reason weather is so hard to predict is 
because it is made up of thousands of variables relating to each 
other in uncertain ways. We only know direction or strength or 
speed with any certainty. The harder we try to be certain of all 
three the less likely we will be. Thus over time a stonn becomes 
less and less predictable. If this principal is removed, then, 
through reasoned deduction, all things are knowable once they 
are measured precisely. If you make things even more uncer-
tain life seems like a crap shoot and all you seem to know is 
one thing about an object. 
Cause and Effect 
Every effect has a cause. Or does it? Mere mortals see some-
thing happen and attribute it to an effect as their perception 
allows for nothing different. Nonnally, they see the glass fall 
off the table and attribute its breaking to hitting the ground. 
What if the glass fell off the table because it was broken? 
Sounds like nonsense and yet, playing with cause and effect can 
give some bizarre impressions and give a truly unworldly feel 
to a plane. This will usually disorient and "freak out"players. 
You may find yourself fiendishly enjoying the suspension of 
cause and effect. 
Inertia 
A body at rest tends to stay at rest and a body that is moving 
continues moving. On Earth, there is air friction and gravity to 
slow things down. Perhaps in your plane, no inertia is allowed. 
You only move when force is applied and then you stop imme-
diately. You can also make inertia high, making it difficult to 
get an object that has stopped moving or change the course of a 
moving object . 
Action/Reaction 
For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When 
a pool ball hits another pool ball its motion is stopped and the 
second pool ball absorbs the energy and moves away from the 
first ball. If you hit the first ball too hard it won't be able to 
absorb all the energy and both balls will continue moving but 
the first ball will slow down equal to the amount of kinetic 
197 

===== PAGE 208 =====
energy it passed to the second ball. If you hit the ball too light-
ly, the first ball will not overcome the inertia as described 
above. So how do you alter this? We!J you can make it so ener-
gy in the form of actions is not transferable at all between 
objects. This means everything is at rest unless propelled by a 
magical means and that when things bump into each other they 
are unaffected. You can make it it so the reaction is twice or 
more the effect of the original action; your plane becomes a 
super billiards game of things bouncing into each other and get-
ting sped up faster and faster. You could also alter it so the 
reaction is not opposite. When something hits something 
instead of going in the direction hit, it goes back the way the 
original object came or a random direction. Imagine pushing a 
baJI and having it push back hard than it was pushed. 
Gravity 
AJI objects attract other objects based on their mass and dis-
tance from each other. Without going into specifics the idea is 
simple: big things attract little things and other big things that 
are close; very big things attract anything in their range of 
effect. What if there was no gravity or crushing gravity? No 
gravity would cause the atmosphere to be disbursed, making it 
difficult to sustain life. Crushing gravity would reduce most 
lifeforms to a puddle of goo. There is magic that alters gravity 
within the game system, but you may want to consider altering 
gravity on your plane such that there are pockets of effect or an 
altered effect throughout your plane. 
Atomic Fore es 
This is what bonds tiny matter together. There is a greater and 
a weaker force, but ignoring that, if there were no atomic forces 
holding you together it would take magic to do so. A plane 
without atomic force would be loose energy from which no 
matter could form. Altering the laws of atomic force produce 
very strange results. Make a more binding force and maybe 
you have an organic crystal or maybe yet another puddle of 
goo. Anything you do with these forces will generally be pure 
speculation but may produce interesting results. 
Relativity 
E = mc2. In very basic terms it means the faster you want 
something to go the harder you have to push it. It also makes 
everything else in the universe relative to the constant of how 
fast light travels since that is set as the threshold by which you 
can't push any harder or go any faster. At some point, even 
Superman couldn't push hard enough to make it move any 
faster. If the law of general relativity is altered, strange effects 
wilJ occur. Visible light will shift to from yellow to blue or red 
depending on whether its moving away from you or towards 
you. In the right conditions, time could flow backwards. That's 
pretty strange and nearly unplayable but perhaps you can set 
your players as observers of the effect and magically separate 
them from interrupting or altering the flow of time. 
Planets anb PlanetaR)? FoRces 
If a spherical world is chosen to house your populations, then 
certain physical effects may manifest themselves due to gravity, 
weather, climate and other planetary forces. These forces are 
listed here along with their possible variations and effects. 
Gravity 
Ttny World (25% of Earth's gravity): -3 Strength, +3 Agility; 
easy flight, jumping x 10. 
Small World (50% of Earth's gravity): -2 Strength, +2 Agility; 
assisted flight, jumping x5. 
Undersized World (75% of Earth's gravity): -1 Strength, 
+ l Agility; many fliers, jumping x2.

attributes.

-1 Agility; few fliers, jumping 1/2.

No fliers, jumping 1/4. 
Huge World (300% of Earth's gravity): +3 Strength, -3 Agility; 
no fliers, jumping 1/8. 
Tectonic Activity 
The tectonic activity of a planet will determine much about the 
qualities of natural disasters such as earthquakes and volcanos. 
No tectonic plates: No mountains or volcanic activity unless 
struck by large meteors. AlJ earthquake effects are halved. 
A few large tectonic plates: Mountains and volcanos exist onJy 
where plates are pushed together. Volcanos are very likely to 
form where one plate slides under another and is remelted 
below the crust of the planet. Mountain size will be equal to 
the amount of pressure the two plates exert on each other and 
the time they have exerted it. 
Many varied plates: Mountains and volcanos are plentiful and 
the volcanos often active. 
Fractured plates: Mountains and volcanos rarely are in whole 
ranges. Instead there are likely to be sinkholes, geysers, lava 
flow, etc. Earthquake effects are doubled on this world even if 
created by magic. 
Hydration 
Desert World (5% or less water content): Food is scarce, life is 
sparse. 
Arid World(] 5% or less water content): Food is rare, only 
pockets of life exist. 
Dry World (25% or less water content): Food is uncommon, 
only a few species can be found and they are highly adapted. 
Balanced World (50% water content): Large areas of habita-
tion, several species can be found. 
Wet World (75-85% water content): Food is common, many 
species to be found. 
Oceanic World (86-95% water content): Food is abundant, 
great diversity of life. 
Water World (96% or more): Food everywhere, life permeates 
everything and is everywhere.

Toxicity 
Worlds are often toxic to life outside their own adapted flora 
and fauna. Below are described some of these toxicities: 
Air: The air slowly poisons all but the most adapted life forms. 
Water: The water must be processed before it is drinkable or it 
will slowly poison life. 
Earth: The soil is toxic to most forms of life, poisoning all but 
the most adaptive plants. 
Life: Most forms of life here employ poisons or are themselves 
toxic to other forms of lives.

sun that occasionally (or often) is a factor in the production of 
weather. Large moons can also affect weather and create tides 
in oceans and other large bodies of water further affecting 
weather. Use these and anything else you would think to apply 
to determine weather patterns for your world. Orbit does not 
apply to crystal sphere worlds.
