Other Planetary Influences 
Fixed Planet: A day-side and a night-side exist forever. One 
side will be much colder and may be uninhabitable. Life will 
have adapted on the dayside to tolerate constant light. 
Strong Magnetic Field: Aurora Borelias effects (color shim-
mering, increased electrical activity in storms, sheet lightening). 
Large Moons: These create eclipses whenever they cross 
between the planet and the sun. These eclipses can be often or 
rare depending on the orbits. 
Violent Air: Tornados and water spouts. 
Complete Cloud Cover: The planet is almost always covered in 
clouds. This cloud layer must be relatively thin or soon the 
planet will undergo a metamorphosis that makes it uninhabit-
ably hot and creates severe pressure on surface dwellers. 
Climares anb Hab,rars 
Climate 
Climate is an average of weather patterns, temperature, humidi-
ty, and average barometric pressure that produces a type of 
environment. Put simply, what the air is like. 
Temperature is provided in degrees Fahrenheit. 
Desert (desert): An area that tends to have relatively light pre-
cipitation that averages between 1 inch and 1 foot of rain per 
year. The most likely weather effect is a wind based sand-storm 
which can easily bury individuals and in extreme cases even 
structures. The air is very dry, having humidity that is rarely 
above 20%. Temperatures vary wildly by season and time. 
Winter nights can be below freezing while summer days can be 
in excess of 130 degrees. 
Highland (mountain): This area is marked by strong winds, 
low pressures, extreme weather patterns such as thunderstorms 
and blizzards in winter. Humidity is fairly low and averages 
between 20-60%. On the slopes opposite the direction of the 
wind, a rain shadow is created, as most storms will dump their 
precipitation on the side of the mountain facing the wind. 
Temperature tends to be brisk being as low as 40 to 60 degrees 
below freezing in deepest winter and as warm as 50 degrees in 
the height of summer. Of course, both pressure and wind speed 
increase with the elevation while temperature decreases. 
Humid Continental: A fairly wet climate that occurs inside of a 
continent, either due to high pressures or large sources of inland 
water. Humidity tends to be between 40 and 80%. Rain is like-
ly, with thunderstorms, snow, sleet, hail and most forms of 
weather, occurring here. Temperatures tend to be relatively 
mild, from 60's to 90's in summer, to at or below freezing in 
winter. Pressure varies but tends to be high, creating many 
storms. 
Humid Oceanic: A climate that receives a daily wet wind from 
a nearby ocean or sea, creating a cooling effect, keeping tem-
peratures and humidity very stable. Seasonal variations are 
moderate here. The temperatures are rarely below freezing, 
even in winter and the ocean breeze reduces heat. Pressure can 
vary throughout the day and storms, usually rain storms, can be 
the result, though most often areas within the climate are passed 
over by bigger storms that drop precipitation farther inland. 
Humid Subtropical Uungle): A wet climate, usually surrounded 
by or near an ocean, receiving constant wet air from the sur-
rounding water. The wet air is further trapped in higher average 
pressures. Temperatures tend to be fairly high, and average 60-
80 degrees on a summer day and rarely dip below 40 degrees 
on a winter's night. 
Icecap (polar): An extreme environment, were most water is 
trapped in the form of ice. Very little humidity exists at all and 
this humidity is usually lower than 10% year round. What pre-
cipitation exists, comes exclusively in the form of snow. 
199 

===== PAGE 210 =====
Storms tend to be blizzards and are extremely deadly to all 
forms of life. Pressure can vary wildly and the winds can shift 
on a whim. Temperature can get as low as 80 below freezing 
and rarely climbs even near the freezing point. 
Semiarid: A fairly dry area, that receives some rainfall each 
year during winter, fall and spring months but tends to be hot 
and dry in summer. Temperatures here can climb as high as 
120 degrees in rare mid summer but average 70-90 degrees. 
Winter months can result in freezing temperatures depending on 
the latitude (how far north the area is). Storms are infrequent 
and winds tend to be light. 
Subtropical Dry Summer: A wet environment that dries out in 
summer. Temperature is mild (50-70's) to high (80-1 lO's), 
pressure varies. Hurricanes are possible in winter. Weather can 
be extreme; being mild one moment and then pouring rain the 
next. 
Tropical Wet (rainforest): An extremely wet environment that 
sees near constant rain. An annual rainfaJI of 36 feet of rain is 
not unheard of. Humidity is often over 80%. Monsoons can 
happen in summer. Pressure remains somewhat constant and 
fairly high. Temperature is usually high but constant between 70 
and 90 degrees. 
Tropical Wet and Dry: Highly seasonal climates. In summer it 
acts as Humid Subtropical, in spring, winter and fall as Tropical 
Wet. Temperature varies by season between lows of 40 in win-
ter highs of 110 in summer. 
Tundra (tundra): A climate that is frozen in winter but thaws 
most summers. It is very arid, rarely going over 30% humidity. 
Tends to be windy and has few weather patterns, most of which 
produces snow or freezing rain. Temperatures tend to be low 
and are usuaJly between 10 to 30 degrees in summer and as low 
as 30 degrees below freezing in winter. 
Exotic: The imagined possibilities are endless. lee caps so low 
that they have zones where carbon dioxide itself freezes and no 
one can breath unaided. There are underground areas so large 
they form their own weather patterns, and places where strange 
gases collect and freakish storms happen. 
Habitat 
Habitat is the surrounding vegetation, and conditions that 
beings and animals live in. Its what's around on or in the 
ground. 
Capitol City: A completely humanoid-made area that has few 
animals, mostly insects, vermin, pets and the occasional domes-
ticated food animal or beast of burden. Plants tend to be in gar-
dens or cultivated trees and some weeds here and there. Most 
food is shipped in. 
City: An area dominated by artificial structures. Animal pres-
ence is reduced to vermin and those owned by a city's inhabi-
tants. Plants vary but are usuaJly those which are cultivated by 
humanoid beings even farms tend to be in outlying areas. 
Coastal: A habitat found along the coast of a sea or ocean. 
Many forms of life survive by feeding on the ocean's abun-
dance from the safety of the land. Land and sea flora and fauna 
meet here. 
Desert: An area that supports few forms of life and has little 
diversity. Plants tend to be hearty survivors that need little 
water. Animals survive mostly off each other and most hide 
from the heat or have long dormant life cycles that survive until 
the occasional wet storm. 
Exotic (clouds): An area where a magical cloud city can be 
found. Some magical races use this environment to hide safely 
away from other races. Plants found here are brought from 
below as are most animals, birds predominate. 
Exotic ( elemental): A habitat dominated by fire, water, earth or 
air where the magical and divine elementals war eternally. 
Animals are in the form of wyrs (small semi-intelligent elemen-
tal-kin). 
Exotic (magical places): An area dominated by magic. 
Creatures thrive only because of the abundant sources of magic. 
Beings tend to be magical in nature and may not even breath or 
reproduce like their more mundane counterparts. 
Exotic ( other planar): An area outside of the prime plane 
where life exists as the plane allows. All life tends to be super-
natural in origin and may be eternal. 
Exotic (space/ether): A habitat that does not itself support life 
and is largely empty. It usually takes some form of magic or 
technology to extend life while a being is in this medium. 
Some very exotic forms of life are possible, but the beings can-
not be respirators nor can they require any abundant forms of 
sustenance. 
Exotic (subterranean sea): An area deep underground so large 
that it supports a sea. Life similar to oceanic life is found here, 
though light tends to be low and visual ability is low or 
enhanced through a secondary means. Plant life is reduced to 
fungus, bacteria, mushrooms and the like predominate. 
Forest: A habitat dominated and protected by trees. Visibility 
is reduced by trees, protecting many forms of life from most 
predators while hiding the predators adapted to arboreal life. 
Other plant life is abundant and survives in the filtered light 
below the trees. Animals and insects are everywhere. This 
habitat can support most forms of life. 
Hills: An area of modest rise that has high visibility to sur-
rounding areas. Predators and birds predominate. Plants of all 
kinds are found, depending largely on the climate and latitude. 
Jungle: A habitant with very dense life and plant life. The jun-
gle is choked with plants and hides a myriad of creatures within 
its foliage. A daily battle for light, food and survival is fought 
by every inhabitant, plant or animal. Humanoids are less fre-
quent here, as disease can spread rapidly. 
200 

===== PAGE 211 =====
Lake: An inland source of water that supports an abundance of 
life in its waters and around its edges. Many forms of life tend 
to gather around the lake to drink from its waters. 
Marsh: A wet habitat dominated by mud and thin waters, usu-
ally fed by a nearby source of water. Insects predominate; 
smaller predators that survive on insects thrive, as do birds. 
Humanoids find the marshy wetlands difficult to live in and 
even traverse. 
Mountain: A region dominated by a mountain or range of 
mountains. Animals and plants adapted to the thinning air and 
higher winds survive. As the mountain(s) rises, less and less 
life is seen, until eventually the highest peaks have none at all. 
Ocean/sea (deep): The most unusual forms of life survive here. 
Plants are rare and float, surviving on chemical processes or 
decay. Animals are blind or carry their own forms of light. 
Pressure is so high that plants and animals brought higher tend 
to burst. 
Ocean/sea (floor): A region where plant life survives on heat 
and chemical reactions. Pressures are so high that very few 
forms of life can survive here. 
Ocean/sea (middle depths): The waters team with life, and ani-
mals (mostly fish) live in abundance. Some plants are found 
here as floaters. Light is dim but usually present. 
Ocean/sea (near surface): Huge kelp and seaweed forests are 
found here. Life is in abundance. Fish and even sea going 
mammals live in these depths. Light from the surface filters 
down at these depths. 
Ocean/sea (surface): Most sea going mammals spend their 
time at the surface as do birds and some insects. Predators are 
more common at the surface, capturing fish and other animals 
that venture up from the middle depths. 
Plains: An area dominated by grasslands and few trees. Herd 
animals predominate with the occasional fast predator. Plants 
survive seasonally, drying or dying in summer and thriving in 
winter months. 
Polar: Very little life can survive in this permanently frigid 
habitat. Some very adapted forms of birds and mammals do 
survive but often migrate to warmer regions as needed for food. 
Rain Forest: A wet habitat that thrives on near constant rain-
fall. All forms of life are in abundance, from trees to insects. 
Most animals are arboreal here, surviving in the trees. 
River: A habitat fed by an abundance of fresh water from high-
er ground. Floods are common in spring. Fish and insects sur-
vive in the water; plants and mammals survive on ground 
around the water. 
Savanna: A dry flat habitat that sees some rain but has only 
pockets of plant life. Most of the savanna is covered in dead 
grasses that came and went with sudden rare storm patterns. 
Stands of trees and shrubs surround drying ponds and dying 
wetlands. Herds of animals move in large groups for protection 
201 
from predators and migrate for sources of foods. 
Scrubland: An area of modest rainfall with isolated groves of 
trees, rolling grasses and shrubs, and desert-like pockets. 
Subterranean (deep): Deep below the surface of the earth ani-
mals live without light, surviving on each other and on mush-
rooms and fungus. Most animal life is blind or carries an inter-
nal light source. 
Subterranean (near surface): Animals from the surface and 
deeper survive here but venture elsewhere for food. Usually 
near surface caves are used for safety during times of rest and 
as shelter from stonns. 
Swamp: A very wet habitat that supports a large population of 
insects and water-borne life. Trees and plant life that can exist 
in and on the water survive by choking off other forms of 
plants. Decay and fungus are everywhere. Very few humanoids 
thrive in swampy conditions. Disease is rampant here. 
Town: A habitat with many structures but still strongly affected 
by the local climate. Wild animals typically avoid these 
humanoid structures but venture in during times of need or in 
the dark of night. Vermin and domesticated animals predomi-
nate. Domesticated plants share their space with the natural 
plant life. 
Tundra: A frigid plan that supports some bird and mammalian 
life as well as seasonal plants. Many animals spend only part of 
their lives on the tundra, migrating to southern latitudes and 
warmer climates during the winter. 
Wasteland: An area nearly devoid of life or recovering from a 
great devastation. Remaining or returning animals feed off each 
other and plant life is rare if seen at all. Most forms of life can-
not survive here for any length of time. 
Volcano: The area on and around an active volcano is filled 
with ash and heat. Some plant life ekes out an existence but is 
always threatened. Animals wisely flee this area. 
Village: An area of humanoid habitation where the natural 
environment is still found within and around the humanoid 
structures. Animals and plants of all varieties (from the sur-
rounding habitats) can be found. Some predators survive on the 
humanoids and their domesticated animals.

Weather adds a dimension to any setting, adding further realism 
to the mix. The tables below are provided to help simulate 
weather for the various seasons in near Earth-like conditions. 
Different worlds or climates might have very different weather 
effects and require a reworking to fit. Use these rules as guide-
lines or a base from which to launch your own world's weather.

Cover, and Precipitation tables (where applicable).

Deines anb SupeRnaruRaL FoRces 
Deities provide Priests and Priest subclasses with their powers 
and abilities. Deities in a fantasy setting can be a tricky subject 
that some are bothered by or refuse to deal with altogether. 
Throughout the ages various cultures have worshiped gods and 
deities, and if necessary, one of the famous pantheons of gods 
could stand in for a particular setting (such as Greco-Roman, 
Norse, Celtic, etc.). Use the following information if you 
would like to design your own pantheon or set of deities. 
CReatmt; Derties 
Being Worshiped 
This is what deities live for. They want to be begged and plead-
ed with, sacrificed to, worshiped and in general thought of with 
great reverence and fear. If a deity has no worshippers, he will 
fade away. Each level of godhood requires a certain number of 
requisite followers (see advancement beyond 15th in the 
Extension Section). Therefore, deities protect their turf from 
other deities and usurping arch mortals. 
Realms of Influence 
These are the areas that an individual deity has influence over. 
They are also used to the match the "'worldly devoted" to the 
deities which most suit them. Each deity should have at least 
one alignment, one attribute, one race, and one class that he has 
within his realm of influence. If deities overlap in these realms, 
a likely conflict may develop as they compete for worshippers.

Choosing a Symbol 
Every deity has a symbol. It is used by the deity's worshippers 
to show each other that they are part of the elite; the special 
people who know the true ways. Make sure the symbol match-
es well the deity's ideals or realms of influence. 
Gaining Experience 
Deities do not often walk amongst the living. They can gain 
experience in the normal fashion; however, in most circum-
stances they gain experience through the actions of their Priests 
and divine skill users. A deity gains l % of whatever experience 
his Priests (or Priest subclasses) gain when the deity's name is 
invoked and/or granted powers, abilities, or divine skills are 
used. He only gains this experience if it is obvious to others 
that the deity's power was used to aid the Priest. Remember 
that a deity stops gaining experience if he does not meet the 
requirements for advancement or loses enough worshippers to 
be demoted to a lower Title. 
ReLK;JOns anb the SouRce OF Drvmlt)? 
Like its magical counterpart, divinity can have many sources. 
These sources can have varied effects upon the setting. In some 
settings, more than one source of divine power is available. 
Each has its own quirks and customs. As long as at least one 
source of divinity is accessible, divine magical skills, powers, 
items and invocations will function. Without them these effects 
do not function or appear to exist at all. It should be noted that 
these divine sources are not meant to represent a real faith in 
anything. Yet still fantasy games can deal with the effects of 
spiritual matters on the character. Some are even set in worlds 
very much like our own where believers follow the adherence 
of a single god and fear a tormentor. C. S. Lewis described 
such an alternate reality in his Narnia series of books. While 
Imagine Role Playing will leave the true believing to you, we 
offer up these faiths from the collected thoughts and works of 
the history and beliefs found within our world and its past. Use 
them to fulfill your goals in creating a mythos you see fit in 
which to set your great morality plays. 
The Dependent Gods (Polytheism) 
"The gods are like children of the mind and sprit. They have 
great power but greater ego. 'Ware the gods at play, for we are 
their playthings. A god's mood is as changeable as the wind." 
The many gods exist but they are created and maintained by the life 
force of their worshippers. They are jealous gods with many of the 
characteristics and foibles that mark their worshippers. They provide 
divine magical skills, and sets of invocations that vary by their devo-
tions or areas of influence. The gods will also deny these same powers 
to punish or control the leaders of the faiths that worship them. It is 
inherently factionistic often with a ruling pantheon of gods and many 
lesser gods vying for a place on the ruling pantheon of deities. This is 
a closed model, where the gods exist only because of the people that 
worship them and their strength is dictated by the number of worship-
pers. Each god has legions of minions that handle the day to day 
affairs of handing out invocations, answering prayers (Commune 
chance) and struggling against the minions of other gods. Piety repre-
sents the connection between the being and the divine forces. A high 
Piety does not mean that being is liked by the gods just that she is 
more connected to their nature and ways. Death of the worshippers of 
the dependent gods involves the soul being claimed by the dependent 
god who the being most served (knowingly or unknowingly). The soul 
journeys to the home plane/place of this guide and is claimed by them. 
Reincarnation only exists if the dependent god allows it. This is the 
standard model used in Imagine and is what is described for the path to 
godhood for all immortal beings above 15th title. Religions are as var-
ied as the gods whose faith they represent. They can be inclusive, 
exclusive, loose, specific, or even sacrificial. 
Game Notes 
I) Operates as described in the Player's Guide and by the path to 
immortality (Title's 16th and above) and deities as outlined in th.is sec-
tion. 
2) The order of these faiths is divided as follows; the believers, the 
Priests, the dead believers, the ranks of minions and then the deity. 
The Dead Gods (Polytheistic Schism) 
"A god never dies he just loses his way and becomes stuck in 
the firmament of creation. Beware awakening the sleeping ones 
for they are as mad a stepped on snake." 
As a by-product of the Dependent Gods their can exist gods who have 
lost their way, ignoring their worshippers too long-or worse, losing all 
of their faithful. These gods enter a kind of limbo. Their existence 
cannot be denied but they are considered dead and not entirely con-
scious most of the time. From time to time new groups of worshippers 
can awaken these dead gods but often-bizarre results such as weakened 
divine powers or even increased divine powers can result. Nothing is 
for certain when one worships a dead god except that anything can 
happen. When the dead god gains enough followers it will rejoin the 
living gods and return to the standard model of Dependent Gods. 
Religions or cults grow up around secret rites and rituals to entice the 
dead god to waken and grant power. 
Game Notes 
I) Dead gods have few, if any minions and usually grant their divine 
powers directly.

The God in Nature (Animism) 
"A waterfall, a flock of birds, the whispers of the ancestors, a 
pride of lions and their prey, a rainbow, a forest '.S' peace, a dev-
astating storm and eve11 an erupting mountain, all of these are 
nature '.S' own, are nature '.S' way. " 
This divine force exists in nature itself, and in the struggle of the natu-
ral order there is divinity. Animals have spirits that collectively have a 
divinity. The earth, air, water and even the burning fire have a divine 
force within them. The living world has a spirit, sometimes referred to 
as Gaia and though not conscious in most settings, instinctively pro-
tects the natural order, promoting life where there is little, destruction 
where there is abundance and defending against the incursions of over 
zealous beings. lnvocations are provided by drawing on the natural 
divinity inherit in the elements, the animal spirits and the spirits of 
ancestors. This divine force is often responsible for the invocations 
and skills of orders of Shaman and Druids in some settings. Piety rep-
resents the connectedness to the natural order-how tapped into the liv-
ing force of life the believer is. Death is a natural occurrence; the spir-
its of ancestors inhabit the places where they died or the descendants 
gather. The spirits themselves are part of the divine force. The skills 
Animal Shape, Evoke and Totem Call epitomize the divine magic of 
Animism, although they can be provided by deities in settings which 
do not use Animism as a divine force. Religions are very ritualistic 
and sometimes involve sacrifices. They can seem almost barbaric to 
outsiders as the Animistic divine force takes more force/control to 
appease and more work to gain power from. 
Game Notes 
1) All invocations must be prayed for in an open area. 
2) Divine Denial is used only for those who destroy the natural order. 
3) The spirit world is made up of spirits of the animal (totems), spirits 
of the elements (elementals), and spirits of the dead (ancestors). There 
is no ranking implied by the order presented. Totems are not consid-
ered above or below the ancestors, together they compose the living 
force of life. 
The Divine in All (Spiritism) 
"We are one. You are in me and I am in you and we are greater 
than all that is seen. We know more than is knowable and share 
more than one lifetime can ever hold. We are the faith of a past 
unrevealed and the promise of a day unseen. " 
This divine force is a shared divinity that exists in all things. There is 
no one consciousness that is above others, no god per se. There is 
instead a collective unconscious that represents the literal will of the 
people acting in their collective interest. There can be a single such 
uniting force (or many forces) by the groupings of beings by race, 
belief, or even one force divided into factions within itself. Some 
beings with higher Piety are more tapped into this collective uncon-
scious and understand it, and can thus direct it to some degree for 
small periods of time. Death is almost a positive event in Spiritisirn 
settings. The only change is a sloughing of the mortal coil, a releasing 
of the grand spirit trapped within. In Spiritisim the spirit wakes up to 
the collective will; no longer unconscious it is part of the conscious 
spirit world, but as such is less involved in the spiritual unconscious-
ness of living beings. The spirit can wander the multi-verse joining 
with other spirits. A spirit can be reborn if it so desires. Sometimes it 
will take the guarding or development of living beings. Invocations 
and divine magical skills come from the collective source and may be 
denied if the being strays too far from the will of collective uncon-
scious. Occasionally one gains power directly from a single spirit who 
is aiding the being. 1n these incidents the spirit guardian has complete 
control of whether the being has access to invocations and divine 
skills. Religions of this type are loose, each being is encouraged to 
seek within the divine nature of all. Some sects will seek to break the 
barrier and seek unconscious will and the spirits that have crossed over. 
Game Notes 
I) No invocation above 10th can be prayed for unless the practitioner 
of Divine Knowledge gains one or more guardian spirits. There is a 
personal relationship between the believer and the spirit that can result 
in many divine denials of skills/invocations depending on the relation-
ship. 
2) Believers that enter a trance (Meditate or Body Control) can have 
limited telepathy (surface thoughts only) with other believers around 
them (l' per will Force point). 
3) Believers that enter a directed trance (Meditate or Body Control) 
while a second practitioner uses Soothe or Cure [nsanity can be 
regressed to remember past lives and events that transpired before the 
most recent birth of the being. 
4) Commune contacts the collective unconscious; it can grant vision 
and manifest itself as a deity but will rarely take direct action unless it 
is for the greater good of many believers. 
5) The order of this religion consists of the believers, the wandering 
spirits and the guardian spirits who watch over and aid the living. 
The Divine in Death (Spiritism/Animism Schism) 
"Life is a temporary mistake, easily corrected. Death is perfec-
tion achieved. The dead feel pain only of their own devising. 
The mortal coil is an imperfect vessel to receive the perfection 
of void." 
These adherents believe that death is a divine force in and of itself. 
They worship and practice the arts of murder and sacrifice. The priests 
of these dark arts draw their power from the life force of the dying or 
dead. Divinity is a force to be shaped almost like magic itself. They 
draw from a kind of unconscious divine source of energy generated by 
the death and suffering of beings everywhere. Their priestly rites and 
acts require bigger and bigger sacrifices, until ultimately they must sac-
rifices themselves to become the highest practitioners of this dark 
belief. Death for them is a thing to be desired in others and to be per-
fected in one's self. The adherents of this practice hope to achieve a 
living death, becoming the undead. Piety is a measure of how directly 
they are tapped into the energy of the negative life force. Religions of 
this type fonn in dark and secret places. They are generally hated, if 
not outright hunted by any other established religion that comes into 
contact with them. 
Game Notes 
I) Adherents may not be Good. 
2) Invocations of I through 10th level require the sacrifice of an ani-
mal when prayed for. 10th and higher require the sacrifice of a living 
being or the intervention of a dead priest granting them power. 
3) Practitioners that have died and crossed over or become undead can 
grant invocations to living priests. 
4) Skill usage and power require a sacrifice of fresh blood, cutting one-
self or another being. One ounce is required per 10% of skill or level 
of power. Each ounce represents (ld4 damage of blood loss) 
Alternately 1 Will Force may be temporarily drained from any willing 
206 

===== PAGE 217 =====
(or just sacrificed source) source per 3 levels of power, or 30% of skill. 
5) When these beings die they usually become undead of one type or 
another depending on which undead fits their beliefs and racial charac-
teristics. 
6) Commune chances are answered by undead who feel compelled to 
help the being until the task/question is answered or a day is passed, 
whichever is first. 
7) The order of death, is the living practicers, the living dark priests, 
the (un)dead servants, the greater (un)dead, the (un)dead priests, and 
the dark force of death. 
The Living Gods (Spiritism/Polytheism Schism) 
"The pharaoh, divine emperor and even true king are gods in 
life, directing divine force for the benefit of their people. We 
will worship them long after they have past beyond the veil of 
death." 
A few are born with the power of divinity within them. These beings 
are thought of as gods in life. This power is usually hereditary though 
in some settings it can be more random in appearance. These great 
ones can call upon internal divinity for invocations and divine magical 
skills. They are, in effect, priests of themselves. They can also call on 
the powers of their ancestors if the ancestors so will. When a living 
god dies he joins the pantheon of deities that have lived before. He 
then gains the power of true godhood and becomes a dependent god as 
described in the Dependent God model. Piety represents one's close-
ness to the gods that have passed on to the other side. A god in life 
cannot grant divine magic to his followers until after he has died and 
joined with the ancestors. Death for those who are not gods means that 
they become minions for the ancestor god they worship. Those that 
worshiped no god are destroyed and remade as dark spirits to be used 
by as any god needs. Religions worship the gods that have died. This 
should not be confused with worship of dead gods. These gods are liv-
ing gods that showed godhood while living in the mortal realm. 
Game Notes 
I) Gods in life: they gain all the divine abilities of the race they are 
and the class they follow but it is internal. They cannot be denied 
access to these gifts. Invocations over I 0th level require prayer to an 
ancestral god (even for these gods in life) and can be denied if mis-
used. When a God in life dies he joins the ancestral god and is now a 
Dependent God as outlined above. 
2) Other worshippers pray to the ancestral gods to receive divine abili-
ties and are treated in all other ways like the worship of Dependent 
Gods. 
Becoming God (Transcendence) 
"To become great one nwst lose all. Loss is gain. Life is a dis-
traction to the greater story unfolding around us. In each there 
is a beginning, in some there is an end-where it goes is for each 
to find." 
Each of us has the "god spark" but must through life (and eventually 
death) find a way to transcend the mundane and join or become divine. 
Souls are recycled, reincarnating again and again until the soul learns 
the lessons of life and transcends, crossing the barrier to the divine 
soul. This divinity can either be a single group being with whom all 
transcended souls can join, or each transcended soul itself can be a 
divine entity (or some combination of both). Higher Piety represents a 
higher ordered being, closer to transcendence. As one approaches tran-
scendence she can call on the powers of divinity in oneself and from 
those who have already transcended. Those that can call on these pow-
ers are called the enlightened. Invocations are granted by the tran-
scended and divine magical skills and powers are from within. Death 
is a time to take stock before returning to the wheel of life or breaking 
it's yoke for all. Religions involve studying and praying to the tran-
scended beings and studying their lives to understand the path of tran-
scendence. 
Game Notes 
I) Divine abilities are granted to the believer from the within and from 
the transcendent. Divine magical skills use the practitioners own 
innate divinity, as do invocations below 10th level. Invocations above 
10th level are granted by the transcendent and can be directly denied. 
2) Divine denial of internal powers can happen. It marks a stepping 
off of the path of enlightenment and the being must return to the path 
and set right what is unbalanced before removing the divine denial. 
3) Believers that enter a trance (Meditate or Body Control) can remem-
ber past lives and events that transpired before the most recent birth of 
the being. 
4) Order of this faith is divided into the believers, the souls in transi-
tion, and the transcended. 
The One God (Monotheism) 
"There is but one god. He is jealous god and will have no 
other gods before him. The one comes to drive out the many. 
Fear the one god. Beware the wrath of god. God is love. God 
will find a way. " 
There is only one god (at least to his worshippers), the alpha and 
omega, the beginning and the end, the source of all that is divine and 
holy. The one god created all that is and all that will be. He is 
omnipresent, omnipotent, all seeing, all knowing and all-powerful. 
The one god is invisible and yet ever-present. He grants the power of 
true divine priesthood only to the saints and prophets. Average priests 
(and worshippers for that matter) have no power but the power of 
prayer (commune). Priests and followers of the one true god have one 
gift; divine magic of any other source has no effect unless their piety 
fails them when encountering other sources of divinity. Death invokes 
the great trial, where one is judged by the actions one has taken in life 
and by one's faith. Those who pass judgement join the heavenly mass-
es. Those that fail are cast out, or worse cast down into torment. 
Religions arising from monotheism are strong because they represent a 
single collection of beliefs handed down to the faithful by the very 
god. By their nature they must deny, destroy or overthrow other reli-
gious beliefs because their beliefs will not allow for the existence of 
other gods. 
Game Notes 
I) Denial of other faiths: when exposed to sources of divinity not from 
the one god the faithful make a Piety save at -5% per (level of effect/or 
10% of divine skill). If the save is made the divine power has no 
effect upon them. If they make this save they literally cannot see, feel, 
touch, taste, hear or experience the divine effect. 
2) Only Saints and Prophets gain Divine ability (always I% or less of 
the faithful). Ordinary Priests and followers have no divine gifts or 
ability to call upon the divine. 
3) Any faithful can pray (commune) but the One God never takes 
direct intervention unless such intervention was part of his plan. 
4) Believers that are effected by other sources of divinity (through fail-
ure of a Piety save). Must make a Will Force save or suffer a crisis of 
207 

===== PAGE 218 =====
faith. The crisis of faith removes the commune chance for the believer, 
as well as a saint's or prophet's divine abilities. This Crisis of Faith 
ends when the Practitioner or indirect source of the other (tainted) 
Divinity is destroyed or disgraced. 
5) This order is divided into the faithful, the priests, the saints and 
prophets, the rewarded dead, minions of god, and then the one god. 
The One God's Fallen Minion (Deviltry, Monotheistic 
Schism) 
"The strongest servant of the true god, envied his place beside 
and below the creator. For his wickedness he was cast out and 
down, forever removed from the holy ranks. With him went a 
third of the hosts of heaven, but the creator was not through 
with these fallen and had a plan all along. Thus he cast the role 
of the Tormentor and his demon minions. Until the end of cre-
ation they will subvert the weak will of the immoral, taking 
those damned souls for playthings. " 
Some forms of Monotheism have a lesser, flawed divine being who 
was cast out from god's judgement and is the tormentor of lost souls. 
The Tormentor has the power of a twisted divine magic, lesser than the 
One God but powerful nonetheless. Dark Priests of this anti-religion 
use the Tormentor's power at the cost of their very souls. When the 
worshippers of the Tormentor die they have no chance for redemption 
and are immediately damned. The Tormentor and his demons also vie 
for the divided souls. Those who have not yet been judged but whose 
flaws may yet deny them salvation. The Tormentor is also seeking to 
take over the world in an apocalyptic destruction that will make a hell 
on earth for those who are left behind when the creator calls the last of 
the faithful to their final reward. Piety when used to such dark purpos-
es measures ones connection to the Tormentor and his demon minions. 
The religion that forms from this belief is an anti-religion, most rituals 
and rites are desecrations of the true faith from whom it steals believ-
ers. These believers are hunted and burned wherever they are found by 
the believers of the one True god. 
Game Notes: 
I) One MUST be evil to use any dark divine magics of the Tormentor. 
2) Death is final for all these worshippers. They cannot be resurrected, 
recovered, wished, miracled or in any other way restored to form 
unless it is the direct will of the Tormentor for some larger purpose. 
3) Commune is costly. Every successful commune also involves some 
form of punishment. 
4) The order of the fallen is as follows. The lost (followers of the 
Tormentor), the dark priest, the tormented dead, the demons, and the 
Tormentor himself. 
God is a Magic God (Gnosticism, Monotheism Schism) 
"God works in mysterious ways. God is the magic within his 
believers. With faith in the one true god comes the power of his 
righteous ways. We are the vessels of holy power." 
This form of Monotheism is less about denial of other religions and 
gods and more about transcendence over them through direct divine 
power granted by the redeemer. The Gnostics practice god's magic-
the divine magic granted to his priests. Death is a judgement as it is 
with the most other practitioners of Monotheism but one can gain 
ascendancy through service of God. Priests of Gnosticism are treated 
like other priests except that the power of prayer is unlikely to produce 
direct intervention. Piety is a measure of control and understanding of 
the magic of god. Religions can be cultish because of the belief 
of their own elitism over other believers of similar faith. 
Game Notes: 
I) Any faithful can pray (commune) but the One God never takes 
direct intervention unless such intervention was part of his plan. 
2) Gnostics gain a + I 0% to saves, resistances and contests against 
divinity not of the One True God or the Tormentor (if applicable). 
3) This order is divided into the faithful, the priests, the rewarded dead, 
minions of god, and then the one god. 
The One God is Dead (Deism, Monotheism Schism) 
"God is dead. He built the mighty engines of creation and 
destruction and started them spinning in their courses. Enjoy 
and wonder at his creation but expect no miracles. " 
God has set the great machine of life and the universe in motion and 
has either retired to make only modest adjustments or has left the uni-
verse entirely, either way he isn't revealing himself to those who seek 
him. Adherents of this belief believe in God, but they do not expect 
him to step forward and make himself known. They do not expect their 
prayers to be answered in life (no commune chance). They believe that 
in death, when they have passed out of the creation then and only then 
will they meet god. The priests and worshippers of this faith have no 
power whatsoever except the denial of all earthly divinity. They accept 
the possibility of miracle but they do not expect to see it. This skepti-
cism in life means that divinity rarely effects them. Piety is irrelevant 
to Deists. 
Game Notes 
I) Denial of earthly divinity: when exposed to sources of divinity 
while on the earthly plane. the adherents of Deism make Piety Save -
5% per (level of effect/or 10% of divine skill). If the save is made the 
divine power has no effect upon them. If they make this save they liter-
ally cannot see, feel, touch, taste, hear or experience the divine effect. 
2) This order is divided into the faithful and the priests while god sits 
alone above it all. 
God is Not (Atheism) 
"That which exists is real. There is no greater power than that 
which we make for ourselves. Gods exist only in our minds. We 
dream them up and we can release ourselves from our own 
folly." 
For good or ill this is a 'faith' in the non-existence of any form of 
divinity whatsoever. It has no priests, no rules, no codes of conduct. 
Death is a release from life, an oblivion, a sleep from which none will 
wake, nothing more. Piety is anathema-an undesired trait, one the 
atheist shuns. 
Game Notes: 
I) No one of higher than 12 Piety can be an Atheist. 
2) No commune chance, no usage of divine skills. 
3) Denial of all Divinity. A Piety save is made, +5% added (increasing 
the chance of save) per (level of effect/or I 0% of divine skill) whenev-
er exposed to any form of divinity. If the save 'fails' then the divine 
power has no effect upon them. They cannot see, feel, touch, taste, 
hear or experience the divine effect. 
4) every divine effect that works on them requires a Will Force save. 
If they fail the Will Force save then they are either struck by an insani-
208 

===== PAGE 219 =====
ty (see Insanity) or they have a "religious experience" leading to a like-
ly conversion into another form of religious belief. 
5) There is no order to this faith. 
God Might Be (Agnosticism) 
"Who can say what is god and what is man? Who claims to 
know the will of a god sets himself up as a god. There may be a 
higher power-of this, none can deny or affirm without entering 
into a belief We believe that we do not believe anything 
beyond what we can sense and even that is suspect. The uni-
verse will reveal itself, we cannot force it to be that which we 
wish it to be. " 
Simply called the unbelievers. The Agnostic has no beliefs for or 
against divinity, makes no claims about its existence of non-existence. 
When experiencing divine events the agnostic will often attempt to 
explain away the effect as some form of natural phenomenon. Their are 
no agnostic priests. There is no religion involved with this non-belief. 
Game Notes 
I) No one of higher than 14 Piety can be an Agnostic. 
2) No commune chance, no usage of divine skills. 
3) + I 0% resistance, or bonus to saves or contests against all things 
divine.

God is in many forms (Mixed Religions) 
"Deity has many parts and offers many paths to enlightenment 
and salvation. The divine cannot be made into a single image 
but defies the explanations of mortals. Only through acceptance 
of alternate belief do we find understanding within embrace of 
divine ways. " 
One or more of the above religions can be combined into a single 
belief structure. It is even possible to combine Polytheistic and 
Monotheistic beliefs if the various deities are seen as aspects of the 
One true God. Vary these as is good for your setting and your desired 
outcome. 
Game Notes 
I) In most settings simple Monotheism (the one god) cannot be com-
bined with other beliefs.

Nanons anb CuLtuRes 
As people evolve through time, they come together through the 
common bonds of race, geography, culture, ideals, religion and 
the like to govern themselves, thus forming nations and realms. 
A game world should be filled with these, and in order to make 
a nation detailed and believable, every detail must be attended 
to. The list below and the pages that follow are intended to aid 
the Game Master in developing rich and colorful nations. The 
following pages cover topics to be addressed when creating 
each country or nation in your game world. 
CuLruRaL A~es 
Nations can be at many stages of cultural development. The 
table to the right shows the historical age in the left margin, and 
gives ideas for the type of politics, social structures and techno-
logical advancements that one might find in those ages to the 
right. Most fantasy setting games fall between the Bronze and 
Iron Ages in the Imperial period. It is recommended not to 
exceed the Steel Age as the game quickly devolves into who 
has the biggest gun. Occasionally you may wish to portray 
Stone Age races. Some races can be at one cultural stage while 
others are in another. For example, Ogre tribes often slip into 
Stone Age cultures if left undisturbed. Dwarves are more likely 
to have harnessed steam power and be able to grind lenses or 
make black powder.

Cult-uRal Phases 
Cultures go through phases. Sometimes they move back and 
forth between phases, but usually they advance through the 
phases until they are replaced by another form of culture or are 
eliminated by other races or cultures. Some examples follow: 
Survivalist: The culture is tenuous at best and can barely sup-
port itself or is losing ground. The culture has not yet defined 
itself but has advanced beyond mere survival. Cultures may 
return to innocence in an attempt to redefine themselves (this is 
very rare). 
Expansionist: The culture has determined its themes, organiza-
tion, reason for existence, belief structures, and is expanding. A 
culture can return to expansionist when a new frontier is open. 
Settled: The culture has found its niche and seeks to better 
itself from within but does not aggressively seek new territory 
and new converts. 
Decaying: The culture has lost some of its values and finds 
itself bewildered or remembering better times. Much of the 
populace is disillusioned and this culture is ripe for takeover or 
return to earlier forms. Dead cultures can sometimes be reborn 
into decaying ones from time to time but rarely are fully 
returned to settled or expansionist. 
Fallen: The culture has collapsed but is stilJ well known. It is 
in the process of being absorbed by other cultures as its cultural 
ideas are supplanted, replaced or suppressed by the more domi-
nant culture. The culture may still be revived to decaying by 
true believers or by overthrowing or escaping the dominating 
culture. 
Lost: Although some individuals still know about or maintain 
the culture, it is essentially non-practiced or has been replaced 
by a more central culture. 
Dead: All members of the culture are dead. The culture 
remains only in ruins and through its effect on other cultures.

Racial Populations and Racial Fertility 
Different races vary greatly in the rate of reproduction and react 
differently to times of relative war and peace. The following 
information is provided for the Game Master for use in world 
building for population gauges and to handle fertilization 
chances in specific individuals. 
Fae (Fairies/Elves)

Fertilization Chance: 2-5%(ld4+1) per attempt 
Gestation: 11 months 
Birth type: Live young 
Gender makeup: 49% male/50% female/I% other 
Multiples: Twins I%, Triples . I% 
War Effects: Fertilization decreases by 2%, male +5%/female -5% 
Peace Effects: Fertilization increases by 5%, Male -5%/Female +5%

lam;uar;es 
Languages should be created for different cultures and races. 
This does not mean that you have to create the actual language 
itself (though some GMs do), but you ought to name the lan-
guages and decide how they have evolved over time and who 
speaks which language. Languages can be racial, such as 
Saurian, Chetahl, etc. They can be national, and there can be 
secret factional languages, such as the language of magic or the 
language of a divine sect. In any case, a list of specific lan-
guages needs to be defined so that characters can choose from it 
and fill their language slots allowed by Intelligence. 
National ResouRces 
Magic Items: Define the major magic items used or created by 
the culture or found within the setting (see Magic section). Set 
the commonality of items based on how likely it is for a player 
in this setting to acquire the item and add histories for unique 
items. 
Herbs: Define the medicinal and magical herbs (see Magic sec-
tion.) Name each, describe how it is found, how it is processed 
and used. 
Hermetic: Pick the special magical ores of your world; pick the 
animal parts that produce special results or the herbs that are 
used as magical components. Decide which spells require spe-
cial components when cast hermetically and which ones gain a 
boost with a special component. Decide which compounds are 
considered magical base compounds and which are ingredients. 
Creatures: Pick your bestiary carefully. Don't just throw 
everything into your world because it is in a book . Make a 
rhyme and reason to why one creature is in your world and 
another is not. How does it eat, reproduce, live, die, etc? 
Races: Any special races for your world can be made now (see 
Design section.) 
Classes: Any special classes for your world can be made now 
(see Design section.) Perhaps you wish to create an eastern 
world and need samurai and ninja, or maybe you just want to 
disallow a few classes for balance within your world. 
Skills: Special skills to support the classes and races of your 
world. 
Magic: New spells or effects for your world. 
Divine Magic: New divine invocations offered by certain 
deities or supernatural beings within your world. 
Arms and Armor: Set the available arms and armor. Create any 
special types of arms or armor found in your setting. 
Economies 
All economies are a system to transfer value between parties. 
As long as a majority of people using their current economic 
system feel that it is working for everybody the system will 
prosper and grow into a better system. When the populace feels 
that the system is being manipulated, it will lead to a change in 
system by getting rid of the government. 
Banks: A private or governmentally run organization that holds 
currency for individuals (who pay an interest rate to the deposi-
tor) that will lend currency (for a fee and interest payment to 
the bank) to borrowers. 
Bank Center: A governmental bank that acts as a bank to other 
banks. 
Borrower: An individual or company that receives currency 
from a bank in return for paying the bank back the amount 
received plus a percentage of the amount received. 
Contracts: A binding agreement between two or more individu-
als that call for each of the individuals to perform certain acts in 
exchange for other goods, services or currency. 
Commodity: A marketable item that is easily found in mass 
quantities. 
212 

===== PAGE 223 =====
Depositor: An individual that leaves currency at a bank. The 
depositor will receive an interest rate payment for holding their 
money at the bank. 
Forward Contracts: This is an agreement whereby one person 
is paid in advance for a good or service. Most forward con-
tracts in an agrarian society involve the payment of currency to 
farmers in the spring to cover the cost of life until the crops are 
harvested in the fall where the crops are delivered for the 
money that was paid in the spring. 
Markets: These are the central places where the purchase and 
sale of goods and services occur for commodity items. 
Taxes: Payments by a citizen to a government for the services 
of the government. 
Tax Collector: A governmental agent who collects the taxes. In 
early environments the tax collector will be a thug and use 
direct physical harm to extract payments. In more developed 
economies the tax collector will use the threats of thugs to 
extract tax payments. In the most developed of economies the 
person will use the threat of regulation or non-physical harm. 
Trade: The purchase and sale of goods between different enti-
ties. 
Development of Market Based Economies 
Subsistence Economy 
This form of economy is the simplest of all forms and generally 
is practiced by nomadic or barbaric tribes. The group size that 
is normally associated with a subsistence style economy is a 
group of 3-40 individuals brought together for mutual protec-
tion from a mutual threat and will sometime work for the com-
mon good of the group. Subsistence style economies require 
the active participation of the group the weak, wounded, 
invalid, or old are left to fend for themselves and are not assist-
ed. Due to the nature of the group dynamics for a subsistence 
economy, they will be nomadic and little if any trading occurs 
between the subsistence economy and other economies. The 
most valuable items that a subsistence economy individual 
owns would be those things that would ensure survival: 
weapons, pack animals, food, and metals. Gold, gems, and 
other means of wealth are of little or no importance. To empha-
size this point, if an individual is asked about the location of 
gold ore and he knows where it is located, he would tell a group 
where it is located just as he would tell them where a stand of 
trees is located. A subsistence economy that has had frequent 
exposure to more civilized (advanced) economies would even-
tually evolve into a barter economy. 
Barter Economy 
The barter economy is a economy based upon the division of 
labor and specialization of jobs. The basis of the barter econo-
my is that John the blacksmith will make one metal scythe for 
Fred the farmer, if Fred the farmer will deliver five bushels of 
com to John the blacksmith. An effective barter economy needs 
large groups to function effectively. A typical barter economy 
will need at least fifty individuals in a fixed location to begin to 
allow for functioning. Once an town of at least fifty individuals 
have gotten their local economy situated for survival and have 
excess resources, they will trade to other villages. Local gov-
ernment in a barter economy will be a local strongman and 
some of his loyal thugs. The local strongman will demand trib-
ute in the form of food and luxuries, the early building blocks 
of a tax system for later growth and development of the city 
economy. The focus of the barter economy is of building a 
home and the care of the family. Large and extended families 
are not uncommon; in larger barter economies (800 or more 
individuals) the apprentice system would begin. 
Hard Currency Economy 
The hard currency economy is based upon the notion of storage 
of value (gold, silver, platinum, diamonds.) The material that is 
used as a storage of value should be either very scarce or very 
hard to mine or grow. You would not want to use dandelion 
flowers as you storage of value because the economy would 
collapse as soon as somebody found a field of the flowers. 
Whatever is used as a storage of value will be the currency by 
which most transactions will occur. Items such as gold or dia-
monds are used because they are valuable as either a currency 
or intrinsically as the base material itself. Within a currency-
based economy there will be sub-specialization of jobs. Fred 
the farmer will sell his crops for currency, Fred the farmer will 
then take his currency and go to Philip the plow maker instead 
of John the blacksmith. The ruling parties in a hard currency 
economy will be able to tax all subjects in an organized manor. 
The collection of standardized taxes will lead to bureaucracies 
and regulations. The focus of the hard currency economy is the 
development and expansion of governmental entities and the 
allowance for economically viable enterprises allowing for spe-
cialization in multiple city systems (5 or more cities of 500 or 
more individuals each). 
Fiat Money Economy 
Fiat money is the final evolution of a market based economy. 
What is used as currency in a fiat economy has no intrinsic 
value (i.e. slips of paper that bear photos of past heroes) and 
can not be easily forged (-60 to -80% applied to the Forgery 
skill roll) . The currency will be tokens that represent value 
such as the paper money currency system of the latter l 900's in 
the United States). When a fiat monetary system is created it 
will begin backed by stores of value (i.e. backing of the fiat 
monetary system will take the shape similar to the early 1900's 
United States currency system where the paper money was back 
by the deposits of gold at governmental warehouse such as Fort 
Knox.). A currency backed by a store of value can have as a 
factor that the fiat money can be exchanged at governmental 
banking centers for the store of value (i.e. such as the silver cer-
tificates issued by the United States in the 1950's and 60's that 
could be exchanged at Federal Reserve banks for silver bullion). 
At later points in the fiat money economy life cycle there will 
be a transition to currency that is not backed by a store of value 
213 

===== PAGE 224 =====
as the size of the economies exceed the economic feasibility of 
the government to own or store the necessary amount of the 
store of value. When the government switches from a store of 
value fiat currency system to one backed by the "faith" in the 
government entity that issues the currency, there is the possibili-
ty of a revolution. The hard currency economies that have sur-
vived and grown will eventually, either by common government 
or from wartime expansion, grow to the size (30 or more cities 
of 10,000 or more individuals each) where continued growth 
necessitates change to the fiat system to grow. 
Types of Market Economies 
Communistic 
A communistic economy operates under the assumption that 
what an individual does should benefit the group and not the 
individual. In this economic environment a majority of choices 
of production and consumption are made by the leadership or 
central planners for its citizens. Raw materials and the means 
of production are owned by the group and can only be used by 
the group, for the group. Individual incentive and greed and 
profit motives are discouraged leading to less innovation in pro-
duction and design. For small groups (3-300 individuals) there 
is relatively little chance for the leadership to become corrupt or 
to make poor planing decisions. As the economy serves more 
people less time is available to properly determine what is pro-
duced and where. The common failure of the communistic 
economy is not the ability to mass produce, but the ability to 
move the finished product to the end users. 
Socialistic 
A socialistic economy is the best and worst of both the market 
based economies and the communistic economy. A socialistic 
economy will allow you to create many convolutions of mix-
tures between market and communistic economies. The raw 
materials and means of production are owned by the govern-
ment but can be purchased or rented by the individual. 
Religious 
The religious economy is run by religious leaders. The deci-
sions of production and sale of goods and services in a religious 
economy is largely determined by the market economy with the 
exception of what is against the morals of the deities. Taxation 
takes the form of tithing, although some governments will tithe 
and tax Black market activities will be heightened under the 
rules of this type of economy. 
Frontier 
A frontier economy is a subset within all of the types of market 
economies mentioned so far. As the government grows their 
boundaries, they expand further out from traditional trade, pro-
duction, and travel areas. Three major draws to the frontier are 
the finding and refinement of materials, acquiring land, and 
(social or religious) freedom. In many cases the frontier is not 
well thought of by the bureaucrats. The amount of money that 
will be apportioned to the frontier for cost of populating the 
frontier will not be sufficient to cover vast projects and. The 
frontier will offer many opportunities for trade with nomadic 
tribes and boarder empires. Since the frontier is on the edge of 
the empire its economy will take on a mixed form of all types 
of economies to fit the needs of the present. Access to finished 
goods from the center of the government will be sporadic, lead-
ing frontiersmen to either make or trade for the goods needed. 
Few if any of the tax Jaws passed will be enforced in the fron-
tier. To keep the frontier economies dependent upon the center 
of government the cost of items delivered to the frontier will be 
expensive, while the price the empire will pay to purchase 
goods will be half to one tenth the low cost for the item. The 
disparity of cost will eventually lead to the frontier leading a 
revolt against the central government or joining their neighbor-
ing government. The economics of the frontier will lead to the 
development of bandit groups developing in the area to fill-in 
the inadequate resources of the government. As the frontier 
market economy matures, these bandit groups will evolve into a 
black market economy. 
Black Market 
A black market economy is an economy existing within all the 
economies mentioned in this section. The purpose of the black 
market economy is to provide goods and services to people in 
spite of the fact that a type of government, political, social or 
religious force does not want the goods around. The black mar-
ket economy is most prevalent in areas where there is totalitari-
an or authoritarian rule. The black market is a mostly word-of-
mouth marketplace where transactions occur in dark alleys or 
private locales. In all economies black market transactions are 
not traceable nor taxable by the government. As the current 
government becomes older in age the governments tends to add 
on regulations that creates a thriving environment for the black 
market economy. 
Effects of Bribery within Economies 
From time to time, people want to have events occur that they 
cannot normally initiate in the financial arena. To facilitate the 
event, people will go to great lengths to convince influential 
individuals by providing gifts of money, sex, goods or services. 
The effect of bribery (if done subtly) will not erode the confi-
dence of the current economy. If bribery is readily detectable, it 
will lead to erosion of the economy. 
Disruption of Economies 
The most common factors to disrupt an economy are wars, 
taxes, over-regulation, and corrupt rulers. These factors have 
the effect of draining resources away from production that leads 
to wealth for the masses, which can lead to the raising of cost 
raw materials leading to inflation. The disruption of an econo-
my is a an event that can radically change the setting of a 
world.

Go~Rnments 
The ways of ruling are as varied as the people themselves. 
Each type is presented individually but often many fonns are 
combined to produce a whole government. They are listed by 
stability from most unstable to most stable. Also the most 
extreme fonn of each type is shown. It is in the realm of possi-
bility to have a benevolent dictatorship. In such cases some of 
the harsher aspects will be lessened and the people may thrive. 
This is the unlikely outcome though and given time the worst in 
governments comes to the front until they are rebuilt, reformed 
or overthrown, or so it is the opinion of this authors. 
Anarchy 
"No one has the right to control my actions. Governments sim-
ply steal your money, make you obey their over powering laws, 
and force you to fight for their causes. All the while the politi-
cians sit in their lavish homes getting fat and lazy off of our 
blood, sweat, and tears. In anarchy we do not believe in gov-
ernment. Instead we believe in ourselves. The things I work for 
are mine to protect and keep, my family follows my laws, and if 
some one wrongs me I settle it my self how I see fit. This is 
what being free is and no one will take that away from me while 
I live." 
Description: There is no government or ruling bodies. The 
people are completely free to do any thing they wish that is not 
stopped by another. Every one lives by there own laws and 
dishes out their own punishments. Due to this there are usually 
many small factions that have come together for protection. If 
someone steals from another it is up to the victim to choose the 
punishment and carry it out. If any one faction begins to grow 
too large within populated area, other factions will often work 
together to take away that power. It is almost as if there is a 
constant internal war to keep every major faction suppressed. 
Due to this all citizens are usually of the same low Social Class. 
It is nearly impossible to gain wealth within this sort of society, 
as anyone that seems to be getting ahead is either targeted by 
thieves or stripped by the public in fear of them gaining too 
much power. The name of the game is survival of the fittest. 
Type: No governing body. Any power is possessed by mobs. 
Leader: No one leads the people as a whole. There may be 
some factions that have come together for protection. 
Stability: Highly Unstable due to no power structure. 
Freedom: Extremely high. 
Economy: Very unstable. With no law or order the economy 
often has large fluctuations, bartering becomes common theft is 
common place. 
Law: Law by might. Disputes are settled between the disput-
ing parties and violence is likely. Strength is found both in size 
and ability, but also in numbers. 
Factional info: This environment is highly factionalized. Most 
are formed for protection or mutual betterment. These factions 
sometimes lead to stronger forms of government. However, 
factions themselves make targets for other factions. 
Co"uptocracy 
"Money is the grease that makes the world roll smoothly. 
Power has a price and often a payment. Loyalty is only 
rewarded locally. The over ambitious man is a fool who 
extends his ability beyond his grasp. The winners sit on the 
plush cushions, sampling the finest vintages and the pleasures 
of the courtesans. The losers are found with their purses emp-
tied, and their throats slit in the backs of alleys or the bottom of 
rivers and sometimes, not at all. " 
Description: The ruler(s) are only as powerful as their criminal 
organization's respect and fear has made them. Respect is 
earned through payment, bribery, kickbacks, and handling prob-
lems well. Fear is earned because of ruthless removal of 'prob-
lems' and the enemies that make them. The average citizen is 
likely to owe allegiance to some criminal faction or will suffer 
some form of retribution. The faction controlling an area regu-
lates nearly any fonn of business endeavor within its bound-
aries. Criminal factions are always vying for control over more 
business, more territory and more money. Crime rates are high 
but punishment can be high as well, though often misdirected. 
The common citizen is very free to act but has limited ability to 
rise without the consent of a criminal faction. 
Type: Government by rule of criminal action. 
Leader(s): Supreme rogues(s) 
Stability: Very Unstable 
Freedom: Very High 
Economy: Very unstable, huge fluctuations in prices and avail-
ability of goods/services. 
Law: By decree of current ruJer(s), loose if it exists at all.

Fascism 
"We are the chosen; the elite of this world. Our race is superi-
or to all others; it only makes sense that we should be the lead-
ers. Our people shall rule these lands and all others that were 
not born one of us will be persecuted. We are strong while oth-
ers are weak, their lives pollute our lands. It is our duty to stop 
this pollution and take our rightful positions as the ruling 
class." 
Description: The people truly believe that their race (or fac-
tion) is superior to all others. Anyone that is not a member of 
this elite has absolutely no rights and will either be killed or 
forced into slavery. The children of these societies are brain-
washed from birth to give full devotion to their race and their 
leader. Anyone rebelling will be killed be subjugated by mili-
tary force. This type of society will often try to expand it views 
across the entire world. The leader is usually a person of great 
charismatic power with true understanding of the loves, hates 
and fears of his own people. He uses this knowledge to control 
them. The supreme ruler is looked upon as a superior being by 
any folJowers. This type of government often has spies every 
where to maintain control of the people. Freedom exists only in 
following the strict orders of the government and any one

caught even expressing an opinion that does not coincide with 
the governments plan is likely to be punished. This type of 
government often arises in strong nations reduced by warrior or

Type: Government by rule of predominant a race (or like 
appearing humanoids). 
Leader(s): The most powerful person of the most powerful

Economy: Stable due to the strict rules and regulations

Law: Very Strict, our leader was born to be leader no one has

Dictatorship 
"When the war ended, in the midst of our celebration, we lost 
our way. So enamored were we of the general who lead us to 
victory we made him our beloved despot. Now there is no work 
he does not take some part of, no coin he does not bite, no joy 
that he has not diminished. He is worse than the conquerors 
for we are a people who cannot stand for ourselves, with out 
first begging his pardon." 
Type: Government by rule of arms or martial power. 
Leader(s): One dictator or supreme warrior. 
Stability: Unstable, rarely outlasts the dictator's life span. 
Economy: Unstable. Prices will vary rapidly. 
Freedom: Low 
Law: Dictatorial whim, harsh punishments, and little leniency. 
Factional info: All factions that do not support the dictator are, 
by necessity, secret. 
Description: A single ruler uses whatever means necessary to 
achieve power. Once in power the direct threat of force is used 
to coerce the ruled to be ruled. This political environment is 
rife with assassinations, favor currying, corruption, deception,

may stabilize. The dictator employs spies, assassins, and mili-
tary forces against anyone he sees as an enemy, even against his 
own people. The society degenerates over time, as the dictator

Feudalism 
"Without the lords we would be ripe for any conquerors blade. 
The lords protect us from those who would take our crops or 
worse our very lives. In peace times the wisest of lords ask little 
in the way of tithes and in war all must contribute as much as 
possible. We work the land the lords provide us. " 
Description: In the times of chaos, when there are few leaders

times even outer walls protect the people's homes. The lords 
maintain a force of men that protect the land from hostile

commit crimes are captured and brought to the lord's judge-

his life. Lords are generally seen either as good or bad, with 
very few perceived in between. Thus Feudalism has difficulty

Type: Government by land owning and serfdom.

Stability: Unstable, only as good as the lord who rules.

Factional info: Any faction against the lord brings his wrath. 
Communism 
"In working together we shall thrive. No man should go hun-
gry while another man gets fat. Every one deserves an equal 
amount of everything. That is why we work for free and give 
every bushel of grain we grow and piece ore we mine to the 
government. It is then distributed evenly throughout the people 
as is required to maintain a stable society. Here all people are

Description: All people are meant to be equal within a com-

thing they possess away they will see how great the return is. 
The goal of communism is to form a utopian society where

Autocracy 
"God save the Queen! She rules over the lords and is the pro-

Description: The Queen is guardian of her people. She must 
retain her own royal troops that protect her from the lords, even

More advanced forms of autocracy also include councils of

Even an heir is not a guarantee of a smooth transition after the

Type: Government by birthright, land owning, and councils.

Democracy 
"Every individual counts and shall be counted. Every thought 
shall be heard. Here the common man has a voice in every 
decision. If a new law passes it is passed; it is because the peo-
ple want it. We are truly free; every man is equal in the eyes of 
a vote. The majority rules. " 
Description: In a true democracy every individual has a vote 
in every decision made by the government. In fact every indi-
vidual is the government. Public forums are assembled to 
decide on all political matters. Every citizen that wishes to 
have his voice heard is allowed a vote at these meetings. No 
man or woman has more than one vote and no man is more 
powerful politically than his neighbor. There is no system of 
leadership, there are only the people and the majority always 
rules. Any one that wishes to change or administer new laws 
simply makes a proposal during these public forums and every 
one attending the meeting votes on it. A simple majority vote is 
all that is needed to pass a new law or to abolish or to amend 
and old. Simple majority likewise handles punishment and con-
viction for crimes. This helps assure a stable economy and
