tends to prevent resentment of power. At first such a society 
sounds nearly utopian and they usually begin that way. The 
critical factor is the will of the people that can be a fickle thing, 
if the people begin to get lazy then they may become less edu-
cated creating worse laws and making poorer decisions. With 
no guidance these bad decisions compound until the economy 
and institutions of life begin to fail. Thereafter the people can 
be so mired in their illusions that real refonn becomes impossi-
ble. Also the disagreeing minority suffers. With none to protect 
them the masses easily ride roughshod over smaller groups and 
individuals. Lack of conformity and popularity has a harsh 
price. 
Type: Direct ruled by the people 
Leader(s): There are no leaders, simply the people that vote. 
Stability: Stable but devolving unless education levels are 
high. 
Freedom: Very high, but likely devolving 
Economy: Stable. In such an environment the consumer econ-
omy flourishes. 
Law: Many laws relating directly to the well being and happi-
ness of the citizens. 
Factional info: All factions that do not directly (or obviously) 
harm the people are legal. 
Magiocracy 
"Power is a force to be wielded, whether it flows from the mind 
or to the people. Magic is the greatest means to power, a potent 
weapon and shield to exert control. Control can be measured 
beyond that which is seen and even unseen. With such vast con-
trol empires follow. Failure to control these forces means anar-
chy, or tyranny if the power falls into the wrong hands. Why 
shouldn't the mag es rule, they already command forces the com-
mon man will never understand?" 
Description: Those with the true power of magic control the 
upper echelons of government. These mages are elitist and see 
their place as earned by their ability. Those who do not have 
the ability are merely another resource, and are otherwise of no 
consequence. The single thing that makes the Magiocracy 
slightly more stable is that the Mages insulate themselves from 
the people and create hierarchies of rulership to handle the day 
to day activities of the governed peoples. This means that what 
is most efficient is usually adopted. Since good laws are gener-
ally (but not always) more efficient they tend to have organized 
laws and rights. The people have some degree of freedom. 
Sometimes in a Magiocracy the rulers are so wrapped up in 
their studies of the Arcane that they become removed from the 
common man and laws can develop which tend to forget the 
human equation. Although this leads to a sense of resentment 
between those that do not have magical power and those that 
have it, it rarely boils over into outright revolution. If revolu-
tion does come it usuaJly comes in the fonn of intervention of 
divine based factions who oppose the wicked ways of the 
mages and have recourse against them. 
Type: Government by rule of magical ability. 
Leader(s): Supreme mages(s) 
Stability: Somewhat unstable due to the rise and faJI of those 
with magical talent. 
Freedom: Average. 
Economy: Stable with a high output for those things that can 
be added by magic. 
Law: Varied, some dictates from the ruler(s) but often a com-
plex set of laws handles lesser commerce and crimes. 
Factional info: All factions which oppose magic are secret. 
Socialist Rule 
"We must provide for the weakest amongst us while still pro-
moting those who have ability and talent. We can choose to 
share our wealth without loosing all of it. We each have rights 
and entitlements and we expect the government to be the shield 
that keeps us from hann. " 
Description: Akin to communism but not to the same extreme. 
What a republic is to a democracy, socialism is to communism. 
Socialistic societies arise as citizens demand minimum stan-
dards that the government must provided. To provide these 
entitlements the governments must then tax (or take from) the 
workers who are productive. Rule is by factional groups who 
must maintain the interests of the people or loose the support of 
the masses. The masses are feared because the militaries are 
often become weak over time due to entitlement programs that 
compete with military organizations for members. Individuals 
stiJI retain freedom and a chance to excel but this is balanced 
against the need to provide for those who cannot provide for 
themselves. An underclass of underprivileged, government 
cared for citizens arises rapidly. There is a fonn of inertia that 
grows with this class that seems to keep them down, keep them 
from educating themselves and applying themselves in produc-
tive ways. Because they know that they will be provided for, 
some individuals will not act. This can and does eventually 
destroy these societies as the productive cannot keep supporting 
the unproductive forever. 
Type: Government by rule of arms or martial power, and 
coercing with entitlements and privileges. 
Leader(s): Factional leaders, sometimes totalitarian in nature. 
Stability: Somewhat stable due to few social classes and regu-
lar enforcement of law. 
Freedom: Moderate. Excess is not tolerated. 
Economy: Stable but can become unstable and devolving if 
entitlements overbalance ability to produce. 
Factional info: There are a many factions within governing 
bodies. Only dangerous and criminal factions are considered 
illegal. 
Bureaucracy 
"There is a form for everything and for everything there is a 
form. There is a line to request permission to be in another line 
to be heard to ask if you can petition to get a hearing for rever-
sal of a previous decision by an official whom no one can find. " 
218 

===== PAGE 229 =====
Description: These types of governments begin simply 
enough. No one is really in charge directly of the 
anything-instead, officials have rules by which they may enact 
other rules which may or may not be laws by which all govern-
ing is then done. Commerce is difficult. Bribery and corrup-
tion follow. The average citizen usually has the illusion of a 
high degree of freedom and yet may become embroiled in petty 
crime disputes for their entire lifetimes. The military is often 
disorganized. This society usually collapses into a corruptocra-
cy or is overthrown by a harsher fonn of government. 
Type: Rule by official procedure and complex law. 
Leader(s): Officials who past tests to prove the can adminis-
trate their portion of the bureaucracy. 
Stability: Stable but devolving as the average citizen is less 
able to function. 
Freedom: Confused. Some consider it high as it takes a long 
process to be convicted of a crime. But official rights may be 
highly restricted. The average citizen may be committing 
crimes without even knowing they are crimes. 
Economy: Devolving, as taxation increased to pay for the 
bureaucracy. Taxmen and officials flourish, all else suffer. 
Law: A mystery, hidden procedure and lost in committee. 
Truly complex laws govern everything. Few completely under-
stand them. 
Factional info: Highly factionalized . 
Judicial 
"If we follow the law it is hard to see how we have a govern-
ment at all. The local militias and magistrates protect the 
peace. High crimes bring the bounty hunters. You can't cross 
the law forever and expect to roam free. Eventually justice is 
served to all. " 
Description: Those that do not break the laws have little con-
tact with the government. The government is seen as militia 
and sheriffs on the streets of the community. It is heard in 
courtrooms were justice is dispensed. The laws must remain 
fair or and a sense that they have become unfair sends ripples of 
dissent through the governed. Mild to extreme forms of protest 
and disobedience follow. If the laws and rulers are corrected 
then life continues as nonnal. Otherwise the people may begin 
calling for justice against the justice makers. Criminals are 
hunted. The services of bounty hunters are in high demand. 
This is a fairly stable fonn of government marred by a lack of 
defense and providing for services of any kind. 
Type: Rule by judicial oversight. 
Leader(s): Supreme judges. 
Stability: Stable 
Freedom: Freedom within allowable laws is high. 
Economy: Strong, because of the safety of law. 
Law: The law is king. Advocates, accusers and magistrates 
administer the laws. Laws are set and adjusted by judicial com-
mittee. 
Factional info: Moderately factionalized. 
Capitalism 
"The root of power is in wealth. Those who create and control 
the most wealth buy their way to power. Every one of us has a 
chance to be wealthy. Freedom is good as it promotes competi-
tion and everyone knows competition is healthy." 
Description: This government is run by the financial numbers, 
taxes are imposed by the richer factions onto the lesser ones. 
Power is wielded by purchasing rights to areas of trade, or to 
individual resources. New business spring up everyday; 
Everyone is selling something. Prostitution is usually legal. 
Armed forces are mercenary in nature. It is all about the 
almighty coin. Religion may suffer because it leads people 
away from the materialistic goals of the society. Birthrights are 
shunned. Seats in ruling commercial entities are purchased by 
the most powerful and influential. Lesser commercial entities 
will band together to financial destroy stronger ones if they are 
seen as having unfair practices. However this is the only reme-
dy and the society often devolves into family or clan run institu-
tions that fall into ruin when the incompetent are allowed to 
continue despite the usual practices of allowing power to be 
purchased. 
Type: Rule by commercial interests. 
Leader(s): Merchant organizations create ruling bodies whose 
seats are purchasable. 
Stability: Stable. 
Freedom: The more you earn the more you have freedom. 
Economy: Strong- the life's blood of this government. 
Law: commercial procedures and criminal activity are defined 
around commerce and what has value. Murder might be 
defined as depriving a family of a stable provider or an employ-
er of a worker. 
Factional info: Highly factionalized commercialized entities. 
Republic 
"We elect our rulers, and ifwe don't like them we can elect oth-
ers. The founders in their wisdom provided for accountability 
and responsibility to the people by their elected rulers. They 
provided us ways to vote the officials out of power if they mis-
use their positions or fail to provide for the common good. It 
would take too long for every citizen to vote on every subject, 
we must trust in those we elect to represent us. " 
Description: In a republic citizens vote for their representa-
tives. The representatives in tum vote on the political issues 
that effect the land on behalf of their people. A different repre-
sentative is elected from the different districts of the lands. If a 
representative is not carrying out the wishes of the people then 
she will either not be re-elected or he will have his position 
stripped from her depending on the severity of her actions. 
There is often a stable economy and the people who obey the 
laws benefit from great freedom. There are few government 
regulations set for conducting business. In theory the people 
when united rule the lands. Various fonns of this government 
can arise. Federalism is a type of republic that has a central rul-
219 

===== PAGE 230 =====
ing body that rules strongly over lesser more provincial ruling 
bodies. 
Type: Ruled by elected representatives of the people. 
Leader(s): The highest elected official. 
Stability: Very Stable, due to the right of the people to vote an 
individual out of office if they do not agree with her actions. 
Freedom: High 
Economy: Stable, often with much variety. 
Law: Laws are set in place for the well being of the citizens. 
Factional info: There are many factions that try to gain politi-
cal power and influence. 
Meritocracy 
"We earn our rights. While the most basic rights apply to all, 
power and privilege comes to those who have shown the 
responsibility to use it properly. Those that rise in ability and 
power have a responsibility to protect those that are less capa-
ble. Yet anyone can prove himself capable through action and 
thought. Idleness is the enemy of all the people." 
Description: This is a highly stratified society of many levels. 
Both tests and service records as well as recommendations cre-
ate rise in social status and responsibility. The lowest members 
of this society may not even be considered citizens if they have 
not performed the required levels of service to society. Those 
born into the lower classes have the same opportunities of 
advancement as those in higher level of society. Everyone is 
born the same but some do get easier recommendations and 
greater opportunities through birth. This society is stable in 
many configurations. If the people become too lazy, those at 
the higher levels suffer and thus will work to get the problem 
corrected. Crime and corruption are dealt with swiftly and 
often harshly. The society has little room for those it cannot 
trust. Criminals are often given the opportunity to serve in dan-
gerous military actions or to serve their fellow citizens. Type: 
Ruled by best candidates. 
Leader(s): The best candidate is elected by proving themselves 
in various tests while having completed various levels of serv-
ice elsewhere and exceeding at each level. 
Stability: Extreme stability. 
Freedom: Ability determines freedom but freedom is generally 
high. 
Economy: Stable, with large yields and quality goods and 
services. 
Law: Laws are set in place to serve all of society, though not 
necessarily equally, and are changed by those that have proved 
they understand the impact of those laws on societies best. 
Enforcers of Jaw also are constantly required to prove they cor-
rectly use the responsibility they have been given. 
Factional info: There are many factions that are generally 
grouped around providing the best training and opportunity for 
each member. 
Utopian 
"We existed in bliss. We accomplished what we needed to and 
supported each other in a harmony that would not be possible 
with less enlightened beings. We have an interdependence that 
allows us to be individuals without losing sight of our common 
interests. Those that came before had good knowledge that we 
cannot forget lest we devolve from this state of grace. " 
Description: A utopia is theoretical state, and without enlight-
enment mortals have difficulty imagining one. It requires great 
understanding by all individuals. Education is the greatest and 
most constant task of the people. Empathy for fellow individu-
als has to be extreme. If a neighbor can feel the blow he would 
strike against his neighbor and knows that it will cause both 
their families great pain to begin a feud, why would he begin it 
unless he is touched by imperfection. The greatest profession in 
this society is the teacher. The society must close itself off to 
those that are less enlightened or face possible dissolution. 
Therefore inferior, untrainable individuals must often be ban-
ished from society. The highest crime is therefore banishment. 
None but the insane would want to lose utopia. The greatest 
fear that remains to the society is boredom. The society can be 
so static that it might eventually welcome change, even if that 
same change may kill it. Most humanoids are incapable of 
achieving a utopian government for any length of time. 
Type: Ruled mutual consent. 
Leader(s): First of equals. Whoever is the most qualified indi-
vidually or as a group to decide a particular issue decides it. 
The decision may be debated but when necessary those most 
capable are empowered to act to preserve the interests of the 
whole. 
Stability: Completely stable. 
Freedom: Complete save the harming of another or the whole. 
Economy: Non-existent. Bartering re-emerges but knowledge 
is the most often exchanged good. 
Law: Very few hard laws. Instead the law is a spirit which 
flows form situation to situation achieving the nest possible 
result because those who can best apply it do so based on the 
situations at hand. 
Factional info: There is an overriding single faction which all 
must feel apart of to keep the utopian ideal going.

HIStOR)? 
Well developed histories make a game world feel well rich and 
realistic, drawing players into legends and myths. Developing a 
full game world history can take years; no matter how much 
you prepare ahead of time, there will always be the need for 
more history. Often you may find yourself jotting notes from 
time to time just before a player finds out something interesting 
from the past that relates to her present or future. Histories 
should begin with a good foundation but can and should devel-
op along the way. The following are the types of subject matter 
you will want to address in your world's history: 
Cultural/National: A history on the beginnings of, early leaders, 
early settlements, etc. 
Heroic: The life and times of a hero or heroine. 
Villainous: The life and times of a villain. 
Factional: The history of the rise (and perhaps falJ) of a faction 
within a culture. 
Settlement: The history of an area, its peoples, their culture, 
leaders and great events. 
Divine: Great writings of deities and their desires and influ-
ences of mortals. 
Prophetic: The story of a prophecy, its place in history and 
how it came to pass or will come to pass. 
Magic: The history of the rise and mastery of magic. 
Martial: The history of the rise and mastery of arms. 
Criminal: The history of the criminal class. 
World: The history of the world as a whole: which cultures and 
leaders dominated when and the progress of all cultures as a 
whole. 
Artifact: The history and making of artifacts and magic items. 
CultuRaL anb Nanonal Hol1ba)?s 
A defining attribute of any culture is its holidays. Holidays 
seem to last sometimes longer than the culture itself and get 
absorbed or incorporated into later or subsequent cultures. 
Several holiday ideas are provided below. 
Seasonal: Occurs based on the solstice and equinox cycles (the 
longest and shortest days and their midway points.) Holidays 
are usually based on festivals like a winterfest celebrating the 
hope of the coming spring in deepest winter or the fall festival 
celebrating the harvests and the end of summer. 
Religious: Based on a proscribed religious observance of days 
for various parts of the religion. Perhaps days of the remem-
brance of prophets, a day when a god or goddess was first seen 
or the day of death or birth of an avatar, etc. 
Leader: The birthday or day of death of a famous leader. 
Founding: The founding day of the culture or the day of its 
separation, liberation or overcoming of another culture. 
Gift Giving: A day to give gifts. 
Freedom: A day to release restrictions, perhaps in a restive 
society. 
Fool's Day: A day where roles are reversed; the fool becomes 
the king Usually used to vent steam against the aristocratics. 
221 
Market Day: A day when markets are filled or a special time in 
which far flung clans gather to trade. 
Day of Masks: A holiday where concealment and costume 
allows frivolity and merriment as well as trying on of different 
roles. 
Planting Day: The day of first planting in an agrarian society 
Harvest Day: The day of harvest in agrarian societies. 
Fertility: A holiday where sexuality runs rampant and the nor-
mal morals are broken or allowed to relax. 
Matchmaking: A day of betrothal where couples are made, 
often by the families of the children long before they are of age 
to decide for themselves. 
War: A day to remember a war, celebrate its victory or remem-
ber those who fought and those who died. 
Death: A day to ward off death or accept iL as part of the cycle 
of life. 
Magic: A day that has magical significance or at which some 
magical phenomenon occurs. 
Warding: A day to ward of evil spirits or the angered dead with 
special rites and/or atonements. Often involving a sacrifice of at 
least symbolic importance. 
Crowning: The day a leader rose to power.

timelines for each culture or nation. This means knowing the 
calendar and time system. What year will it be? When and why 
did this system of time come into effect? Making a new time 
and calender system can be burdensome on the players, as they 
attempt to convert everything from their current mindset to the 
new one you have created for your world. You can change

date systems you have invented. The table below shows the

Factional membership 
Some factions are wide open and others only replace members 
upon the death of a current member. Below are several mem-
bership styles: 
Loose: Membership is unrecorded and unspecific. If someone 
thinks they are a member of this faction, they probably are. It 
reduces stability by 2 levels but is likely to increase the number 
of people in the faction dramatically. 
Open: Anyone can join anytime. Random effect on stability 
(increases or decreases randomly depending on whim of the 
people, current ideology, etc.). 
Elitist: Some characteristic or perceived difference allows 
entrance to the faction. All other membership is closed. 
Seasonal: The faction has a specific period where membership 
is encouraged. At other times membership is not open. 
Application: The character applies for membership and is 
approved by a set process. There may be ways around this 
process but the most predominate way to join this faction is 
through application for membership. Stability is improved by 
one level. 
Approval: The prospective member gets the approval of the 
faction or portion of the faction and is let in. Stability is 
improved by one level. 
Arbitrary: No set rhyme or reason determines why someone 
gets into the group or faction. Stability is lowered by 2 levels. 
Merit: Through an award or meritorious conduct an individual 
becomes a member of the faction. Stability increases 2 levels. 
Appointment: Another person appoints members to this faction. 
Stability increased by one level. 
Sponsorship: The prospective member must find someone to 
sponsor them to become members of this faction or group. 
Stability is increased by one level. 
Talent: Through demonstration of a talent membership is 
gained. Stability decreases by one level. 
Nobility: One must be seen as a noble to enter this faction. 
Stability increases by one level. 
Hereditary: Membership is based on family name, clan or 
place of birth. Stability lowers by one level. 
Replacement: When a member dies or is removed another is 
chosen to take his or her place. Stability increases by 3 levels. 
Test: A test of faith, friendship, trustworthiness, belief, etc. is 
taken by the prospective member to gain entrance. Stability is 
increased by one level. 
Event: Some event happened which all members participated in 
or were affected by, binding them as a faction. Initial stability 
is +2 and then, per year, is reduced by one level.

Flora: Define tree types, bushes, flowers, grasses, roots, water-based, carnivorous and insecta-
vorious. Create magical varieties for use as herbs. Place by region within your world or set-
ting. Use the herb section for defining magi-
cal herbs useful for Hermetic Lore. 
Fauna: Define more common life 
fonns, insects, small animals, medium 
animals, large animals, herbavores, 
insectavores, carnivores, etc. Combine 
with Flora to create a food chain. Use the 
monster design section to create the larger or 
more dangerous animals. Use hermetic to define 
magical properties of animal parts. 
Creatures: Add "monsters" to the top of the current food chain and . define which 
flora and fauna supports each creature (see Design section for creature creation 
process.) Define the magical properties of creatures for use in Hermetic Lore. 
Races: Decide which races you will use and/or design (see the Design section for 
the race creation process). 
Magic: Set the magical level of the world and determine magic sources (see Magic 
section.) Determine which of your races or beings can use magic and which cannot. 
Those who cannot should not be a magic using class like mage, trickster, etc.

f 1LL1m; the Settm~ with People 
Populating a game world with individuals that will directly interact 
with other characters is a Herculean task. Rather than spending years 
developing a population of individuals, each with an intricate back-
ground, there is a method available to gradually develop characters. 
There is a three-stage, layered approach to building up a unique popu-
lation, with each stage going more indepth than the stage before. These 
stages produce the Game Master Extra (GME), the Game Master 
Personality (GMP), and the Game Master Character (GMC). 
GMEs 
Every race has average Joes and Janes. These are the extras who rep-
resent the baker and farmer, the students and the teachers, or the con-
scripted warrior and the sea-going pirate. A Game Master Extra starts 
his life with a first name, race, basic attributes and random social skill 
based on his occupation (see Player's Guide). Noticeably lacking from 
a GME is a last name, history, family, and any distinguishing details 
other than perhaps a single quirk. These individuals have very limited 
knowledge of the world, as their experiences are often limited to the 
area where they grew up and/or currently reside. A GME is intended 
to interact with other individuals only in the most basic of ways and 
generally fulfills some basic role within the world. Tim the rope mer-
chant or Jennifer the fish monger are two basic examples of Game 
Master Extras. 
The average extra has her attributes generated with 5d4 only. If you 
wish, you can roll up any specific attribute that you may need to know 
for this individual, or you can simply use the average of 5d4 (consid-
ered to be 13). Whichever method, any relevant attributes can be mod-

Occupation Effects 
GMEs may have attributes modified based on their profession. 
Use the table below to determine these modifiers. Attribute 
points gained for occupations are treated as drilled points. If 
the common person stops their occupation, these modifiers are 
lost after two weeks of non-activity per drilling rules. These 
modifiers do not apply to classed characters as they are 
assumed to have left their previous occupation to become their 
current class(es). 
For GMEs Endurance is always (Strength +Vitality/2) with 
racial modifiers. Except for militia and conscripts, Weapon 
Knowledge is treated as base chance or as a non-acquired skill. 
They can wield weapons at a -10% penalty unless they make 
their Weapon Knowledge roll, after training, in which case the 
penalty drops to -5%. No common person can ever partially 
learn more than two weapons through using non-acquired 
Weapon Knowledge. Militia and conscripts automatically get 
one weapon they can use without penalty and may learn up two 
more by the methods above. 
Additional GME rules 
Apply these additional rules to your GMEs, or common people: 
1. Choose one social skill reflective of his profession. No more than 
l /2 of their normal racial skills are defined. 
2. They can use any armor that they could reasonably find or own. 
3. They have a -10% to morale (including conscripts and militia.) 
4. They may have 1-3 additional class skills as a failed class type, as 
well as normal racial and social skills by Knowledge.

Game Master Personalities(GMPs) 
A Game Master Personality is a GME that has all attributes, a 
class, multiple social skills, all racial skills and a short history 
defined. GMPs have a developed mood and attitude and can 
have their own social flair or clothing style defined as well. 
While they have some knowledge of world events, they are 
most often focused on capitalizing local opportunities for their 
own advancement and because of such are most often well 
known locals. GMPs often serve the surrounding locale as 
source of knowledge or act as the local expert of an intermedi-
ate skill such as blacksmithing or healing and can even act in a 
small leadership role. A GMP is intended to interact with other 
individuals on an occasional basis and often influences the 
events of a scenario. Dan D. Lion, the protector of the forest 
and Lord Gathor, the landlord, are two basic examples of a 
Game Master Personalities. 
Game Master Characters (GMCs) 
A Game Master Character is a GMP that has been fully devel-
oped to the same level as a player character and should be treat-
ed as if roleplayed by a player. Most notably, a GMC has a free 
will and as such his actions are not directly dictated by a situa-
tion as they are with a GME and GMP. As such, a Game 
Master Character is instrumental in helping or hindering player 
characters or creating different paths for a player character to 
take to reach a goal. GMCs are usually well known individuals 
with reputations within an organization or a large geographic 
area. A GMC is intended to interact with other individuals on a 
day-to-day basis and is often a primary focus of an adventure or 
campaign. Tony Tanissa the short but mean Midfolk mob-boss 
of the capital city, Casandra O'Connor the queen of the northern 
gypsies, and Prince Estharkin, the first in line for the Elven 
throne are three very basic concept examples of a Game Master 
Character. 
Retired GMCs 
Because they are too old, too wounded or just too tired of the 
adventuring life GMCs can retire to regular society. They may 
lose their edge (- 1 or -2 attribute points in the required attrib-
utes for their class), but they still retain their skills and skill 
chances (minus any lost for attribute reduction) and can be 
extremely helpful or hindering to other adventurers. 
Roles (ChaRacteR Concepts) 
The most fundamental aspect of character is personality. Role 
playing is the assumption and acting out of a defined role. In 
the real world people take on roles; they are generally based on 
life experience, birth order, accomplishments, recognition, study 
and hard work, and even the perceptions of others. As you cre-
ate and evolve beings in your world, be cognizant of the charac-
ter concepts you want to portray. You can choose one or more 
of the roles below that suit your character concept. Remember 
to change some of these roles as the being matures and grows, 
keeping some of them as core or central to the overall concept. 
Roles are not to be confused with alignment which represents 
the being's larger world view and place therein. 
Heroism/Cowardice 
Coward: Afraid of any danger and never a risk taker. Does not allow 
what others perceptions are to force him to take risks. He invites a 
bully and will be incapable of action in most extreme situations. 
Traumatized: Some action or misdeed done upon her in the past has 
caused an irrational fear to grow within the character. She will rarely 
take risk unless others push her into it. The irrational fear causes inac-
tion in some difficult situations. 
Self-preserving: Fear comes only in those circumstances that are likely 
to lead to death. His fear is not irrational and stems from the wish to 
continue, to survive. He will remove himself from truly dangerous situ-
ations. 
Reluctant Hero: She has reasonable fears but risks anyway. She will 
not be comfortable in heroic roles, but recognizes the necessity of the 
role needing to be fulfilled during times of great need. 
Self-sacrificing: Out of a sense of duty or a love of all life he is will-
ing to take some risk to save others. He will not take risks just to take 
them, but will balance the risk with the reward to others. 
The Hero: A risk taker. If she has fear, she never shows it or allows it 
to cloud judgment. The hero often takes risks that involve little reward 
or small overall gains for her cause. 
Luck 
Born Loser: He seems to make the wrong choices at the wrong times. 
All those crucial situations tum at the worst possible time with the 
worse possible result. Often this being is so used to bad luck he seems 
to make bad luck on his own. 
Loser: Bad luck has struck enough times for the being to be labelled a 
failure. She now has a low self-esteem and does not believe in his or 
her past accomplishments. Bad luck will strike again or so she feels. 
Average: This person makes his or her own luck, bad or good. It is 
just as likely he will do well as poorly. Chance does not seem to play 
a large role in this being's life. 
Winner: Luck strikes this person when she seems to need it most. Just 
when things are going bad they tum around. She finds ways of making 
the worst situation seem better and then feels lucky. 
Born Winner: Always on top, this person enjoys the lion's share of 
luck and never seems to be beaten. No matter what happens he or she 
seems to get the best of it. These beings are immensely self-assured. 
Talent/Fame 
Destined Star: This individual has a recognizable talent and is des-
tined for greatness. She is known for their extraordinary ability in a 
particular area. 
Rising Star: This individual is recognized for his talent, but has yet to 
fulfill his full potential. He is well on his way towards becoming a 
success and is now at least regionally famous. 
Star: The accomplished talent. She has reached the brass ring. Few 
ever are as famous as a star but this being has achieved greatness 
through blind luck, talent, gift, and perseverance. She is recognized 
even over and above her talent. 
Falling Star: The talent has begun to suffer. He is considered past 
their prime, though still accomplished. Age and time has taken its toll. 
Fallen Star: The individual has lost talent, lost fame and is now only 
thought of for past deeds and achievements. Occasionally the talent 
may resurface but not enough to recover what once was.

===== PAGE 238 =====
Attention Needs 
Drama Queen: This person must be the center of attention and will 
create all kinds of havoc just to continue being in the spotlight. The 
being will resort to the worst of tricks just to gamer continued atten-
tion. She is happiest when surrounded by admirers. 
Victim: This person plays the victim for the negative attention. 
Always suffering imagined slights, insults and ailments. Happiest 
when being cared for and fawned over. 
Wolf Crier: This person is always telling awful stories and big whop-
pers because of the momentary attention. He or she will be ignored by 
those who know them well, thought to be a liar or paranoid. 
Everybody's Friend: This being makes sacrifices to stay in the good 
graces of even the slightest of acquaintances. He is known as generous 
but it is a defense mechanism to keep from losing a friend's attention. 
Friendly: This being gets the attention of friends and loved ones in a 
healthy normal way, by earning it. She will not stay in an unhealthy 
relationship for long. 
Loner: Prefers to avoid attention and remain to oneself. Can accept a 
certain amount of individual attention but never seeks it out. 
Isolationist: The being avoids the attention and company of others and 
finds ways to avoid lasting relationships of any kind. He may have a 
low opinion of others. 
Separatist: A hermit. Cannot abide the company of others. Leaves 
civilization or finds a way to hide within it. Cannot maintain any rela-
tionship whatsoever even with blood relations. She does not under-
stand others or has become so obsessed with her own problems or 
struggles that she cannot handle another's. 
Organization 
Mess Maker: Cannot stay organized or maintain discipline. He lets 
things go until they are beyond salvageable. Give them more than one 
thing to do or keep at a time and something will inevitably be lost. 
Disorganized: Is unable to handle larger tasks or life situations in an 
ordered fashion. As soon as this individual becomes overloaded, 
organization is the first to suffer. Inevitably, lesser importance items 
are lost in the shuffle. 
Organized: This person survives difficult situations and task through 
organization and planing. She is not known to forget a task nor to be 
late for an activity. 
Over-planner: This being has plans for plans. He is likely to call a 
meeting just to plan out the next meeting. They are compulsive plan-
ners and are rarely ever spontaneous about anything. 
Love 
Dispassionate: Does not enjoy feeling any strong emotions and there-
fore avoids situations which would evoke or involve extreme emotion. 
He is often thought of as cold or uncaring and this may or may not be 
true. He may have suffered from past strong or forceful relationships 
that caused anxiety or unease. 
Capable of Love: She can love and will if the situation presents itself 
but is reserved until such a situation is obvious or likely. 
Loving: The being feels love and emotion greatly and will often make 
the first move to ensure love. He is a risk takers with his emotions and 
is capable of passion in appropriate situations. 
Passionate: The being feels love or strong emotions, often at inappro-
priate times. She is just as likely to hate those that reject her as feel 
even stronger love. This passion will bleed over into other aspects of 
her life. 
Hate 
Despise: Everyone will eventually do something to agitate this being. 
No one is immune, especially those that are nice or caring towards the 
being, as they are most likely to betray. Never forgets or forgives any 
slight, however small. 
Hot Tempered: Easily upset, this being is likely to react to betrayal or 
have frequent misunderstandings with others. Anger is seething just 
below the surface, likely to hold a grudge for long. 
Even Tempered: Will forgive and forget when appropriate and be 
angry when appropriate but never for long. Unlikely to hold a lasting 
grudge. 
Forgiving: Unlikely to hate or keep anger for any length of time. 
These individuals forgive to their own detriment. Others often take 
advantage of this. 
Zest/Zeal 
Doom: For this being the world is an awful place. It and all in it are 
dying. There is no point to anything because it won't last. Why bother? 
Life is tasteless, odorless, and bland. No experience is wortb the effort. 
Gloom: These individuals see little reason to do much more than hope 
for a better life. They think that it is possible to achieve great things 
but now isn't the right time. Perhaps another day will be better. Some 
things should be experienced, but one needs to be careful. 
Bloom: Life is getting better all the time. Trying new things in order 
to learn and experience is a must. They think the world will get better 
over time, no matter how bad it is right now. 
Loom: Life is a loom to be weaved full of new experiences and 
knowledge. They want to suck the marrow from life, to see it all and 
feel it all. The world is a great place and detractors are mere distrac-
tions. 
Outlook 
Pessimist: These beings believe that people are essentially bad. 
Things will get worse and the only thing one can rely on is one's self. 
If the job is to be done right, they have to do it themselves because 
everyone else will louse it up. 
Wait and See: They trust only after it is earned. The believe only after 
it is proven. They wait and they see. If they don't see, they may not 
wait forever. 
Plan for the Worst but Hope for the Best: These beings are not sur-
prised when others fall down but they hope that it doesn't happen. 
They hope people will be true and situations will improve but they 
plan for contingencies. 
Try and See: These people take the first step. They trust first and find 
out later. They will get out of bad situations once they realize it has 
gone bad but will try similar things anyway because each situation is 
unique. 
Optimist: These people are optimistic even in the face of disaster. The 
forest fire makes way for new trees. The death of a loved one is prut 
of the great cycle. Most situations will be positive. Do not be distract-
ed by the bad things in life. 
Political 
Leftist: Change for change sake. The establishment is wrong and 
should be torn down and replaced, preferably with something new. 
The old ways are wrong and the new ways are the only salvation for 
all. Those that disagree are just part of the problem. 
Liberal: Would like to see the establishment change at the proper 
pace. The changes should support people and people issues. Those that 
228 

===== PAGE 239 =====
are less fortunate should be aided by the establishment or the establish-
ment has no real reason to exist in its present form. Individuals should 
be protected from the heavy-handed dealings of an oppressive society. 
Moderate: Change when change is needed. Status quo when the 
establishment is doing a good job. Swayed by a rousing speech, or 
personage of integrity. 
Conservative: One who would maintain the establishment and way of 
life as it is or needs to be. One who believes that people must take 
care of themselves and it is not the establishment's role or responsibili-
ty to do so. Establishment programs to aid common people would only 
rob them of their self-reliance. Believes society should be protected 
from the evils of the depraved individuals. 
Reactionary: These individuals want to make the establishment even 
more rigid. They want the politics of the past to prevail and replace the 
current establishment. These individuals often use hate to sell their 
message and point to certain individuals in society who are responsi-
ble. 
Power Seeking 
Power Grabber: This individual seizes power at any cost and by any 
means. He does not care how it affects others. Others are beneath him 
and not destined for higher position. Those who stand in his way can 
be sure that every ounce of power he have will be directed at them in 
order to gain more power. 
Ambitious: Seeking power and carefully plotting to get it but not to 
the permanent detriment of others. This individual will step on toes to 
get where she wants to be. 
Opportunist: Waits patiently for the right situation; then seizes it and 
uses it to their advantage. The opportunist is the one who makes the 
best of the right situation but does not set the situation up. Constant 
preparation is their motto. 
Responsible: Meets his responsibilities and earns his keep. Does not 
take power or use situations but will accept responsibility or position 
when they are offered, or required. 
Denial: Doesn't want power but will handle it momentarily if forced. 
Rises to meet challenges they are forced to and then quickly slips out 
of power when possible. 
Escapist: Doesn't want power and responsibility. Flees if necessary to 
avoid it. Likes the bottom rung just fine and thinks freedom is worth 
it. Responsibility brings danger and can only lead to her shortcomings 
being made public. 
Group Rank 
Follower: Follows when called. Joins when asked but never volun-
teers. Likes the comfort of being part of the crowd. 
Joiner: Easily joins causes or groups that sound interesting or fulfill 
some internal need. 
Leader: Leads groups. Find themselves thrust into or seeking leader-
ship positions within groups. Others look up to them. 
Founder: Someone who creates groups and or factions. The highest 
leader or overall focus. 
Overall Ability 
Incapable: Unable to complete tasks in an efficient or correct manner. 
Inept: Unlikely to produce anything but shoddy work or service. 
Average: Neither likely or unlikely to produce good work or service. 
Practiced: Likely to produce good work or service. 
Capable: Always completes tasks in an efficient and correct manner. 
Seriousness 
Careless: This being is too relaxed about life to worry about the 
details. The details are for the serious and depressing work-a-day 
drones. These beings will have difficulty focusing on tasks for long 
periods of time. 
Carefree: Less likely to be cautious in their actions. These individuals 
shoot from the hip and figure life works itself out anyway. They will 
typically abandon long term projects and or tasks when they become 
too much work or when something more interesting comes along. 
Careful: Cautious when acting. These individuals are likely to plan 
actions and or at least think them through carefully. They work for 
their rewards and expect little luck to come there way unearned. 
Serious: Life is about work and careful planning. You don't get any-
where through dumb luck, or so they believe. They distrust the less 
serious and openly oppose those who are careless. 
Commitment 
No Commitment: These individuals are incapable of committing to 
any cause, person, place or relationship. They drift through life and 
even the pain of loneliness will not get them to overcome their fears of 
commitment. 
Uncommitted: These individuals reserve commitment for only the 
most special of times or the best of relationships. Most of the time 
they are on the outside looking in. They often wait too long to com-
mit and lose their chance. 
Committed: Can commit to causes and relationships when they are 
worthy. Bases the level of commitment on the worthiness of the cause 
or relationship. 
Over Committed: Tend to commit to a level that allows the individual 
to be taken advantage off. Will rarely back down from a commitment 
and hates being seen as a quitter. 
Empathy/Sympathy 
Detached: These individuals avoid feeling emotions relating to others. 
They may feel strong feelings about themselves or their own situations 
but are either incapable of or choose not to feel for others. 
Sympathetic: Can feel others but only from a distance. Stronger emo-
tions and/or feelings are denied. 
Empathetic: Can feel other's pain and joy and is very affected by the 
emotions of those around them. Sometimes overly so. 
Internalized: Feels the emotions of others around them deeply. They 
can imagine themselves as the other person often suppressing their 
own feelings for the emotions of another. 
Risk 
Refuser: Avoids all risk. When pressed by outside influence they 
refuse to take a risk. Only those situations where no real risk is 
involved will they attempt or get involved in. 
Weigher: Weighs all risk very carefully. Only if the reward matches 
the risk or the risk is low will they take the chance. If the risk can pro-
duce permanent harmful results they are unlikely to attempt it regard-
less of the reward. 
Gambler: Takes risks that others would consider chancy or dangerous. 
The risk will often outweigh the reward, but this individual will chance 
it anyway. They do weigh extremely dangerous situations but may try 
anyway. 
Risk Taker: These beings believe you can't have rewards without 
risks. They are often reckless and will take the most dangerous risks 
for average rewards.

===== PAGE 240 =====
Authority 
Rebellious: Hates all authority. Does not accept nor bows to authority. 
Would live free or die before submitting. Escapes, avoids or removes 
all authority they encounter. 
Reluctant: Dislikes authority. Reluctantly follows when necessary or 
if the authority is deserved. Unlikely to accept any dissenting opinion 
or faction long term . 
Merit: Authority earned is authority respected. If they agree with the 
authority they will follow it steadfastly; otherwise, they will see the 
authority as lesser or without merit and act accordingly. 
Observer: Follows authority until it proves to be wrong. This individ-
ual is always surprised when the politician is caught with his hands in 
other's pockets. 
Hard Liner: Authority for authority's sake. lf you don't like it, that's 
too bad. It's not ours to question why. These individuals are the 
guardians of authority and as such are often the scapegoats when 
someone takes a fall for an authority figure. 
Loyalty 
Betrayer: A betrayer of causes or relationships. His own reasons are 
more important than the cause or relationship such that when the loyal-
ty is tested loyalty fails. 
Disloyal: Likely to be disloyal in difficult or unforeseen situations. 
When tested, morale may be the deciding factor between loyalty and 
disloyalty. 
Elitist: The being typically has a select group of friends for whom she 
would risk life or limb, but has no regard for the well being of those 
outside that group. While not desiring harm upon anyone, the Elitist 
would think nothing of the destruction of a town. To 
become a member of her group, one must almost prove 
their merit. 
Loyal: A being who is unlikely to betray a cause or 
relationship. Only the most heinous of situations, such 
as kidnapping of a loved one, etc., would ever make the 
being consider betrayal. 
Martyr: The individual would die for the cause or rela-
tionship. There is no circumstance the being would 
betray. He can be tortured, etc. and will still be unlikely 
to give away a secret or betray another. 
Past, Present and Future 
Obsessed with the Past: Some event or imagined splen-
dor of the past has the individual living solely for the 
past. He neglects present circumstances, often letting 
appearance and current relationships and responsibilities 
suffer in order to daydream about the past. 
Living in the Past: Passionate for a previous time or 
age and is likely to dress or act based on that time or 
perception of that time. Dislikes the present state of 
affairs and would happily trade it all in for a ticket to 
the past. 
Fondness for the Past: The being is nostalgic about old 
times or elder days. He is likely to know more about 
the past then others, but does not lose sight of the fact 
that he lives in the present. 
Remembers Past: The past is a memory and is to be 
cherished if deserving or remembered as needed, noth-
ing more. 
Forgets Past: The past is the past and has no bearing on 
the future. Why worry about what has gone before 
when you must live now is this individual's feeling. 
Non-spontaneous: An inability to live in the now. Unable to seize the 
current day and make it one's own. These individuals have little inter-
est in new experiences or immediate gratification and are willing to 
forgo either for other endeavors. 
Spontaneous: Can enjoy new experiences on the spur of the moment. 
Likes immediate gratification of needs or wants. This individual does 
not like to wait for outcomes. 
Living in the Present: Trapped in the eternal now. The being is 
unwilling to consider the future or remember the past and how it 
relates to current activities. He needs immediate gratification and is 
unable to wait for any long term outcomes. 
Obsessed with the Future: Some imagined splendor of the future has 
the individual living for a better day. He or she neglects present cir-
cumstances. Often letting appearance and current relationships and 
responsibilities go to daydream about what will come. 
Living in the Future: Has a passion for all things new and is likely to 
dress or act based on perception of a possible future. Dislikes the pres-
ent state of affairs and would happily trade it all in for a ride to the 
future. 
Planning for the Future: The being is curious about times to come. 
She is likely to know more about trends and projections then others but 
does not lose sight of the fact that she lives in the present. 
Future Aware: The future is yet to come. To be planned for if needed 
or decided upon if necessary, nothing more. 
Ignorant of Future: The future is beyond understanding so why bother. 
After all, the future has no bearing on the now. One must live in 
today's world or there will be no future.

In order to create a believable game world, two things must be 
considered above all else: depth and consistency. In order to 
hold the attention of good role-players, the world must have 
depth and consistency and the players must be have access to 
enough information to perceive this. Too often a GM designs 
an interesting game world but finds that the player's do not 
seem to "get it". This is generally because they were not given 
enough information to hook them in the first place. But how 
does the GM give enough information to the player's to hook 
them, yet not give away all the great secrets of the game world? 
The Tier Storyline system offers a way for the GM to handle 
this problem and keep a good game running for years. 
There are four Tiers, each moving to a deeper and more exclu-
sive level. These tiers are used for both creating a good game 
world, as well as implementation of adventures in the game 
world. The first part of the tier system deals with information 
and writing plotlines. 
Informational Tiers 
Creating Depth 
Tier 1: Common Knowledge 
This is the most common level of knowledge about the game 
world, and every player should have access to information on 
this level. This level involves general histories, world maps and 
the like. This is the stuff that all players should know just so 
they can understand the basic context of the game world. Even 
if a player's character will not know all of this information, the 
player should still know it for purposes of understanding the 
context in which his character will be interacting. This infor-
mation should be presented to the players in the form of a sev-
eral page overview of the world which includes the races and 
where they are from, as well as the general realms of the world. 
This information does not necessarily have to be "correct", as it 
is for the players to read and know. 
Tier 2: Factional Information 
Tier 2 is the area of information that is relevant to factions and 
being a member of a group. It contains in-depth, detailed racial 
and class information as well as skill information that allows 
characters to specialize in all sorts of esoteric areas of knowl-
edge. Most good roleplayers are going to want to know their 
races' history, and will learn this information as well as the gen-
eral Tier I common knowledge. Players should have an idea 
about any faction that may have taught them their skills, as well 
a knowledge about the land or country they came from. Tier 2 
information should also include special knowledge which 
comes from skills, such as the History skill. A separate sheet or 
packet should be created for each faction or skill information 
231 
which a character might know, and these can be handed to spe-
cific characters so that they know information specific to their 
character. For example, a human Priest would get special infor-
mation about the country he was from and how the humans 
interact with other races. He would also have information about 
his religious faction, and would probably have a special sheet 
prepared that contained information about the skill Theology. 
For skills like Theology and History, its a good idea to let a 
player know one body of Tier 2 knowledge per 10% of the skill. 
Thus at 35% Theology, a Priest might know three types of the-
ology: his own and two others of a god from a surrounding 
area. A 35% History skill might allow the player to have three 
history handouts: one of his culture, and two others he had cho-
sen to study. Of course players are free to discuss all of this 
information, and this will make for a better roleplaying environ-
ment. 
Tier 3: GM World Information 
This Tier contains information documents about the world the 
GM knows, but does not want to allow the players to read. 
Instead, the players find out about this information usually over 
time and through role-playing. The GM should have his own 
Tier 3 book which contains detailed information on the factions 
and world and maps which contain things the players should not 
know about. The bulk of a game world will be this information, 
and letting the player's see it will ruin things for them. Often 
the GM will release a Tier 2 history which is written from a 
very strong bias of one race. He might then have a document 
in his Tier 3 information which contained "what really hap-
pened". This information wiU provide the basis for adventures 
and the story of the world. 
Tier 4: The Secrets of the Universe 
This is the level of the deepest darkest secrets that only the 
designer(s) of the world should know. These are things that 
drive the game world in ways that no player knows. They 
should never be revealed unless the player intends to not play in 
the game world, or at at least if he does not care about losing 
much of the entertainment value of the world. If these ideas are 
shallow and trite, the game world wi11 be weak all the way 
down the line. Tier 4 is the body of ideas that contain how the 
world was created, and perhaps the secrets of how to gain ulti-
mate power in the game world. Often when and if this informa-
tion comes out, it is at the end of a great epic campaign which 
involves immortal characters when the GM plans to end his cur-
rent game world and begin another.

Des~rnm; Races 
Perhaps you would like to make a special version of an existing race, 
or perhaps a lost darker cousin. Maybe you have a completely new 
race in mind. The following information follows the design form and 
should be helpful in making sure that you have included all the neces-
sary elements of a race. First, an overview of the general flavor and 
theory of classification for types of Imagine races is provided. Expect 
to see many more races in future supplements which will flesh out 
these concepts. 
The Wild Ones 
Also called Famorians, these are the races of animal spirit, affected by 
the conflicts of time. It is up to the GM and his setting if these beings 
were drawn from other realms or created during great clashes of the 
order and chaos. Whether the world or the creatures themselves were 
altered, it remains that these wild ones have aspects of beasts and 
beings both-something of the animal remains and something new is 
gained. They appear as mongrels, part humanoid, and part any number 
of beasts (generally one primary type).

The Fae 
Just as the prime plane is made up of earth, air, water and even fire so 
too are the eldest of races. The Elves are all of these elements brought 
into a racial whole. They feel the ebb and call of sea, the love of the 
earth and what grows in it, the winds that cool and sing and even the 
tamed power of fire, harnessed for good works. They are the highest 
of the Fae, and have earned the name High Fae. Around them and 
closer to the very elements is a myriad of Fae races. Some of the Fae 
are further divided by serving either order or chaos, or as some would 
say, seelie and unseelie. This divides the Elves themselves, with the 
High, Gray and Wood Elves generally following their seelie beliefs, 
and the fallen Dark Elves with their unseelie ways. 
Of Air Fae there is the named Fairy. The Fairy is properly called a 
Sprite if female and a Pixie if male. Of Earth Fae there is the Gnome. 
The Fae orders of fire and water will be addressed in future books.

Goblin-Kin 
A fiercely divided hierarchy of clans and tribes, sharing a common 
ancestry, Goblin Kin are born for conflict. They fight even amongst 
themselves and have difficulty forming any lasting social order larger 
than a clan, while most are found in disorganized tribes or lesser 
groups. They know power when they feel it, and fear is the greatest 
Goblin-Kin motivator. So it is that a single strong leader can occasion-
ally unite them toward a common enemy or purpose. It is these times 
when the Goblin-kin are the most dangerous to other races. The larger 
Goblins are often referred to as Ores. Thus, a Mountain Goblin is 
often called a Black Ore but a Forest Goblin never is. The Goblin 
share a kinship with their larger and more dangerous cousins, the 
Ogres and Trolls. They lead shortened lives, mitigated only by their 
prodigious breeding volume and speed. Many a race has defeated a 
horde of Goblin-Kin only to have a similar problem just a few score 
years later. Few races look on Goblin-Kin with anything but fear and 
repulsion; even the darker races that truck with them are reviled by 
their presence. 
Races of this type in the Players Guide or Masters Manual:

Earthkin 
Born of earthen works in ages past, the Giant and Dwarf share a com-
mon ancestry, despite their differing stature. Though Dwarf dwells in 
the earth and the Giant on it, each has stone lacing and fortifying their 
amazing bone structures. Either sinks in water with no hope of swim-
ming. Neither can tap into or shape the weaves of magic, for their 
gifts are primal and much older. They share an understanding of the 
song of stones and the magic trapped within minerals. Their gift for 
building and crafting are legendary; from the smallest Dwarven lens to 
the Giant's stone bridges that span mighty rivers, they are unrivaled. 
Some even say that these two Earthkin were shaped from the rock 
itself, the Giants from the Mountain rock and the Dwarves from the 
boulders below. Certainly their cultures revere the ancient stone over 
tree, over animal, over any other magic. Though their kinship is little 
recognized by the other races the oldest scholars know that once Dwarf 
and Giant were one peoples crafting, building and separate from the 
other races.

Mundanes 
The last group of races shares only a lack of true magic. Though the 
Midfolk have a touch of it and the humans can shape its ways, neither 
is born to magic. Both would survive in dismal places were magic 
cannot go. Both have gifts of community and striving that make them 
more ambitious and self-serving than other races. Where the Fae know 
their place amid the elements, the humans instead seek to tame all 
themselves, shaping the world to their image, instead of finding a place 
within it. There is an aged time that the other races share-a history 
and a past longer than the more recent Mundanes. Yet this lack of his-
tory only seems to free the Mundanes more to strive for their place in 
the sun. They would never even accept the label Mundane for they see 
theirs as a great destiny to sweep the land and sow the seeds of immor-
tality in their deeds and their works. In this they may be right for only 
time will tell who emerges from the swirling chaos of the racial strug-
gle to reign supreme over the whole of creation.

Race Design Guide 
Race Name: The name by which the race is known. 
Background/Flavor Info: Information pertaining to the culture, habi-
tats, alignment restrictions, habits, their relationship to other races, how 
they came to be, etc. 
Attribute: Modifiers to attribute rolls of this race. Optimally, the 
penalties and bonuses should even out unless other strengths and weak-
nesses are being factored in, as is often the case. It is a good idea to 
start with a balanced attribute modifier section and then adjust it as the 
race seems to get stronger or weaker than Civilized Human. Civilized 
Humans are considered the baseline race, and generally most races end 
up with a cumulative negative number for attribute modifiers due to 
their extra abilities. Only Civilized Humans are afforded a general 
bonus that can be applied to any attribute, as well as the ability to 
move attribute points around. It is not recommend to create future 
races with these abilities. 
There are a few guidelines that you can follow to determine attribute 
modifiers. Any race that is thought of as barbaric, or lives in a tough 
natural environment, will often have bonuses to physical attributes and 
possibly a small bonus to Will force. These same races may tend to 
have lower personal attributes. Personal attributes modifiers can be 
difficult to nail down without some frame of reference. The following 
information should give you a context to work with. 
• Charm modifiers are based on how the race treats or feels about other 
races in general, and thus the power of influence they will be able to 
exert over other races. The following information should be applied:

Racial Skills: Those skills to which a race has access and has passed 
down from generation to generation. This does not mean that every 
individual possesses every one of these skills, just that the more 
learned (high Knowledge) individuals in the race can have access to a 
complete set. The choice of racial skills is one of the strongest defin-
ers of a race. Decide whether the race is a civilized one with many 
street abilities-Steal, Lie, etc., or a magical one with Detect Magic and 
similar skills. Or perhaps you have a whole new skill design in mind. 
The amount of skills can vary from 3 to 4 for the simplest of races to 
15 for the most highly magical or advanced. 
Resistances: Here is where you will decide if the race has any weak-
nesses or strengths against magic, control, illusion, poison, or disease. 
Barbaric races are often more resistant to poisons but less so to magic 
and illusions. Stubborn races are less likely to be controlled. 
Special Abilities/Powers: This is where lnfravision, Night Vision, spe-
cial sensing abilities, racial powers and other positive benefits are list-
ed. This is also subjective, but no race should more than a few. The 
greater the penalties in attributes, the more special abilities can be cho-
sen. Special attacks can be included for races with claws and such. 
Special Modifiers: Modifiers that alter game mechanics for the race. 
Starting Age and Maximum Age: The random age of intellectual 
maturity or age when play starts, then the highest age the race is 
expected to live. 
Perception, Affinity, Fortune and Endurance Modifiers: In general, 
the more barbaric the race, the lower its perception modifier and affmi-
ty, and the higher its Endurance. Endurance modifiers should also take 
into account the races size to a large degree. Read the sections on 
Affinity, Perception and Fortune to better understand these modifiers. 
Aging Table: The true age of the race and the apparent aging rate in 
as compared to humans. If the being is human-like in aging then this 
is unnecessary. If a current race has an aging table that will suit list 
you may wish to use or emulate it. 
Beginning Equipment: If the race is considered barbaric it will not 
be granted money, and so some starting equipment must be added 
(based on social class). It is recommended that an existing table be 
used as a base and converted if necessary. 
Attribute Maximums: The maximums this race is allowed by attrib-

ute. This is intended to be after all calculated modifiers. ll is listed 
from Strength to Will Force. Piety and Will Force should always be 
allowed to have a maximum of 20 unless there is an extremely good 
reason to change it (such as a race hated by the gods). Barbaric races 
will be physically stronger and civilized races will be stronger mental-
ly, mystically or both. 
Male/Female Modifiers: Attribute modifiers based on gender. 
Characteristics: The odds and ends that affect a race's height, frame, 
weight, physical appearance, and movement ability. If at all possible, 
current races can be used as models. If not, let racial flavor guide you. 
Available Classes: The types of classes this race is restricted to. 
Barbaric races tend to not have access to intellectual and speUcasting 
classes such as Mage, Mentalist, etc. Instead these cultures tend to be 
more divine in nature, having shamans and using older forms of magic 
such as runes. Also make sure that the no class is allowed for the race 
when racial attribute maximums keep it from meeting the required 
minimums of a class. 
Halt1Mixed Races: List the races this race can breed with. The type 
of offspring is also listed: sterile or fertile. 
Body Type: The name of the body chart. Use an existing racial chart 
if it exists or name the chart after your new race. 
Special Body Chart: (YIN) If you are filling out the special body 
chart then check Y here. 
Body Chart: 30 areas are provided. It is difficult to imagine a race 
that would have more than 30 body areas and still be viable as a player 
race. A Body Chart should include numbers for body areas used for 
random rolls. Each body area should have a name and a multiplier 
against Endurance for the area. Also decide whether or not the area is a 
limb or a vital area. Wounded limbs slow opponents, vital areas kill 
them. 
Racial Specials (Abilities): List a few special positive traits that rare 
individuals have for random rolling or for character building. 
Racial Specials (Disabilities): Show a few special negative qualities 
that rare individuals live with, to be used for random rolling or for 
character building. 
Class Des191 Sfstem 
Classes provide the vehicle for characters to choose an advance-
ment path they will follow as they interact within a setting. 
Adding depth and variety, new classes allow the GM to breathe 
life into the factions that inhabit his campaign setting. The 
building blocks provided in the class creation system are power-
ful. Wielded in the wrong way, they could easily topple the bal-
ance within a game. The class creation system is not about cre-
ating characters with minimum weaknesses and maximum ben-
efits by taldng the best of all possible skills. It's about adding 
flavor to the story, helping mesh rules and roleplaying. 
Name and Description 
The class name should be evocative of what the class does or 
for what it is known. Try to encompass the range of the class. 
For instance, 'Rogue' represents the full range from the alley-
way cutpurse to the merely opportunistic adventurer. 
Classes are defined as a grouping of skills that reflect a charac-
ter's learning path within an environment. If the environment 
to learn the set of skills defined by a class does not exist within 
a world setting, then the class will not be available. A mini-
mum of 250 words should explain how the concept of the class 
exists and interacts within a game setting. Describe the day to 
day activities and special talents known to the class. 
Skills 
Skills are grouped together in six skill categories: combat, disci-
plined, divine magical, informational, magical and stealth/intru-
sive. In the pages to follow, skills are first listed in order by 
minimum Title and then are listed alphabetically with minimum 
Title and skill requirements. 
Requirements 
Each skill always has a Title requirement and may have a skill 
requirement. Both the Title and all skill requirements must be 
met in order for a class to obtain a skill. The minimum Title 
requirement is the earliest point in experience advancement that 
a class may obtain the skill. Skill requirements may be a spe-
cific skill or some number of a type of skill (or both). Skills 
such as Ritual Lore, Candle Lore and Potion Lore that belong to 
two skill categories may be counted for both categories when 
determining if skill requirements are met. Also, skill require-
ments may be met at the same Title that a skill requires it. For 
example, Cause Disease has a minimum Title requirement of 3 
and a skill requirement of Wounding before it may be obtained. 
If Wounding were to be obtained at 3rd Title, then Cause 
Disease may be obtained at 3rd Title as well. 
Number of Skills 
A class has a minimum of thirty and a maximum of fifty skills 
between 1st and 10th Title. A class may have a number of skills 
available at a Title equal to or lower than the number of skills at 
the previous Title. For example, a class may have four skills at 
8th Title and then three skills at 9th Title, but the reverse is not 
permitted. No more than five skills are permitted per Title and 
each Title should have at least three skills. At 11th through 
15th Titles, only one skill per Title is permitted. 
Environment 
Any skills that have different environment types such as the 
urban and wilderness varieties of Detect Trap, Set Trap and 
Remove Trap need to be chosen by the designer at the time the 
skills are selected. The environment type (urban or wilderness) 
should be selected based on the flavor of the class.

Alignment 
Some classes have a given disposition based on their skill set. 
For example, classes centered around healing arts are less prone 
to be malicious than those with destructive skills. A basic con-
cept exists that some divine magical skills use positive lifeforce 
and others negative life force. The metaphysical idea here is 
that when positive or negative lifeforce is channelled by a mor-
tal, they tend to polarize that being's spirit towards the positive 
or negative, respectively. The more powerful the skill, the more 
powerful this polarization. A mortal can only tolerate a certain 
degree of this violent metaphysical "pushing and pulling". 
Positive Lifeforce Skills: Bless, Healing, Detect Evil, 
Protection from Evil, Turn Undead, Cure Disease, Cure Poison, 
Regeneration, Resurrection, Recover, Empathy, Empathy 
Magic, Remove Fear, Light, Sacred Grove. 
Negative Lifeforce Skills: Blasphemy, Wounding, Detect Good, 
Protection from Good, Control Undead, Cause Disease, Call 
Undead, Withering, Destruction, Plague, Sympathy, Sympathy 
Magic, Fear, Darkness, Haunted Grove. 
In order for a class to have skills from both categories, its align-
ment restriction must be some type of neutral. A class with 
only positive skills cannot be evil, and a class with only nega-
tive skills cannot be good. A class may contain skills with a 
minimum Title requirement of 6 or higher from only one of the 
two lifeforce categories, but not both. Flavor of the class 
should also guide the alignment requirement. For example, 
Assassins cannot be good, as their primary purpose is to 
methodically kill people, while Rangers cannot be evil, as they 
are protectors of animals and woodlands. 
Core Skills 
Choose the top five that define the center of the class. Each 
core skill should further define the role of this class within the 
campaign setting. 
Rules for selecting class core skills: 
1. There are always five core skills. 
2. Core skills cannot come from more than three skill categories 
(combat, disciplined, divine magical, informational, magi-
cal and stealth/intrusive). 
3. All skill requirements can be ignored. The Title requirement 
may be reduced by up to two Titles. If both Divine 
Knowledge and a spellcasting skill (Scroll Knowledge, 
Hermetic lore Lore and Wild Magic) are taken as core 
skills, only one of them may have the Title requirement 
reduced. 
4. All core skills must be taken within the first six Titles. 
241 
(Therefore, it follows that any skill with a minimum Title 
requirement of 9 or higher may not be taken as a core 
skill.) 
S. Only one of the five core skills may have a minimum Title 
requirement of 6, 7, or 8. 
In order for a character to advance past 10th Title (the point of 
entering the supernatural realm), his skill chance for core skills 
must meet certain minimum requirements. The skill chance 
requirements are determined by the Title at which the core skill 
was acquired:

To emphasize a class' expertise in an area, all core skills receive 
a 30% bonus when acquired. A class also receives a + l 0% 
bonus to a primary skill category and a +5% bonus to a second-
ary skill category. To determine which skill categories should 
receive a bonus, count up the number of skills for each of the 
six skill categories. The top two categories will receive the pri-
mary and secondary bonuses. The designer may ignore the dis-
ciplined and informational skill categories if he so chooses, but 
neither should ever be selected as the primary skill category. 
The skill category with the highest number does not have to 
receive the primary (the designer may choose from either of the 
top two). Different skill categories are to be used when deter-
mining bonuses. For example, a class may have a +5% or 
+10% bonus to combat skills, but never a combined +15%. 
Optionally, a tertiary skill category bonus of +5% may be given 
if the class is diverse enough to warrant the bonus.

classes (Warrior, Rogue, Priest or Mage) a class "belongs" to.

The subclass of a class will influence the armor and weapons 
usable by the class. Skill category bonuses are cumulative with 
the bonus given to core skills. 
Attribute Requirements 
Ultimately, the goal of attribute requirements is to minimize the 
number of skills on average that a character will start out with a 
negative skill chance. For all twelve attributes, count up the 
number of class skills that use each attribute. The three attrib-
utes with the highest values determine which attributes will 
have minimum requirements for this class. 
In order to determine the minimum rating for an attribute 
requirement, an association between the requirement attributes 
and the six different skill categories must be established. 
Attributes are loosely associated with the certain skill cate-
gories, as listed below. The number listed in parenthesis is the 
average skill rating of the all the skills in the game of that type. 
Combat (13): 
Divine Magical (15): 
Disciplined (14): 
Informational (13): 
Magical (15): 
Stealth/Intrusive ( 12): 
Strength, Agility 
Wisdom, Piety, Will Force 
Agility, Wisdom, Will Force 
Intelligence, Knowledge 
Intelligence, Knowledge, Aura, 
Will Force 
Agility, Intelligence, Knowledge 
Using the above information, associate the top three attributes 
with the skill categories where a skill category bonus is given 
(done during the Special Modifiers step). Once the first attrib-
ute has been associated with a category, it is assigned a mini-
mum rating of the average rating for that skill category (the 
number in parenthesis). If the attribute can be associated with 
more than one skill category, choose the category with the high-
er number. Follow the same steps for the second and third 
attributes, only all the secondary or tertiary attributes which are 
15 can be reduced to 14, as these attributes are not as vital to 
the class. 
For example, the skills for the Minstrel class primarily use the 
Intelligence, Knowledge and Agility attributes. From the 
Special Modifiers step, two skill categories receive a bonus: 
Magical and Stealth/Intrusive. Intelligence and Knowledge 
attributes map to both the Magical and Stealth/Intrusive skill 
categories, so the higher number of these two categories (15) is 
set as the rating requirement for these attributes. The primary 
attribute (Intelligence) must remain a 15, but the secondary 
(Knowledge) can be reduced to a 14. The Agility attribute 
maps to the Stealth/Intrusive skill category (because the class 
receives a bonus for that category), so this attribute is assigned 
the average rating (12) of the Stealth/Intrusive skills used by 
this class. 
Class Extensions 
In order to progress past 10th Title (the point of becoming 
supernatural), a character's attributes must meet certain mini-
mum requirements. The first attribute requirement should be 
set to a rating of racial maximum (RM). This means that if a 
race has a 16 rating for the attribute, then the character must 
have a 16 rating as well. The second attribute requirement 
should be set to a rating of racial maximum minus one (RM-1). 
Suppose an attribute for a race has a maximum rating of 18. In 
order to advance, the character would have to have at least a 17 
rating. Similarly, the third attribute requirement should be set 
to a rating of racial maximum minus four (RM-4). Will Force 
and Knowledge, if not already one of the three requirement 
attributes for the class, have mandatory minimum requirements 
of 15 each. 
Goal Advancement 
This reflects the fundamental progression made by a character 
as he advances through experience. Advancement is rewarded 
with additional skill points and attribute increases. 
Skill Points 
The base number of skills points awarded to a character upon 
advancement to a new goal is based upon the number of skills 
available to that class:
