Three modifiers to the base skill points per Goal exist. The first 
modifier is a +2 bonus to a primary class. This bonus provides 
a slight advantage to the primary classes versus their respective 
subclasses. 
The second modifier is applied to keep classes balanced with 
one another. From the Special Modifiers step, multiply the 
number of class skills in the primary skill category by 10. 
Then, multiply the number of class skills in the secondary skill 
category by 5. Add both numbers together and then divine by 
30. This number represents the average number of skill points 
awarded to a class each Goal by special modifiers (not includ-
ing core skill bonuses). If the number is less than l 1.0, then 
additional skill points are added to the base skill points per Goal 
until the number is greater than 11.0 (but not greater than 12.0). 
For example, the Monk has a base of 18 skill points for having 
50 class skills between 1st and 10th Title. 
The Monk has an average of 3 skill points per Goal for Divine 
Magic skills (primary), 2.66 skill points per Goal for Combat 
skills (secondary) and 1.66 skill points per Goal for Disciplined 
242 

===== PAGE 253 =====
skills (tertiary). Totalled together, this equals an average of 
7.33 skill points per Goal from special modifiers. Four skill 
points (7 .33 + 4 = 11.33) are added to the base of 18 skill points 
giving the Monk a total of 22 skill points per Goal. 
The third modifier is subjective and left up to the designer. A 
+ 1 or +2 bonus is given to non-combative "scholarly" classes 
(the Seer and Sage are two such examples). 
Attribute Increases 
The two highest attribute requirements (see Attribute 
Requirements) receive a 5% chance of permanently increasing 
by one at each Goal. In cases where the second and third attrib-
ute requirements have the same rating, the choice is balanced 
between two factors. The attribute that is used more frequently 
(see Attribute Requirements) and the attribute more strongly 
associated with the primary class is chosen. Class attribute 
associations for Warriors are a high Strength and Agility, 
Rogues have a high Agility and Intelligence, Priests have a high 
Piety and Will Force, and Mages have a high Intelligence and 
Aura. 
For example, the Knight has attribute requirements of Piety 14, 
Agility 13, Will Force 13. Since the Knight is a Warrior sub-
class and both Agility and Will Force are equally distributed, a 
5% chance is given to increase Piety and Agility (instead of 
Piety and Will Force). 
In cases where two attribute requirements have the same value 
and neither is tied to the primary class, then the attribute used 
more frequently determines which attribute gains a chance to be 
raised. For example, a Ranger has attribute requirements of 
Agility 13, Intelligence 12, and Knowledge 12. Since neither 
Intelligence nor Knowledge are tied to the Warrior class, but 
Knowledge is used more frequently in skills than Intelligence, a 
Ranger has a 5% chance to increase Agility and Knowledge 
(instead of Agility and Intelligence). 
Title Advancement 
If the class starts with or acquires Scroll Knowledge, Hermetic 
lore Lore or Wild Magic, then advancement of Aura Control 
should be listed as a reminder. If the class starts with or 
acquires Divine Knowledge, then a reminder of Piety Control 
increases should be listed here. Remember that these bonuses 
do not begin until the character acquires the skill (Practitioner 
Title). Any additional bonuses that relate to some special skill 
or ability can be listed here as well. For example, if the class is 
extremely divine-centric, an increase in commune chance is list-
ed by Title ( usually + 1 % ). 
Armor Usable 
Any class with Scroll Knowledge is restricted to armor that 
does not restrict the spellcaster's movements. Any armor with 
combat penalties is considered too restrictive to be used by a 
spellcaster and still allow him to cast spells. Generally, this 
means a Scroll Knowledge practitioner may wear leather or 
hide of any type, and may only wear plate in the form of arm 
bracers, leg bracers, helms or composite helms. Such classes 
may be allowed a to wear a half shirt of any kind, and even a 
full shirt or long shirt of ringmail, if it is expected that this class 
will be apt to get into close combat. Shields may be used as 
long they do not violate a deity restriction or flavor aspect of 
the class, or if it would be near impossible for the class to per-
form its major duties with the shield. 
All non-Warrior subclasses must follow the above armor rules 
unless at least half of their skills are combat skills (the Priest is 
exempt from this rule, but not Priest subclasses). Any further 
restrictions may be imposed if it is felt that they run contrary to 
the spirit or flavor of the class. For example, it was decided 
that the Ranger would not be able to perform some functions in 
certain cumbersome pieces of plate armor. 
Weapons Usable 
Warrior and Rogue subclasses should be allowed to fight with 
any weapons, unless there is a flavor reason for creating a 
restriction (such as the Knight not using missile weapons). 
Priest subclasses should have their weapon selection based on 
the flavor and restrictions of their deity. Mage subclasses, as 
weIJ as any other class who's only combat skill is Weapon 
Knowledge, should be given a selection of no more than seven 
weapons from the following list: club, dagger; knife, quarter-
staff, rod, sling, and a choice of any one sword. Exceptions can 
be made, if it is believed that the character has some class fla-
vor reason as to why they would be able to use additional 
weapons, or if it is thought the class may be exposed to close 
combat. However, such character's weapons useable list should 
include large melee weapons such as battle axes, warhammers 
or polearms.

Warrior subclasses with more than half of their total skills as 
combat skills are ranking l. Warrior subclasses with half or 
less of their total skills as combat skills are ranking 2. 
Rogue subclasses should fall in rankings 3 through 6. The more 
combative the class is expected to be, the higher the ranking 
within this range may be. If the class is expected to try and 
avoid combats, the ranking should be lower. 
Priest subclasses should generally fall in rankings 5 through 8; 
however, due to the variable combat nature of Priest subclasses, 
a Priest subclass whose primary function is combat may be as 
high as ranking 4, but a Priest subclass who is totally non-com-
bative can be as low as ranking 12. 
Mage subclasses should fall in rankings 8 through 12. Only 
Mage subclasses with several combat skills should be allowed 
to be of ranking 8. Classes who would be expected to avoid 
combat completely should be ranking 12.

Availability 
Just because a class has been created specific to a game setting 
does not automatically make it available for players to choose 
from. If the class is specific to a race or a faction, then it fol-
lows that only those characters that belong to that race or fac-
tion (or those with an appropriate background) have the oppor-
tunity to learn the class skill set. 
Special Requirements 
Any unique tests or conditions required to advance beyond 10th 
Title should be detailed here.

Desu;nmr; Class an b Racial Skills 
Creating your own classes and races may necessitate the need to create 
new skilJs. You can also create skills as alternates or substitutes for 
existing class or race skills to give the class or race a subtle twist. For 
instance, Hermetic Lore was created originally to give to Alchemists 
and Witches instead of Scroll Knowledge. The listings below describe 
how to use the Racial/Class Skill Design Form. 
Class / Racial Skill Design Guide 
Skill Name: The name of the skill should be something that stands out 
from other skills and something that makes one understand its use. 
Lore is generally saved for the higher of two skills when it is deemed 
to break an ability into two skills. 
Attributes: The one or two attributes required to achieve the base 
rating. 
Rating: The level of difficulty of a skill relative to other skills. 
Magical and divine magical skills are usually higher. Rating are usual-
ly between I and 20. 
Start Bonus: The dice rolled to determine starting bonus (doubled 
when rolling a race skill). The table below determines starting bonus 
by rating:

Time: This is the time the skill takes to execute in normal 
circumstances. 
Type: Kind of skill (combat, stealth/intrusive, magical, divine magi-
cal, disciplined or informational). 
Restricted: Can the skill be taught outside the restrictions of class 
under normal circumstances, and is the skill treated as a common skill: 
Yes or No?. 
Learn Time: Time required to learn the skill in total hours, if the skill 
is unrestricted. It is usually 4x the rating of the skill. Adjust by +/-8 
hours depending on a perceived difference in the ability to learn the 
skill versus the difficulty of using the skill; i.e. a skilJ may have a rat-
ing of 12 for use but the designer may determine that it is an easy skill 
to learn and so subtracts 4 hours off the 48 hour learn time for a rating 
12 skill. 
Description: Summary of what the skill accomplishes. 
General Usage: A full description of how the skill is generally used, 
including all game mechanics and subskills or products of the skill. 
Special Uses: Tricks that this skill can be utilized for. 
Notes: Wormation about its use with other skills or situations. 
Special Notes: Any special warnings about the use of this skill, etc. 
Critical Failure: The effects if the skill is failed by more than 20%. 
Critical Success: The effects if the skill is made by more than 20%. 
Repeat Failure: What if the skill fails consecutive times? (3 is usual). 
Repeat Usage: Any effects if the skill is used multiple times.

Desrc;nmr; Weapons 
Adding cultures or special materials to your world will necessitate cre-
ating new weapons. The listings below detail use of the Weapon 
Design Form. 
Weapon Design Guide 
Weapon Name: What the weapon is called. 
Description: A description of how the weapon is used, made and/or 
its composition. 
Damage: The amount of damage this weapon does in normal combat 
situations. 
Strength: The amount of damage a weapon can take before breaking 
above its object threshold. 
Speed: The normal speed of the weapon. List reloading speeds in 
parenthesis if it is a projectile weapon. Very few weapons should have 
a minimum speed of I or 2 seconds. Weapons which are very light 
(21b. or less) and do under 2d4+2 damage may be used in a I second 
minimum attack. Weapons which weigh less than 4 lb., do slight dam-
age ( 4d4 or less) or are very well balanced and require little recovery, 
may be used in a 2 second attack. Weapons generally meant to be used 
two-handed for a human but that can be used one handed usually have 
+ I second added to their minimum weapon speed. Weapons generally 
expected to be used two handed have a minimum speed of 4 and a 
maximum 0f7 to 10. 
Minimum Speed: The lowest speed the weapon can be lowered to by 
any means. 
Weight: The weapon's weight. 
Length: The length of the weapon. 
Object Threshold: The amount of damage the weapon will absorb 
before taking damage itself (see Damage to Weapons and Non-Armor 
Material in the Combat section of the Player's Guide for examples). 
Modifiers: Some weapons cannot be used for certain types of attacks 
(notated by "non") or are considered better or worse to hit with certain 
types of attacks. 
Missile Damage: If the weapon does a different amount of damage 
when used as a missile, list that damage here. 
Projectile Type: If the weapon can be used as a missile, this is filled 
out. 
Projectile Modifiers: Adjustments to hit or damage for a particular 
type of projectile. 
Ranges: The missile weapon range distances for the weapon, with 
extra spaces to show ranges for special projectiles types. 
Cost: Price at low, medium and high if cost applies. (Some early 
weapons may be bartered or traded for, not purchased.) 
Special: Special uses or skill modifiers are listed here. 
Desrc;nmr; ARmoR 
Adding special materials or introducing new races or cultures may 
cause you to need new or different armor styles. The information 
below describes how to use the Armor Design Form to full advantage. 
Armor Design Guide 
Armor Piece Name: What the armor piece is called. 
Description: A description of how the armor is worn, made, etc. 
Type: The type of armor piece: flexible, semi-flexible or rigid. 
Material: The base material the armor is produced from. 
Weight: The weight of the entire piece. 
Modifiers: Heavy or cumbersome armor pieces may cause penalties. 
Skills: Modifier to combat skills while wearing the piece. 
Defensive Adj.: Modifier to be hit while wearing the piece. 
Initiative: Modifier to Initiative rolls while wearing the piece. 
Weapon Speed: Modifier to weapon attack speed while wearing the 
piece. 
Armor Value: The amount of protection this armor provides and how 
much damage it receives from a particular type of strike. 1/20 means 1 
point is taken for every full 20 points done. Attack types are cut, 
thrust/missile, smash/crush and constrict. A sample of types is shown 
below. 
Areas Protected: A complete listing of all areas this armor protects. 
Cost: Price at low, medium and high if cost applies. (Early armor may 
have been bartered or traded for.)

Magical Metals 
When making a piece of armor from magical metal, add the magical 
bonus of the metal to the armor value of the type of armor being made. 
Then, because magical metals have their armor value doubled, the new 
value is doubled. This bonus is only doubled when the value is inher-
ent to the metal, so that +2 magical steel still only doubles to 40. 
Example: Chain mail has an armor rating of IS. When made from +2 
Mithreel, this becomes 17, then doubled (for magic) it becomes 34. 
Thus plate mail made from the same material would be (20+2) x 2 = 
44.Armor damage is listed in the form of a ratio. 
Mithreel: +I, +2. Adamantium: +3, +4. Crysteel: +5, +6.

Des,r;mm; Spells (The Spell CReanon Spsrem) 
There are two main uses for the spell creation system. The first is when 
the Game Master wishes to create new spells for his world and allow 
them to be found and used by the players within that world. In this 
case the spell creation system is simply a way to make sure that the 
spell 's Aura level is balanced relative to other spells, and that the Game 
Master knows which of the types of magic the spell contains. 
The second and much more exciting use of the system involves an 
interaction between the Game Master and a player who is trying to 
have his character create a spell. In this case, the character must have 
one of the following skills: Spell Lore, Wild Magic or Hermetic Lore. 
Once these requirements are met, the GM can decide exactly how he 
wishes the character to proceed within the game world itself. The fol-
lowing are guidelines that should be used for each skill. 
Spell Lore 
The player starts by telling the GM that he wishes to create a new 
spell, and states basically what he wants the spell to do. The GM 
decides to give the player whatever leads that would be appropriate 
within the Game Master's World. The player then begins doing 
research. The character should have some study area such as a tower 
or home where he can begin keeping notes and books on the subject. 
Depending on the size of the magical library that a character has, the 
GM can judge how much research the character must do outside of this 
workshop. The time necessary for research is based on the eventual 
Aura level of the spell ( 1 week of research per Aura level) as is the 
cost of research (20-50 gold pieces per week { ld4 x 10)). In the case 
where a Spell Lorist is studying a spell that has already been made 
somewhere else and the Game Master already knows the Aura level of 
the spell, he can determine the research time as stated in the skill Spell 
Lore. However, if the player is attempting to create an entirely new 
spell then the Game Master has a couple of options: 
1) The Game Master runs the concept of the spell through the Spell 
Creation System without the player's knowledge and then gets a final 
level. Now that the GM knows what the Aura Level of the spell 
should be, he can determine research time accordingly. 
2) The nature of the spell creation system is such that spells with simi-
lar effects could be created in many different ways. For example, the 
spell Trip could be attempted by using magic to physically grab a 
being's leg and hold it instantaneously so that he loses his balance. 
Another way would be to attempt to control the mind of a being and 
force his motor control system to fail on one leg for just a split second 
so that he would lose his balance. Depending on the approach, the 
spell may come out a different Aura level. 
A much more interesting method of research is to force the player to 
describe in exact detail how the spell idea will work, and over an 
extended period of time (research time) the GM slowly "builds" the 
spell. informing the player bit by bit how the research is going. If at 
some point the player realizes that the approach is inefficient, and will 
make the Aura level far too high, he may abandon his research and 
start over. In both cases, the GM must make his best guess based on 
the route the player is taking through the spell creation system as to 
what level the spell will probably be and judge research time accord-
ingly. If the player starts over or backs up, the GM can recalculate the 
predicted Aura level and add whatever research time he feels is neces-
sary. It is up to the player and the Game Master to make the research 
process vibrant and interesting role-playing. 
When the process is complete, the player makes a Spell Lore roll. If 
successful, the spell can then be recorded in the form of spell notes (in 
a spell book), or on a magical scroll (with the use of Scroll Knowledge 
and the Spell Runes). He can then memorize the spell whenever he 
desires, share it with other mages, etc. If unsuccessful, see the skill 
Spell Lore for details. 
Wild Magic 
When using the skill Wild Magic, no research is done at all. The play-
er makes her best guess at a good approach and the Game Master runs 
the spell concept through the system. Whatever level is arrived at is 
the one that the player is stuck with. If this winds up being over her 
Aura Control, then the caster can try and abort (Intelligence save) or go 
ahead and try the spell. The spell is then cast, and if it was over her 
Aura Control then a spell failure chance is rolled (based on the spells 
Aura level). If the spell fails, a roll is then made on the magical 
mishap table. If the spell does not fail, the caster then makes a Wild 
Magic roll to see if the creation process was successful. Careless 
Wilders tend to have short Ii fespans ! 
If the spell is cast successfully, the caster may have a far easier time 
casting this spell again. It is up to the player to record the approach 
that she used, and if she does so, she can cast the spell later without 
having to go through the system all over again. 
Hermetic Lore 
With Hermetic Lore, the caster does not do research, but instead choos-
es an approach and explains to the GM just as with Wild Magic. The 
player must also use the correct materials (based on the 16 qualities of 
magic). He then spends time grinding and mixing during a ritual 
process whose time is explained under Hermetic Lore. A Hermetic 
Lore skill lore is then made, but at half chance without a recipe. If the 
roll is failed the spell does not work, and if it exceeds the caster's Aura 
Control there will be a spell failure chance. The character can record 
the spell as a recipe to use it again. 
With all three skills, the creator can always re-create the spell without 
making a new skill roll if he met the requirements for keeping the spell 
recorded. 
Creating a Spell 
Whatever skill is being used, the Game Master must run the spell 
through the list of tables and charts which make up the Spell Creation 
System. The system is divided into specific steps. Use the Spell 
Creation Worksheet found (in the Appendix) to aid you along the way. 
STEP I: Define the spell. 
The first step is to determine the entire effect of what the spell is to be. 
The general desired effect of the spell should be written down and stat-
ed in a clear and concise sentence. If written by the player, the Game 
Master then examines the sentence and asks for any clarifications that 
he feels are necessary. 
STEP II: Determine the focus. 
The next step is to decide what the focus of the spell is. The focus of a 
spell is that which the spell is attempting to create or directly affect in 
some way. This usually involves finding the subject of the sentence. 
What is the substance that the caster is attempting to produce or affect? 
Of the sixteen aspects of magic, ten of them are focus types, and six 
are action types. The focus types will define what is affected, and the 
249 

===== PAGE 260 =====
action types define how it is affected. Once you have decided what 
aspect the focus falls under, you wilJ also find which action aspects can 
affect that focus. Only certain action aspects can affect certain focus 
aspects. This is best illustrated in the diagram below. The black cir-
cles represent the focus aspects and the white rings the action aspects. 
Action aspects may only affect focus aspects that are within their ring. 
Of the IO focus aspects, six: within the action aspect rings are called the 
primary aspects. The four others outside of the rings are the metaphys-
ical foci, and are based on the advanced principles of metaphysics. 
STEP ill: Add the modifiers to produce the Aura level 
Once a focus has been chosen, the next step is to go to the tables listed 
with that type of magic and find the desired effect. Reading through 
the tables should help you understand which combinations of action 
and focus types will produce the result you want. Beside each effect is 
a modifier, either positive or negative. When all the effects have been 
chosen, they add up to make the Aura level of the spell. Added to this 
should then be all the modifiers for the spell 's parameters, as well as 
any specialized effects created with metaphysics. 
Though the information in the tables covers a myriad of situations, it 
certainly does not address every possible spell idea. Thus you should 
feel free to use the numbers in any particular table to determine a new 
value for any effects you do not see listed. As a general guideline, if 
the desired effect generally seems easier to accomplish than the one 
chosen from a table, you may subtract one from the that effect's modi-
fier. If it seems much easier, you may subtract two points, and so on. 
Conversely, if an effect seems more difficult in relation to a specific 
effect, then add a few points to the modifier in the same way as above.

Aspect: Natural 
Spells which have this type as their focus are things which come from the earthly plane. Anything which can be found on the earthly plane in a 
solid or liquid form can be included under this category. The only exception are the five types of elemental energy (fire, ice, acid, electricity and 
Aura energy), light and sound. This category also includes natural forces such as weather and gravity. 
Spells of Type: Natural, Alteration 
The List for Altering nature is nearly endless. The following should be looked at as guidelines for many of the possibilities. If you wish an alter-
ation which is not listed, make your best estimation based on the given modifiers. Alterations are not based on what is being changed, but on what 
the focus is being changed into. An important note about these type of spells is that normally they when an alteration spell is cast on a living being, 
the being's Aura field will take control of the spell. Thus you cannot normally make a spell which causes someone to unwillingly fly. Making such 
a spell is called overriding metaphysics, and has a cost of +8.

This category includes the five types of elemental energy: ice/frost, fire, acid/chemical energy, electricity/lightning and pure Aura energy, some-

Spells of Type: Energy, Creation 
Creating energy and harnessing the raw power of the elements can be very powerful but dangerous as well. After an energy type has been chosen, 
a value for its damage must also be chosen which will affect the Aura level. A spell cannot normally be made which causes energy to be created in 
another being's Aura Field. However, energy can be created in free form around the being and then displaced towards the being (as in a storm). 
This effect can be overriden by adding+ 11 to the Aura level of the spell. If created onto a being, energy affects 4d6 random regions. An example 
of this would be the spell Incinerate.

Since energy cannot effectively be created within another beings Aura Field it is easiest to create it and displace it towards a target. The following 
displacement options are available: 
a. It can be displaced in free form, in which case it will appear as a stream if given a duration or as a bolt if the duration is instantaneous (such as 
the finger spells). If in stream form, damage must be spread out over the entire combat round, with targets getting a Magic Resistance save each 
round. So if the spell a finger of fire is created with a duration of IO seconds per Aura and a damage of I die per Aura, at 20 Aura it will do 20 
dice of damage over a period of 200 seconds, or I die per 10 seconds. This can simply be assigned to the first target hit if dividing this small 
amount of damage becomes cumbersome. Formula: Total damage/total seconds = damage per second. 
b. It can be kept in free form then be displaced into a high state of turbulence, called a storm. 
c. Energy can be compressed to create explosions. 
d. When created normally, energy is in a volatile state. It can be locked, so that its shape can be treated as a solid (walls of fire would be an exam-
ple). Locked energy, however, cannot be displaced.

I) Affected targets make a Magic Resistance save or be blinded for the 
duration of the storm. 
2) Affected beings make an Agility save to continue standing.

4) No missiles may be fired, and any fired into the storm from the outside will hit a random target within the storm. 
5) Damage is assessed to 4d6 random regions instead of normal 2d4. 
6) Energy will only do 1/2 damage in a storm of its opposite element.

Aspect: Death 
Death magics are those which use negative life force, or the spirit or essence of an undead being. This type of magic is generally used to affect 
undead or to damage living beings, as it is the opposite of positive life force. This can includes mystical attributes of undead being's as well. The 
effects are generally the opposite of life spells.

Aspect: Dimensional 
The realm of dimension is that of the soul as well other dimensional places. Spells that attempt to control a being's soul require a true name. For 
beings without a soul, only some form of that being's essence is required (such as fire for a Fire Elemental, etc.). Other types of spells that fall 
under this category are spells which transfer the soul through a dimensional medium (such as all summoning and teleportation spells). Whenever 
the soul or essence of a being is transferred to the earthly plane, it demands a home. Thus, the soul will reform the body if it is connected to one, or 
make or attempt to take over one if it does not have a natural physical form. It is this phenomena that allows for teleportation and summoning. 
Spells which affect time are also included here, as are spells that affect personal attributes.

STEP IV: Metaphysics 
The spells based on the six primary aspects and their actions form the core of spell creation, but they also allow for only very singular effects. 
Examples of singular effect spells would be the simple creation spells such as Produce Food and Produce Water. Below is a list of basic principles 
of metaphysics which can be used with any spell which could have been made with the system up to this point. Some of them are the basis for the 
concept of parameters. If a spell creator is creating a spell and wants to use these principles, he can simply incorporate them into the spell during 
the creation process. If complex effects wish to be created, then these can only be done with advanced metaphysics (explained later). A spell 
which alters earth so that it changes its form is part of the basic system, but a spell that alters earth enough to actually destroy it would require more 
than the basics. In singular effect spells there can be several actions done to the same focus, but always only one focus. For example, Finger of 
Fire creates fire and then displaces it towards a target.

The Advanced Principles 
If one wishes to create spells with more complex effects, then the principles of metaphysics will have to be applied. Suddenly a caster is able to do 
all sorts of complex things. Two separate spells can be created and merged into one. Spells can be set so that they do not take effect immediately. 
Creation of these types of spells involve the application of the principles of metaphysics, and if a player wishes to make such spells, his character 
must have the Metaphysics social skill. 
The advanced principles are combined with other effects in the previous sections to create new effects. They can also be used by themselves to cre-
ate spells called meta-spells, such as Dispel Magic and Set. Specifically, illusions are created with masking in order to send out a false signature, 
and generally also use repulsion of a sense which would identify the true nature of the masked object or being Wards are created by applying the 
repulsion principle, in order to repel something that the spellcaster does not want to affect the focus. Shifting is used in any case where the focus 
will leave the plane that the caster is on. Teleporting is included in this, as the teleported object actually leaves a plane and returns to a different 
location on that plane. For convenience, the tables for the advanced principles are Listed below, as well as tables for the basic principles. The spell 
creator does not require Metaphysics to use the basic principles. 
Aspect: Meta-spells 
Of these advanced principles, three of them are significant enough to be considered there own aspect of magic. These are Masking (Illusion), 
Repulsion (Warding), and Meta-sense (Sensing). All other principles are considered to be part of type Meta-spells. All four of these types do not 
need to have an action, only a focus. They can also be added to any spell made with a focus and one or more of the actions. For example, the spell 
Dig is type: natural, alteration (because it alters a natural solid) but because it destroys the solid (the Resonation principle), it has Meta added to it.

Example: The area affected of I 0ft3/ Aura is chosen. A mage decides to fix this to make it more useable for his apprentice. He has an Aura control 
of 16, so he uses this full number and directs it into the spell; 10 ftJ/ Aura x 16 Aura points= 160 cubic feet. So now whenever this spell is cast it 
will always affect 160 ftJ of material. This may not be too useful, so he might simply want to fix it at 5 Aura, or 50 ft. ln any case this number 
cannot now change during casting time. 
Terraci11g: If several fixed choices are desired for a parameter, the caster can choose to plug in several different Aura point values, none of which 
can exceed his Aura Control. Ex. A mage decides that she will terrace the area affected in a spell she is making, (which has a proportional area 
affected of 10 ftJ/Aura). She chooses 4 different Aura values: 4, 8, 12, 16. Plugging these numbers in she gets 40 ft, 80 ft, 120 ft, and 160 ft. The 
spell behaves like this: 
At 4 Aura it affects 40 ft., At 8 Aura it affects 80 ft., At 12Aura it affects 120 ft., At 16 Aura it affects 160 ft. 
Surface Areas and Perimeters: The spell creator is allowed to designate that he only wishes the focus of the spell to fill the surface area of a vol-
ume (or the perimeter of an area) instead of the entire shape. This is the basis of the circle spells in the this manual.

Resistances 
Anytime a spell is cast upon an unwilling subject, even if the spell was 
intended to be friendly, they get a saving throw of the appropriate type 
(called a normal save) with the following modifications: 
a. Control Resistances are used against control spells. Only sapient 
beings (5+ mental attributes) get an automatic Control Resistance save. 
b. Spells which are illusion-based (spells which used the meta-princi-
ple of Masking) give an Illusion Resistance save. 
c. All other spell types offer a Magic Resistance save.

STEP IX. Anomalies 
Anomalies are side effects of spells that occur during creation. They 
become a part of that spell and will happen each and every time that 
exact spell is cast again. Some are good and some are bad. A mage 
who creates a spell and gets a certain anomaly may find this new effect 
to be a bonus, or so detrimental that the spell becomes useless.

Anomalies can be controlled in several ways. If the creator of the spell 
has done excellent research, the chance can be lowered. Hasty research 
will raise the chance. Each spell added with a merge increases the 
chance by +5%, (roll for each spell). Each advanced metaphysical 
principle used other than merge increases the chance by 1 % (per prin-
ciple) and adds +5% (per principle) to the roll on the number of anom-
alies table. Each apprentice used will lower the chance by 2%. 
Feel free as a Game Master to modify the chance for anomalies for 
your world and have fun with this concept. For example, if a hermeti-
cist is using poor quality materials or exceptional materials you may 
wish to modify the chance for anomalies as well as the chance of 
success. 
Once it has been determined that an anomaly has occurred then roll 
once for each anomaly on the Anomalies Table. If the creator wishes, 
2% can be subtracted from the roll for each apprentice used. Do not 
immediately tell the spell creator what the anomaly is, but make him 
make a Intelligence save to see if he has guessed the anomaly. 
Otherwise, he will just have to wait till the spell is cast to find out!

STEP X. GM Modifications and Notes 
After a spell has been created, the GM may wish to add any 
notes about its effects (or side effects) that he feel should be 
included, either for flavor or for game balance. For example, it 
was decided that the spell Clean would harm earth elementals. 
Some players will try and abuse the system, either with 
extremely liberal interpretations of the rules, or by finding actu-
al loopholes. As the GM, feel free to modify the Aura level by 
a few points if you feel that the spell is too powerful for your 
world. Creative explanations can be used to explain these mod-
ifiers based on the specifics of your setting. Be careful not to 
overdo it, however, and stifle the inventiveness of the player. 
Often a spell may seem too powerful when in reality the player 
simply devised a clever effect. 
Spell Name 
The name of the new spell. It is recommended that you use the spell 
naming conventions offered in the magic section (and repeated below) 
for spells which are modifications of existing spells. If you are allow-
ing a player character to create a new spell, then allow her to name it; 
otherwise, use an appropriate name that describes its function in a gen-
eral way.

Invocations can be created with the same basic guidelines as spells, 
with two major exceptions: 
1. Avoid effects that are direct; divine magic is indirect and subtle. 
2. Mages have a hard time dealing with lifeforce, especially positive 
lifeforce. Divine magic deals with both forces easily, and thus positive 
and negative lifeforce effects are should be much lower level.

DesK;nmr; Mar;1e ltems 
Players lust for items of power and Game Masters agonize over how 
many such items should become available in a setting. Imagine allows 
for the creation of some very unusual magic items, even without creat-
ing new spells or effects. In the Imagine Role Playing System™ nearly 
every spell can be placed into a magic item in one form or another. 
Magic items can be made by exceptional characters with skill such as 
Weave Magic, Metal Lore, Stone Lore, Wood Lore and Empower, as 
well as with the spell Enchantment. The general magic item design 
rules are provided under the spell Enchantment in the Player's Guide. 
These rules are supplemented in this section by rules expansions, as 
well as by the Spell Creation System that allows for completely new 
spell effects. You as the Game Master can choose from the extensive 
list of magic items as well as design new items for your setting. The 
following material will provide information about creating items as 
well as a worksheet (in the appendix) to help you along. A Magic Item 
Form has been provided as well, meant to be filled out and given to 
your players after a magic item has been completed. In the later mate-
rial, design information for divine items, combined items and magical 
instruments is dealt with as well. Forms for these are also provided. 
Rules Expansion for Enchantment 
The following rules are an expansion of the basic magic item creation 
rules found in the Player's Guide under the spell Enchantment. The 
Magic Item Design Worksheet is meant to parallel this section. 
Step 1: Item Material 
The quality of the material has a great impact on the success of the 
enchantment. Only magical material will not introduce a failure 
chance into the casting of Enchantment.

Failure Chance: Record the failure chance based on the material being 
used, and modify this number by -I% for each servant necessary to 
meet the caster's needs during the casting. If this item is being created 
by a character, then roll this failure chance after the character has com-
pleted the casting. This is different from a spell failure and does not 
require a roll on the magical mishap table; the spell simply does not 
work and the character must recast the spell, spending all of the same 
time and money again as required by power points. 
Step 2: Determining Power Points 
The amount of powers and abilities which may be placed into an item 
is based on the power points which the caster is able to generate. 
Base PP: The initial base of power points is determined by multiply-
ing the amount of Aura directed into the Enchantment spell by I 0. 
Weakening the Item (Base Aura Level): Additional power points can 
be gained by reducing the Base Aura Level of the item below 20. For 
each point below 20 the Base Aura Level is reduced, JO power points 
will be gained. The caster does not gain additional power points if the 
spell is cast at higher than 20 Aura; even if the Enchantment spell is 
cast at higher than 20 Aura, additional points are granted based on 
reducing the Base Aura Level below 20 Aura only. 
Magical Material: For each + 1 bonus of magical material, IO power 
points are gained. 
Caster's Ability: For each and every attribute rating point above 16 
for Intelligence, Wisdom and Knowledge, 5 power points are gained. 
Clean: If the item has the spell Clean cast upon it, 10 power points are 
gained. 
New Item: If the enchantment begins within one hour of the creation 
of the actual item being enchanted, 20 power points are gained. 
Enchant Area: If the caster performs the enchantment in an area where 
he has cast Enchant Area, 20 power points are gained. 
Total Power Points Available: The power points generated from the 
above steps should be added together and recorded. If the enchanter is 
mortal and has no supernatural aid, the maximum power points 
allowed are 400. The only way an item may be created with more than 
400 power points is: 
a) with supernatural aid 
b) a deity himself creates the item, 
c) A mortal expends all of his Will Force upon the completion of the 
Enchantment spell, thereby dying instantly and irretrievably. A Wish 
or Miracle cannot bring the being back, as the being has expended all 
life force (Will Force) and can no longer inhabit a corporeal form. 
Step 3: Creating Powers 
There are four types of effects which can be created with the 
Enchantment spell, and each effect is bought with varying amounts of 
power points. The four types of effects are powers, usages, charges 
and abilities. All are created by casting one or more spells (or in some 
cases skills) into the item during the enchantment process. The pow-
ers can be enchanted so that they are activated by the wearer, or so that 
the only the item itself uses or activates the power (designated by 
"item only"). 
Powers 
Powers are spells that when enchanted into an item can be activated 
without draining Aura from a being's Aura Pool. Though they do not 
actually drain Aura, they do require a minimum amount of Aura to be 
available in a being's Aura Pool, but do not actually drain that Aura 
from the pool (called activating). Because the wielder ios not provid-
ing the Aura, the actual spell is cast from the item itself. Since powers 
are spells, they have an Aura Level which is the same level as the 
263 

===== PAGE 274 =====
equivalent spell. The base cost for a power is equal to its Aura Level 
modified by how often the power can be used:

"At will" means that the power can be activated as many times as the 
wielder desires, each activation taking 5 seconds. Note that for a 
power to work "at will", the spell Permanency must be cast during the 
enchantment process. This casting does not require additional Will 
force to be spent, as Will force is being used in the Enchantment spell 
already. Only spells which may be made permanent can be made to 
work at will (see Permanency in the Player's Guide). 
The sum of the Aura Levels of all powers that are activated or in use 
cannot exceed the amount of Aura available in the being's Aura Pool. 
It is possible to create an item which does not need free Aura to be 
available in the wielder's Aura Pool. This is decided by the enchanter, 
and will automatically double the base cost of the power. Instead of an 
Aura Level, NR can be placed after the power on the worksheet for 
"not required."

A charged item is one that has had one power cast into it, and when 
activated it will be gone from the item. A charged item can only have 
one power but may have multiple charges. For example, a charged 
item might have the power (spell) Finger of Fire in it. There can be no 
other powers in this item, but it might contain ten charges of Finger of 
Fire. Thus the wielder could use Finger of Fire ten times before 
exhausting all of the items charges. All charges take 5 seconds to acti-
vate and are cast from the item as opposed to the wielder. An item can 
recharged by casting the appropriate spell into the item with an amount 
of Aura equal to or greater than the Base Aura Level of the item (once 
for each charge). Overfilling the item with more charges than the item 
can hold causes the item to explode per the spell Explosion, with an 
amount of Aura points equal to two times the number of charges in the 
item. The Enchanter determines the number of charges during casting. 
The power point cost for charges is determined by multiplying the 
number of charges by the Aura Level of the spell. 
Charges PP cost = number of charges x the Aura level of the power. 
If a charged item is destroyed, it will also explode as the spell 
Explosion at 1 Aura point per charge in the item. 
Abilities 
An item can have a power or any other effect enchanted into it in such 
a way as to make it constant. This means that the effect no longer has 
a limited number of uses, but acts as a continuous effect and is now 
called an ability. An item made by a mortal can never have more tl1an 
two abilities (items with more than 2 abilities are considered artifacts). 
Abilities take the wielder one second to turn on and one second to turn 
off. Turning a power or effect into an ability requires that the spell 
Permanency be cast on the item as well. Because of this, only spells 
which can be made permanent can be turned into abilities (see the spell 
Permanency in the Player's Guide). This casting does not require addi-
tional Will force to be spent, as Will force is being used in the 
Enchantment spell already. 
The power point cost for turning a power into an ability is 20 times 
the Aura Level of the power. 
Abilities PP cost = Aura level of power x 20 
Abilities can be enchanted so that they will take their effect on the item 
or the wielder. This is decided by the enchanter during the casting and 
cannot be changed later. 
Activating an ability requires a thought, word, or deed. This method of 
activation is decided by the caster during the enchantment process and 
will modify the base power point cost:

Power, Usage, Charge and Ability Notes 
Several spells have special modifiers and costs of their own: 
Cache: The item may be the key to the Cache, per the spell Cache 
but may not have the ability to cast the spell Cache. 
Creation: If made the power of a magic item, it will only be able to 
produce a specific creature already produced by the caster and will 
take I /2 the normal time listed for that particular creature under cre-
ation. 
Delay: Cannot be the power of magical item. 
Enchant Area: Must be a constant power. Under no circumstances can 
a magical item create other enchanted areas. 
Change Self/True: The particular creature that the object will change 
into may be chosen at the time of the enchantment. Statistics of the 
new form may be determined in advance and remain the same no mat-
ter who uses it. 
Change Other: May be used normally or a specific random table 
could be created showing the various types the victim of this power 
will be transformed into. 
Endow Intelligence: Cannot be the power of a magic item. 
Enhance Speed: Double normal power point cost. 
Explosion: Double normal power point cost. 
Incinerate: Double normal power point cost. 
Intensify: Cannot be the power of a magic item. 
Non-Detection: Can be set to make the magic item unable to be identi-
fied. If the magical item is intelligent, it can choose to hide its powers. 
Rebirth: Double normal power point cost. 
Repair: The item gains the ability to instantly foe itself when broken. 
Reincarnation: Double normal power point cost. 
Set: Cannot be the power of a magical item. 
Symbiosis: Can only be used if a second magic item is used for the 
purposes of the symbiosis, and then the owners of the items would be 
symbiots while they possessed the magical item. 
Teleport: Could be used to Teleport the item back to the last owner by 
thought, command, deed or automatically as a constant power. 
Wish: Used only at GM discretion and then at triple normal cost. 
Step 4: Creating Special Abilities 
Special abilities are created when magical skills or effects are used to 
grant unusual effects while enchanting the item. Each special ability 
has a power point cost associated with it. Unlike powers, the cost is a 
set cost and can be activated by anyone with whom the item itself has 
affinity. The caster must choose this overall affinity before adding 
abilities. Choice of affinity has no bearing on the cost of each ability. 
265 

===== PAGE 276 =====
The GM may take liberty in creating his own special abilities and 
should detennine a reasonable power point cost based upon the exam-
ples given. Non-artifacts may only have one special ability, and this 
counts as one of the two abilities that non-artifacts are allowed to have. 
Animation: Cost: 50 power points. 
The enchanter must possess Telekinesis in order to enchant this 
ability. It allows a weapon to attack under its owner power as if 
wielded by the item's owner. If the item is not a weapon it can be 
moved by the owner's thought if it is within sight. 
Cold: Cost: See below. 
This ability causes the magical item to burn with a freezing touch. 
To create this ability the enchanter must have the skill Cryokin-
esis. Victims struck or touched by the item must make a Magic 
Resistance or suffer ld4 per 6 power points used in creating this 
power ( I Od4 maximum). It takes one second for the user to turn 
the power on or off. The user is immune to the frost touch. 
Curse: Cost: 50 power points. 
During the enchantment process, a curse is placed on the item per 
the skill Curse. Any wielder meeting the conditions of the curse 
is affected by it. A successful Remove Curse removes only the 
current curse on the afflicted item holder, not the curse on the 
item itself. Curses cannot directly kill a wielder, though they may 
lead to conditions that result in the wielder's death. A cursed item 
can never be gotten rid of, and will always come back to the 
wielder who it cursed. 
Electricity: Cost: See below. 
This ability causes the magical item to become electrified. To 
create this ability the enchanter must have the skill Electrokinesis. 
Victims struck or touched by the item must make a Magic 
Resistance or suffer ld8 per 10 power points used in creating this 
power (10d8 maximum). It takes one second for the user to turn 
the power on or off. The user is immune to the electricity. 
Fire: Cost: See below. 
This ability causes the magical item to burn with a magical flame. 
To create this ability the enchanter must have the skill 
Pyrokinesis. Victims struck or touched by the item must make a 
Magic Resistance or suffer ld6 per 8 power points used in creat-
ing this power (10d6 maximum). It takes I second for the user to 
tum the power on or off. The user is immune to the fire.

This ability can only be given to items that are weapons. This 
effect is produced by immersing the weapon in the blood of the 
particular being type, race, alignment or class the item is going to 
be created to slay. Anytime the weapon is considered to have 
struck the flesh of the particular type it has been set to slay, that 
being must make a Magic Resistance or perish. Immersing the 
weapon in the blood of a deity allows the weapon to be able to 
slay all mortals; this last ability is completely at the discretion of 
the GM. 
Thought Projection: Cost: See below. 
The enchanter must possess Thought Projection in order to 
enchant this ability. It allows the item's user to attempt Thought 
Projection at +5% per 5 power points used.

When time is finished and costs are paid, the item is finished and ready 
to be used.

The divine magic item creation rules are almost identical to the rules 
for creating magic items; however, all the rules have been fully 
detailed here for those unfamiliar with the Enchantment rules. 
Rules Expansion for Imbue Divinity 
The following rules are an expansion of the basic divine magic item 
creation rules found in the Player's Guide under the spell Imbue 
Divinity. The Divine Magic Item Design Worksheet is meant to paral-
lel this section. 
Step 1: Item Material 
The quality of the material has a great impact on the success of the 
enchantment. Only magical material will not introduce a failure 
chance into the invoking of Imbue Divinity.

Failure Chance: Record the failure chance based on the material being 
used, and modify this number by -1 % for each servant necessary to 
meet the invoker's needs during the invoking. If this item is being cre-
ated by a character, then roll this failure chance after the character has 
completed the invocation. If the roll is failed, the invocation simply 
does not work and the character must repeat the process, spending all 
of the same time and money again as required by power points. 
Step 2: Determining Power Points 
The amount of powers and abilities which may be placed into an item 
is based on the power points which the invoker is able to generate. 
Base PP: The initial base of power points is determined by multiply-
ing the Piety Control of the invoker by IO. 
Weakening the Item ( Base Piety Level): Additional power points can 
be gained by reducing the Base Piety Level of the item below 20. For 
each point below 20 the Base Piety Level is reduced, 20 additional 
power points will be gained. 
Magical Material: For each + I bonus of magical material, 10 power 
points are gained. 
Invoker's Ability: For each and every attribute rating point above I 6 
for Intelligence, Wisdom and Knowledge, 5 power points are gained. 
Clean: If the item has the invocation Clean upon it, 10 power points 
are gained. 
New Item: If the imbuement begins within one hour of the creation of 
the actual item being imbued, 20 power points are gained. 
Sacred Location: If the caster performs Imbue Divinity in an area that 
has been consecrated by his deity, 20 power points are gained. 
Total Power Points Available: The power points generated from the 
above steps should be added together and recorded. If the imbuer is 
mortal and has no supernatural aid, the maximum power points 
allowed are 400. The only way an item may be created with more than 
400 power points is: 
a) with supernatural aid 
b) a deity himself creates the item, 
c) A mortal expends all of his Will Force upon the completion of the 
Imbue Divinity invocation, thereby dying instantly and irretrievably. A 
Wish or Miracle cannot bring the being back, as the being has expend-
ed all life force (Will Force) and can no longer inhabit a corporeal 
form. 
Step 3: Creating Powers 
There are three types of effects which can be created with Imbue 
Divinity, and each effect is bought with varying amounts of power 
points. The three types of effects are powers, charges and abilities. All 
are created by placing one or more invocations (or in some cases 
skills) into the item during the imbuement process. The powers can be 
imbued so that they are activated by the wearer, or so that the only the 
item itself uses or activates the power (designated by "item only"). 
Divine Powers 
Divine powers are invocations in an item that the user activates from 
the Piety of the item itself. Since divine powers are invocations, they 
have a Piety Level which is the same level as the equivalent invoca-
tion. The base cost for a divine power is equal to its Piety Level modi-
fied by how often the power can be used:

generate the base power points. 
"At will" means that the power can be activated as many times as the 
wielder desires, each activation taking 5 seconds. Note that for a 
power to work "at will", the invocation Permanency must be cast dur-
ing the imbuement process. This invoking does not require additional 
Will force to be spent, as Will force is being used in the Imbue

Items can be made such that the item itself activates the power in the 
item, but the the wielder has no control over the activation. Such items 
are generally designed to create effects that activate when a being 
enters an area which the deity does not wish defiled. 
Charges 
A charged item is one that has had one power invoked into it, and 
when activated it will be gone from the item. A charged item can only 
have one power but may have multiple charges. For example, a 
charged item might have the power Protection From Undead in it. 
There can be no other types of powers in this item, but it might contain 
ten charges of Protection From Undead. Thus the wielder could use 
Protection From Undead ten times before exhausting all of the items 
charges. All charges take 5 seconds to activate and are invoked from 
the item as opposed to the wielder. An item can recharged by invoking 
the appropriate spell into the item up to the maximum number of 
charges the item can hold. Overfilling the item with more charges than 
the it can hold causes the item to explode per the invocation Divine 
Blast, with a Piety Control equal one per the number of charges in the 
item. The imbuer determines the number of charges during invoking. 
The power point cost for charges is determined by multiplying the 
number of charges by the Piety Level of the spell. 
Charges PP cost = number of charges x the Piety level of the power. 
If a charged item is destroyed, it will also explode explained above. 
Charges can be made to be activated at the Piety Control of the wielder 
and not the Base Piety level of the item: 
If activated at the Piety Control of the wielder: power points x 1/2 
Abilities 
An item can have a power or any other effect imbued into it in such a 
way as to make it constant. This means that the effect no longer has a 
limited number of uses, but acts as a continuous effect and is now 
called an ability. An item made by a mortal can never have more than 
two abilities (items with more than 2 abilities are considered artifacts). 
Abilities take the wielder one second to tum on and one second to tum 
off. Turning a power or effect into an ability requires that the invoca-
tion Permanency be put on the item as well. Because of this, only 
invocations which can be made permanent can be turned into abilities 
(see the invocation Permanency in the Player's Guide). This invoking 
does not require additional Will force to be spent, as Will force is being 
used in the Imbue Divinity process already. 
The power point cost for turning a power into an ability is 20 times the 
Piety Level of the power. 
Abilities PP cost = Piety Level of power x 20 
Abilities can be imbued so that they will take their effect on the item or 
the wielder. This is decided by the imbuer during the procedure, and 
cannot be changed later. 
Activating an ability requires a thought, word, or deed. This method of 
activation is decided by the imbuer during the Imbue Divinity process 
and will modify the base power point cost:

The GM or advanced players may want to create magic items which 
grant or enhance skills to add to the uniqueness of an existing type of 
item. A few examples are a sword that grants the skill Critical, a rapi-
er that adds to Focused Attack or a cup that blesses any water put into 
it and has a chance of making holy water once per day. The item's 
imbuer must have the skill to put it into the item, or he must find a 
master of that skill to participate during the imbuement process. The 
time necessary to add a skill into an item is the same as the learn time 
for that skill. To find the power point cost for putting a skill into an 
item, first determine whether or not the wielder of the item will get a 
bonus to an acquired skill, a bonus to a common or non-acquired skill, 
or if the item will grant the skill itself. Decide what percent increase 
the item will give to a skill (+20% to Potion Lore, etc.) or how much it 
will give the wielder at base chance (50% Potion Lore, etc.). Divide 
this chance by 5%, and multiply this number by the rating of the skill. 
Example: An item will give the wielder Awaken Plant at 60%. 60% divided 
by 5% = 12; the rating of Awaken Plant is 18, so the power point cost for this 
ability is 12 x 18 = 216. This number would be the same for an item that gave 
a +60% bonus to the Awaken Plant skill as well.

Step 4: Creating Special Abilities 
Special abilities are created when divine magical skills or effects are 
used to grant unusual effects while imbuing the item. Each special 
ability has a power point cost associated with it. Unlike powers, the 
cost is a set cost and can be activated by anyone with whom the item 
itself has affinity. The caster must choose this overall affinity before 
adding abilities. Choice of affinity has no bearing on the cost of each 
special ability. The GM may take liberty in creating his own special 
abilities and should determine a reasonable power point cost based 
upon the examples given. Non-artifacts may only have one special 
ability, and this counts as one of the two abilities that non-artifacts are 
allowed to have. 
Holy/Unholy Water Sprinkler/Producer: (Cost = 50 power points) 
A container is filled with or an item bathed in holy or unholy water 
(whichever is appropriate to the invoker's deity) for the duration of 
Imbue Divinity. If the item is a container, it will fill with holy or 
unholy water once per day. If the item is not a container, once per I 0 
seconds it will sprinkle holy or unholy water when swung at high 
velocity. Anyone hit by the item is also considered showered by holy 
or unholy water. Holy or unholy water produced by sprinkling loses its 
divinity after 10 seconds. 
Healing: (Cost= 20 power points per ld6+1 of healing relief) 
The skill Healing is successfully used to imbue the item with the abili-
ty to magically heal someone it is held against. This ability has the 
same restrictions as the skill Healing and can not have a potency 
greater than the invoker's Healing ability. 
Wounding: (Cost= 20 power points per ld6+1 of wounding damage) 
The skill Wounding is successfully used to imbue the item with the 
ability to magically wound someone it is held against. This ability has 
the same restrictions as the skill Wounding and can not have a potency 
greater than the invoker's Wounding ability. 
Talisman: (Cost= JOO power points) 
When the skill Talisman is successfully used during the time of imbu-
ing, it makes the item a talisman to the invoker's deity and can be used 
as such by anyone who worships that deity. The power of the talisman 
is defined within the skill description for Talisman. 
Protection from Undead: (Cost 50 = power points) 
The skill Tum Undead is successfully used while the item is being 
imbued. The ability prevents undead from getting within 60' of the 
item unless a Control Resistance is successful. 
Protection from Evil/Good: (Cost 50 = power points) 
The skill Protection from Evil or Protection from Good is successfully 
used while the item is being imbued. The ability prevents the appro-
priate alignment from getting within 60' of the item unless a Control 
Resistance is successful. 
Curse: (Cost = 50 power points) 
During the imbuement process, a curse is placed on the item per the 
skill Curse. Any wielder meeting the conditions of the curse is affect-
ed by it. A successful Remove Curse removes only the current curse 
on the afflicted item holder, not the curse on the item itself. Curses 
cannot directly kill a wielder, though they may lead to conditions that 
result in the wielder's death. A cursed item can never be gotten rid of, 
and will always come back to the wielder who it cursed. 
Insanity: (Cost= 100 power points) 
If the skill Insanity is successfully used while the item is being imbued, 
the wielder of the item has the ability to cause insanity in mortal 
beings the item touches. If the mortal fails a Will Force roll, a random 
(or Game Master determined) insanity is inflicted upon the unfortunate 
victim. Each victim is only required to make one save against the item 
and is thereafter immune.

Once the number of power points to spend has been calculated, use the 
table to determine the final costs in time, money and Will Force. 
When time is finished and costs are paid, the item is finished and ready 
to be used.

Dual Ma9c Jr-ems 
A dual magic item is an item that is both magical and divine magi-
cal in nature. There are basically two ways that such an item can be 
created: 
1) The enchanter/imbuer has both Scroll Knowledge and Divine 
Knowledge, the spell Enchantment, and the invocation Imbue Divinity. 
These can then be used concurrently by casting the Enchantment first, 
and then as the Enchantment process ends (6 hours to I year later), 
Imbue Divinity is immediately invoked. This is simply one spell fol-
lowed by one invocation, and all costs for both must be paid. 
2) A separate enchanter and imbuer both begin the spell Enchantment 
and the invocation Imbue Divinity in the same second, and the process 
is performed concurrently. 
Either of these methods must be approved by the GM. This type of 
item is completely optional, as it can lead to some very powerful items. 
To create a worksheet for this type of item, simply fill out both the 
Magic Item Design Worksheet as well as the Divine Item Design 
Worksheet, plus the additional information located at the bottom of the 
latter sheet. For explanations of the Magic Item Design Worksheet or 
the Divine Item Design Worksheet please see those areas. Only the 
summary section explanation is provided here. 
Highest Power Point Cost: The higher power point cost used of the 
two methods, then this number is used to determine the classification 
of the item. 
Classification: This is the one time that mortals can create an item 
which has more than 2 abilities. This is only because they are added 
together, thus both the Enchantment and Imbuing are still limited to no 
more than 400 power points and no more than two abilities each. 
Therefore a dual item would never have more than four abilities and 
cost no more than 400 power points. In this case, the item is stilJ 
counted as an Arch item, even though it has four abilities. 
Total Time to Create: If one being is doing both tasks, this is the sum 
of the time for both processes. If a separate enchanter and imbuer 
work together on the item, then the time taken would be the greater of 
the two (listed on the separate design sheets). 
Total Will Force Cost: The sum of the Will Force costs listed on both 
sheets. 
Total Exp. Value: The Total Experience Value of the item listed on 
both sheets, if its effects are fully understood. See Setting. 
Total Gp. Cost: The sum of costs listed on both sheets. This will 
include any foodstuffs, etc. needed by the enchanter during the this 
process.

Rules Expansion for Weave Magic 
By use of the skill Weave Magic, magical goods can be created 
(anything from clothing to swords to wine bottles.) These goods are 
considered to be + I magical where relevant. lf the item created is an 
instrument, the power of a magical song can be placed into the magical 
instrument at the time of weaving. The power of the song can then be 
activated by playing one note or chord by anyone with the skill Play. 
One song can be enchanted per 2 full Practitioner Titles. Each song 
enchanted causes a loss of 1/2 of a Will Force point and requires an 
additional Weave Magic skill roll at -20% while the instrument is being 
created. Activation time for the song is I d4+ 1 seconds, and is set at 
the time of weaving. The power is always activated at the Class Title 
of the player using the skill Play. 
In addition, this ability of Weave Magic can be combined with the 
speIJ Enchantment or the invocation Imbue Divinity so that the item 
wilJ activate a power when a note or chord is played. Use the normal 
rules of magic item creation but for powers only (no abilities, usages, 
skills, etc.), except that the activation time will be ld4+1 seconds 
(fixed and determined during the enchanting). Because playing a note 
or chord is a deed, the power is always at half Power Point cost. The 
gold piece value of these items should be determined by the economy 
of the game world, but a rule of thumb is 2d IO x I 00 gold per song or 
power. The enchantment time is based on the material being created, 
as listed in the Weave Magic skill (p.135 of the Player's Guide).

ARROW OF TRUE SLAYING 
Description: The arrow is made from the strongest wood with an adamantium

addition to the normal damage the arrow does when tired from the bow (dam-
age is dependant on the type of bow). The arrow will do double damage on nat-
ural 18+. 
Each Arrow of True Slaying is in fact specific to one particular race, class, 
alignment, or whatever else the creator wished. Thus, one arrow might be an 
Arrow of Giant Slaying, while another might be an Arrow of Evil slaying. Any 
being which fits the requirements and is struck by or touches the arrow forces 
the being to make a Magic Resistance or die. (this effect only activates against 
the particular race, class, alignment, etc., and is decided upon at the time of 
enchantment). The Magic Resistance must be repeated each IO seconds that the 
being touches the arrow, including a being who has the arrow lodged in him. 
In addition, 3 times per day the wielder may point the arrow at any intended 
target for 7 seconds and the arrow will then follow the target around all obsta-
cles (and circle waiting for it if it hides) for up to three times its range in order 
to strike it. In this case, a normal roll to hit must still be made (though the 
arrow follows the target, the hit is not automatic). The wielder must have 8 free 
Aura in his Aura Pool in order to use this last power. 
Base Aura Level 16 
Abilities

bonus. There can be many different Books of Arcana, and each one teaches a

RINGS OF FRIENDSHIP 
Description: The Rings of Friendship are two identical mithreel rings with 
ornate carvings of two beings entwined upon them. Once the rings have been 
put on by two separate individuals, they cannot be removed until the death of 
one of the pair. Until such time as both rings are worn they will have no power 
alone. When a ring is placed on any beings finger, it will change size to fit that 
persons finger exactly. Once two people are each wearing a ring, they gain the 
following powers and detriments: 
1) Telepathy between the two beings, if within 20 miles of one another. 
2) Both beings lose I Will Force point permanently. 
3) The being with the lower Intelligence has its intelligence rating raised to that 
of the higher being's. The same goes for Wisdom. 
4) If either being affected possesses supernatural powers, they are shared by 
both. Skills which are afforded Wisdom and Intelligence bonuses are 
shared by both beings. 
5) Both beings are granted 2-7 additional Endurance. 
6) If either being is an animal, surprise becomes -50% against the other being. 
7) Both beings can see through each other's eyes when desired. 
8) If either being affected dies for any reason, the other must make a Magic 
Resistance or die as well. If the save is made, the survivor loses 3d4 
Endurance and I d4 Will Force, and the ring loses its power until two indi-
viduals once again wear the rings.

Des191mr; CReatuRes 
The most important element in creature design is the concept of the 
creature you are making. The tables below provide mechanics for that 
concept, but they cannot replace your idea of what the creature is all 
about. Use the tables below to express the creature in game terms, but 
always allow the flavor of the concept be the final judge in deciding on 
numbers and mechanics; this system is intended to be a guide, created 
to give the player at least a ball-park range of creature stats. 
Creatures do not use the Title system, but instead are classified by 
level. As you go through the system, you will find many cases where 
you must choose a range of numbers (such as Strength;Jd4+10). In 
these cases, record this range so that when you are finished, you will 
have created a "creature template" for that type of creature. For exam-
ple, if you created a wolf, then the when finished you would a range 
for the Wolf's strength, weight, Endurance, etc. This way you can cre-
ate many wolves which are all different. It is also a good idea to 
record one specific instance of a wolf; that is to say, go ahead and 
work out one number for each range of numbers. This single number 
should be as close to average as possible; thus Strength ld4+10 might 
be "13(1d4+10)". Thus you will always have at least one pre-generat-
ed creature to use at a moments notice. 
The CReatuRe CReanon Gwbe 
The following pages offer a guide for designing creatures. By 
guide, it is meant that the following tables are meant to be used as 
guidelines to help you create an interesting and believable fantasy crea-
ture. Guidelines are not hard and fast rules, and the designer has some 
freedom in modifying the numbers where they do not make good 
sense. 
The first step in creating a creature is to start with the basic overall 
concept. No doubt you have some general idea for the creature con-
cept. Think about such questions as: What size is this creature? How 
big is it? Does it require magic to support a huge frame, or to make it 
fly? What does it eat? What eats it? Is this a creature which would 
not exist in the earthly realm, i.e. supernatural? These questions will 
help you determine the first two things you need to know: within 
which of the nine creature types should the creature be classified, and 
what is the habitat, climate, basic habits and life cycle of the creature. 
Power Point Cost (Determining Creature Level) 
Throughout the guide, certain factors have a power point cost (PP) 
associated with them. A record should be kept of these points whenev-
er the designer chooses an entry from a list with a PP cost next to it. 
These PP's should be added together, and for every full 40 PP, the 
creature should have one level added to its base level. The base level 
for a creature is determined by the size of the creature, and can be 
found on the same table where its Endurance is located. 
Creature Type 
Animal: Animals are natural creatures of a world that are non-sapient. 
Magical Animal: Magical animals are animals that could not exist 
were it not for the power of magic. They can have larger forms than 
normally allowable, and can fly with a body structure which should not 
be able to fly. Some have sapience or minimal intelligence. 
Humanoid: Humanoids are those races which have the basic body 
structure of a human but may have many varieties of size and shape. 
They are usually intelligent, and are the creatures which make up many 
of the character races. 
Magical Humanoid: Magical Humanoids have the basic humanoid 
form, but are endowed with magical powers and abilities and could not 
exist were it not for the power of magic. 
Magical: These are creatures which are either magically created or 
animated through spells or effects, or which can exist only through the 
means of magic, and which are not part of another creature category. 
Plant: Plants are basic non-sapient flora which exist on the earthly 
realm. 
Magical Plant: These are plants which have been enhanced or exist 
through the power of magic. Sometimes they are sapient. Many herbs 
are magical plants. 
Slime: A slime is an odd creature which is partially magical plant and 
partially magical animal. 
Undead: Undead are creatures that were once living but exist in their 
present form only through the power of negative lifeforce. There abili-
ties and forms vary greatly. 
Supernatural: These are creatures which come from other planes of 
existence than the earthly realm, and which are usually the servants of 
deities and are sometimes summoned by priests. They form a tenth 
category of creatures which is not identified by Bestiary Lore, but 
reserved for the skill Planar Lore. 
Habits/Life Cycle 
Some thought should be put into how the creature reproduces and rais-
es its young, as well as how the creature interacts socially. Is it a soli-
tary creature? Does it live in packs? This information will aid the 
Game Master in creating realistic encounters with the creature(s). 
Climate 
Desert (desert), Highland (mountain), Humid Continental, Humid 
Oceanic, Humid Subtropical Gungle), Icecap (polar), Semiarid, 
Subtropical Dry Summer, Tropical Wet (rain forest), Tropical Wet and 
Dry, Tundra (tundra). 
Habitat 
Coastal, desert, exotic (clouds), exotic (elemental), exotic (magical 
places), exotic (other planar), exotic (space/ether), exotic (subterranean 
sea), forest, hills, jungle, lake, marsh, mountain, ocean/sea (deep), 
ocean/sea (floor), ocean/sea (middle depths), ocean/sea (near surface), 
ocean/sea (surface), plains, polar, rain forest, river, savanna, scrubland, 
subterranean (deep), subterranean (near surface), swamp, tundra and 
wasteland. 
Body Type 
Each table describes the body areas and the modifier to base 
Endurance for the specific areas, whether a limb or a vital region, the 
effect upon loss of the area and finally any chance for special injury 
effects. Choose the body area which is most appropriate to the size 
and shape of the creature. ln some cases you may even need to create 
a new body type. 
Tiny 
Creatures less than about a foot in average length or height have the 
tiny body type. These creatures typically have 2 or fewer Endurance 
regardless of the makeup of their body structure, although they may 
have more through magical means. They are considered to have one 
body area, and it must be struck with a hit to the center target region in 
the attack charts (see Player's Guide). Since nearly any blow will 
destroy the body of such a creature, vital areas do not produce addi-
tional chances to incapacitate.

Small 
Creatures over a foot but less than three feet in average length or 
height have a small body type. These creatures will usually have 10 or 
less Endurance regardless of the structure of their body unless the crea-
ture is magical. These creatures are considered to have one body area 
but it may be struck by any hit on the attack chart (see Player's Guide). 
Each blow has a I% chance per point of damage actually taken of 
causing an incapacitating or disabling blow to the creature. Of these 
blows, 50% are said to strike a limb and 50% are said to strike a vital 
area. Vital hits can cause incapacitation for 4d6 seconds. Limb hits can 
disable the limb, slowing movement and removing usage of the limb 
until healed.

mined from the magical abilities section.

Mollusk 
Mollusks have soft bodies which are often enclosed in a hard shell. They have 
a muscular foot which in some cases (such as the octopus) has developed into 
multiple limbs. Mollusks include slugs, snails, octopi, squid, clam and oysters.

Hybrid 
Any mixture of the above body types can be created by pulling the 
appropriate body regions out from each chart and combining them. In 
such cases, a new chart must be made by pulling groups of areas from 
the appropriate body charts. For example, a new creature might be a 
quadruped/reptile hybrid. This creature might have the following from 
the quadruped: Head, neck, forequarters, right foreleg, left foreleg, right 
Jo ref oot, left forefoot; 
And these from the reptile: Hindquarters, underbelly, right hindleg, left 
hindleg, right hindclaw, left hindclaw, upper tail, lower tail. 
Insubstantial 
Used for spirits. See Insubstantial in the magical abilities list. Pick an 
Endurance value from the weight table and and use the base level. 
Height/Length, Weight 
The weight of a creature is the basic factor that will determine the 
combat information for any creature. Because of this, if you are creat-
ing a creature based upon a real life example, then any accurate infor-
mation for weight that you obtain from research on that animal should 
come first. However, if no information can be found, or the creature is 
entirely new, then the following table below will aid in determining the 
weight of a creature. The information is approximate and can be 
adjusted if the math produces skewed results. The height of the crea-
ture will determine its base weight. This base weight will be multi-
plied by 3 modifiers; one for its body type, one for its frame, and one 
for its density. Humanoids, Saurians, Centaurs and birds are measured 
standing up, quadrupeds are measured by their height at the shoulder 
when standing, and giant lizards, snakes/worms, sea mammals, mol-
lusks, fish, spiders and insects are measured from head to tail or tip.
